title: Turkish  Intervention  Fails to Stem Lira Sell-Off
text:
ISTANBUL--Turkey's central bank resorted Thursday to direct currency sales for the first time in two years to prop up the lira, but the currency kept on spiraling to record lows amid a broad-based investor exodus from emerging markets.

Policy makers in Ankara started selling dollars in the European morning as the dollar jumped to 2.2973 against the lira, according to traders familiar with the transaction. The lira bounced back somewhat in response, but plunged again within hours. That drew in the central bank for a second time, traders said, but again the lira quickly sank, with the dollar soaring above 2.30 to the lira.

Mounting expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve will increase the rate at which its scaling back monthly bond purchases has hit economies dependent on international investors to plug external funding shortfalls, such as Turkey and South Africa. The pressure also spread to other developing nations like Argentina, which faces rising inflation and social unrest, as well as Russia and Mexico.

"It's been a concerted selloff in emerging market currencies, a day of big losses for the high-yielding pack across the board. Turkey is the classic example. Current account is still huge and we have political layers," said Luis Costa, a Citigroup strategist in London. "The story in the lira is extremely complicated and at 2.3 is has much further to go. We are short of the currency. The move has been way too fast and has broken all forecasts."

In a one-sentence emailed statement after the first intervention, the central bank said it was taking this action because of "unhealthy price developments." A spokesman declined further comment and the policy makers haven't provided an update.

"The central bank has wasted precious foreign-exchange reserves today on what was--and would always be in the absence of meaningful rate hikes--a futile intervention effort," said Peter Kinsella, senior foreign-currency strategist at Commerzbank in London. "The move higher shows no signs of stopping and unless we see aggressive countermeasures from the central bank, there could be a more aggressive run on the currency in the coming weeks."

Turkish markets have been hit hard by the Fed's tapering plans and by local political tensions. A corruption probe launched Dec. 17 has targeted Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan's allies, forced a cabinet shuffle, further fueled the lira selloff, and sent borrowing costs soaring.

One easy, though not risk-free fix would be to raise interest rates. But on Tuesday, Governor Erdem Basci budged an outright bump to his key policy rates, instead introducing a new lending tool that economists said amounted to a backdoor rate hike. Mr. Erdogan has repeatedly blamed a so-called interest-rate lobby of economists, investors and journalists of seeking to destabilize Turkey and its markets for their own profit.

"It appears that political pressure has been brought to bear on the central bank not to hike rates. Markets did not react well, and the central bank was forced to step up its foreign-exchange intervention," said Brown Brothers Harriman & Co. strategists led by Marc Chandler in New York.

The International Monetary Fund, which has recently criticized Turkey's central bank for its opaque monetary policies, urged policy makers to stick to a flexible exchange rate and argued that an interest-rate increase should be the immediate priority to tame near-rampant inflation. Turkey saw price increases of 7.4% in 2013, compared with its 5% official target.

"What matters is that monetary policy avoids second-round effects to inflation by ensuring a strong nominal anchor," IMF spokesman William Murray said.

Turkey's lira is in its longest losing streak since August 2001, which had triggered an economic crisis and caused the banking system to collapse. Still, the country is at a much stronger financial position now: the government sold a $2.5 billion bond Wednesday that was four times oversubscribed, the Treasury said Thursday.

But the lira's future direction largely depends on the central bank's ability to persuade investors that it will use its new extraordinary days of additional monetary tightening, which Mr. Basci says will effectively raise borrowing costs. Monday is poised to be the first such day, followed by Thursday.

"The market sent a very clear message to the central bank today: it wants monetary tightening. The remedy is in long-term extraordinary days, otherwise the currency sales will not be effective," said Murat Yardimci, head of foreign-exchange at ING Bank in Istanbul.

"The central bank was a lot more aggressive in the past, the intervention is actually strong but markets find the national lender's stance weak," said Ozlem Derici, chief economist at Deniz Invest in Istanbul. "The markets still lack trust in the central bank, I expect it to continue its direct intervention."

Policy makers have already burned through at least $19 billion, a third of the central bank's net reserves, in an unsuccessful effort to halt the lira's slide since last June. The currency declined 21% against the dollar last year, making it one of the worst performers in emerging markets and a leading loser among developing economies with a 7% drop this year.

"Rule number one of direct currency intervention, when you intervene, do it in massive size and make sure it is effective. I guess the message from today's move is that the central bank of Turkey just did not do enough," said Tim Ash at Standard Bank in London. "The cover for Turkey's central bank is that we are seeing broader-based emerging-market currency weakness, including the ruble and the South African rand, which makes the intervention more difficult to understand."

title: U.S. Stocks End Broadly Lower
text:
Stocks suffered broad declines as weak data out of China spooked investors, triggering a flight out of riskier assets.

The increase in market volatility, which included sharp selloffs in emerging markets and the biggest tumble in Argentina's currency in over a decade, came as U.S. stocks has struggled in recent weeks to regain the upward momentum seen at the end of 2013.

On Thursday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average slid 175.99 points, or 1.1%, to 16197.35, the lowest close since Dec. 19.

The S&P 500 index shed 16.40 points, or 0.9%, to 1828.46, and the Nasdaq Composite Index dropped 24.13 points, or 0.6%, to 4218.87. Materials and financials led declines in all 10 of the S&P 500 sectors.

The S&P 500 ended the session 1.1% below its Jan. 15 record-high close.

Data showing China's manufacturing activity contracted in January sparked worries that the recent slowing momentum in the world's second-largest economy is carrying over into the new year.

That triggered a selloff in riskier emerging-market shares and currencies, and helped bolster prices of Treasurys and gold, which are viewed as safe-haven assets.

"We had some really weak data out of China, and that's scaring people," said Ian Winer, director of equity trading at Wedbush Securities. He said that since the global rally in equities is predicated on global economic growth, "if you get weakness [in China], it's something [stock] bulls have to question."

The iShares MSCI Emerging Markets exchange-traded fund tumbled 2.5% to the lowest level since September 2013.

Several emerging-market currencies also sold off sharply in unison. The Argentine peso suffered the biggest one-day drop against the dollar in a decade, as Argentina faces heightened concerns about its own dwindling foreign currency reserves. In addition, the Turkish lira sank to another record low against the U.S. dollar. The lira tumbled even after Turkey's central bankintervened directly in currency markets for the first time in two years to slow its fall, raising questions about the central bank's ability to fight currency losses.

The lack of confidence spilled over into other emerging-market currencies, with the Russian ruble and South African rand dropping to multiyear lows against the greenback.

"China is still the growth engine of the global economy," said Chris Gaffney, senior market strategist with EverBank Wealth Management, which manages money across asset classes for high-net-worth individuals. "The [currency] sell-off is the result of worries about China's growth, and that's also leading to broader stock-market declines."

Meanwhile, Treasury prices rallied, with the yield on the 10-year Treasury note settling at 2.774%, the lowest seen since Dec. 3. Yields fall as Treasury prices rise. Front-month January gold futures ran up 1.9% to a two-month high of $1,262.60 an ounce.

The attention placed on China and its effect on global risk assets marks a sudden change for investors, who have grown accustomed to focusing on U.S. corporate earnings.

"This is the first time in many weeks that we've seen this kind of across-the-board volatility," said Adam Grimes, chief investment officer at Waverly Advisors, which provides tactical research and advisory services to traders and money managers. "There is a clear theme here, that the market doesn't like risk today."

Mr. Grimes added that while the selloffs in emerging-market currencies have his immediate attention, in the context of the bigger picture for stocks, he believes nothing has changed.

"If this continued for two to three days, then we might be rolling over into a bigger-scale pullback," Mr. Grimes said. But for anyone with a more than one-week view, "this is nothing; it's still business as usual, " he said.

In corporate news, U.S.-listed shares of Finland's Nokia slumped 8.7% after the company said handset sales declined in the fourth quarter. Nokia is expected to transfer its handset business this quarter to Microsoft this quarter. Microsoft shares edged up 0.4%.

Also in the Dow, McDonald's reported flat fourth-quarter earnings and a 0.1% drop in global same-store sales, hurt by a 1.4% decline in U.S. sales.

Economic data were mixed. Weekly jobless claims edged up slightly less than forecast, while sales of existing homes increased less than expected.

In Europe, the Stoxx Europe 600 lost 1%, pulling back from a six-year high, as the weak Chinese data overshadowed data showing a pickup in activity in the euro zone.

Asian markets fell on the back of the weak Chinese data. China's Shanghai Composite shed 0.5%, after running up 3% over the previous two sessions.

title: Turkey Intervenes  to Halt Lira Slide
text:
ISTANBUL--Turkey's central bankintervened directly in the currencies markets Thursday for the first time in two years in an effort to slow the lira's free fall.

Policy makers in Ankara started selling dollars as the lira hit a record low of 2.2973 against the dollar before noon local time, and slumped to an all-time nadir of 3.1342 against the euro, said three traders familiar with the transaction. The lira bounced back somewhat in response, but didn't immediately recoup all the day's losses.

In a one-sentence emailed statement, the central bank said it was intervening with direct foreign-exchange sales because of "unhealthy price developments."

"This is pretty forceful. And the last time they did this, they didn't do it just once. But these sorts of interventions tend to just give people the opportunity to buy more dollars," said Bartosz Pawlowski, head of emerging market strategy at BNP Paribas in London.

The move comes as Turkey's lira is in its longest losing streak since August 2001, which had triggered an economic crisis and caused the banking system to collapse. To be sure, Turkey is at a much stronger financial position now: the government sold a $2.5 billion bond Wednesday that was four times oversubscribed, the Treasury said Thursday.

Still, the sustained lira selloff shows the market's discomfort with the central bank's refusal to raise benchmark interest rates to curb currency losses and target inflation. On Tuesday, Governor Erdem Basci did a backdoor increase by announcing a new 9% funding rate that will be applicable in so-called extraordinary days of additional monetary tightening. The central bank is poised to hold the first such day on Monday, and then again on Thursday, which Mr. Basci says will effectively raise borrowing costs.

"I think it's just a waiting game. They are trying to keep the lira steady and calm the market down until the 9% funding rate kicks in on Monday," Mr. Pawlowski said.

"I expect more high-amount, direct dollar sales, but even if that curbs losses a little bit I do not expect it to have a lasting impact. The central bank needs to raise interest rates or apply additional monetary tightening more frequently for a sustainable appreciation in the lira," said Gizem Oztok Altinsac, chief economist at Garanti Securities in Istanbul.

The central bank has already burned through about $19 billion, a third of its net reserves, in an unsuccessful effort to halt the lira's slide since last June. The currency declined 21% against the dollar last year, making it worst performer in emerging markets, and is leading losses in developing economies with a 7% drop this year.

"In essence, the current bag of Turkey's central bank policies has not been working. It is falling back on more tried and tested methods, and resorting to direct intervention, as opposed to selling via managed foreign-exchange auctions," said Tim Ash, head of emerging markets strategy at Standard Bank PLC in London. "This might ultimately slow the pace of depreciation...but it will not change the trend, unless we see some improvements in the underlying drivers of the weak lira."

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Rouble hits 4-1/2 year low vs basket, lira tests record low
text:
LONDON, Jan 14 (Reuters) - The rouble hit a 4-1/2 year low against its dollar-euro basket on Tuesday after Russia's central bank said it would scale back its forex interventions, while the lira tested a new record low as Turkey's current account deficit widened further.

Broader emerging markets also slipped, taking their cue from a firmer dollar and Wall Street's 1.2 percent decline late on Monday, with MSCI's main emerging equity index down half a percent.

Emerging markets have been under pressure for more than six months on expectations - which become reality this month - that the Federal Reserve will scale back its bond-buying programme, encouraging investors to return home.

"A lot of foot-loose institutional capital has gone into emerging markets, and we're not sure that has come out yet," Kevin Gardner, European CIO at Barclays Wealth, told a briefing.

"Markets have cheapened up, but we are not yet too bullish on EM stocks."

Russian stocks fell more than 1 percent, but losses in the broader index were tempered by gains in its largest constituent, China. Mainland Chinese shares broke a four-day fall to end 0.9 percent higher.

The rouble hit 4-1/2 year lows against its dollar-euro basket and four-month lows against the dollar after the central bank said on Monday it would end 'targeted' interventions on the currency market as part of a strategic shift towards letting the rouble float freely.

The reduction to zero of its interventions, which had been set at $60 million per day, will increase the flexibility of the exchange rate corridor used by the central bank and reduce its presence on the market.

"As rouble volatility rises, the spot is likely to weaken at current interest rate levels," Commerzbank analysts wrote in a client note.

The lira fell more than half a percent to the dollar and Turkish stocks dropped more than 1 percent following data showing the current account deficit widened to $3.94 billion in November. The widening came in below expectations, however.

"The good news is that the deteriorating trend has stopped, the bad news is that the deficit remains very large," said Tim Ash, emerging markets strategist at Standard Bank, in a client note.

title: Turkish Markets Vulnerable After Fed Tapering
text:
ISTANBUL--Turkey's markets were volatile Thursday after the U.S. Federal Reserve decided to start scaling back its monthly bond purchases, a move which initially prompted a selloff in Turkish assets and forced the central bank in Ankara to take action.

Turkey's central bank said it will sell on Dec. 23 a minimum $250 million, up from $100 million previously, as part of additional tightening to support the lira. Ankara's move followed the Fed's decision Wednesday to taper by $10 billion its bond-buying program, which had helped flood emerging markets like Turkey with cash, as the recovery in the world's largest economy gains traction.

Turkey's lira slumped by almost 1% against the dollar following the Fed decision, weakening to 2.0624 per dollar early Thursday and nearing a record low, before reversing losses to gain 0.2% after the central bank said it would more than double its currency intervention.

Turkey's benchmark two-year bond yields surged to 9.42% from 9.36% before easing to 9.25%, and Istanbul's benchmark stock index was flat at 71,357.1 at 0920 GMT, after losing nearly 2% in initial trading before recovering on the central bank announcement.

Analysts warn Turkey is still in the firing line, as the Fed tapering may lead investors to start differentiating between developing economies and choke off capital inflows into some countries. Turkey is in the so-called "Fragile Five" group, with Brazil, India, South Africa and Indonesia, due to its external vulnerabilities, led by a current-account deficit at 7.5% of its $786 billion gross domestic product.

"Now, while emerging markets might be able to take this initial move to taper on the chin, individual emerging-market country fundamentals still matter--probably more so now. And therein Turkey and the lira's problem still is the current account deficit, a wide external financing gap, a central bank that is kicking and screaming to avoid narrowing the gap by hiking policy rates and slowing domestic demand," said Tim Ash, head of emerging market research at Standard Bank PLC.

Aside from global developments such as Fed tapering, Turkey is also facing rising political risks at home that could pressure the domestic markets, analysts say. Turkish police on Tuesday detained 52 people, including the sons of three cabinet ministers and the chief executive officer of a state-owned bank, as part of a corruption investigation. The probe, which analysts say is part of a tug of war between Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan and an influential Islamic cleric, is rattling Turkey just three months before critical local elections and putting additional pressure on Turkish assets.

"This [Fed tapering] will eliminate the uncertainty for the markets and the sooner the tapering started the better for the markets in our view, despite the headwinds such as weaker lira and higher rates we may see for the short run...We think that political risks could further escalate until the elections, especially equities' performance could be highly volatile which would lead Turkey to decouple from emerging-market peers in terms of asset prices," said Tera Brokers in Istanbul.

ISTANBUL, Sept 4 (Reuters) - The Turkish lira gave up some of its earlier gains on Wednesday after the central bank failed to reassure investors on its strategy to support the currency and military strikes on neighbouring Syria moved a step closer.

Russian President Vladimir Putin signalled a readiness to drop his opposition to potential U.S.-led strikes on Syria if Damascus were proven to have carried out a chemical weapons attack.

Putin's comments come after U.S. President Barack Obama clinched the backing of key figures in Congress for his plan to punish the Syrian government with limited strikes, though no vote on that proposal is due until next week.

The lira eased to 2.0606 against the dollar by 1433 GMT, from 2.0520 earlier and not far off last week's record lows. It was also near record lows against the dollar/euro basket at 2.3873.

Financial markets have been concerned about possible U.S. intervention in Turkey's southern neighbour, thinking it could push oil prices higher in the short term, further increasing Turkey's import bill and its gaping current account deficit.

The lira hit a record low of 2.07 against the dollar on Aug. 28, around 15 percent down from its peak this year, after central bank Governor Erdem Basci ruled out interest rate hikes to defend the currency.

That surprise announcement left economists wondering how the bank would support the currency in the face of fears about an imminent tapering in U.S. stimulus, the conflict in Syria, and the current account gap.

The deficit makes Turkey particularly vulnerable to cuts in the U.S. Federal Reserve's stimulus programme because further falls in the lira would make it more expensive to finance.

The central bank suggested at a meeting with economists on Wednesday that more surprises lay ahead in its unorthodox efforts to manage the lira, including the use of gross reserves, but investors were unconvinced.

"They seem very, very reluctant to raise rates, even in a situation with the lira going through 2.4, 2.5 ... against (the euro/dollar) basket," said Standard Bank economist Timothy Ash.

"So the mix now is basically fixed/anchored policy rates, and willingness to live with a weaker currency," he said.

The central bank has sold $8 billion at forex auctions to support the lira so far this year.

title: DJ  Emerging Markets Hope to Get Some Attention at G-20, Too
text:
Leaders from the Group of 20 economies have been preoccupied by Syria ahead of their summit this week, but some are still hoping to find a way to steady the suddenly shaky fortunes of emerging markets.

In recent years, most of the economic threats tackled by the G-20 have stemmed from large flows of capital from developed countries to developing ones in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis. But now that flow has begun to reverse, posing new challenges to the global recovery.

The turnaround has accelerated in recent weeks as investors anticipate an end to the U.S. Federal Reserve's period of extraordinary monetary stimulus this year. The result has been sharp falls in developing-country currencies.

The central banks of three G-20 members-Brazil, Indonesia and Turkey-have raised interest rates, intervened in currency markets or both in recent weeks to try to stem the declines.

In India, where the rupee has suffered the most-precipitous decline among large Asian economies, the central bank has also taken the step of selling dollars to state-run oil refiners via a commercial bank to shift demand for dollars away from the open market.

The Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development on Tuesday warned that an already subdued recovery in global economic growth could be weakened further if the outflow of capital from developing economies intensifies.

Some leaders are hoping that the issue can still be addressed, even if the meetings in St. Petersburg on Thursday and Friday are dominated by the crisis surrounding the alleged use of chemical weapons in Syria's civil war.

For instance, a person familiar with Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff's thinking said she hopes the summit will produce agreement on ways to ease the impact of the anticipated change in Fed policy.

"The tone of her speech [at the summit] will show how upset she may be with U.S. policies," said a Brazilian government official.

Brazilian officials say they have the backing of other developing countries in seeking moves to address recent currency volatility, although they are unclear about which among the G-20 members will be offering support. In particular, they want the Fed to improve the way it communicates its intentions to reduce market swings.

With the U.S. government focusing on efforts to boost support for its approach to Syria, those developing economies may be left frustrated. But even without Syria, the U.S. would have been unlikely to make major concessions, economists say.

"Other than a vague commitment to take into account the effects of its monetary policy on other countries, the Fed is in practice likely to make no concessions to developments elsewhere," said Capital Economics, a London-based research firm.

In an effort to exercise more control over their currencies, the governments of Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa have been working on a joint proposal to set up a $100 billion Contingency Reserve Arrangement by pooling central-bank reserves.

Leaders may make some progress in St. Petersburg, since that doesn't require input from the U.S. or other developed countries, although the new fund is unlikely to be launched until next year.

In March, finance ministers of the five "Brics" countries signed an agreement to kick-start the arrangement during their annual meeting in South Africa. China will contribute $41 billion, followed by Brazil, Russia and India with $18 billion each, and South Africa with $5 billion.

The focus on Syria will also probably mean that developed-country members of the G-20 pay less attention to a long-running dispute over whether to set binding deadlines for stabilizing their budget deficits and beginning to cut their debts.

In recent months, German officials have pushed the G-20 nations to agree to hard targets for reducing debt after the current deficit-cutting agreement expires in 2016. But the effort ran into strong U.S. opposition when finance ministers met in Moscow in July, with Treasury Department officials insisting that the priority had to be boosting jobs and growth as opposed to reducing debt.

Rather than a hard target, the G-20 countries are expected to lay out "medium-term fiscal strategies" to show how they will achieve "sustainable growth" after 2016, a German official told reporters in Berlin on Monday.

"This is better than no strategy, but these aren't binding targets," the official said.

G-20 leaders are also set to produce a plan for supporting growth and creating jobs.

A U.S. administration official said an overriding U.S. goal at the summit is persuading other nations that they need to help boost demand world-wide. Global demand is "improving," but "remains weak," the official said.

"We need to rededicate ourselves to promoting a lasting rebalancing of global demand," the official said. "We welcome signs that Europe's long recession is ending and their critical steps to restore financial stability. But important challenges remain, including boosting demand and addressing record-high unemployment levels."

Beyond that, the U.S. wants to make progress toward another goal: cracking down on tax evasion.

That issue was front-and-center at a separate meeting of the Group of Eight nations in Northern Ireland in June.

"We will also be working in St. Petersburg to get support globally for the kinds of measures that we have laid out for countries to close tax loopholes and avoid a race to the bottom where tax competition leads countries to lose revenue and companies to make inefficient decisions when they locate where they pay the lowest tax, rather than where it's most productive for them to produce," an Obama administration official said.

title: Turkish assets firm on Syria delay,  central bank  eyed
text:
* Central bank has signalled Monday could be key day

* Additional forex may be sold at auction

* Delay to Syria intervention brings some relief

By Dasha Afanasieva

ISTANBUL, Aug 29 (Reuters) - Turkish assets firmed on Monday with a delay to possible U.S. military action in Syria bringing some relief and investors expecting further measures from the central bank to curb currency volatility.

The lira firmed to 2.0160 against the dollar by 0806 GMT, from 2.0320 late on Thursday. Markets were closed on Friday for a national holiday.

The 10-year benchmark bond yield fell to 10.02 percent from 10.28 percent at Thursday's close. The main Istanbul share index rose 2.48 percent to 68,040.48 points, outperforming emerging markets peers.

Central Bank Governor Erdem Basci hinted last week that additional monetary tightening measures, including a forex auction, to be implemented on Monday could be a template for its future policy moves.

"The tightening on Monday should be watched closely. We put it out there as an example," Basci told state-run Anadolu news agency in an interview last Tuesday (www.aafinans.com("http://www.aafinans.com")).

As part of the tightening, the bank is not holding a one-week repo auction and will hold a minimum $100 million forex auction to give the lira additional support.

Economists interpreted Basci's comments as meaning the bank could increase the volume of its forex auctions.

"As he stressed the extensive forex reserves at the bank's disposal there is a high likelihood of even more aggressive forex intervention today," Commerzbank analysts said in a note.

Markets were pricing out the risk of an immediate military intervention in Syria after U.S. President Barack Obama said that he would not attack Syria before seeking approval from Congress, which reconvenes on Sept. 9.

Financial markets have been concerned about possible U.S. intervention in Turkey's southern neighbour, fearing it could push oil prices higher in the short term, further increasing Turkey's import bill and its gaping current account deficit. title: Indian Rupee, Indonesian Rupiah Gain on  Central-Bank  Moves
text:
The Indian rupee lead gains among emerging-market currencies Thursday on the back of new central-bank measures aimed at supporting the currency.

The Reserve Bank of India late Wednesday said it would sell dollars to the country's three state-run oil refiners through a designated commercial bank, shifting the bulk of the refiners' demand for dollars away from the open market. Oil refiners are India's biggest buyers of dollars, which they use to pay for crude-oil import.

As a result, the rupee soared 2.7% against the dollar, which bought INR66.98 in offshore trading, according to CQG.

"This has provided some relief, as this is taking care of a big chunk of the local corporate demand for dollars," Societe Generale analysts said in a note.

But they warned it may not be enough to sustain prolonged gains in the rupee. "While this measure may help alleviate tensions in the FX market, this is not a game changer, however," they added.

The Indonesian rupiah also gained modestly after the country's central bank raised interest rates at an extra policy meeting Thursday.

The rupee and rupiah have been among the hardest-hit currencies this month. India and Indonesia's reliance on foreign money to fund their wide trade deficits has made investors particularly nervous about these currencies, since a drawdown in U.S. Federal Reserve stimulus could result in less capital flows into these countries. The Fed is poised to start dialing down its bond-buying stimulus program as soon as September, analysts say.

Bank Indonesia raised its main policy rate by a half-percentage point to 7% Thursday, reflecting a growing realization that defending the country's plunging currency amid the emerging-market selloff is a more pressing need than maintaining rapid economic growth. The rupiah advanced a modest 0.2% to trade at IDR10,925 per dollar, after hitting four-year lows the previous session.

The Brazilian central bank's interest-rate increase, however, didn't have the same desired impact on its currency. The real slipped 0.6% against the dollar, which bought BRL2.3585, according to CQG. Late Wednesday, Brazil's central bank raised its benchmark Selic rate by 50 basis points to 9%, as was widely expected by analysts. But analysts say the rate hike may not be enough to stem inflationary pressures

"With the considerable amount of [real] depreciation over the past three months and a high likelihood of a gasoline price hike towards year-end/early next year, inflationary pressure down the road should remain high," Nomura analysts said in a note.

In Europe, the lira was among the few gainers, despite data showing a wider-than-expected trade gap. Turkey's trade deficit widened to $9.8 billion from $8 billion in July, the Ankara-based state statistics agency TUIK said, compared with the market consensus of $8.4 billion. Turkey's central bank has been intervening consistently to support the currency, which has fallen on concerns about its current account gap. It sold $50 million in a foreign exchange auction Thursday.

The lira strengthened 0.3% against the dollar, which bought TRY2.0318.

title: UPDATE 3-Turkish  central bank  says won't defend lira with interest rates
text:
* Basci all but rules out interest rate hike

* Lira hits record low, bond yields jump, stocks slide

* U.S. Fed, Syria, elections weigh on Turkish appeal

* Lira slide hits corporate earnings (Adds analyst comment, updates market reaction)

By Seda Sezer and Nick Tattersall

ISTANBUL, Aug 27 (Reuters) - Turkish Central Bank Governor Erdem Basci said on Tuesday he did not intend to hike interest rates to defend a sliding lira, which hit record lows on concern about the outlook for U.S. stimulus and the conflict in neighbouring Syria.

In an interview with the state-run Anadolu news agency (AA), Basci said the central bank had $40 billion in reserves which it could use to shore up the lira and would intervene defensively as needed to reduce exchange rate volatility.

The lira weakened to a record low of 2.037 to the dollar as markets wondered whether the bank had the firepower necessary to defend the currency.

The main Turkish share index slid 4.7 percent to close at its lowest in a year.

The 10-year benchmark bond yield spiked to 10.83 percent during Basci's interview, which was broadcast live on Turkish financial TV stations, from 10.18 percent on Monday. It closed at 10.28 percent.

"We will not be using our interest rate weapon against the exchange rate. We are very clear on that and we have said there will not be any uncertainty about interest rates," Basci told AA Finans (www.aafinans.com("http://www.aafinans.com")).

"Since we will not be using this then we are left with the balance sheet weapon, and that is a very powerful weapon. That means we will use our foreign exchange reserves against the slide in the foreign exchange market."

His comments surprised many economists.

"Turkey's central bank is digging itself into a deeper hole. For a country whose forex reserves barely cover its short-term external debts, this is highly imprudent policymaking," said Nicholas Spiro of Spiro Sovereign Strategy.

Emerging markets have borne the brunt of heavy selling in recent weeks amid concern that the U.S. Federal Reserve will soon start reducing its massive bond-buying programme, which had flooded developing economies with cheap liquidity.

Turkey is particularly vulnerable because it is heavily dependent on foreign inflows to finance its current account deficit, running at over 7 percent of national output.

Concern about the consequences of a possible U.S.-led intervention in neighbouring Syria and political uncertainty ahead of an election cycle beginning next year have further dampened its appeal as investors shun riskier assets.

Basci said he was not overly worried about the exchange rate, forecasting it would recover by the end of the year to around 1.92 to the dollar, and that long-term bond yields would also be back in single digits.

"Don't expect a shock from us on the interest rate side, just expect interesting manoeuvres on the forex side that will result in an appreciation of the lira," Basci said, in characteristically cryptic comments.

"I am neither a hawk nor a dove," he said when questioned about his policy stance. "I am not a bird."

WEAK LIRA TAKES TOLL

The central bank raised its overnight lending rate, the upper end of the interest rate corridor it uses to control monetary conditions, for a second straight month last week, hiking it by 50 basis points to 7.75 percent in a surprise move to try to prevent an uncontrolled slide in the lira.

Basci said the average cost of lira funding would remain between 6.75 percent, the rate at which it funds primary dealers, and 7.75 percent until inflation drops to its year-end forecast of 6.2 percent.

"The central bank is once again demonstrating it is unwilling to raise rates much further, and that will continue to drag (the dollar/lira rate) higher," Luis Costa, head of CEEMEA currency and debt strategy at Citi, referring to more lira weakening.

Economy Minister Zafer Caglayan, a vocal supporter of low interest rates and champion of Turkish exporters, who benefit from a weak lira, said the central bank did not need to intervene to support the currency, saying the 2 to the dollar level it breached on Tuesday was only a psychological barrier.

He also dismissed suggestions that any Turkish participation in an international coalition to intervene in Syria would have a negative impact on the economy.

But the effects of the weak lira - which has fallen 14 percent against the dollar from a peak this year of 1.7455 on Feb. 1 - are already being felt by some of Turkey's top firms.

A weak lira cut net profit at national flag carrier Turkish Airlines by almost a third in the second quarter despite a sharp rise in sales, sending its shares tumbling more than 2 percent on Tuesday.

The country's largest telecoms group Turk Telekom , whose liabilities are in dollars, euros and Japanese yen, said last month its net profit fall 56 percent in the same period due to foreign exchange losses.

The weakening lira and Basci's comments helped knock the main Istanbul share index down by more than 3 percent to a year low although it later recovered somewhat to trade down 2.4 percent by 1030 GMT.

"Combined with the uncertainty over a multi-party military intervention in Syria, the comments are negative for Turkey's financial markets," said Ibrahim Aksoy, economist at Istanbul-based Seker Securities. title: UPDATE 1-Turkish lira weakens beyond 2 per dollar on Washington's Syria comments
text:
* Lira at record low

* Syria weighs

* C.bank governor to speak

By Seda Sezer

ISTANBUL, Aug 27 (Reuters) - The Turkish lira weakened beyond 2 to the dollar on Tuesday after the United States signalled possible military intervention in Syria and the market waited for central bank action to halt the currency's fall.

U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry, in the most forceful reaction yet to last week's suspected gas attack outside Damascus, said President Barack Obama "believes there must be accountability for those who would use the world's most heinous weapons against the world's most vulnerable people".

The lira was at 2.0045 against the dollar by 0544 GMT after dropping as low as 2.0095 earlier and from 1.9918 late on Monday.

Turkish central bank governor Erdem Basci was expected to appear on television at 0730 GMT, and investors are looking for more guidance on how he will act to stop the lira's decline.

Turkey's central bank has been tightening monetary conditions to support the lira through a range of tools, but has left its main benchmark rate - the one-week repo rate - unchanged at 4.5 percent.

"The recent developments in Syria signal possible military intervention and this is negative for economies like Turkey," said Fatih Keresteci, a strategist at HSBC Bank in Turkey.

"The Turkish central bank's hyperactive monetary policy, which aims to reduce the selling pressure, creates a second wave of selling tendency because it creates uncertainties. The lira will remain under pressure unless the central bank switches to an orthodox policy and makes lira relatively attractive again."

The central bank held a forex auction on Monday and sold $350 million, in line with additional monetary tightening steps announced last week. The bank also held its first one-week, fixed-rate repo auction in almost a week, with a volume of 1.5 billion lira ($755 million).

It also said it would launch a forex-selling auction on Tuesday with a minimum volume of $50 million.

Growing expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve may soon start tapering its stimulus programme has hit appetite for emerging markets, with Turkey's gaping current account deficit leaving it particularly vulnerable.

The country is dependent on foreign inflows to finance the gap, which is equivalent to around 7.1 percent of Turkey's economic output.

Raising interest rates makes lira assets more attractive to foreign investors, but could also crimp growth, something Prime Minister Tayyip Erdogan's government is eager to avoid before local polls next year and a general election in 2015.

title: Syria Roils  Foreign-Exchange  Markets
text:
--Lira, rupee plunge to new record lows against the dollar

--Market participants seek safety in Swiss franc, yen


 
   By Clare Connaghan 
 

The Turkish lira and Indian rupee remained under intense selling pressure Tuesday as fears of possible U.S. intervention in Syria ramped up the pressure on these currencies and drove traders into perceived safe retreats in times of stress, such as the yen and Swiss franc.

The lira and rupee--two currencies that have already been hit hard in the past few weeks due to concerns over how their economies will cope when the U.S. Federal Reserve starts winding down stimulus measures--slumped to new record lows against the dollar Tuesday as political tensions between Syria and the U.S. escalated.

The Israeli shekel also came under pressure, falling to a near seven-week low against the dollar, after U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry said the U.S. and its allies are considering military strikes on Syria after "undeniable" evidence of a chemical attack.

"Foreign-exchange markets have reacted further overnight to fears of military intervention in Syria," said Elsa Lignos, senior currency strategist at RBC Capital Markets in London.

Across financial markets, the crisis in Syria weighed with stock markets in Europe and the Middle East tumbling, while yields on U.S. 10-year Treasury bonds fell to their lowest level since mid-August.

For the lira, additional pressure came from the stance of Turkish central bank Governor Erdem Basci, who ruled out raising core interest rates to defend the bruised currency. In response, the lira weakened by more than 1% against the dollar which surged to a new record high of TRY2.0339. The euro also broke new ground, rising to TRY2.7163 against the lira, as the governor failed to calm market nerves.

"Basci rules out further overnight lending rate hikes, which is negative for the lira in our view given the Fed uncertainty," says Ibrahim Aksoy, an economist with Istanbul-based brokerage Seker Invest.

The Fed is preparing to wind down policies that flooded financial markets with cheap cash, which is raising concerns about how countries such as Turkey, which relied on these inflows to pay for imports and finance debt, will cope without it. As a result, investors have been selling the lira aggressively and so far this month, the currency is down more than 3% against the dollar.

Turkey's central bank has increased sales of dollars to support the lira, but ultimately this measure will only dampen depreciation, not reverse it, says Thu Lan Nguyen, a currencies strategist at Commerzbank.

"If markets are in a risk off mode there is hardly anything you can do as a central bank," says Ms Nguyen.

The situation is the same for India, where the rupee sunk to new life-time low against the dollar Tuesday of INR66.07 despite the central bank intervening, according to local dealers. India, which like Turkey has seen its currency swoon in anticipation of a shift in Fed policy, also faces the extra burden of higher oil prices, which are also climbing amid the Syrian tensions.

Caught up in the emerging-markets tension, the South African rand sank close to a four-year low against the dollar, which hit ZAR10.4394.

In other news, data showing business sentiment in the euro-zone's largest economy--Germany--leapt in August amid an improving export outlook, had limited impact on the euro which remained weaker against the dollar on the day.

Looking ahead, aside from watching the situation in Syria, Case Shiller house prices and consumer confidence data are due for release at 1300 GMT and 1400 GMT respectively.

"The market is digesting the weak durable good orders we had from the U.S. yesterday which has put uncertainty back on the agenda leading up to the FOMC meeting," said Michael Sneyd, a foreign-exchange strategist at BNP Paribas in London.

Data showed total orders for durable goods such as cars and furniture dropped 7.3% in July after three months of gains, worse than economists had predicted. The weak report complicates the outlook for Federal Reserve policy, as Fed members are debating whether the U.S. economy is healthy enough to begin winding down its post-crisis stimulus measures as early as next month.

Against this backdrop, price action is likely to remain choppy with investors not really wanting to commit to new trades, Mr Sneyd added.

At 1101 GMT, the euro was trading at $1.3346 against the dollar, compared with $1.3370 late Monday in New York, according to trading system EBS. The dollar was at Y97.80 against the yen, compared with Y98.50, while the euro was at Y130.525, compared with Y131.72. The pound was trading at $1.5515 against the dollar, compared with $1.5573 late Monday in New York.

title: DJ Turkish Lira Sinks as  Central Bank  Rules Out Further Rate Hikes
text:
ISTANBUL--The Turkish lira slumped to yet another record low against the euro and dollar Tuesday as the country's central bank governor rules out further rate hikes.

The lira weakened over 1% against both the dollar and euro following the governor's speech. The dollar surged past TRY2.03 against the lira for the first time ever, while the euro rose to a new record high of TRY2.7163.

By 0810 GMT, the dollar was trading at TRY2.0285, up from TRY2.0050 before the governor's speech. The euro was trading at TRY2.7055, up from around TRY2.68 before the speech started.

In an interview with state-run news agency Anadolu Agency, Mr. Basci said the central bank will fund the market at 6.75% until the inflation rate falls to the 6.2% from the current 8.8% by the end of this year. He said the central bank will fund the market at 7.75% on additional tightening days, but he said the cost of funding for the banks won't be more expensive than the 7.75% rate. He said the central bank will use foreign exchange reserves to defend the lira, but won't use interest rates to stem the currency's slide.

"USD/TRY will be 1.92 by the year end and don't be surprised when you see that level," Mr. Basci said. He said markets shouldn't expect interest rate hikes but should expect rates to remain steady.

"Basci rules out further overnight lending rate hikes, which is negative for the lira in our view given the Fed uncertainty. The Central Bank Governor has also said that the currency movements may be rapid, but the currency would likely gain value once again should the central bank be successful in controlling short-term interest rates," said Ibrahim Aksoy, an economist with Istanbul-based brokerage Seker Invest. "Overall, the comments so far are negative for the lira, bond and equity markets," Mr. Aksoy said, combined with the uncertainty over a possible U.S. military intervention in Syria, the comments are negative for Turkey's financial markets.

title: Mexican Peso, Emerging-Market  Currencies  Slip on Fed Worries
text:
The Mexican peso and most other emerging-market currencies slumped Monday, resuming the selloff that has plagued them in recent weeks.

Investors returned their focus to the Federal Reserve's September policy meeting, where the Fed could start to trim its bond-buying stimulus program that had sent investors on a hunt for yield in past years. The threat of less Fed stimulus has rapidly tamped investors' enthusiasm for higher-yielding emerging-market assets, and has caused many to reinvest in U.S. assets.

Several emerging-market currencies recovered slightly on Friday in the wake of larger intervention efforts on the part of Brazil's and Turkey's central banks over the course of the week. However, these currencies once again took on a bearish tone Monday, with little sign of such interventions having an effect as Brazil's and Turkey's currencies weakened.

"September's getting closer and closer," said Win Thin, global head of emerging-market currency strategy at Brown Brothers Harriman in New York. "It's pretty much a full-scale emerging-market selloff continued."

Mexico's currency led the way, diving 1.8% against the dollar, which bought MXN13.1827, according to CQG. The peso often acts as a proxy for emerging-market currencies, since it is one of the more heavily traded and accessible currencies in the asset class.

Brazil's currency also weakened sharply, despite the Brazilian central bank's heightened efforts to stop the real's seeming one-way decline last week. Brazil's central bank on Thursday said it would provide at least $60 billion more in dollar liquidity through the end of the year. Under the plan, the bank will offer $3 billion of dollar loans and swaps per week in regular auctions starting Friday. Still, the real fell 1.4% against the dollar, which bought BRL2.3813 late Monday.

In Asia, the rupee weakened, though India's central bank was suspected of intervening in the foreign-exchange market toward the close of local trading Monday. The rupee slid 1% against the greenback, which traded at INR64.32, according to CQG.

The rupee and Brazilian real have been severely punished by traders this month as their countries have large current account deficits. These current account gaps force them to rely on foreign portfolio inflows to meet financing needs, but these flows could lessen if the Fed pulls back stimulus, analysts say.

The Indonesian rupiah, however, saw some recovery in response to a group of measures the government announced last week aimed at narrowing the country's current account gap. Indonesia's central bank announced additional measures Friday aimed at stabilizing local markets and the economy as well.

The rupiah fell 1.7% to IDR10,845 against the dollar.

"The measures from both the government and central bank are certainly well-intentioned and a step in the right direction,' said HSBC ASEAN economist Su Sian LIM in a note Monday.

In Europe, the Turkish lira underperformed, despite continued intervention by Turkey's central bank, which sold $350 million in foreign exchange to support the lira Monday. After hovering near record lows earlier in the session, the lira slipped 0.5% against the dollar, which bought TRY1.9982, according to CQG.

title: South African Rand, Emerging-Market  Currencies  Edge Lower After FOMC Minutes
text:
Emerging-market currencies extended losses against the dollar Wednesday after the recently released Federal Reserve's July monetary policy meeting minutes did nothing to dispel expectations that the central bank could begin winding down its stimulus efforts as soon as next month.

The U.S. dollar gained 1.2% versus the South African rand to ZAR10.2776 late in the New York trading day. The greenback also climbed against Latin American currencies, strengthening 1.8% against the Brazilian real to BRL 1.436 and 1.6% against the Mexican peso to MXN13.1739.

The Fed's $85 billion-a-month bond buying program has added liquidity to the market and driven investors toward high-yielding emerging-market assets. But as the U.S. its economy shows signs of recovery--and given the prospect of higher interest rates as the Fed ends its bond buying--investors are putting their money back into U.S. assets amid concerns over how developing countries' economies will fare once this global liquidity is drained.

Asian currencies were hit particularly hard, with the Indian rupee falling to fresh record-lows against the dollar, which gained 2.3% to INR64.59. The Indonesian rupiah slid to IDR10945 per dollar, down from IDR10729.0 late Tuesday.

title: Indian Rupee Defies Broader Emerging-Market  Currency  Slump
text:
The Indian rupee surged against the dollar Wednesday on the back of the Reserve Bank of India's latest efforts to shore up the currency, while most other emerging-market currencies fell.

The rupee soared more than 1% to a one-week high against the U.S. currency, which recently bought INR59.12.

The RBI late Tuesday put new restrictions on commercial banks' access to cash. Banks now are permitted to borrow cash up to only 0.5% of their net deposits from the central bank daily at 7.25%, the central bank said in a news release posted on its website. It also said banks must set aside more cash with it than they did before.

These measures are only the latest in a series of steps to prop up the currency, which has been pummeled by concerns about the Federal Reserve withdrawing its stimulus that had helped drive investors to higher-yielding assets.

While these latest measures helped drive the rupee higher, they actually dragged down India's local bond and equity markets and raised concerns that further liquidity-tightening could hit these markets even harder.

"We do think it's going to stem the short-term pressure on the rupee," said Ilan Solot, emerging-market currency strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman. But he warned that additional tightening could cause "collateral damage" in other markets and spook away much-needed short-term equity flows.

Other emerging-market currencies, however, broadly weakened on the back of disappointing Chinese economic data and positive U.S. housing data. HSBC's Chinese manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index dropped to an 11-month low at 47.7 in July, from 48.2 in June.

Meanwhile, U.S. new-home sales surged 8.3% in June, renewing worries that the Fed could start tapering its bond-buying stimulus if the economic outlook improves in the world's largest economy.

The Brazilian real suffered the largest slide against the dollar, despite intervention by Brazil's central bank. The central bank held a currency swap auction Wednesday aimed at supporting the real, which slumped more than 1% against the dollar. The U.S. currency bought BRL2.2433 from BRL2.2133 late Tuesday, according to CQG.

The Mexican peso also slid significantly as a rise in U.S. Treasurys lent support to the dollar. The peso slumped 1.2% against the dollar, which traded at MXN12.6485.

The Turkish lira was the top decliner among emerging European currencies, despite the recent rate hike by its central bank and continued market intervention. On Tuesday, Turkey's central bank raised its overnight lending rate by 0.75 percentage point to 7.25% and signaled that it could tighten further, in an attempt to halt the lira's relentless decline. But that, along with foreign-exchange selling auctions Wednesday, wasn't enough to halt the lira's dive. The lira weakened 1% against the dollar, which changed hands at TRY1.9194, according to CQG.

The South African rand slid as well, despite better-than-expected inflation data. It fell 0.6% against the dollar, which bought ZAR9.7377. The annual inflation rate ticked down to 5.5% from 5.6% in May, according to South Africa's statistics agency.

title: DJ Turkey Expected to Raise Rates Tuesday to Stem Lira's Decline
text:
ISTANBUL--Turkey is expected Tuesday to join a number of emerging economies, such as Brazil, India and Indonesia, with a rise in interest rates in an effort to support the local currency, but economists are split on the extent of the expected increase, with forecasts ranging from 50 to 100 basis points.

The central bank has spent billions of dollars in foreign-exchange interventions and auctions in an effort to stem the lira's slide but with little effect. The bank is now considering a rate increase--its first since October 2011--to prop up the currency.

The lira has plummeted about 8% since the beginning of this year and hit record lows against the dollar, largely as a result of a broader sell-off in emerging markets in the spring, fueled by fears that the Federal Reserve would soon start scaling back its monthly bond-buying program. Widespread clashes between police and anti-government protesters in June also weighed on the currency.

At 1145 GMT Monday, the lira was steady against the dollar at TRY1.9169.

A poll of ten economists by Dow Jones Newswires showed that half expect Turkey's central bank to raise its 6.50% overnight lending rate by 50 basis points, while the other half expect an increase of 100 basis points, when its Monetary Policy Committee meets Tuesday. All ten expect the central bank to keep its overnight borrowing rate at 3.50% and one-week benchmark rate at 4.50%.

"I think the benchmark for the market will be the 100 bps move point--less than this and Turkish assets are likely to come under renewed selling pressure, more than this and they are likely to rally as the market will assume that the central bank is finally looking to get ahead (or rather "on") of the curve in terms of required tightening," said Tim Ash, head of emerging markets research at Standard Bank PLC in London.

Last week, Central bank Governor Erdem Basci said policy makers would consider "a measured step to widen the interest-rate corridor" that ranges from 3.5% to 6.5% at its regular monthly meeting July 23. The corridor allows policy makers to vary borrowing costs daily in an effort to meet targets ranging from economic growth to financial stability.

"If a move of 50 basis points or less is announced, we expect TRY [the lira] to sell off very sharply with USD/TRY highly likely to breach the 2.00 handle. However, the risk of this is too great and given that forex intervention has proven ineffective and Turkey's foreign reserves are very limited, the bank has little choice," said Christian Lawrence, emerging market strategist at Rabobank.

The central bank has spent more than 10% of its net foreign-exchange reserves in market interventions, and has sold $6.6 billion in foreign exchange auctions, since June 11.

title: DJ Performance of Emerging-Market  Currencies  Improves as Dollar Weakens

The pro-growth focus of the Group of 20 countries over the weekend has given investors confidence and prompted a recovery of most emerging-market currencies against the dollar on Monday.

The Turkish lira gained 0.3% on the day, according to CQG data, on a combination of improved global outlook and expectations of a rate increase in Turkey.

In addition to the G-20 conclusion, Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe's party saw a strong showing in parliamentary elections which also served as a referendum to his administration's reforms and weakening of the yen.

This set off a weakness in the dollar that has lingered through the New York trading session.

Standard Chartered analysts note that the recent protests have exposed Turkey's vulnerabilities to investors, and at the same time diminished its policy options.

Investors who previously had held Turkish bonds have sharply lowered their exposure as a result and this has resulted in a selloff in all Turkish assets, especially the lira. Though Turkey's central bank has intervened regularly to defend the lira, much of the recent retracement in the currency's value was due to the expectation of rate increases. Some analysts, though, worry that such a move would pressure Turkey's growth, which already is sluggish due to the recession in most of Europe.

Also, in anticipation of central bank action, Hungary's currency continued to gain. It recently traded at 294.11 forints, up 0.5% on the day to the euro. Also, Hungary's central bank is expected to continue easing, with analysts projecting a 25 basis-point cut to its key policy rate to 4%, in a bid to support growth at a time when inflation is low.

Even at the 4%, investors say Hungary is an attractive carry play as its yield is higher than comparable European peers.

title: CORRECTED- Central bank  reserves perilously low in some developing countries
text:
(Corrects Chinese reserves figure to over $3 trillion)

LONDON, July 18 (Reuters) - Severely depleted central bank reserves are putting Ukraine, Egypt and Venezuela at risk of balance of payments crises while reserves in many other developing countries are also steadily declining.

Based on a comparison of monthly import needs and maturing short-term debt, most emerging economies - with a few exceptions - still have ample reserves, as the following graphic, based on Bank of AmericaMerrill Lynch data, shows:

For a graphic, click on: http://link.reuters.com/sef79t("http://link.reuters.com/sef79t")

One yardstick of reserve adequacy is the number of months of imports the reserves will buy, with three months deemed to be the safe minimum. The second, based on the so-called Guidotti-Greenspan rule, requires reserves to be at least equal to external debt payments due in the coming year.

The rationale is that countries should have enough reserves to resist a sudden stop in foreign financing.

By the first measure, Egypt and Venezuela, with less than two months apiece of import cover, and Ukraine, with three months, look most vulnerable. Ukraine's reserves are also insufficient to cover debt maturing before mid-2014.

Another possible weak link is Turkey, which on the face of it has five months' import cover and a reserves-to-short-term debt ratio of 1. But Turkey's net usable reserves are actually far lower, with HSBC estimating the figure as low as $40 billion, giving import cover of just 2.3 months.

David Hauner, head of EEMEA debt strategy at BofA Merrill Lynch says Turkey also looks vulnerable by the other measure, of maturing foreign debt.

"Turkey ... barely covers the one-year period. That is why people get so nervous when Turkey intervenes in the market and that is why you are seeing such a huge underperformance of Turkish assets in the external debt market," Hauner said.

"But among big emerging markets very few are running a ratio of less than 2. Clearly they have raised the bar on themselves."

Emerging markets hold the lion's share of central banks' combined $11.1 trillion reserves, recent IMF data shows - a legacy of the past decade's trade and investment boom. Over $3 trillion of this is in China.

But as exports and capital inflows slow, accumulation has stalled and is even reversing as central banks from Brazil to Poland are forced to sell dollars to support falling currencies.

It is unclear exactly how much emerging central banks have spent on currency interventions since the sell-off started in May but they range from Brazil's sale of $20 billion in derivatives to $6.2 billion in Turkey and $5 billion in Russia.

Reserves have therefore fallen since the figures above were compiled. Latest data shows Indonesia's stash at $98.1 billion, down $9 billion over May-June, while India now has $280.1 billion compared to $296 billion in early May.

Some of the moves reflect valuation effects such as exchange rate changes and a lower gold price. But further falls could send more countries into risky territory. India and South Africa both of which have 4.5-5 months' import cover, reserve/debt ratios of 2 or less and large current account gaps, look especially vulnerable. title: DJ Brazilian Real Turns Volatile as More Rate Hikes Are Projected
text:
The Brazilian real see-sawed on Thursday as it moved from strength to weakness and back as investors' digested the central bank's latest take on the country's economic health.

The real recently traded at BRL2.2206, a gain of 0.2% on the day to the dollar, according to CQG data.

Market participants were surprised at the hawkish message from the minutes of Brazil's central bank's recent meeting released Thursday. The central bank acknowledged that the currency's sharp fall in recent weeks added to rising inflation but suggests the resulting adjustments to prices is good for the economy, said Tony Volpon, head of emerging-market research Americas at Nomura Securities International Inc.

Further, the minutes suggested Brazil would continue to tighten monetary policy. It already has raised key policy rates by 100 basis points.

In minutes released Thursday of the central bank's July 10 decision, policy makers said weakness in the Brazilian real versus the dollar "constitutes a strong source of shorter-term inflationary pressure." However, the longer-term effects of a weaker real can be limited through "adequate" monetary policy measures, the bank said.

These comments have prompted Citi analyst Marcelo Kfoury to suggest Brazil would raise rates to 9.25% in the current cycle.

Meanwhile, an auction of foreign-exchange swap contracts on Thursday helped the real strengthen against the dollar.

In other central-bank actions, the South African central bank kept its key policy rates unchanged at 5%. The bank's governor said slower growth is making the bank more tolerant to inflation, which is heading close to its comfort level of 6%.

Meanwhile, the bank once again reduced its growth forecast for the year to 2% from its previous estimate of 2.4%, and to 3.3% from 3.5%% for 2014.

South Africa's growth has stumbled after last year's mining strikes that have triggered labor unrest and extended labor negotiations. Also, the fall in commodity prices has hurt the exporter of precious metals.

The dollar rose 0.5% to the South African rand to ZAR9.8774, according to CQG data.

In Turkey, the central bank continued to intervene in an attempt to reduce volatility in the lira. The dollar rose 0.44% to TRY1.92, according to CQG data.

Market participants believe despite the day's weakness, emerging-market currencies will be supported in coming weeks as investors take advantage of these lower levels. Already, many investors have said they have bought local bonds of Mexico and Brazil.

In Mexico, the peso has rebounded below MXN12.4558, for the first time in more than seven weeks, according to CQG data. Investors cite the administration's renewed focus on reforms and the country's close ties to an improved U.S. economy.

In the debt markets, some emerging-market issuers tiptoed back in, including Asia's first high-yield deal since June. PT Multipolar TK of Indonesia is in the market with a $200 million, five-year note that has a guidance in the area of 9.875% yield.

Other issuers include Russian Agricultural bank and Banco do Brasil. The Russian bank is selling a $500 million bond that has a guidance of 5.4% yield. Banco do Brasil expects to sell a EUR500 million, five-year bond at a yield of 4%.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Stocks eye positive week, lira eases
text:
LONDON, July 12 (Reuters) - Emerging stocks were heading for a rare week of gains on Friday, buoyed by hopes the Fed would not turn off the liquidity taps any time soon, while Turkey's lira edged towards record lows despite recent intervention.

Attempts by U.S. Federal Chairman Ben Bernanke this week to row back on previous comments about the tapering of the Fed's money-printing programme have given support to high-yielding emerging markets.

The MSCI emerging stocks index has risen 2.7 percent this week though it remains 11 percent down from May 22, the date of Bernanke's initial remarks about tapering.

The index was steady on Friday after soaring 3 percent in the previous session, its largest one-day gain since Sept 2012. Russian stocks  rose more than 1 percent to hit their highest in over a month, South African stocks hit three-week highs and Turkish stocks rose 0.3 percent.

Chinese shares  fell, however, ahead of GDP data due on Monday.

China's finance minister signalled that Beijing may be willing to tolerate second half economic growth significantly below 7 percent, the most sobering comment to date on the country's slowdown from a senior policymaker.

Emerging sovereign debt spreads inched out 1 basis point to 358 bps over U.S. Treasuries.

Equity and bond funds saw outflows of $2.2 billion and $1.3 billion respectively in the week to June 10, according to banks citing EPFR data.

"The rest of the summer may continue to be challenging for emerging market fixed income assets," said Barclays in a client note.

"Growth concerns, overshadowed by the Fed's tapering of asset purchases and large EM fund outflows, are taking the front seat in our risk...metrics."

The Turkish lira edged towards recent record lows, despite more than $6 billion spent by the central bank in its support this week.

Concerns about the Fed's stimulus plans and anti-government protests across Turkey last month have driven the losses in the currency, leaving investors worried about the country's wide current account deficit and the lack of rate rises.

Benchmark bond yields fell almost 30 bps from the previous session however.

Most emerging European currencies were slightly weaker, though the forint briefly hit a three-week high.

title: EUROPE'S PULSE-A daily note from our Economics Editor
text:
(A daily view of what's eye-catching in Europe from EMEA Economics Editor Mike Peacock. The views expressed are his own.)

July 11 (Reuters) - How much time does massive central bank currency intervention buy? About a day at a time in Turkey's case. It spent $1.3 billion of its reserves yesterday to stop the lira going into freefall having thrown a record $2.25 billion at the market on Monday.

So far this year, the central bank has burned over $6 billion of its reserves which have now dropped below $40 billion. So that can't go on for long, meaning an interest rate rise which a slowing economy really doesn't need must be on the cards. The lira hit a record low versus the dollar on Monday.

Much of this is to do with the global emerging market sell-off sparked by the Federal Reserve's exit plan from money-printing but Ankara has sown the seeds of crisis too, first with the very public standoff with protesters in its main cities who railed against what they see as Prime Minister Tayyip Erdogan's increasingly authoritarian rule.

Erdogan has come out fighting, blaming "foreign circles", and an "interest rate lobby", foreign media and terrorists for Turkey's problems - not the sort of language likely to encourage foreign investors. It also means the if rates do rise, Erdogan is probably going to have to blame someone.

Yesterday, the banking watchdog launched an investigation into recent foreign exchange deals. Justified or not, that could well scare the horses too. Then, there is the already yawning current account deficit which leaves the economy acutely vulnerable to investment outflows. So Turkey is at the centre of the emerging market storm, partly due to its own actions, and it's not clear the government is going to change tack.

German Bund futures have risen after minutes of the Fed's last meeting showed chairman Ben Bernanke saw easy policy for the foreseeable future, while about half his colleagues thought a halt to QE should be called by the year-end. Bernanke has said that is more likely by mid-2014.

In the round, markets are taking that as a more dovish stance (?). European stock futures are pointing substantially higher.

Italy will sell up to 6.5 billion euros of fixed-rate bonds and floating-rate certificates after one-year borrowing costs rose to their highest since March at a one-year debt sale on Wednesday.

A ratings cut by S&P on Tuesday gives an unhelpful backdrop. The ratings agency's forecast of a deeper economic downturn this year - with the pressure that will put on Italy's deficit - is in line with the IMF and most other forecasters. With the government at odds over issues ranging from demands to cut an unpopular housing tax, to an order for F-35 combat jets and the legal problems of centre-right leader Silvio Berlusconi, prospects of concerted political support for reform appear weak.

ECB policymakers Benoit Coeure and Jens Weidmann are both speaking and their words will be parsed for any more clarity on what keeping interest rates at record lows for an "extended period" actually means. Executive Board member Joerg Asmussen told Reuters on Tuesday that the pledge was good for "beyond" 12 months but the ECB then rushed out a statement insisting he had not intended to give any guidance on exact time frames.

Since Draghi announced "forward guidance" a week ago there have been shades of mixed messages from his colleagues which shows just how difficult it is. Coeure has already said the ECB stands ready to act flexibly to new developments while Weidmann has stuck to his line that monetary policy can only do so much. There is an element of smoke and mirrors here. In the end, if growth and inflation start rising, the ECB will tighten policy, regardless of timelines. 'Twas ever thus.

ECB reaction to yesterday's messy banking union developments will also be interesting. The European Commission proposed a cross-border agency to salvage or shut failing banks which, because it will have no funds for some time, suggests it will find it very difficult actually to demand the closure of any bank, no matter how stricken, because the bill will fall squarely on the home government. Ergo, the "doom loop" created by weak sovereigns propping up weaker banks is utterly unbroken.

However, even that was too much for Germany which demanded again that such decisions should rest squarely with member states, not an overarching body. The ECB is likely to take over its supervisory role late next year. It does not want to be exposed without parallel structures in place. European Commission President Jose Manuel Barroso is in Warsaw and may have something to say too. (Editing by Susan Fenton)

title: Turkish Lira Extends Losses Despite  Central Bank Intervention
text:
The Turkish lira's losses couldn't be tamed Wednesday, despite continued intervention by its central bank.

Turkey's central bank sold $1.3 billion at six separate foreign exchange auctions Wednesday in an effort to halt the lira's precipitous slide against the dollar. For most of this week, Turkey's central bank has been actively trying to limit the lira's losses as it could trigger outflows and raise the cost of borrowing for the government.

Even measures to check speculative trading haven't been enough, however, to counter investors' growing wariness of Turkey and most emerging-market assets. Countries that have been particularly hit hard are those with current account deficits, like Turkey, India and Brazil.

"Everyone's... focusing on the fundamentals rather than on yields right now," said Win Thin, global head of emerging-market currency strategy at Brown Brothers Harriman in New York.

The lira slid 0.6% against the dollar, which bought TRY1.9532, according to CQG.

On Wednesday, minutes of the Federal Reserve's June policy meeting showed about half of Fed officials believed the central bank should end its $85 billion-a-month bond-buying program by the end of this year. The dollar pared some of its gains against some emerging-market currencies as the minutes also showed that some Fed officials didn't believe the labor market has improved enough for the central bank to start pulling back on its bond purchases.

But longer-term, the potential for Fed tapering has led investors to reduce their exposure to emerging markets, and as a result, asset prices are under pressure. In a vicious cycle, this leads to further widening of emerging economies' current account deficits and a weakening of their currencies, which makes refinancing existing debt more expensive for these countries.

"Barring any complete collapse of the U.S. economy in July or August, I think tapering's on track," Mr. Thin said. "Overall that's still dollar positive."

Brazil's currency also underperformed Wednesday, falling to its weakest level against the dollar since April 2009. That spurred the Brazilian central bank to call a snap auction of foreign-exchange swap contracts, which typically help support the real. Still, the real was 0.6% weaker against the U.S. currency, which bought BRL2.2735, according to CQG. Brazil's central bank will conclude a rate-setting meeting later Wednesday, where it is widely expected by analysts to raise its benchmark Selic rate by at least 50 basis points to 8.5%.

The Mexican peso also weakened, slipping 0.5% against the dollar, which bought MXN12.9530.

Among Asian currencies, the Indian rupee bounced back on Wednesday to trade below INR60 to the dollar for the first time since the release of strong U.S. payrolls data last week. The dollar recently traded at INR59.84, according to CQG data. The partial recovery came after the Reserve Bank of India took measures Tuesday to reduce volatility in the foreign exchange market and halt the rupee's relentless losses. The central bank said Tuesday it had barred banks and currency dealers from using their proprietary funds to trade in currency futures and options, though they can trade on behalf of their clients.

Meanwhile, China's weaker export data had little impact on other Asian currencies, as weaker growth in the Asian giant was mostly priced in.

Still, Indonesia, which has commodity trade ties to China, saw a weakening of its currency. The dollar was at IDR9965 against the rupiah, compared with IDR9959.0 the previous session, according to CQG data.

Indonesia also was in the market with an international bond issue. The sovereign bond had an initial guidance of 5.45% yield on the $500 million deal that could potentially increase, based on demand. The deal, rated BB+, is expected to price later Wednesday.

While investors may be willing to buy, the price they demand for the debt will be the highest Indonesia has paid since 2010, when it sold its 10-year bond at a 6% yield.

--Victoria McGrane contributed to this article.
