title: DJ Turkey Examines Lira Trades
text:
(FROM THE WALL STREET JOURNAL 7/11/13) 
   By Emre Peker and Kerim Karakaya 

ISTANBUL -- Turkey started an investigation of foreign-currency transactions, building on a probe of stock trading, as the central bank broadened a fight to shore up the lira, moves analysts say threaten to undermine confidence in the country.

The Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency has asked Turkey's major banks for detailed information on clients who sold the lira on Monday and Tuesday, as well as the sums of money and profit margins involved in the currency trades, three bankers said. The BRSA said in a statement that the probe is "routine." The central bank declined to comment.

The probes come as Turkey's central bank is selling record amounts of dollars in daily auctions to counter a slide that has weakened the lira by about 9% in the past two months, a move that makes it one of the worst-performing emerging-market currencies. Analysts say both the intervention and the investigations threaten investors' confidence in Turkey's ability to weather a global selloff in developing economices.

The effort to stabilize markets follows antigovernment protests that roiled Turkey in June, just as international investors were pulling out of emerging markets because of concern that the U.S. Federal Reserve will end policies that had encouraged investment there.

"Turkey is always a higher risk country than other emerging markets when we talk about portfolio outflows and in a sudden stop, Turkey is always the most vulnerable one," said Valentina Chen, who helps manage $4.5 billion of emerging-market debt and currencies at Aviva Investors in London. "With these investigations, I think they're making the situation worse. Turkey is an accident waiting to happen."

Since June 11, when the central bank began auctioning dollars for lira, Turkey has used about 12% of its net foreign-currency reserves. Economist estimate the total has fallen to just above $40 billion. Erdem Basci, governor of the Turkish central bank, has declined to raise interest rates, a tactic countries often use when their currencies are plunging.

The country's Achilles' heel is its chronic current-account deficit, which climbed to $51.3 billion -- 6.5% of Turkey's $786 billion gross domestic product -- in April, a total that exceeds the central bank's net reserves of foreign currency. In 2011, when the deficit grew to 10% of GDP, the currency dropped 20% against the dollar and helped push inflation to double-digit percentages.

On Monday, the lira sank to an all-time low of 1.9736 against the dollar, prompting the central bank to sell the greenback, slightly tightening monetary policy by reducing the amount of the local currency in the market. The central bank sold a record $2.25 billion in seven auctions on Monday, and followed up with another $1.3 billion on Wednesday, but the lira barely budged. It was at 1.9609 to the dollar in late afternoon trading.

"The central bank's firepower. . .is extremely low by emerging-market standards," said Neil Shearing, chief emerging-markets economist with Capital Economics. "In the end, we suspect the market pressure will win out, particularly given the small size of Turkey's foreign-exchange reserves."

The government, which has been quick to blame speculators for the rout, seemed to acknowledge this week that broader factors are behind the selloff.

"If the Turkish lira weakness is sustained, it would tend to get inflationary pressure up," Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek said Wednesday at a European Policy Centre event in Brussels. "The fallout so far is very limited, but how we move from here is important. The faster Federal Reserve policy normalization is actually. . .problematic for all emerging markets."

Mr. Simsek said in a message from his official Twitter account that the protests and the prospect that the Fed will scale back its easing efforts were the two causes behind rising borrowing costs in Turkey.

Still, despite the recognition that broader factors are at play, the government continues to investigate traders' actions.

Two weeks ago, the Capital Markets Board, Turkey's securities regulator, launched an investigation into a selloff in stocks in June that caused Turkey's main share index to plummet 24% from a record high on May 22.

Meanwhile, Turkey's two-year borrowing costs have been climbing steadily from an all-time low of 4.79% on May 17, when Moody's Investors Service gave the country a second investment-grade credit rating. Fitch Ratings raised Turkey to investment grade in November.

Yields on benchmark two-year debt rose to 9.25% on Wednesday, the highest level in more than a year.

Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan has blamed what he calls the "interest-rate lobby" for the protests, saying the unrest is intended to allow investors to profit from Turkey's instability. He has repeatedly warned investors who have sold Turkish assets that the authorities will punish them.

title: CURRENCIES : Dollar Extends Rally As Fed Talks Slower Stimulus
text:
By William L. Watts and Sara Sjolin, MarketWatch

The U.S. dollar trimmed an earlier surge but remained higher versus most major currencies Thursday, building on gains triggered a day earlier after Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke said the bank could begin to slow its stimulus-providing program of bond purchases by the end of the year.

Emerging-market currencies tumbled sharply, with the dollar surging to an all-time high versus the Turkish lira, as a stampede out of emerging-market assets continued after the Fed remarks. The dollar's overall rise was aided by a weaker-than-expected Chinese purchasing managers' index.

"The bottom line for the dollar is that heightened tapering risks reinforce the 'stronger U.S. dollar' theme that we expect to gain traction into 2014 as U.S. cyclical leadership becomes more evident and U.S. [Treasury] yields rise for the 'right' reasons," said Syed Mansoor Mohi-uddin, strategist at UBS. "Expect broad-based dollar gains in the G-10 space."

The ICE dollar index (DXY), which tracks the greenback's performance against six rivals, rose to 81.823 from 81.301 late Wednesday in North America, and traded as high as 82.140.

The dollar extended gains after data showed May existing-home sales rose to their strongest pace since Movember 2009 and the Philadelphia Fed index also beat expectations.

The dollar (USDJPY) changed hands at 97.38 yen, up from Yen96.36 in North American trade late Wednesday, when it surged versus the Japanese currency. The dollar traded as high as Yen98.28 in earlier action Thursday. Meanwhile, the euro (EURUSD) fell to $1.3221, down from $1.3294.

The British pound (GBPUSD) managed to shake off early weakness to rise to $1.5492, up slightly from $1.5482.

Meanwhile, the dollar traded as high as 1.9503 Turkish lira (USDTRY), setting an all-time high, and remained up 1.5% in recent action at 1.9346 lira. The move came even as Turkey's central bank added to intervention efforts aimed at propping up its currency, selling $350 million into the market, according to Dow Jones Newswires.

Most of Thursday's across-the-board weakness versus the dollar "can be attributed to the spike in global bond yields, which boosted the cost of borrowing around the world. This accelerated deleveraging in the forex market with dollar strength only adding to the pain," said Kathy Lien, managing director of FX strategy for BK Asset Management.

The WSJ Dollar Index , which uses a slightly wider comparison basket, rose to 73.86 from Wednesday's close at 73.39.

Included in the WSJ Dollar Index is the Australian dollar, which was hit hard after the Federal Reserve said if the U.S. economy improves in line with its forecasts, then it will have scope to reduce the pace of monthly bond purchases. The purchases, directed at stimulating growth, are currently set at $85 billion a month.

The Aussie (AUDUSD) changed hands at 92 U.S. cents in recent action after trading as low as 91.63 cents versus 93.01 late Wednesday. The Aussie hadn't traded below 93 cents since September 2010, according to FactSet data.

"[A]nyone wanting to know where the AUD/USD is headed needs to firmly have a view on the U.S. fixed-income market," IG chief market strategist Chris Weston wrote to clients Thursday.

If the yield on the U.S. 10-year note (10_YEAR) is headed for 3% "over time then the [currency] pair will head firmly below [90 U.S. cents], despite every hedge fund and leveraged player being max short already," said Weston.

A currency with a higher yield tends to appreciate faster than its rivals. Treasury yields soared as prices fell Thursday, pushing the yield on the 10-year note to 2.42%, the highest yield in 2013.

While the dollar had pulled back recently on uncertainty about the Fed's plans for bond buying, analysts have said the quantitative-easing purchases overall have weighed on the dollar's value.

The Fed said it may end asset purchases around mid-2014, depending on economic data.

"The move by the Fed yesterday might in fact be the beginning of the first dollar uptrend in years not driven by financial market stress," analysts at Danske Bank said in a note.

title: DJ  FX  HORIZONS: This Ain't No Emerging Market Crisis
text:
By Michael J. Casey

Don't confuse the recent rout in developing countries' currencies with an "emerging market crisis."

In a period of slowing global growth in which the Federal Reserve is seen reining in its monetary stimulus, most developing world governments are more than happy to see their currencies weaken. In fact, it's part of a natural and necessary rebalancing in the world.

As U.S. bond yields rise and American growth prospects appear to outshine those of other places, money is being reallocated back to dollar assets. Meanwhile, with the Japanese yen still down 20% from its lows of September, emerging market producers are worried about lost competitiveness for their exporters. It's why many central banks are holding off on intervention and letting their currencies fall. Softer exchange rates are just what the doctor ordered.

That is, unless you belong to a group I'll call the TIBS.

With apologies to Jim O'Neill of BRICS coinage fame and to whomever came up with that jarring PIGS acronym, TIBS stands for Turkey, India, Brazil and South Africa. The currencies of these countries have borne the brunt of the emerging market selloff this month. That's because domestic political and economic problems make them more vulnerable to outflows of money--to the point that the currency sell-off risks igniting national crises. The TIBS are the exceptions that prove the rule.

Turkey, India and Brazil have all aggressively intervened in foreign exchange markets to bolster their flagging currencies. They simply can't afford to take the sanguine view of depreciation that, say, Chile or Malaysia are taking.

In Brazil's case, it's an inflation problem. Brazil's failure to tackle rigidities in its labor market has left its inflation rate at the very top of its central bank's acceptable range, which is why it hiked rates by an unexpectedly large half-percentage point two weeks ago even as economic growth was showing signs of grinding to a halt. The last thing the central bank needs is a plunging Brazilian real, which would generate inflation via higher import prices.

Turkey and India, the other prominent interveners, have successfully beaten back the inflation bogey that nagged them two years ago, but the legacy of that fight and the problem of large current-account deficits mean investors continue to fear a loss of market confidence in the Indian rupee or Turkish lira. (Complicating matters for Turkey is the political uncertainty sown by the violent protests against Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan.)

The TIBS member that's really in trouble, however, is South Africa. As with Brazil, South African inflation is stubbornly high -- just a hair below 6%, the top of the central bank's target range. But unlike the other three countries, it doesn't have a deep pool of dollars with which to prop up the South African rand. Following a 4.3% plunge last month, the country's foreign exchange reserves stood at a modest $48 billion at the end of May. It means that South Africa's authorities can only pray that the rout in the rand doesn't go so far as to fuel imported inflation. That would simply add to the country's long list of problems, which include industrial strife in its all-important mining sector and international declines in prices of the minerals its sells.

Yet one of the principal causes of South Africa's pain--a slowdown in China--provides a kind of mixed blessing to other emerging markets. Few are happy about weaker Chinese demand, of course, but at least it means they don't have to worry about inflation. Over the weekend, China reported that producer prices were down 2.9% on the year. For a country that manufactures so much of what we all buy, that's a powerful disinflationary force to unleash on the world. It means that for almost all countries outside the TIBS group, emerging market currencies will be free to keep falling if they have to.

title: DJ 2nd UPDATE: Turkish Police Move to Clear Istanbul Square
text:
ISTANBUL--Turkey's prime minister defended a police push to clear protesters from a central square in Istanbul on Tuesday that had sparked clashes in the heart of the city, following more than two weeks of nationwide demonstrations.

Security forces moved into Taksim Square, the Istanbul epicenter of protests, around 7:30 a.m. on Tuesday, firing tear gas and water cannons, while protesters threw rocks and Molotov cocktails. Battalions of police, which had ceded control of Taksim the day after nationwide protests flared on May 31, were positioned around the square's perimeter by 8 a.m.

As clashes began to break out and scenes from the square broadcast live on television, Turkey's currency sank to fresh 2011 lows, prompting the central bank to swiftly intervene to stabilize the lira.

Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan offered a robust defense of the police incursion, reiterating that the protests were illegal and being spurred on by radical groups and shadowy foreign elements.

"This is an illegal uprising but some are trying to mask it," Mr. Erdogan said in Ankara. Delegates at the party headquarters chanted "Turkey is proud of you," in a stronger sign of the polarization between party supporters and the demonstrators around Taksim.

"These protests were used on purpose and on a systematic basis. There is a huge game they want to play on Turkey," the prime minister said, telling his party base that democracy was thriving in the country in a way unimaginable a decade ago, when his party swept to power.

Mr. Erdogan spoke shortly after Istanbul Governor Huseyin Avni Mutlu convened a news conference to draw a distinction between violent protesters at Taksim who the government says are damaging the country's image, and peaceful demonstrators at the adjacent Gezi Park, a patch of grassland that activists are trying to save from a government rebuilding project. Protests there spawned wider demonstrations.

The comments, coupled with the police action, could be aimed at isolating the more radical protesters, analysts said.

"The police intervened to dismantle barricades," Mr. Mutlu, the governor, said. "Some individuals have clashed with the police...We are trying to normalize the scene in Taksim. We are not going to intervene in Gezi Park."

Turkey's demonstrations, the broadest challenge to Prime Minister Erdogan's party in 10 years, have brought to light a vibrant contingent of secular and middle-class Turks who are chafing at what they see as an increasingly heavy hand in the prime minister's rule.

They have also underscored the strong support Mr. Erdogan enjoys in a vast stretch of the country, largely among nationalists, the religiously pious, and a section of the business class that has profited from his rule.

Turkish officials on Tuesday emphasized the damage to the country's unity, image, and financial stability that they say the protests at Taksim have caused. Governor Mutlu said authorities "will not allow a siege" around a statue at the square of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, founder of Turkey's republic, and a nearby cultural center, vowing not to allow protest material back around the statue.

"The Ataturk statue and cultural center have become like an advertisement board. It's very bad for the image of Turkey and Istanbul," the governor said, adding that the authorities are committed "to be very careful and sensitive in handling the situation."

Intervening to stabilize the currency, Turkey's central bank sold $50 million at an intraday auction after the lira had plummeted in the morning. The move came shortly after the bank said in a statement it would hold intraday forex selling auctions, which it hasn't done since January 2012, to raise the value of the lira against the dollar.

By early afternoon in Taksim, police forces withdrew from the square's center and clashes calmed down. Demonstrators gathered on the steps of Gezi Park chanting anti-government slogans. Inside the park, protesters who had camped overnight grew agitated, and fearful of the escalation in violence.

Some began to question whether demonstrators were egging on the police force with violence. Others in the park chanted, in unison, to the police: "Go ahead and gas us."

"The authorities are trying to turn us into the guilty party as we currently stand on the right side of history," said a 40-year-old tourist guide, who said he rushed to the area after seeing broadcasts of security forces amassing to move into the square earlier in the day.

"They know there will be resistance in the park, they know there will be people who throw stones at the police. If they thought people wouldn't respond, they wouldn't send thousands of cops to clear the square. How could people keep calm in the park? It's being gassed," he said.

Istanbul Governor Mutlu reiterated that the aim of the police incursion Tuesday was to remove banners from around the area. He also said the government was open to dialogue not just with the country's youth, but with other political parties as well, "for the sake of our nation and for peace."

"Do you think Gezi Park hasn't been provoked?" he asked, praising those sitting in at the park for not yielding to provocation by the "marginal groups' to join violence.

"Again, I want to publicly state that we are thankful for their sensibility," he said, adding he was optimistic the scene would settle.

Earlier Tuesday, police moved to clear barricades and disperse crowds on Siraselviler Avenue leading up to Taksim Square. Security forces fired tear gas at protesters as they fled the area, with one vehicle catching fire in the process.

An armored police vehicle mounted with a water cannon, which had also been used to spray demonstrators with pepper gas, tore down an unmanned, makeshift protester barricade at the entry of Siraselviler and doused the burning vehicle with water.

The police action came a day after Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan made his first conciliatory gesture toward the protests that are entering a third week over concerns that new government policies will restrict lifestyles.

Mr. Erdogan defied protesters with back-to-back rallies drawing tens of thousands of his supporters in three cities over the weekend. He continued to say the protests were being hijacked by extremists, while also conceding that the he is open to hear the democratic demand of environmentalist groups. The prime minister and his deputies have said that they won't allow illegal demonstrations to continue.

"We have been waiting for this to happen," said protester Ugur Hacan, a 24-year-old artistic director for TV series and movies, who was sleeping at the park with friends when police entered the square.

"As long as the police don't interfere with Gezi Park, the protests will continue. I believe more people might come after this action," Mr. Hacan said. He and three other friends at the park said police didn't confront the protesters directly.

Taksim Square subway was still functioning Tuesday, and some commuters emerging from the metro were caught in the melee.

"We need to talk rather than fight each other. I hope this can be resolved quickly," said Can Ozdemir, a hotel waiter, as his eyes streamed from the tear gas.

Speaking after a weekly cabinet meeting in Ankara Monday, Deputy Prime Minister Bulent Arinc said Mr. Erdogan would meet some demonstration representatives Wednesday and others at another time, without providing additional details.

--Yeliz Candemir and Gokce Sanlialp contributed to this article.

title: WSJ Blog:Turkey Protests: What to Expect From the Markets?
text:
(This story has been posted on The Wall Street Journal Online's MoneyBeat blog at http://blogs.wsj.com/moneybeat/)

By Yeliz Candemir and Joe Parkinson

ISTANBUL-- After a weekend of protests that have shaken Turkey, pollsters and analysts are trying to decipher what the demonstrations mean for the country's political future.

But what about Turkey's economy, which even before the protest movement began on Tuesday, was reeling from one of its worst weeks in the past two years?

Turkish assets have plunged in recent days in line with an emerging markets selloff driven by investor concerns of an early end to the U.S. Federal's bond-buying program.Turkish bond prices have risen dramatically signalling declining investor confidence, while stocks are under pressure. Market jitters sent the lira on Friday to its lowest level in one-and-a-half years, prompting central bank Governor Erdem Basci to verbally intervene to shore up the currency.

Turkey's economy has won plaudits in recent years and was recently awarded its second investment-grade credit rating by Moody's. But it also remains acutely vulnerable to a decline in foreign investor confidence as it carries a large current account deficit equivalent to 6% of GDP.

Middle East Real Time interviewed four analysts to see what they thought the nationwide anti-government protests would mean for Turkish assets when the market opens on Monday. Economists were unified that the lira would be under pressure, but divided on how seriously the market would take the weekend's demonstrations given that Turkey's Prime Minister retains broad support across large parts of the country.

Tim Ash, head of emerging market research at Standard Bank PLC in London: "I think most investors know Turkey quite well and understand that Erdogan and the AKP are still the dominant political force in the country...I actually think that given the demonstrations over the weekend, the central bank and the Turkish authorities will be more interventionist and eager that the currency does not move much weaker, as they will be fearful that markets could becomevicious."

Tufan Comert, a strategist with Istanbul-based brokerage Garanti Securities: "We may see some further sell off in Turkish assets. Bourse Istanbul 100 Index may start trading Monday with a sharp drop. However, after the first reactions, the protests wouldn't have a dramatic impact on the market as the central bank is likely to tighten liquidity policy further."

Inan Demir, chief economist with Finansinvest: "The prevailing shaky sentiment towards risk assets implies that Turkish lira denominated assets could be subject to the same risk as well. So the continuation of large scale protests could exacerbate the pressure on the currency and TRY denominated assets, particularly if this week's loaded data agenda which includes inflation at home and non-farm payrolls in US sustains the negative sentiment."

Ugur Gurses, an economics columnst at Turkish daily Radikal: "There was a sharp volatility in global markets before the protests. With growing protests we may see significant capital outflows and the central bank may implement tightening policies. Inflation data may remain subdued if capital outflows accelerate."

By Joe Parkinson

ISTANBUL--Turkey's real effective exchange rate rose in March, edging closer to the level at which the central bank has said it would take action to prevent further appreciation of the Turkish lira.

The measure of the lira's strength against several other currencies rose to 119.95 in March from 119.69 in February, though was lower than a revised 120.39 in January, the Ankara-based central bank said in a report on its website Tuesday.

The news come after central bank Governor Erdem Basci Wednesday said the national lender would consider easing monetary policy if the lira's real effective exchange rate rises above the threshold level of 120. After his comments, the lira weakened to 1.8111 against the dollar and the yield on two year bonds traded at 6.35% compared with 6.47% early Wednesday.

At its monetary policy committee meeting March 26, the central bank cut its overnight lending rate by 100 basis points, in a surprise move, while it kept its key policy interest rate and overnight borrowing rates steady.

The bank cut its overnight rate to 7.50% from 8.50%; it left its one-week benchmark interest rate at 5.50% and its overnight borrowing rate at 4.50%.

title: UPDATE: Turkey  Central Bank  Cuts Overnight Borrowing, Lending Rates
text:
ISTANBUL--Turkey's central bank continued to ease monetary policy on Tuesday as Moody's Investors Service suggested Ankara was edging closer to capturing an investment-grade credit rating, bolstering a growing investor confidence that the emerging economy is successfully managing its imbalances.

The bank stopped short of cutting its benchmark rate for a second consecutive month but surprised markets by reducing overnight borrowing and lending rates in a bid to prevent speculative capital inflows.

The central bank cut its overnight borrowing rate to 4.75% from 5%, and its overnight lending rate to 8.75% from 9%, while holding its one-week benchmark interest rate steady at 5.5%, the bank said in a statement on its website.

The moves briefly sent stocks to a record high--extending a rally which has seen the IMKB index rise by 11% since the beginning of this year--and pulled the lira and bonds weaker. Turkish assets have been buoyed by anticipation of more investment-grade credit ratings following the November decision by Fitch Ratings that granted Turkey the first such status since 1994.

The 0.2% decline of the lira after the rate moves reversed earlier gains against the dollar spurred by an announcement from Moody's , which said ratings firm would hold a teleconference on Jan. 28 to discuss, among other things, Turkey "shifting closer to an investment grade sovereign rating".

Economists said the central bank was likely trying to moderately weaken the lira to propel growth without spooking markets with a second consecutive cut to the benchmark rate.

"The central bank's signal via cutting the overnight borrowing rate hints that it will not allow Turkish lira to become an overvalued currency," said Ozgur Altug, chief economist with BGC Partners in Istanbul. "We think that the lira might be slightly under pressure, although the approaching Moody's conference will limit this pressure in the short-term."

The recent rally of the lira, which hit a ten month high against the dollar last week, prompted exporters to call for the central bank to intervene and support the biggest factor in Turkey's economic rebalancing: sales abroad. Companies argued that the lira's strength is beginning to undermine international competitiveness after record exports in 2012 helped Turkey narrow a record current-account deficit to 6.5% of gross domestic product from 10% of GDP in 2011.

Turkish Exporters Association Chairman Mehmet Buyukeksi said at the turn of the year that over appreciation of the lira would negatively affect the economy and exporters' competitive strength.

The call for a less valuable lira comes as the real effective exchange rate--the measure of the lira's strength against several other currencies--fell to 118.3 in December from a revised 119.4 in November.

In November, central bank Governor Erdem Basci said the monetary policy committee would gradually ease policy if the lira's real effective exchange rate continued to rose to a range of 120 to 125. The central bank would take "strong" steps to halt the currency's gains should the measure hit 130, he said, indicating the bank could consider interest rate cuts.

Some economists said by engaging in a limited easing, the central bank was trying to keep its options open, but cautioned that the scope for further cuts was limited, given that a global recovery would spur credit growth, likely levy pressure on Turkey's key economic weakness: a bloated current account deficit.

"The bigger picture, however, is that the central bank has only limited room to reduce market interest rates," said Capital Economics, the UK-based economic consultancy. "If anything, the Central Bank Republic of Turkey would be more inclined to tighten policy to ensure that rising credit and domestic demand don't cause the current account deficit to widen to unsustainable levels."

title: UPDATE 1-Some IMF directors say Turkey should raise rates
text:
(Adds details from IMF review, background on Turkey)

WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - Some directors on the International Monetary Fund's executive board on Tuesday recommended that Turkey return to a positive real interest rate to target inflation.

The board's annual discussion of the Turkish economy came before Turkey's central bank trimmed the highest of its main rates on Tuesday to prop up a slowing economy.

"Many directors saw merit in returning to a positive real policy rate under a conventional inflation-targeting framework, supported by a strengthened communication policy," the IMF said in a statement following the board discussion on Turkey, which happened on Nov. 16.

Many of the IMF's directors also recommended that Turkey should use more sterilized intervention to manage risk from capital inflows, since it has a low level of international reserves. Central banks use sterilized intervention to prevent the currency from appreciating without affecting the money supply.

Turkey's economy, the fastest growing in Europe last year, has slowed this year as domestic demand weakens. With recent rate cuts, the central bank has been trying to boost growth without allowing the lira to strengthen too sharply.

The prospect of a surge for the currency grew last week when rating agency Fitch gave Turkey its first investment grade credit rating in 18 years, pushing the lira to a three-month high. While the ratings upgrade is a positive sign, it also increases the risk of cash from abroad flooding the country in the short term, further widening the current account deficit.

Turkey's current account deficit is its main economic weakness, reaching 10 percent of national output in 2011.

The central bank in the past has also had to act strongly to counter a jump in the lira's value - due in the past to ultra-low interest rates in the developed world - that would cripple both Turkey's exporters and economic growth.

But inflation still remains above target, the IMF board said. In its visit to the country earlier this year, the IMF said Turkey's annual inflation was around 9.2 percent in September, well above the central bank's year-end target of 5 percent.

Earlier this month, the Turkish central bank said it expects inflation to moderate to around 7 percent by the end of this year.

IMF directors welcomed Turkey's plans for a tighter fiscal policy, as proposed in its budget for 2013, and called on it to increase its primary surplus to boost national savings, which could reduce the economy's vulnerability to volatile capital flows.

title: As Fed Readies QE3, Foreign Governments Brace for  Currency  Onslaught
text:
--As with QE2, a weaker dollar is predicted for QE3

--Emerging market central banks might retaliate by weakening their currencies, but that could stoke inflation

--The risk is that this descends into an-out race to the bottom with tit-for-tat currency depreciations

The Federal Reserve's plan to embark on an open-ended round of asset purchases to bolster the U.S. economy has put financial authorities in other countries on high alert.

Looking back to the last time the Fed printed dollars to finance bond buying, which sent the U.S. currency on a year-long decline against most of its counterparts, officials are bracing for an unwanted flood of speculative money into their markets and a possible cycle of tit-for-tat retaliatory measures. The biggest fear is that it triggers a self-reinforcing and self-destructive race to the bottom in which monetary policy and direct interventions are used to prevent other countries from gaining a competitive advantage through weaker exchange rates.

The Bank of Japan provided fodder for such concerns Wednesday. Just six days after the Fed said it would purchase an additional $40 billion in mortgage bonds a month for an indefinite period, Japan's central bank announced it would add another 10 trillion yen ($127 billion) to its asset-buying program and extend it out to the end of 2013. Although the BOJ didn't explicitly cite the yen's strength as a motivating factor, Japan's currency immediately fell to a one-month low versus the dollar. Last Friday, following the Fed's announcement a day earlier, Finance Minister Jun Azumi forcefully complained that the strong yen was hurting the Japanese economy and hinted at direct intervention by vowing to "take decisive steps when it is deemed necessary."

Some emerging market governments have also taken matters into their own hands this past week. Brazil has conducted so-called "reverse dollar swaps" to prevent its currency, the real, from appreciating; Peru adjusted its intervention strategy toward weakening the Peruvian sol; and Turkey cut interest rates by more than expected.

Others have been notably more muted in their response. Officials in South Korea, Thailand, Singapore and the Philippines took a cautiously sanguine view of the uptick in their currencies, though they all asserted a readiness to smooth out market movement if capital inflows become excessive.

The moves from the Fed and BOJ come after the European Central Bank announced its own plan to buy bonds, in its case those of struggling governments in the periphery of the euro zone, in a bid to contain the region's debt crisis. Unlike the Fed and BOJ's actions, which will result in a net addition of fresh currency into global financial markets and are widely described as "quantitative easing," or QE, the ECB will "sterilize" its transactions by selling certificates that mop up the additional euros. Nonetheless, the moves are seen boosting the willingness of investors to take on risky investments generally, which typically results in large-scale transfers of funds out of dollars and into other currencies.

"All of this cash generated by the Federal Reserve is going to be entering foreign shores," said Komal Sri-Kumar, chief global strategist at TCW. "Emerging markets are going to be tempted to cut interest rates...to offset their currencies appreciating too much."

Emerging market currencies are in the crosshairs of speculators during such times because their interest rates tend to be higher than those in the U.S., European countries and Japan, allowing investors to book a profit on the difference between the two. But such countries often depend heavily on exports, which become more expensive when exchange rates rise. The dilemma for their central banks at times when global liquidity is rising is that they also face inflationary pressures from rising commodity prices and inflows into their real estate and other markets. If they were to combat those rising prices with higher rates, it would only further increase the appeal of their currencies.

In the previous round of Fed quantitative easing, which was dubbed "QE2," the dollar weakened significantly. In the 13 months from June 2010, when expectations of more Fed stimulus first began to rise, until the $600 billion bond-buying program wound up the following summer, the Wall Street Journal Dollar Index, a measure of the dollar's value against a basket of major currencies, lost 18% of its value. It dropped 20% against the Brazilian real over the same period and 18% versus the Korean won.

The dollar followed a similar, but slower path leading up to the QE3 announcement last week. The WSJ Dollar Index hit a 22-month high in July and then started to slide gradually before dropping sharply once Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke signaled the central bank's plans at his speech in Jackson Hole, Wyo, on Aug. 31. The index is now nearly 6% off its July high.

The fallout during QE2 in 2010 and 2011 prompted an especially bellicose response from a few foreign officials, with Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega famously declaring that the world had entered a "currency war," an allusion to the highly damaging competitive-depreciation policies that undermined world trade during the Great Depression. This time around, Mr. Mantega has been less bellicose, though he remains critical of Fed policy. Speaking in Paris on Tuesday, he said, "I don't believe that the new monetary easing will resolve many problems for the U.S., but it could cause several problems for emerging market countries."

The Fed declined to comment Wednesday. In the past, Fed officials have defended their actions by saying that efforts to strengthen the U.S. recovery help the global economy. Mr. Bernanke said in 2010 that different monetary policies may be appropriate for different groups of countries, drawing a distinction between advanced economies and countries with emerging markets that may see more inflation pressure. But he also noted that disparities between exchange rate policies had led to global spending imbalances as "those countries that have allowed their exchange rates to be determined primarily by market forces have seen their competitiveness erode relative to countries that have intervened more aggressively."

In general, the latest response from other emerging market governments has been muted. That may be because those countries' currencies are already well down from their 2011 highs, a function in part of the interventionist actions many undertook in the wake of QE2, with Brazil in particular resorting both to dollar purchases and taxes on short-term foreign investment.

Yet this hands-off response could merely embolden foreign investors. Paresh Upadhyaya, director of currencies at Pioneer Investments with $200 billion under management, said his firm has increased bets on the Korean won, Indian rupee, and Turkish lira over the past week, on expectations they'll benefit from monetary easing in the U.S, Japan, U.K. and euro zone. He says he doesn't expect as much of a backlash from emerging markets as there was during QE2.

The stakes may even be higher this time around. A much slower global growth environment and weakening international trade will make export-driven emerging market countries more protective of market share. And unlike the time limits that were placed on previous such programs, the Fed's new QE plan is open-ended, allowing the central bank to effectively print money until the employment picture in the U.S. meaningfully improves.

Meanwhile, other major central banks beyond the Fed, ECB and BOJ have programs in place that tend to steer money away from their currencies. The Swiss National Bank has been regularly entering the market to buy euros and sell francs since September 2011, setting a floor on the pair. And the Bank of England has conducted Fed-style "unsterilized" bond-buying that pumps extra pounds into financial markets.

Faced with such barriers, investors will tend to go for higher-yielding currencies that are allowed to float more freely.

"Within the EM universe there clearly are going to be relative value trades," said Jonathon Griggs, global chief investment officer of the currency group at J.P. Morgan Asset Management. In choosing currencies from "laissez-faire" countries over those that are more interventionist, Mr. Griggs said one interesting trade is the Mexican peso against the Korean won. Other investors cite the Polish zloty, Norwegian krone and Canadian dollar.

The problem for policy makers in such countries, however, is that with so many other currencies off limits, theirs could end up bearing an even bigger burden from exchange rate appreciation.

And if China, the world's biggest goods exporter, gets into the currency devaluation game--either through direct moves to weaken the yuan or through a more aggressive round of monetary easing--the temptation for other countries to retaliate with their own actions could become even more intense.

"Three of the four major central banks have now acted and the last shoe to drop will be China," said James Rickards, partner at JAC Capital and author of the 2011 book "Currency Wars: The Making of the Next Global Crisis."

--Matthew Walter and Kristina Peterson contributed to this article.

title: Turkish c.bank says lira at reasonable levels
text:

title: DJ After Scrambling to Lira Rescue, Turkey May Shift to Growth
text:
-- Turkey's central bank may loosen monetary stance to boost growth

-- Traders betting on central bank rate cut drive down bond yields

-- Turkish central bank must be vigilant on lira to keep credibility

By Emre Peker

ISTANBUL--Barely six months after being forced to intervene to shore up the embattled lira, markets are betting Turkey's central bank may loosen monetary policy to aid the government's economic growth target. That could undermine the credibility Turkey's rate setters worked hard to build as investors questioned their unorthodox policies to combat inflation and restore financial stability.

Traders already expect Governor Erdem Basci to cut borrowing costs for banks and encourage credit growth. That pushed the benchmark two-year bond yield down 12 basis points to 8.16% on Thursday, the lowest since October. Turkey's central bank has been varying interest rates daily between its benchmark rate of 5.75% and market rate of 11.5% since October to tame inflation and stabilize the lira. The funding rate has plummeted to about 8.5% in July from as high as 10.2% last month.

"The market sees more and more chances for the rate to come down," said Viktor Szabo, who helps manage $8 billion in emerging-market debt at Aberdeen Asset Management in London. "Even if the central bank will ease, it will stay behind the curve. The market will price in more cuts than what the central bank will deliver; they would lose much credibility if they try to be ahead of the market and do a huge cut."

In recent months, Turkey's central bank has been buoyed by an economic rebalancing in line with its expectations, driven by rising exports, declining domestic demand and slowing inflation. That, investors say, is increasing the likelihood Turkey will join its global peers by cutting its rate ceiling to boost growth.

The European Central Bank cut benchmark rates Thursday, citing no short-term inflationary risk as the euro zone faces a double-dip recession. Meanwhile, the Bank of England announced another round of stimulus and the Chinese central bank cut its benchmark rate for the second time in less than a month.

Turkey's gross domestic product expanded 3.2% in the first quarter, at about a quarter of the pace in the first three months of 2011, and consumer price inflation slowed to 8.87% in June from a three-and-a-half-year peak of 11.1% in April.

"If I was the bank, I'd wait a bit to see how things work out in the euro zone, but I suspect they might be keen to make an adjustment after those CPI numbers," said Caroline Gorman, who helps manage more than $7 billion in emerging-market assets at GAM Ltd. in London. "It's important that they maintain signals to the market that they are vigilant about lira stability because it plays an important psychological role."

To support Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan's 4% economic growth target for this year, Governor Basci may seek to release his hold on domestic credit growth and boost spending, investors and economists say.

Last year, credit-fueled domestic spending saw Turkey's ballooning current-account deficit hit a record $78.6 billion--more than 10% of gross domestic product--in October. Investors doubting Turkey's ability to finance the gap bet against the lira, driving it down 18% against the dollar in 2011. The lira's decline, the worst of any emerging-market currency in the world, caused inflation to spike and prompted the central bank to intervene, spending precious reserves to buy liras and squeezing lenders to curb consumer spending.

"We expect domestic demand to recover from second quarter onwards," said Nilufer Sezgin, chief economist at Ekspres Invest, the Istanbul-based brokerage owned by Dexia SA's Denizbank.

Domestic private consumption didn't grow in real terms in the first three months of the year, BGC Partners Chief Economist Ozgur Altug wrote July 2, when the GDP figures for the first quarter were unveiled. Private-sector investment demand will be a main driver of economic growth in the second half of the year, said Sengul Dagdeviren, ING Groep NV's Istanbul-based economist.

"The overall tone with slower global growth and emerging-markets growth, and lower inflationary pressures all point to the possibility of keeping pretty loose monetary policies everywhere," Aberdeen's Mr. Szabo said in an interview. "And then, the search for yield starts, and Turkey stands out as one of the highest yields."

title: WSJE(5/9) Turkey Report: Turkey Has Posted Record Growth, But Is It Really Doing What It Says On The Tin?
text:
(From THE WALL STREET JOURNAL EUROPE) 
   By Joe Parkinson 

ISTANBUL -- In a lofty gallery in Istanbul's bustling Beyoglu district earlier this month, Kerimcan Guleryuz was putting the final touches to his latest exhibition and forecasting another record year. Promoting local artists whose works now sell at up to 10 times the value of two years ago, Mr. Guleryuz has seen demand for Turkish art explode while many other markets have been choked by financial crisis.

"I've worked in art markets around the world for two decades and I've never seen an expansion like this . . . and it feels like we are just at the beginning," Mr. Guleryuz said as he toured the gallery's exhibition spaces and 100-seater auditorium. "The art market is booming but no-one really expected it to happen this way . . . many people think it's too good to be true."

Ignored for decades but now underpinned by a domestic consumer boom and a wave of foreign capital, Turkey's booming art sector is just one pocket of an economy that has rebounded spectacularly from the financial crisis; an apt metaphor for a country emboldened by its economic performance but simultaneously concerned that its expansion may be unbalanced and unsustainable.

Turkey grew 8.5% last year, posting the fastest growth of any major world economy except China. That followed an expansion of 9% in 2010, powered by a consumer boom and an industrial sector firing on all cylinders. The auto industry has emerged as an alternative auto production hub to established production bases in Eastern Europe and Russia, while free-spending consumers have sucked up easy credit from comfortably capitalized banks, helping to fire growth.

Turkey's government expects growth to slow to a 4% expansion this year, but consumer indicators underscore the nation of 75 million's re-emergence as a regional economic and diplomatic power.

According to a study by the Boston Consulting Group, shopping malls and airline passengers in Turkey have tripled in the past decade. Auto sales rose 120% during the same period, while consumer loans surged to 129 billion Turkish lira ($81.55 billion) from 2 billion lira. The value of private pensions rose more than eightfold in the five years to 2010. Meanwhile, Istanbul -- Turkey's booming metropolis driving the recovery -- has developed into a fashion and tourism hub and recently ranked above four Chinese cities as the world's most dynamic metropolitan center, according to the Brookings Institution.

Turkey's policy makers have been quick to take praise for the expansion of the economy, which stands in stark contrast to neighbors in the European Union and the Middle East, where debt woes and political uprisings have darkened the outlook. Turkey's popular but polarizing prime minister, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, has repeatedly predicted that Turkey will jump six spots to become one of the world's top 10 economies by nominal gross domestic product by 2023, the centenary of the founding of the Turkish Republic.

Many investors have been seduced by an unfamiliar political stability in Turkey. That consistency has been provided by Prime Minister Erdogan's ruling Justice and Development Party, or AKP, sculpted from banned Islamist parties into a Muslim version of European-style Christian Democracy. The AKP has dominated the political landscape since sweeping to power in 2002, securing its third straight landslide election victory last year.

Turkey still has deep political divides. Hundreds of top military officers, including generals and a former chief of staff, are currently on trial charged with plotting against the Islamist-leaning government. Concerns over weak government have been replaced with fears that politics has become dangerously predictable, with the ruling party, and particularly Mr. Erdogan, increasingly autocratic and intolerant of dissent.

But gone, it seems, are the bad old days of the 1990s when squabbling coalition governments sidestepped structural reforms and triple-digit inflation erased savings.

"There's still significant political noise in Turkey which investors take note of, but, from a historical perspective, the political risk now is very low and that's a more important driver of investment decisions," says Simon Quijano-Evans, chief emerging-markets economist at ING in London.

"There are concerns about some aspects of policy but the government has put into place some solid reforms and from a long view it seems like it's an economy of strength," he says.

Underpinning political stability is economic potential; with a youthful population of 75 million and a relatively cheap labor force, Turkey likes to market itself as more of a BRIC than a bubble.

If only it were that simple.

For a growing number of investors, Turkey's boom is looking increasingly unstable. One side-effect of the boom is an inflation rate that has risen sharply to hit 10.4% in March, spurred by a dramatic cut in interest rates and a weak currency. The double-digit figure, though expected to ease in the months ahead, is well above the central bank's target and the inflation rates of most of Turkey's emerging-market peers. The bigger problem, however, is that the country's rapid growth rate is supported almost entirely by demand, sucking in imports and pumping the current-account deficit to 10% of gross domestic product.

The rapid widening of Turkey's current-account deficit is in one sense symptomatic of the country's strong rebound from recession, as the economy is unusually dependent on imports and domestic demand. But the scale of the deficit -- and particularly the speculative or "hot money" assets that are financing it -- has unnerved some investors and Turkish policy makers, while ratings agencies regularly cite the imbalance as a reason for keeping fast-growing and fiscally disciplined Turkey below investment grade.

The issue of funding Turkey's current-account deficit with speculative financing has been magnified by near-zero interest rates in the developed world, which has sent waves of hot money flows seeking higher yields toward emerging markets with higher interest rates, such as Turkey.

Economists and ratings agencies have repeatedly warned that the short-term money funding Turkey's current-account deficit could exit fast if market sentiment turns negative, leaving the economy vulnerable to a hard landing, or hefty correction, that could prompt panic and send asset values tumbling.

Analysis by research institute Tepav shows the ratio of Turkey's current-account deficit to foreign-exchange transactions, a measure of the deficit's unaffordability, is at 37%, well above peaks reached just before Turkey's past four economic crashes.

Market confidence in Turkish assets wobbled at the end of last year as sentiment dived amid fears over the euro zone and its banks. The central bank stepped in to defend the lira, which briefly touched a historic low against the dollar.

But Turkey has limited foreign exchange reserves for this kind of intervention and is restricted in its capacity to fend off any big decline in its currency. Its problem is that economic growth has not been driven by exports, which bring in dollars when goods are sold abroad. Some analysts say Turkey's foreign-exchange reserves would soon have approached critically low levels had it continued to sell dollars to support the lira.

In times of positive market sentiment, the central bank has also moved to keep the currency from appreciating, which offered a lift to exports. But that boost is unlikely to come to the rescue; the European Union remains Turkey's biggest export market, while its fastest growing market was -- until the Arab Spring -- the Middle East. Both are in trouble.

Turkey's central bank has also since 2010 tried to curb hot money and damp inflation while maintaining growth with a new policy framework: tightening monetary policy by varying overnight borrowing rates for commercial banks within a wide corridor of 5.75% to 12.5%, while leaving the main policy rate unchanged.

But for many international economists this so-called interest rate corridor has simply raised more questions about the wisdom of the country's monetary policy, which they fear could drive its fast-growing economy toward a hard landing and even recession later this year.

"Turkish policy is unclear and the recovery is unbalanced; it's obvious where Turkey's vulnerabilities lie. When the two are combined it builds a perception among investors that the economy's success is built on an illusion of stability," says Atilla Yesilada, an analyst at Istanbul-based Global Source Partners, an economic research firm. "We're not sure how vulnerable the edifice is yet," he says, "but I guess we'll find out."

The central bank has defended the economic logic of its decisions, stressing that policy has tightened significantly in recent months and that an unorthodox response was required to curb surging domestic demand and shore up the Turkish lira, which weakened some 20% against the dollar last year.

Still, many economists and bankers believe monetary policy can't fix what ails Turkey. The country produces minimal quantities of oil and gas.

Meanwhile, manufacturers face high costs relative to competitors, economists say, and so tend to use imported semi-finished goods rather than produce their own components. As a result, as Turkey produces more, it imports more -- 85% of Turkish imports are commodities and semi-finished products, fueling the current-account deficit, which unnerves investors.

Despite the imbalances and growing specter of risk, the strength of Turkey's rebound has shifted perceptions that the economy is a perennial underachiever.

9 May 2012 00:30 EDT  WSJE(5/9) Turkey Report: Turkey Has Posted Record -2-

Turkey remains a rare bright spot among European economies; its vast economic potential is obvious. The raw materials are in place: a strategic location between Asia and Europe, a democratic political system and age-old tradition as a trading hub.

But market skepticism about the sustainability of Turkey's growth story is rising, and the stakes are high. The government's electoral success and increased international clout are based largely on growing prosperity, successes that a sudden downturn could damage.

Policy makers must overcome structural imbalances and concerns over monetary policy if Turkey is to convert an impressive growth spurt into a sustainable expansion.

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: Emerging-Market Investors Faced With Fewer 'Carry'  Currencies
text:
--Central bank interventions limit carry-trade options

--Investors continue to seek higher-yielding paper

--Focus turns to Mexican peso and South African rand


 
   By Prabha Natarajan 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Investors remain bullish on emerging-market currencies and now that Greece has concluded its debt restructuring, low volatility in global markets offers an ideal time to initiate trades.

The problem, however, is these investors' options are less plentiful now that central banks in emerging markets have built walls to protect their currencies.

One favorite play, selling the dollar and buying Brazilian real assets, lost its luster recently after a rash of central-bank actions to prevent further appreciation of the Brazilian currency. Central banks in Turkey, Colombia and Peru also have intervened either directly or indirectly to stop their currencies from rising too quickly.

The genesis of this "currency war" is the rapid gains among emerging-market currencies in the first two months of the year. Investors, especially those in developed countries like the U.S. and U.K. with a capacity to borrow cash at ultra-low yields, sought out assets in emerging currencies that also offered the added bonus of currency appreciation. This so-called carry trade resulted in emerging-market currencies gaining 5% to 10% in the first six weeks of the year.

Earlier this year, a broad basket of emerging-market currencies including the real, Turkish lira, Indian rupee, and Indonesian rupiah were viewed as the best carry currencies. The purchases were funded either through the dollar or euro.

Now that central banks in many of these countries are resisting, investors are hesitant to go for the same play. After all, no one wants to bet against the central bank. Rather, they are keen on currencies like the rand and Mexican peso, whose central banks don't intervene on a daily basis in the market. Both also offer higher interest rates on local bonds.

"That story of broad risk-on, risk-off way of looking at currencies is changing," said Guillermo Felices, head of European currency strategy at Barclays Capital. "Investors have to be much more discerning in the way one picks carry. Lazy carry will be penalized."

Central banks' protectionism, of course, isn't expected to end carry trades based on the wide yield differentials. Over the medium to long term, emerging-market currencies are expected to gain against the dollar and other developed-world currencies. And as central banks in the U.S., Europe and Japan keep interest rates low and continue with their quantitative-easing policies, investors will be on the lookout for higher-yielding paper.

"There's a competitive nature to this game," said Stephen Jen, partner at SLJ Macro Partners, an investment company that also manages a hedge fund. "Money will go to places where capital flows are welcome, where policy makers are more tolerant."

For many investors that place is Mexico. The currency has gained 10.2% this year, and its central bank hasn't indicated any shift in policy to curb the appreciation. And Mexico's close trade links with the U.S. make it an automatic beneficiary of a recovery here.

In addition, Thanasis Petronikolos, head of emerging-market currency and debt at Baring Asset Management, sees opportunities in dollar-denominated bonds of Chinese companies and so-called dim sum bonds, which are listed in Hong Kong but denominated in Chinese yuan.

But he doesn't recommend backing out of Brazil or Hungary, especially if investors got in early.

"The fundamental story on the strength of the real is still there," he said. "With high-yielding local bonds, investors should be ready to cope with short-term volatility."

-By Prabha Natarajan, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2468; prabha.natarajan@dowjones.com [ 03-13-12 1633ET ]

--IMF: Currency intervention can be helpful tool against volatility

--IMF paper counters conventional view of FX intervention

--IMF study includes Korea, Turkey, Poland, Brazil, other emerging markets

By Ian Talley

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--Turning decades of conventional wisdom on its head, a new research paper published Wednesday by International Monetary Fund economists builds a case for emerging markets to intervene in their exchange rates.

The IMF research paper advocates central banks in emerging markets smoothing out strong movements in their exchange rates, particularly when caused by external economic shocks that fuel hefty cash flows into or out of their economies.

The paper reflects a broader shift in IMF economic policy thinking that has given credence to some emerging market actions that have come under advanced-country censure, including a new backing of the use of capital controls.

"If two policy instruments are available (the policy interest rate and foreign exchange market intervention), then they should be used in tandem to achieve both price-stability and exchange-rate objectives," the economists wrote.

In the paper, "Two Targets, Two Instruments: Monetary and Exchange Rate Policies in Emerging Market Economies," the economists argue that instead of undermining central bank credibility for inflation targeting--long a conventional view--currency intervention can actually support central bank credibility. Such trust built by central banks makes their policies more effective.

"The idea of using more tools to address economic problems is one that has been gaining traction in the wake of the financial crisis," said Jonathan Ostry, deputy head of the research department and one of the three IMF economists who authored the paper.

"A narrow view in which all will be well as long as central banks deliver stable consumer prices simply doesn't hold water," he said.

The paper studied 14 countries and the currency policies, including Brazil, South Korea, Turkey, Poland, Hungary and Thailand. Many of the countries have come under criticism for their currency intervention.

In fact, the authors say that foreswearing intervention in the face of wild swings in currencies "might actually serve to undercut rather than boost credibility."

title: UPDATE:IMF Paper Advocates Temporary Emerging-Market  FX Intervention
text:
--IMF: Currency intervention can be helpful tool against volatility

--IMF paper counters conventional view of FX intervention

--IMF study includes Korea, Turkey, Poland, Brazil, other emerging markets

(Adds IMF economists' comments, background and details throughout, starting in the third paragraph)

By Ian Talley

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--Turning decades of conventional wisdom on its head, a new research paper published Wednesday by International Monetary Fund economists builds a case for emerging markets to intervene in their currencies.

The IMF research paper advocates central banks in emerging markets smoothing out strong movements in their exchange rates, particularly when caused by external economic shocks that fuel hefty cash flows into or out of their economies.

Far from being reluctant to use exchange rate intervention, "central banks should embrace its use as being fully consistent" with inflation-targeting, the economists said.

The paper reflects a broader shift in IMF economic policy thinking, giving credence to some emerging-market actions that have come under advanced-country censure, including a new backing of the use of capital controls.

"If two policy instruments are available (the policy interest rate and foreign exchange market intervention), then they should be used in tandem to achieve both price-stability and exchange-rate objectives," the economists wrote.

In the paper, "Two Targets, Two Instruments: Monetary and Exchange Rate Policies in Emerging Market Economies," the economists argue that instead of undermining central bank credibility for inflation targeting--long a conventional view--currency intervention can actually support central bank credibility. Such trust built by central banks makes their policies more effective.

"The idea of using more tools to address economic problems is one that has been gaining traction in the wake of the financial crisis," said Jonathan Ostry, deputy head of the research department and one of the three IMF economists who wrote the paper.

"A narrow view in which all will be well as long as central banks deliver stable consumer prices simply doesn't hold water," he said.

The paper studied 14 countries and their currency policies, including Brazil, South Korea, Turkey, Poland, Hungary and Thailand. Many of the countries have come under criticism for their currency intervention.

In fact, the authors say that forswearing intervention in the face of wild swings in currencies "might actually serve to undercut rather than boost credibility."

The authors argued against sustained exchange rate intervention, saying it would prove too costly to an economy. Rather, under permanent market pressures, policy makers should allow the currency to adjust. Unlike Brazil or South Korea, which are largely recognized as floating economies despite some currency intervention, China's yuan has long been seen as persistently undervalued as the central bank buys foreign currency and sells yuan to give it a competitive advantage.

"You should not be intervening to sustain a misaligned exchange rate, you should be intervening to mitigate misalignment," Ostry said.

Emerging markets are particularly exposed to large international capital flows because government balance sheets don't have the depth to offset such investments and their economies aren't as flexible as industrialized countries. Like reeds in the wind, emerging markets have had to weather massive capital movements in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis and euro debt woes.

The Institute of International Finance, an industry group representing more than 400 of the world's largest financial firms, expects capital flows to emerging markets to fall this year by an estimated $164 billion, contributing to a near-30% plummet in cash flows to those regions since 2010. That's likely to mean continuing pressure on their exchange rates. Earlier this month, Brazil's finance minister revived fears of an international currency war.

But the IMF staff said that as long as countries are simply seeking to return their currencies back into equilibrium with underlying economic fundamentals, intervention can play a stabilizing role in regional and global economies. By combining forex intervention with policy-rate decisions, central banks can afford to weaken their rate actions to achieve the same objective. That prevents a competition of too-low interest rates across emerging markets and avoid the resulting competitive interventions, the authors say.

The shift in perspective also highlights the growing say of emerging markets within the fund and the academic fallout from the financial crisis that eroded many long-held economist assumptions. The condoning of currency intervention--on a limited basis--addresses complaints from many developing countries that advanced nations should take into account the international impacts of monetary and economic policy. Brazil, for example, repeatedly cited the U.S. Federal Reserve's easing as helping to drive capital flows damaging to its economy. Brazil has intervened to prevent the real from further harm, drawing criticism from abroad.

title: WSJ UPDATE: China And Turkey Sign Six Business Agreements
text:
ISTANBUL (Dow Jones)--China and Turkey set aside differences on how to quell escalating violence in Syria on Tuesday, as Chinese Vice President Xi Jinping began the final leg of a diplomatic tour by overseeing a series of bilateral business deals, including a central bank swap deal to boost trade in local currencies.

Mr. Xi, widely presumed to be China's next top leader, signed the three-year currency-swap pact between the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey and the People's Bank of China alongside Turkish President Abdullah Gul in Ankara on Tuesday.

The two leaders, who signed five other business agreements, didn't make any public statements before the Chinese vice president headed to Istanbul to meet Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan, but Turkish officials were expected to relay their growing concerns over the gathering violence in neighboring Syria.

(This story and related background material will be available on The Wall Street Journal website, WSJ.com.)

Ankara has repeatedly said the world can't remain silent in the face of an 11-month revolt against Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, which appears to be degenerating into civil war. China, along with Russia, has vetoed two United Nations Security Council resolutions backing Arab League plans seeking an end to the conflict and condemning a crackdown on protests that killed 5,400 in 2011 alone, according to the U.N.

Ankara reacted furiously when Beijing, along with Moscow, vetoed the second resolution earlier this month, proposing a summit on Syria to help coordinate policy outside the Security Council.

As activists reported that Syrian government troops continued to shell restive districts in the opposition stronghold of Homs, killing at least 16 people, official communication from Mr. Xi's diplomatic visit made no mention of Syria or the stalling diplomatic attempts to halt the violence.

China's state news agency Xinhua reported that Mr. Xi and the Turkish president discussed "regional and international affairs of common concerns," though neither side initially offered details.

The conspicuous silence on developments in Syria disappointed Turkish analysts, who had hoped the meeting of two rising powers with expanding interests in the Middle East could offer some clue on whether Beijing would soften its objection to intervention to quell the violence, with growing fears that the revolt against the Assad regime is degenerating into civil war.

China in recent weeks has given little indication it would support Western intervention, despite heightened criticism in Turkey, Europe and the U.S. that it was serving as an obstructionist to restoring peace there. Rather, senior Chinese leaders and state media have delivered unusually direct defenses of China's position.

China has a strict foreign policy of noninterference in other countries' internal affairs, which in recent years it has used to block international intervention on humanitarian grounds alone. Additionally, China fears unrest toward authoritarian regimes in the Arab world could spread to Beijing if aided by the West, analysts say.

"Our position hasn't changed," said Foreign Ministry spokesman Hong Lei at a news briefing Tuesday. He said China was willing to work with the international community to resolve the crisis in Syria, but said China didn't welcome external arms or interference in the conflict.

Mr. Hong confirmed China had received an invitation to a "Friends of Syria" meeting backed by Western powers and the Arab League set for Friday in Tunis, but didn't say whether China would participate. Russia confirmed on Tuesday that it wouldn't participate in the meeting because the Syrian government wouldn't be represented, stoking fears that the group would struggle to gain legitimacy.

Mr. Xi, who will become China's Communist Party chief in a once-a-decade leadership transition that begins late this year, will have to forge a consensus on sensitive foreign-policy issues among powerful political forces in China, including state-owned enterprises and the military.

Many questions remain about his approach to policy, though he is viewed by U.S. officials and other political analysts as a business-friendly politician, perhaps less driven by communist ideology than his predecessors.

Nonetheless, analysts said Mr. Xi wouldn't be able to stray significantly from the prevailing party line on Syria and other Middle East issues, lest he risk upstaging China's current leadership, including President Hu Jintao.

Chinese leaders, including Premier Wen Jiabao, have said China isn't defending the Assad regime. They argue the U.N. Security Council resolution calling for Mr. Assad's resignation ran afoul of the U.N. charter. In addition to vetoing the Security Council's resolution, China last week was one among just 12 U.N. member states to oppose a nonbinding resolution condemning the Syrian government.

Earlier Tuesday, Mr. Xi was confronted with one sensitive domestic issue, as a group of protesters gathered outside his Ankara hotel to demonstrate against Beijing's crackdown against Turkic-speaking Uighurs in China's northwestern Xinjiang province, according to Turkey's state Anadolu Agency. Violence between Muslim Uighurs and Han Chinese, China's dominant ethnic group, left nearly 200 dead in western China in 2009 in the worst riots in the country's far west in more than a decade.

Turkey's Parliament Speaker Cemil Cicek earlier said that Ankara respects China's "sovereignty and territorial unity" in an apparent reference to the issue. [ 02-21-12 1509ET ]

30 Jan 2012 03:01 EDT DJ  Turkey Central Bank Governor Content With Lira's Rise


 
   By Geoffrey T. Smith and Joe Parkinson 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

DAVOS, Switzerland (Dow Jones)--Turkey's Central Bank governor said this weekend that he is happy with the lira's recent surge as it should push down on inflation, but cautioned that prices could remain elevated this year, possibly preventing the bank from loosening policy if sentiment turns negative.

Speaking in an interview with Dow Jones Newswires at the World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, Switzerland, Governor Erdem Basci offered a robust defense of Turkey's controversial monetary policy, stressing that the bank's moves had last year simultaneously pushed the lira lower to help exports, popped a burgeoning consumer lending bubble that threatened to destabilize the economy and improved Turkey's mushrooming current account deficit. That deficit is currently almost 10% of gross domestic product and is considered a key weakness of the economy by investors.

The governor stressed the lira's recent rise, gaining some 5% against the dollar since the beginning of the year, meant that the bank had stopped selling its scarce foreign currency reserves and could begin rebuilding them if global confidence remained optimistic.

"We are content with the appreciation, to speed up disinflation. Just by base effects, inflation is going to fall by 3 percentage points, but for the rest we need time. The earlier the fall in inflation starts, the better," Basci said.

"Price stability will be the main focus of attention this year," the governor added.

Basci's comments come amid a surge in the value of Turkey's currency since the beginning of 2012. Last year, the lira weakened more than any currency in the world versus the dollar. Since January it has posted one of the world's strongest performances, buoyed by rising global sentiment and last week's Federal Reserve move to boost liquidity.

The rising lira should help push down inflation, which hit 10.45% on the year in December, moving into double digits for the first time in three years and feeding fears of a pronounced rise in prices. But pressures keeping prices elevated later this year could hinder the bank from responding to potential shocks from the euro zone or other events that may decrease global risk appetite.

Tighter policy could keep upward pressure on the currency, cutting into the competitiveness of Turkish exporters and making imports more costly; adding upward pressure to the economy's gaping current account deficit.

Despite that prospect, Basci said that he had become "rather more optimistic" about the prospects for solving the crisis in the euro zone after several top policy makers from some of the bloc's new governments assured him of their commitment to fiscal consolidation.

"Now it seems that there is a unanimous voice and determination about fiscal austerity. All the new governments have the same opinion that fiscal contraction would help rather than hurt," the bank chief said, adding that "now everybody talks like a German."

Emerging markets across the world may be enjoying a robust rally, but not all investors share Basci's confidence that Turkey's stellar start to the year is sustainable. Some caution that the recent rebound of the lira and Turkish bonds hasn't been driven by a shift in investor perceptions of Turkey, but by hefty central-bank intervention and a recovery in risk appetite.

The cost of insuring Turkish debt has firmed, underlining investor skepticism that Turkey's imbalances are no longer a risk. Governor Basci's strong intervention in the markets in January was deemed necessary despite the bank tightening its policy through an unconventional widening of its interest-rate corridor, which allows it to constantly shift the cost of borrowing between 5.75% and 12.5%, rather than raising benchmark interest rates, which remain at a record low of 5.75%.

The central bank may have shored up the currency, but concerns over fundamentals, policy priorities and external risks mean that if sentiment turns negative, Turkish assets could be back in the crosshairs.

Meanwhile, the central bank's increasingly complex economic policy has fed investor fears that the economy, which grew at an 8.2% pace in the third quarter, could be headed for a hard landing. Although the governor is more upbeat than many international investors, he concedes that Turkish debt is unlikely to be elevated to investment grade any time soon.

Top Turkish policy makers have long berated ratings firms for what they see as a perceived bias against Turkey, which has posted remarkable economic growth as it rebounded from a steep recession in 2009.

"It's a little bit too early to talk about" an investment-grade rating," the governor said.
