title: WSJ(1/12) Dismay Over Turkish Rates
text:
(From THE WALL STREET JOURNAL) 
   By Joe Parkinson 

ISTANBUL -- Economists expressed dismay Wednesday at a pledge from Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan to strike back at an "interest-rate lobby" that allegedly seeks to stifle Turkish growth.

In comments late Tuesday, Mr. Erdogan also said market interest rates should be lower. High interest rates, he said, cause inflation -- contrary to orthodox economic theory accepted around the globe. "We will make the necessary sharp responses against the interest-rate lobby. We won't let the interest-rate lobby work in comfort," he told reporters in Ankara.

The Turkish leader hasn't outlined who he believes constitutes this lobby. But he is commonly understood to be referring to foreign parties -- including investors, economists and journalists -- who have called for an increase in Turkey's benchmark policy rate in order to tame inflation and cool an overheating economy. Government ministers have suggested the call for higher rates comes from those who want to park their money in Turkey and "suck Turkey's blood."

Mr. Erdogan's intervention comes as economists covering Turkey say they are struggling to understand the country's monetary policy, which they fear could drive its economy, which grew 8.2% in the third quarter of 2011, toward a hard landing and even recession later this year.

The stakes are high. The government's electoral success and increased international clout are based largely on growing prosperity, successes that a sudden downturn could damage. Turkey, which conducts roughly half of its trade with the European Union, has also been a rare bright spot among European economies.

"Markets find these comments a little disturbing. . . . There's absolutely no evidence of a speculative attack on the lira, or some foreign-markets plot against Turkey," said Tim Ash, chief emerging-markets economist at RBS in London. "Worse, it comes as the market is increasingly confused by the central bank's policy strategy; it's either going to win them a Nobel Prize or it's a road to nowhere."

At issue, as the inflation rate has risen above 10% for the first time in three years, is the central bank's reluctance to raise its main policy rate. That benchmark overnight rate controls lending for all institutions, and now stands at 5.75%. Instead, the bank has employed a wider interest-rate corridor -- a rate that it says will vary between 5.75% and 12.5% -- that it can change daily, enabling it to tighten and loosen policy according to market conditions.

Turkish ministers have called for the policy rate to be equal to the rate of inflation -- in effect, for a 0% real interest rate. In May, Mr. Erdogan said Turkey should have real interest rates at zero, prompting some economists to speculate the central bank has been keeping its policy rate artificially low to accommodate that goal.

The central bank didn't respond to calls to comment on Mr. Erdogan's speech.

Confusion over the central bank's intentions have contributed to a rapid fall in the Turkish lira's value. The central bank has attempted to stem that fall by spending scarce foreign reserves in currency-exchange market operations. The bank says it spent some $4.5 billion in the last week of December, bringing its reserves to $78.3 billion.

"However cruelly the interest-rate lobby works, the spending power of citizens of this country who consume declines by the same amount," Mr. Erdogan said. Market interest rates should fall to the 5.75% policy rate, he said.

Lenders such as Garanti Bankasi AS are now charging Turkish borrowers as much as 20% annually for loans, up from a little over 10% a year ago, crimping consumer borrowing.

In a year when the government hopes to adopt a new constitution, likely in a referendum, any shadow over Turkey's economy could pose a direct political threat to the government. Analysts say that could explain Mr. Erdogan's finger-pointing at an alleged interest-rate lobby.

A representative for the prime minister declined to comment.

Markets shrugged off Mr. Erdogan's comments, with Turkish assets rising on news that the economy's bloated current-account deficit in November narrowed for the first time in more than two years.

What Mr. Erdogan says on interest rates shouldn't matter, as Turkey's central bank is legally independent, with a mandate to fight inflation and ensure financial stability. But speculation over the bank's independence has risen since April, when Erdem Basci, a childhood friend of Turkish economic czar and deputy prime minister Ali Babacan, was named bank governor.

text:
-- Turkey's central bank continued its fight to prevent further lira appreciation Wednesday

-- Concerns rising the banks reserves are being depleted too quickly 


 
   By Yeliz Candemir and Clare Connaghan 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

LONDON (Dow Jones)--Turkey's central bank kept up its fight to prevent a precipitous slide in its currency Wednesday but with foreign-currency reserves being quickly depleted doubts are surfacing over how long they can keep up this aggressive assault.

For the fourth straight session, the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey propped up the lira by directly intervening in the foreign-exchange market and selling $100 million at its daily foreign-exchange selling auction.

"While Turkey's central bank measures might support the lira short-term, it is however questionable how long the bank will be able to continue with these levels of foreign-currency sales without depleting its foreign-currency reserves too quickly," said Carolin Hecht, a currency strategist at Commerzbank in Frankfurt.

Prior to Wednesday, the central bank is estimated to have spent around $4.5 billion in just three trading days via direct intervention and FX selling auctions to limit depreciation of the Turkish lira.

"There is a considerable meltdown in forex reserves.... Foreign capital inflows are limited and the central bank needs its forex reserves," said Mehmet Besimoglu, chief economist with Oyak Research.

According to the latest data, the central bank's forex reserves were $82.8 billion in the week to Dec. 23.

The lira sunk to a fresh record low against the dollar last week as investor concerns mounted over the prospect of the fast-growing economy overheating and effects of the intensifying euro crisis. With fears over the impact this could have on inflation, which broke double digits in December, the central bank stepped in Friday and launched a large-scale intervention for only the second time in five years.

The bank has directly intervened in every trading session since Friday, keeping up its strong opposition to lira weakness. In further measures to prop up the lira, the bank has continued to hold its daily foreign-exchange auctions.

"We assume that it will use its ammunition more carefully over the coming days, which is likely to disappoint some market participants," said Hecht.

Signs of this are already emerging given that Wednesday's dollar-selling auction was much lower than Friday's $750 million. In addition, the bank's direct intervention also appears to be on a much smaller scale Wednesday, traders said.

Should this continue, the lira is likely to come under further pressure, according to market participants. In fact this already looks to be the case with the Turkish currency trading down around 1% against the buck Wednesday.

Turkey's central has been under fire for months by some economists, who say the bank has been too sanguine about inflation risks and too reluctant to increase its central policy rate.

Instead, the bank has pursued a less orthodox policy, tightening monetary policy by varying overnight borrowing rates for commercial banks within a wide corridor of 5.75% to 12.5%, while leaving the main policy rate unchanged.

At 1658 GMT, the dollar was trading at TRY1.8834 against the Turkish lira compared with TRY1.8738 late Tuesday in New York.

title: MIDEAST MONEY-Turkey to stay course on monetary policy--but for how long?
text:
* Unorthodox policy has so far supported fast growth

* C.bank suggests ultra-low rates needed given global uncertainty

* But inflation is not responding, weak currency a concern

* Many analysts would prefer simpler, traditional policy mix

* Other countries with unorthodox policies ran into trouble

By Seltem Iyigun and Seda Sezer

ANKARA, Jan 4 (Reuters) - Turkey bade farewell to the old year promising to stay the course with its unorthodox monetary policy, but some analysts expect that before long, it may have to rethink its stance because of economic threats lurking in 2012.

The central bank's policy, which consists of keeping interest rates low, raising required reserve ratios for commercial banks and widening the gap between its borrowing and lending rates, aims to counter a huge current account deficit while balancing the risks associated with the volatile lira currency.

The policy has helped keep Turkish growth robust over the past year while other economies, particularly in Europe, have wilted. But it has left many investors confused over the complex mix, and many are worried about the risk of a "hard landing" -- a sudden, destructive slowdown of growth -- in 2012.

The central bank, which has been criticised by foreign fund managers for what it calls its "flexibility", has been reluctant to raise interest rates because this would hamper growth, even though inflation was above 10 percent at the end of 2011, its highest level in three years.

Meanwhile, the bank has been intervening heavily in the foreign exchange market by selling dollars to prop up the weak lira, which lost more than 20 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar last year.

"Turkey will have to make a choice on whether its priority will be growth or inflation," said Imran Ahmad, emerging markets foreign exchange strategist at RBS.

"In the end policy makers can't have it all. Turkey can't have it both ways. There has to be a trade-off. There is going to be more pressure this year on policy makers to respond."

PERFORMANCE

Turkey, which until a decade ago was viewed by international investors as a financial basket-case, was one of the world's best-peforming economies in 2011, propelled by roaring domestic demand from its growing middle class. While Europe has struggled with anaemic growth and a sovereign debt crisis, Ankara estimates growth was 8 percent last year.

But the economy is widely expected to slow considerably in 2012 -- the International Monetary Fund predicts growth will fall to 2 percent. The Turkish government's medium-term economic plan anticipates growth of 4 percent in 2012.

By reducing the expansion of domestic demand, an economic slowdown could help to solve Turkey's problems. It could help to bring down the current account deficit, which at around 10 percent of gross domestic product is one of the biggest threats to economic stability. It might also cut inflation, which the government wants to limit to 5 percent in 2012.

Policy makers insist Turkey's slowdown and the crisis in the European Union, to which Turkey sends over 40 percent of its exports, will vindicate their approach. But analysts fear the numbers may not add up.

"Even with a reasonable growth rate of 2-3 percent, the current account-to-GDP ratio would only decrease 2-2.5 percent," said Haluk Burumcekci, chief economist at EFG Istanbul.

Many economists would therefore prefer a simpler, more traditional monetary policy mix: higher interest rates to strengthen the currency, which would help to bring down the current account deficit and inflation, combined with lower reserve ratios if necessary to encourage banks to lend.

Other emerging economies tried unorthodox monetary policies last year and got themselves into trouble. Kenya, once a darling of emerging market investors, cut interest rates early in 2011 to spur growth; when inflation surged, it responded by adjusting money market liqidity rather than raising rates. The result was a confidence crisis in Kenya's markets that dragged its currency to record lows.

Turkey has a much stronger and more diversified economy than Kenya, but as the lira's volatility suggests, it risks its own loss of investor confidence.

STAY THE COURSE

Announcing monetary and exchange rate policy for 2012 at a news conference on Dec. 27, central bank governor Erdem Basci said the bank would stick to its current policy in a climate of global uncertainty.

That means the bank will continue to use reserve ratios -- the proportion of their funds which commercial banks must hold back from lending -- and the gap between its borrowing and lending rates as major policy tools, although its main policy interest rate could be adjusted. That rate, the one-week repo, is at a record-low 5.75 percent.

"The central bank tries to be clear about its policies but the framework of its new monetary policy is so complex that the bank can't avoid the uncertainty," said Nilufer Sezgin, chief economist at Ekspres Invest.

Tufan Comert, a strategist from Garanti Securities, said the bank's policies were having a limited impact on inflation because Turkey's inflation had deep structural roots. The country has a large energy import bill, and among emerging economies, it is believed to be one of the most susceptible to having currency weakness pass through into inflation.

"The Bank is going to press ahead with the flexible policy," with even more flexibility," Comert said. "This means markets will carry on trying to see the way ahead. Medium or long-term planning will not be possible for some time. This is not what markets want."

The results, analysts said, is likely to be inflation remaining uncomfortably high. The World Bank's Turkey representative Ulrich Zachau has said Turkey's 5 percent inflation target for 2012 will be hard to reach because of the pass-through effect from the weak currency.

Burumcekci of EFG Istanbul expects inflation to start decreasing significantly only after October. And the lira, despite the central bank's market intervention, looks set to stay under pressure.

"Turkey has been using FX to defend the currency but that policy might not be sustainable," said Ahmad at RBS. "In the context of a weak global growth and deleveraging, the central bank might have to use monetary policy to defend the currency."

(Writing by Ibon Villelabeitia; Editing by Andrew Torchia)

ISTANBUL, Jan 3 (Reuters) - Repeated central bank intervention helped the Turkish lira firm below 1.88 against the dollar on Tuesday, while shares benefitted from a recovery in global risk appetite to gain nearly 3 percent.

The Turkish lira traded at 1.8765 in late trade compared with 1.8900 on Monday afternoon, but it was unable to hold onto its strongest level of 1.8697.

Since last Friday, the central bank has sold between $4-4.5 billion through direct intervention in the currency market and in daily forex auctions to support the ailing lira.

On Tuesday, the bank sold $350 million at auction and traders reckoned it sold a further $400 million in several bouts of intervention. The bank confirmed intervening in the market, without disclosing amounts sold.

The lira weakened nearly 22 percent versus the dollar in 2011, adding to inflationary pressures, and on Dec. 28 hit its weakest ever level of 1.9215 against the greenback.

Against its euro-dollar basket, the lira was quoted at 2.1595 in late trade, compared with 2.1676 late Monday. At its strongest, the lira strengthened to as much as 2.1481 against the basket, coming down from 2.1731 earlier.

"For the moment, neither the forex sales nor the tightening in lira liquidity had significant impact on the currency. The lira basket currency (0.5 dollar-lira + 0.5 euro-lira) declined by 0.5 percent in a day to 2.16 vicinity, but this was also related with the strengthening risk appetite in international markets," said Erkin Isik, a strategist at TEB-BNP Paribas.

Central Bank Governor Erdem Basci said last week the bank may sell foreign currency directly on "exceptional days", without specifying what would make a day exceptional.

During a meeting with economists on Tuesday, the bank said unsterilized forex sales and interventions could be used to complement monetary tightening.

The central bank can decide not to sterilize forex sales by not providing the amount of lira drained from the market through repo auctions, decreasing lira liquidity in the market.

Istanbul's main stock index closed 2.96 percent up at 52,859.07 points, outperforming the MSCI emerging markets index, which was up 2.52 percent.

"The increase is mostly related with recovery of the global risk sentiment. The central bank's interventions and the increase of daily forex selling auctions amounts also supported the index," said Serdar Pazi, fund manager at Ata Invest.

Shares of Turkish lender Yapi Kredi rose 7.04 percent on Tuesday and banking index surged 4.04 percent as the lira's strengthening supported banking shares, analysts said. Foreign investment in Turkish shares is concentrated in the banking sector.

The yield on Turkey's benchmark bond maturing on Dec. 4, 2013 closed at 11.53 percent, up from a previous close of 11.48 percent.

"The increase of funding costs resulted in a sell-off in front-end of the yield curve. So long as the central bank increases the funding yield above 5.75 percent, it's hard to see bond yields declining," said a fixed income trader of a bank.

Turkey's consumer price index rose 0.58 percent month-on-month in December, exceeding a Reuters poll forecast of a 0.3 percent rise, for a year-on-year rise of 10.45 percent, data showed on Tuesday.

title: Emerging-Market  Currencies , Debt Rally On Positive Global Data
text:
--Latin American currencies lead emerging-market currency rally

--Emerging-market debt strengthens

--Hungarian assets underperform on uncertainty about government policies


 
   By Erin McCarthy 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging-market currencies and debt kicked off 2012 stronger, as positive global economic data boosted market optimism.

Some Latin American currencies jumped about 2% against the dollar, while emerging European currencies also bounced back from last week's weaker levels. The Hungarian forint, however, was an outlier, again punished for concerns surrounding recent government policy making.

Emerging-market sovereign debt strengthened across the board, with the premium investors demand to hold such debt shrinking modestly. The spread on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global, or Embig, tightened by eight basis points to 418 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms, its index rose 0.1%.

Venezuela and Argentina's debt outperformed, as they often outpace wider market swings. Argentina's spread shed 24 basis points to 902 basis points over Treasurys, and its index jumped 1.8%. Venezuela's spread narrowed by 25 basis points to 1234 basis points over Treasurys, while its index climbed 0.9%.

Helping prop up riskier assets was a slew of better-than-expected economic data. An official reading of China's purchasing managers' index released over the weekend showed manufacturing activity swung from a contraction to a mild expansion in December, while data showed unemployment in Germany falling more than expected last month. In the U.S., the manufacturing sector expanded in December, according to data released Tuesday, which added to the improved market sentiment.

Analysts warn, however, that the positive start to the year for emerging market currencies may only be temporary.

"It's a bit of a risk-on move but it's definitely not going to last," said Carolin Hecht, emerging markets strategist at Commerzbank, who warns that euro-zone debt crisis concerns will likely return to the forefront.

Still, investors took advantage of the risk rally. The Brazilian real and Mexican peso both soared about 2% against the U.S. currency, tracking gains in U.S. stocks. The real hit a three-week high against the dollar, which traded 2.1% lower at BRL1.8320 late Tuesday, according to CQG. Against the peso, the dollar slid 2% to MXN13.6494 from MXN13.9224 late Monday.

The Turkish lira also bounced against the dollar, but largely in response to central bank intervention. Turkey's central bank waded into the foreign exchange market Tuesday for a third straight day to support the lira, and also sold $350 million at its daily forex auction. Turkey's relentless inflation rate, which hit a three-year high in December, and large current account deficit have pushed investors to punish the currency in recent months. The dollar slid 1.2% against the lira to TRY1.8716, according to CQG.

The Hungarian forint, however, could not latch on to the general risk rally, as investors continue to flee the country's assets on concerns about its government's unpredictable economic policies. The forint fell to a five-week low against the euro Tuesday, while the cost of insuring Hungarian debt against default hit a record high. On the Embig, Hungary's spread widened by a whopping 46 basis points to 651 basis points over Treasurys, while its index dove 3% in price.

The government's defiant passage, despite criticism from the European Union and the International Monetary Fund, of a central bank bill that analysts say undermines the independence of Hungary's central bank, has made foreign investors wary. Earlier in December, the EU and IMF broke off informal talks on a possible aid package for debt-laden Hungary due to the proposed bill. Uncertainty whether the talks will resume has put Hungarian assets under further pressure.

Hungary's government is "continuing their very explosive fiscal policy measures," said Commerzbank's Hecht. "Certainly it will be very difficult for the Hungarian government to get IMF aid now."

-By Erin McCarthy, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2712; erin.mccarthy@dowjones.com; @djfxtrader [ 03-01-12 2044GMT ]

--Hungary's policy missteps lead to massive selloff

--Investors forcing government to accept external help

--Key trigger is if there is no deal with IMF


 
   By Erin McCarthy and Prabha Natarajan 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Hungary stands at the brink of a currency crisis, leaving its government little time or room to reverse policy missteps that have prompted a massive selloff in the forint.

Market participants are consciously pushing the government against a wall by ridding themselves of the currency, which hit an all-time low of HUF321.67 against the euro Wednesday. With the forint falling nearly 1% or more daily, local government bonds yields trading in the double digits, and the government meeting with the International Monetary Fund in a matter of days, Hungary's make-or-break moment may soon be approaching.

"We are on the road to a currency crisis, but we haven't arrived there yet," said Viktor Szabo, portfolio manager at Aberdeen Asset Management. "The markets are forcing the government to accept external help."

The risks intensified talks over a precautionary credit line from the European Union and IMF broken down because of the government's move to strip the central bank of some of its independence. While markets still expect Hungary to wrangle a credit line of at least 15 to 20 billion euros, a definitive failure to achieve that could send the forint into a freefall.

"The key trigger is basically when it becomes fully evident there can't be compromise," said Peter Attard Montalto, emerging markets economist at Nomura.

Aberdeen Asset Management's Szabo believes the evaporating confidence could feed on itself in currency markets.

"If [the forint] starts to lose 1-2% of its FX value daily, that's what I would call a crisis," he said. "A couple of more days like this week is bad for Hungary and the forint."

That critical juncture could come on Jan. 11, when a delegation from Budapest is expected to visit IMF chief Christine Lagarde in Washington. The IMF has said next week's meetings aren't negotiations, and no decision has been made on resuming formal talks.

If nothing pans out from these meetings, it could set off a selloff that could widen risk premiums by as much as 200 basis points on local government bonds and depreciate the forint to HUF340 against the euro, wrote Michal Dybula, an economist at BNP Paribas in Warsaw, in a note to clients. This would push Hungary into a deeper recession with a negative economic growth of 3% for this year, he said.

Another focal point for those betting against the forint: Hungary's shaky balance sheet. Its central bank holds only EUR2.5 billion in cash reserves and yet this year some EUR4.3 billion in foreign debt will mature (most of it owed to the EU and IMF) with a further EUR5.5 billion of local debt also falling due.

Add to this the risk of more sovereign ratings downgrades for Hungary to compound those announced by Standard & Poor's and Moodys Investors Service late last year and the pressure is on for large holders of Hungarian debt--among them the Templeton Global Bond Fund, which held $3.35 billion as of Sept. 30, 2011.

Analysts say the government could potentially fund itself with short-term debt issuance until at least the third quarter, but after a series of failed debt auctions, yields are now above 10% for 10-year debt, a level that's fundamentally unsustainable.

Alternatively, Hungary could raise interest rates to attract capital back into the country and boost the forint--and it is expected to do so the tune of 50 basis points on Jan. 24. But that will only worsen an already deteriorating economic outlook.

Against such risks, both sides in the EU-IMF standoff with Hungary have strong incentives to compromise.

A sharp drop in the forint would hurt Austrian and Italian banks with a strong presence in Hungarian assets, adding to contagion risks in a euro zone that is grappling with its own nail-biting crisis. But it would also be a political blow for the government as it would stoke inflation for Hungarian households and could add to the domestic unrest that is already burgeoning in the country.

Partly because neither side is expected to be suicidal and partly because Hungary, despite everything, is seen with the potential for rapid growth over the long term, some long-only investment funds have held onto their positions in Hungarian debt.

It's "not that we are impressed by government initiatives so far," but rather that "we see longer-term value at these valuations," said Michael Hansen, strategic portfolio manager at Global Evolution A/S, a Denmark hedge fund with $40 million in Hungarian assets.

Nonetheless, both currency and bond markets are signaling anxiety over how much capital flight will be needed before Hungary backtracks on its policy stance to achieve rapprochement with the IMF and EU.

"You actually have to have the crisis" before you get the support from the IMF, said Nomura's Montalto.

-By Erin McCarthy and Prabha Natarajan, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2712; erin.mccarthy@dowjones.com

--Gordon Fairclough, Veronika Gulyas and Jessica Mead contributed to this article. [ 04-01-12 2244GMT ]

title: Emerging Europe  Currencies  Fall; Emerging-Market Debt Down
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging European central banks took advantage of light trading conditions to prop up their currencies Friday, after the region's currencies came under pressure.

Both Turkey and Poland were seen intervening in the foreign exchange market, as their currencies underperformed despite quiet trading. No one, however, came to the rescue of the Hungarian forint, which fell more than 1.5% against the euro on Friday.

Latin American currencies made only modest gains on the last trading day of 2011, while emerging-market sovereign debt weakened slightly.

Analysts say that markets could demonstrate more negative sentiment when trading picks up next week, and emerging-market currencies, especially in Europe, could see more downward pressure. Meanwhile, the euro-zone sovereign debt crisis remains in focus, as France and Germany both have government debt auctions next week. Emerging-market currencies' performances have largely been taking cues from external developments for much of this year.

"The market risk is still the main factor," said Ilan Solot, currency strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman.

Meanwhile, the premium that investors demand to hold emerging-market debt increased slightly Friday. The spread on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global, or Embig, widened by six basis points to 425 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms, its index was flat. Egypt's debt was little changed despite a cut further into junk territory for its credit ratings from Fitch Ratings on Friday.

Among currencies, the Turkish lira soared after Turkey's central bank held a $750 million dollar-selling auction and intervened directly in the foreign exchange market. Investors have favored shorting the lira this year because of Turkey's large current account deficit, the central's bank unique monetary policy mix and concerns about inflation.

The dollar slid 1.3% against the lira to TRY1.8927, according to CQG.

Poland also took steps to rescue its currency from further weakness for a second day in a row, in order to keep its foreign debt at bay and avoid the necessity of introducing painful austerity measures.

The foreign debt, making up for around one-third of Poland's total public debt, is priced based on the zloty's last fixing each year. To strengthen the currency just ahead of that time, the finance ministry's agent, BGK bank, was heavily buying zlotys. The zloty was still down more than 1% against the euro, which traded at PLN4.4685 from PLN4.4072 late Thursday.

The Hungarian forint slid to a five-week low against the euro, after Hungary's parliament passed a controversial central-bank law Friday that the European Central Bank, the European Commission and the International Monetary Fund have criticized for threatening the central bank's independence. The defiance of Hungary's government in pushing the bill forward could derail the country's bid for financial support from the IMF and European Union, analysts say.

"The IMF deal went from being uncertain to very unlikely to happen, at least in the short term," Solot said. On the Embig, Hungary's debt weakened significantly, its spread widening by 22 basis points to 624 basis points over Treasurys. Its index dove 1.2% in price.

In Latin America, the Mexican peso advanced mildly against the dollar in thin trading, while Brazil's real was nearly flat against the U.S. currency on the day. Both currencies posted a depreciation of more than 12% against the dollar this year, according to CQG.

-By Erin McCarthy, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2712; erin.mccarthy@dowjones.com

--Euro falls to lowest level against yen since June 2001, below Y100

--Turkish lira rockets as central bank steps up pressure on currency weakness

--Polish monetary policymaker says rates likely to be on hold in January and February


 
   By Jessica Mead 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

LONDON (Dow Jones)--The euro sank to its lowest level against the Japanese yen since June 2001 in European hours Friday but extremely thin dealing conditions protected the single currency from a broad-based selloff during the last trading session of 2011.

The euro remained under the cosh against other currencies, hovering just above its 2011 lows against the dollar and slipping to its lowest level against the Swiss franc since Nov. 4, but investors were reluctant to add to any negative bets on the currency amid thin volumes.

"While most investors have probably pared back exposure approaching the end of the year, what positions there are appear to be biased to the downside, which may go some ways to explaining why the euro has been unable to extend losses," said Todd Elmer, currency strategist at Citigroup.

The fall in the euro against the yen also weighed on the dollar. It fell as low as Y77.28 against the Japanese currency, extending losses suffered in Asian hours on the back of last-minute settlement orders by Japanese exporters.

Overall, though, the currency markets remained very quiet. Even survey data showing a continued contraction in Chinese manufacturing activity in December failed to have any impact. "It caused a bit of interest, but nothing dramatic," said Steven Saywell, chief currency strategist at BNP Paribas in London

"People are sitting on their hands and waiting until the end of the year," he added.

Still, some excitement came from Turkey, where the central bank intervened to support the wilting lira. The dollar dropped sharply from TRY1.92 to just under TRY1.86 by 1127 GMT as the central bank sold foreign currencies.

Elsewhere, the Polish zloty was weaker against the euro, which traded above PLN4.44, despite zloty-supportive intervention by state-owned bank BGK. Anna Zielinska-Glebocka, a member of Poland's monetary policy council, said Poland's interest rates are likely to remain on hold in January and February as risks to the Polish economy balance each other out. She added that the zloty is currently undervalued but expects it will trail the single currency in 2012.

At 1137 GMT, the euro was trading at $1.2944 against the dollar, compared with $1.2960 late Thursday in New York, according to trading system EBS. The dollar was at Y77.38 against the yen, compared with Y77.62, while the euro was at Y100.18 compared with Y100.70. Fitch's decision to change the outlook on Turkey's BB+ long-term foreign and local currency ratings from positive, citing the challenge of reducing a large current account deficit and above-target inflation, dashed expectations the country could soon gain an investment grade rating. title: Turkey's  Central Bank  Attempts To Fight Financial Markets
text:
ISTANBUL (Dow Jones)--Turkey's central bank stepped back into the ring this week in the latest round of what's turning into quite a dust-up.

In the red corner: heavyweight financial markets that have persisted in selling the lira despite repeated signals from Turkey's policy makers that they will intervene to put a floor under the embattled currency.

In the blue corner: Ankara's plucky central bankers -- a determined bunch not afraid to throw some big punches, as on Tuesday when the bank directly intervened in the market for the first time in five years after a record foreign exchange auction failed to lift the currency.

The battle to bully the historically volatile lira, which has fallen close to 20% against the dollar this year, is nothing new. But it has intensified since August as the market focused on fast-growing Turkey's structural weakness: a soaring current account deficit forecast to top 9% of GDP this year. The central bank since the summer has repeatedly offered bulky dollar auctions to shore up the currency, which was under strong selling pressure as a toxic combination of global economic fears and escalating euro-zone debt worries led investors to fold their bets in emerging markets on a colossal scale.

But there's a problem. Those interventions don't seem to be working, and markets are increasingly nervous the bank has started a fight it doesn't have the firepower to finish.

That's because Turkey is running one of the lowest levels of foreign-exchange reserves relative to short-term debt exposure of any emerging market, giving it limited resources to defend the lira. That, in turn, is boosting market expectations that policy makers will have to begin raising rates aggressively to offset the depletion of reserves.

"The Turkish Central Bank is laying out its stall, showing a willingness to take on the market... [it] is clearly aimed at sending a message to the market that the central bank will have no truck with speculation, and speculators, against the lira," said Timothy Ash, an emerging markets strategist at Royal Bank of Scotland Group PLC in London.

"Markets will definitely continue to test them, and the bank will need to stay on the market for some time," said Simon Quijano-Evans, chief economist for Europe, the Middle East and Africa at ING in London. "That begs the question: How long can they continue?"

Certainly, Turkey's approximately $86 billion reserves set against its ballooning current account deficit appear to leave the economy more exposed than many other emerging market economies.

South Africa, which also faces a marked depreciation of its currency, holds reserves of $43 billion but only runs a current account deficit of 3% of GDP. Resource-rich Brazil has reserves of $351 billion and runs a 2% deficit, while Russia, which also recently intervened to manage the ruble, holds a whopping $510 billion and runs a current account surplus of $100 billion.

Markets will be watching closely for clues whether Turkey's top bankers will try to stare down the traders or move to raise rates, and risk slowing growth, to shore up the lira. [ 10-21-11 1049ET ]

title: DJ UPDATE: Turkey  Central Bank  Holds Key Interest Rate At 5.75%
text:
(Rewrites, adding market reaction, economist comment, further detail throughout.)

By Joe Parkinson

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

ISTANBUL (Dow Jones)--Turkey's central bank Thursday held its key interest rate at a record low as expected, but increased the overnight lending rate and issued a hawkish statement in an effort to shore up the embattled lira.

Policy makers kept the one-week repurchase agreement interest rate unchanged for the second straight month at 5.75%, according to a statement on the bank's website.

That decision was in line with the expectations of seven economists surveyed by Dow Jones Newswires, who unanimously forecast no change.

The bank also held the overnight borrowing rate steady at 5%, but in a surprise move, raised the overnight lending rate to 12.5% from 9%.

The central bank summarized its decisions in a statement Thursday that was markedly more hawkish than those made previously, dropping all mention of any potential policy loosening and stressing that the lira's recent depreciation would spur a significant rise in inflation in the coming period.

The lira initially jumped on the news, but gains were short-lived, with the currency moving back up to where it was trading before the central bank's announcement. At 1114 GMT, the dollar was trading at TRY1.8617 against the Turkish lira, after falling to as low as TRY1.8564 immediately after decision.

Economists said the bank's more hawkish tone showed policy makers were regearing away from a loosening bias to combat intensifying pressure on the lira.

"The tone is clearly much more hawkish and this is the first step towards a key interest rate hike... the removal of the talk about rate cuts and general tone on the inflation outlook is clearly more hawkish," said Simon Quijano-Evans, chief EMEA economist with ING in London.

Turkey's central bank Tuesday intervened directly to support the lira for the first time in five years, amid persistent pressure on the currency which has seen it fall some 20% against the dollar since November.

That move was intended to demonstrate the central bank's determination to halt the lira's depreciation by buying the currency, rather than raising interest rates which would risk curbing Turkey's economic growth, economists said.

Although Thursday's statement has bolstered the central bank's position, some economists still question whether policy makers are doing enough.

Turkey has among the lowest levels of foreign-exchange reserves relative to short-term debt exposure of any emerging market, giving it limited resources to defend its currency. As a result, there is much skepticism among market participants over the central bank's ability to continue supporting the lira.

"The question in terms of today's move by the CBRT is whether it is hawkish enough... the underlying concern is that the CBRT is still too dovish to raise the interest rates that really matter... this is more a signalling story than serious effort to stop a speculative attack," said Tim Ash an economist at RBS.

title: Turkey Maintains Resistance To Lira Weakness
text:
LONDON -- Turkey's central bank kept up its strong resistance to lira weakness Wednesday after announcing for the fourth time this month that it will offer a record $1.35 billion at its daily foreign-exchange selling auction.

The high volume on offer comes a day after Turkey's central bank directly intervened in the foreign exchange market for the first time in more than five years, as part of its latest efforts to stem weakness in the lira.

"At this stage the central bank is clearly concerned and keen to cap any further lira losses," said emerging market strategists at UniCredit in a note to clients.

So far, the measures have guided the lira over 1.5% higher against the dollar from the lows it hit earlier this week.

But with the central bank running down reserves rapidly, concerns are rising it won't be able to keep up the fight, market participants say.

"It would be relatively unrealistic to expect that it had sufficient currency reserves to prevent a depreciation of the lira over an extended period of time," said Thu Lan Nguyen, an emerging market strategist at Commerzbank in Frankfurt.

Unless you have unlimited ammunition, it will be difficult to prevent the lira from further weakness, she said. "All you can do is smooth out losses, you cannot prevent a depreciation," she added.

The lira, like several other emerging market currencies, has come under intense selling pressure in recent weeks as a toxic combination of global economy fears and escalating euro-zone debt worries led investors to fold their bets in emerging markets on a colossal scale.

Until now, the bank had avoided intervening directly on the currency market and had instead been selling dollars at a daily auction to stem the depreciation of the lira.

But continued selling pressure spurred its first intervention since May 2006, something which market participants expect to continue, for the time being at least.

"Turkey's central bank is likely to carry on with sizeable daily auctions and direct interventions for the time being, keeping lower foreign exchange reserve requirement ratios in its pocket for now," said Turker Hamzaoglu of Bank of AmericaMerrill Lynch, adding that in 2006 the bank called an emergency meeting and raised rates 225 basis points in three interventions.

Since November 2010, the lira has fallen 30% against the dollar after the bank began an unorthodox monetary policy that cut the benchmark interest rate to deter speculative inflows while increasing bank reserve ratios to slow a gathering credit boom.

Eyes will be on Turkey's central bank's interest rate decision, which is due Thursday at 1100 GMT. Analysts expect the central bank to keep interest rates and the reserve requirement ratios on lira and foreign currency holdings, unchanged.

title: WSJ:  Turkey Central Bank Intervenes  To Boost Lira; First Time Since 2006
text:
ISTANBUL (Dow Jones)--Turkey's central bank intervened directly to support the lira for the first time in five years Tuesday, taking on skeptical currency markets after an earlier U.S. dollar auction failed to lift the currency.

The move aimed to demonstrate to markets the central bank's determination to halt the lira's fall by buying up currency, rather than raise interest rates, which would risk damping Turkey's rapid economic growth, economists said.

Turkey, however, has among the lowest levels of foreign-exchange reserves relative to short term debt exposure of any emerging market, giving it limited resources to defend the lira. As a result the bank is fighting growing skepticism over its ability to see the policy through.

"Markets will definitely continue to test them and the bank will need to stay on the market for some time. That begs the question: how long can they continue?" said Simon Quijano-Evans, chief economist for Europe, the Middle East and Africa at ING in London.

(This story and related background material will be available on The Wall Street Journal website, WSJ.com.)

Traders reported that the bank began buying liras around 4 p.m. local time, sending the currency almost 1% higher to TRY1.85 to the dollar, after an earlier sale of $750 million at auction failed to have any significant impact. By evening the lira had lost part of that gain, trading just above TRY1.86 to the dollar, though it was still up on the day.

The central bank later confirmed in an emailed statement that it had intervened in the market due to "speculative activity" and "unhealthy price moves." The statement also said the bank might hold another large dollar auction Wednesday, after Tuesday's record offering of $1.35 billion.

The statement didn't name the size of the Tuesday's direct intervention, however, and a bank spokesman also declined to give the size. The last time the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey intervened directly in currency markets was June 26, 2006, when it spent $848 million.

Turkey's lira, like several other emerging-market currencies, has come under intense selling pressure in recent weeks as a toxic combination of global economy fears and escalating euro-zone debt worries led investors to fold their bets in emerging markets.

Turkey's central bank isn't the only one to have sold reserves to stem the tide. The central bank of Russia this month bought 10 billion rubles after the currency tumbled. South Africa's central bank, by contrast, appears to have taken the view that intervention is futile, economists said.

While a weak currency is good for exports, it also makes imports of energy, raw materials and consumer goods more expensive, stoking inflation. Turkey's central bank currently forecasts inflation to hit 7.5% at the end of the year, above its 5.5% target.

What makes Turkey vulnerable, despite an otherwise healthy economy, is the size of its current account deficit, now above 9% of gross domestic product, economists say. The International Monetary Fund has advised the central bank to raise interest rates and stop selling dollars--the opposite of what it is doing--so that it can build up reserves against any sudden withdrawal of external financing for the roughly $70 billion deficit.

The scale of the current account deficit reflects Turkey's rapid recent growth--10.2% in the first half of 2011--and traditionally low savings rate, a structural problem the government says it is aware of and preparing to address.

The bank's lira policy will fail unless good news in Europe or the U.S. reverses the current flow of money from emerging-market currencies, says Atilla Yesilada, an Istanbul-based economist with Global Source Partners. "There is no speculative attack on the Turkish lira in particular. This is like trying to resist a tsunami using sandbags," he said.

Mr. Yesilada estimates that the central bank has at most $10 billion in its war chest that it can use to defend the lira. "If they run through that, then foreign investors would become concerned by the very level of the Turkish reserves and start selling the lira on that," making the problem worse rather than better, he said.

The lira has weakened 30% against the dollar since November 2010.

-By Joe Parkinson and Marc Champion, The Wall Street Journal

-Yeliz Candemir contributed to this article. [ 10-18-11 1331ET ]

title: EMERGING MARKETS-China, euro zone fears snap winning run
text:
* China GDP, French rating warning spark 2 pct emerging-share drop

* Turkish central bank launches forex auction after lira slide

* Hungarian forint falls, debt insurance spikes up on rating fears

By Sebastian Tong

LONDON, Oct 18 (Reuters) - Disappointing Chinese third-quarter GDP growth and a warning on France's credit rating sent emerging markets reeling on Tuesday while Turkey's central bank launched a foreign-exchange auction to steady the lira from a record low to the euro/dollar basket.

The darkened outlook for the global economy knocked Russian stocks and its currency lower while Hungary's risk premiums rose and its forint slid on fears of an imminent ratings cut.

Emerging shares dropped 2.2 percent by 1130 GMT, more than double the one-percent loss on developed markets

and snapping a nine-session rally that saw the benchmark leap over 14 percent to Monday's four-week highs.

Optimism for a speedy resolution to the euro zone debt crisis all but evaporated after Moody's warned it may slap a negative outlook on France's Aaa credit rating in the next three months should bailout costs stretch its budget excessively.

"The market had clearly been a little too optimistic about a solution to the euro zone debt crisis. This is a complicated problem and with so many voices, the solution will take time and be painful," said Gaelle Blanchard, emerging markets strategist at Societe Generale.

"Even if the Europeans manage to come up with a unanimous plan with strong measures, how will credit agencies react to the further burden on their government budgets? We could have a negative impact on that front even if we have good news on debt resolution."

Data showing China's economic expansion slowing to its weakest pace since early 2009 in the third quarter further renewed fears of a global slowdown that were alleviated last week after retail, manufacturing and employment readings showed signs of improvement in the U.S. economy.

Adding to the gloom, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development cut its forecast for 2012 GDP growth in its 29 countries of operations which includes Central and Eastern Europe as well as Central Asia.

Steep share losses in the Asian session, which saw Hong Kong's Hang Seng plummet over 4 percent and the Shanghai's key stock index drop more than 2 percent, moderated slightly by the European trade.

The Thomson Reuters Emerging European stock index

eased 0.3 percent lower though Polish and Hungarian shares were 1 percent lower.

Weaker oil prices kept Russia's dollar RTS Index down for its second day while the rouble-denominated share index

waned from Monday's three-week highs.

TURKEY ACTS, HUNGARIAN WORRIES

The threat of weaker Chinese demand for commodities also weighed on the rouble, which fell nearly 1 percent against its euro/dollar basket and slipped from Monday's four-week high versus the greenback .

Emerging currencies were otherwise mixed with the Polish zloty stabilising after weakening three straight sessions against the euro and Romania's leu at a two-week low versus the common currency.

Israel's shekel drooped half a percentage point after touching a six-week high against the dollar on Monday.

Hungary's forint slid for its fourth straight session

while the cost of insuring the country's sovereign debt for five years rose some 10 basis points higher from the previous close.

Officials from credit rating agencies Standard & Poor's and Moody's are due in Budapest this month in meetings that BoA-Merrill Lynch has warned could lead to the loss of its investment grade status by one agency.

BoA-Merrill Lynch estimates that Hungary's total financing needs in 2012 is at 13.2 billion euros, up from 12.3 billion this year. Foreign investors now hold a significant chunk of local and foreign-currency Hungarian bonds but their exposure will need to increase further as the ability of local players to absorb new paper is limited, the bank said.

"However, this could prove challenging given the potentially lower rating and an unfavourable global backdrop," it warned.

A $1.35 billion forex selling auction helped to steady the lira further after a two-percent fall versus the dollar on Monday.

Earlier, the unit sank to a record low of 2.2261 against its euro/dollar basket on high corporate demand to meet import payments .

JPMorgan is recommending a short dollar/lira trade, with an entry of 1.87 and a target level of 1.79 with stop losses triggered at 1.91.

"In the short-run, the (Turkish central bank) has the determination and capacity to support the lira in periods of risk aversion. Turkey has been amongst the most determined to cap depreciation pressure on the lira, particularly since the start of October, with both verbal and physical intervention intensifying," it said in a note.

On Monday, Turkey defied market volatility to raise $1 billion with a 10-year dollar-denominated bond that attracted demand totalling over $3 billion.

Turkey's share of the JPMorgan EMBI hard-currency bond benchmark traded 6 bps wider over U.S. Treasuries, underperforming the index which was 5 bps wider at 371 bps.

(Reporting by Sebastian Tong; editing by Anna Willard)

title: Emerging-Market  Currencies  Mixed, Debt Steady With Euro-Zone Focus
text:
-Global growth worries, euro-zone crisis continue to dominate riskier assets' performance

-Turkey's central bank intervenes in foreign exchange market

-Emerging-market currencies mixed


   By Erin McCarthy 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging-market currencies were mixed Tuesday after euro-zone officials dismissed reports of an agreement to bolster the euro zone's rescue fund, while debt was little changed.

Emerging-market currencies had been slightly down for most of the session, after Chinese data showing slower-than-expected third quarter growth and ongoing euro-zone sovereign debt crisis worries pressured riskier assets.

Reports that France and Germany had agreed to expand the region's bailout fund to EUR2 trillion triggered a reversal in some of those currencies late in the session. But those gains were limited as various euro-zone sources refuted the report and said no deal on the bailout fund would be reached until Friday.

Still, market watchers warn that euro-zone policymakers must take more decisive action in order to ease investor jitters.

"The near term concern is that without some solution we're looking at a more likelihood of a [Greek] default," said Brian Dolan, chief currency strategist at Forex.com. "If you get one [default] it raises the question of a whole domino effect."

The risk premium on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global, or Embig, tightened by three basis points to 408 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms, its index fell 0.1%.

Euro-zone worries have weighed more heavily on emerging-market currencies, especially in emerging Europe. Turkey's central bank stepped into the foreign exchange market Tuesday to support its falling currency, while other currencies' gains were muted.

The Turkish lira advanced about 0.4% against the dollar, which changed hands at TRY1.8573 late Tuesday, according to CQG. Earlier, Turkey's central bank directly intervened in the foreign exchange market for the first time in more than five years, its latest effort to prop up its embattled currency. It also sold $750 million at its daily forex-selling auction. Investors wary of Turkey's large current account deficit and its exposure to the euro zone continue to sell the lira in times of risk aversion.

Eyes are also on Brazil's central bank, which is widely expected to cut its Selic base interest rate by 50 basis points Wednesday, to 11.5% from 12%. That has pressured the real, but the currency got a last-minute boost from heightened hopes for a euro-zone plan and a late-day rally in U.S. stocks. The dollar fell 0.4% to BRL1.7530 from BRL1.7600 late Monday, according to CQG. On the Embig, Brazil's spread was little changed, just two basis points tighter at 230 basis points over Treasurys.

The Mexican peso led gainers, largely tracking the rise in U.S. equities. The dollar slipped 0.8% to MXN13.3755 against the peso, which often serves as a proxy for risk among investors. Chile's peso, meanwhile, tumbled more than 1% on lower international copper prices and fears of slowing growth in China, a main source for commodity demand. Chile's currency often tracks the red metal's prices, since the Andean nation is the world largest copper producer.

-By Erin McCarthy, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2712; erin.mccarthy@dowjones.com

-Joe Parkinson and Clare Connaghan contributed to this article. [ 18-10-11 2042GMT ]

title: UPDATE 2-Turkish c.bank  intervenes , boosts ailing lira
text:
* C.bank sells more than $1 billion to support lira

* C.bank says "speculative behaviour" behind lira moves

* Lira firms to below 1.85 before slipping back

(Adds analyst comments, background)

By Seltem Iyigun

ISTANBUL, Oct 18 (Reuters) - The Turkish Central Bank sold over $1 billion to support an ailing lira on Tuesday, and said it was stung into action by unhealthy currency moves based on speculation.

The bank began by selling $750 million at its daily forex selling auction, but when that failed to relieve pressure on the lira the bank intervened directly with sales exceeding $600 million, traders said.

The lira firmed to below 1.85 against the dollar after the intervention from 1.8675 beforehand and compared with Monday's interbank closing level of 1.8520.

However it subsequently lost ground back to 1.86, bringing losses this year against the dollar to 17 percent. Intervention continued around 1435 GMT. The yield on the benchmark bond fell to 8.50 from 8.60 percent and the share index ended up 0.5 percent.

The lira has come under considerable selling pressure in recent months, losing almost as much as 20 percent against the U.S. currency, as a result of a flight from risk.

Daily forex-selling auctions have been at the centre of the central bank's response to the depreciation and it has sold more than $5 billion since it started the auctions on Aug 5.

The bank said in a statement it could hold a high-volume forex-selling auction on Wednesday.

"Selling intervention is being carried out in the market due to unhealthy exchange rate price formations, resulting from speculative behaviour linked to a loss of market depth," the central bank said.

INTERVENTION SUSTAINABLE?

Analysts questioned how long the central bank could maintain such intervention.

"I don't know how long the bank could continue this way. If people start questioning the sufficiency of its forex reserves, then the real speculation could start," said Mehmet Besimoglu, chief economist at Oyak Securities.

Turkish central bank gross forex reserves stood at $85.1 billion lira on Oct. 7, down from $93 billion at the end of July.

The intervention has heightened investor interest in Thursday's monetary policy committee meeting amid speculation it could take further measures to support the currency.

"In its monthly meeting, the central bank may consider increasing its borrowing rate in order to implement a tight monetary policy," Besimoglu said.

In a Reuters poll conducted last week, all 14 analysts polled forecast the bank would keep its policy rate at a record low of 5.75 percent. One forecast a reduction of 50 basis points in required reserve ratios (RRR)and another forecast a hike of the overnight borrowing rate.

The Turkish economy, which surged close to 10 percent in the first half, is expected to slow dramatically in the next year and the central bank has said it would loosen monetary policy if the slowdown becomes more pronounced.

At the same time, the lira depreciation has fuelled fears about rising inflation which were ignited by recent public sector price hikes and consumer tax increases.

(Reporting by Seltem Iyigun; Writing by Daren Butler)

MADRID (Dow Jones)--Turkey's central bank was right to intervene in currency markets to help temper speculative attacks against the lira, Turkish Economy Minister Zafer Caglayan said at a conference here Thursday.

"The bank intervened at the right time and speculative attacks were killed off," he said. "The central bank, when is necessary...does its work in an appropriate way."

The bank cut reserve requirements on lira and foreign currency deposits, sold hefty amounts in its daily dollar auctions and allowed banks to use foreign currencies to satisfy more of the reserve requirements for lira deposits.

On Thursday, the central bank didn't hold a foreign exchange auction and declined to explain why. But it sold $70 million at its daily foreign-exchange auction Wednesday, after offering to sell as much as $140 million.

Despite his support for the bank's moves to put a floor under the currency, Caglayan also said he that what he called "devaluation," a weakening of the currency, was important for Turkey and other countries.

However, lira depreciation is stoking investor concerns over the country's inflation, which the government expects to reach around 8% this year.

title: DJ UPDATE: Turkey August Industrial Output Eases More Than Expected
text:
ISTANBUL (Dow Jones)--Turkish industrial production--a leading indicator of economic output--slowed sharply in August, significantly undershooting market expectations and suggesting that momentum is easing in one of the world's fastest-growing economies.

According to data published Monday by the national statistics institute TUIK, industrial output rose 3.8% on the year in August, almost halving the 6.9% expansion record in July. The annual easing, which substantially undershot the 5.0% growth expected by the market, was driven by a 7.1% contraction on the month amid broad-based declines across the production subsectors.

The news had little effect on Turkish assets, initially trimming the lira's early gains against the dollar but failing to erase Turkish stocks' morning advance.

Despite the pronounced easing, economists said the data indicated that Turkey's economy was increasingly likely to navigate a soft landing from a rapid growth rate that many had feared was overheating the economy.

"The soft landing continues," said Ozgur Altug, chief economist at BCG Partners in a research note, adding that "while the data look worse than expected, it is clear that the economy is normalizing after a sharp growth in the first half of 2011."

Turkey outstripped China to post the fastest growth of any group-of-twenty economy in the first half of 2011, confirming its position as Eurasia's rising tiger as rampant consumer demand propelled an expansion of 10.2% versus the first six months of 2010. The pace of domestic demand, underpinned by a rapid expansion of consumer lending, had in recent months spurred fears in the market that Turkey's economy was overheating and could face a painful correction.

But recent indicators have pointed to a pronounced slowdown, underscoring the central bank's prognosis that output would ease significantly in the second half of the year.

Turkey's central bank, which intervened strongly in the market last week to stop an abrupt slide in the lira, worries that a global downturn--particularly in the European Union, Turkey's dominant trade partner--could take Turkey's booming economy down with it.

As the global economic outlook has darkened, Turkey's central bank has turned to foreign-currency auctions to stabilize the lira, rather than raising interest rates, which could damp growth.

title: RPT-ANALYSIS-Turkey defending lira with limited  FX  ammunition
text:
(Repeats without changes to text)

ISTANBUL, Oct 6 (Reuters) - Turkey has upped the ante in defence of the lira, but with hard cash reserves far smaller than those of many developing economy peers, FX intervention may not be feasible for long should investors resume their exodus from emerging markets.

Faced with year-to-date lira losses of almost 20 percent to the dollar and rising inflation, the central bank this week mounted its most aggressive defence of the currency yet, selling a record $1.1 billion on Wednesday and Thursday and making changes to banks' reserve requirements.

The action succeeded in lifting the lira well off record lows. But any further FX interventions will put Turkey in serious danger of depleting a reserve stash that is its primary buffer against a large balance of payments deficit.

Reserves stand now at around $85 billion, far short of the hundreds of billions of dollars held by other comparable emerging market countries and down more than 10 percent from July as a result of the central bank's daily dollar auctions.

"This speed of reserve drawdown is not sustainable," said Manik Narain, emerging markets strategist at UBS in London. "Turkey's reserves in terms of external debt coverage or import coverage are among the the lowest in emerging markets."

In contrast, South Korean interventions throughout September cost it $9 billion but made a dent of less than 3 percent in its reserves, the world's eighth-largest.

Central bank data shows $132 billion in external debt payments due in the coming year, mostly private sector. Add in the huge current account gap and the liability mounts to over $200 billion -- more than double its current reserve level.

Turkey in fact is one of only four emerging countries whose FX reserves are insufficient to cover annual trade balance needs and maturing short-term debt, a UBS study shows. The other countries in this position are Bulgaria, Latvia and Belarus.

"The Turkish central bank ... is not Brazil or Korea which have a lot more firepower," said Alia Yousuf, a bond portfolio manager with ACPI Investments in London.

"If this (reserves decline) continues it will obviously lead to more uneasiness with investors. Ultimately if global market uncertainty remains, funding the Turkish current account deficit will become an increasing worry."

BANK UNEASY?

BNP Paribas analysts note that the gross reserves-imports ratio stands at 37 percent while the reserves to short-term debt ratio is at 98 percent, just above levels it says are mentioned by the bank in its reserve management guidelines.

"Our back-of-the envelope calculation yields that if the central bank sells $10 billion more, all FX reserve ratios will decline to or below their critical levels," BNP told clients.

Though the central bank deliberately engineered a depreciation in the lira in the early part of the year, it has appeared increasingly uncomfortable with the scale and pace of the currency's fall.

On Thursday it attempted to soothe analysts' worries, saying in a presentation that its reserve position was quite strong, judging by the ratio of reserves to short term FX debt.

But signs are it is uneasy; hence the decision to allow banks to hold more reserves in dollars, a step that may add $3.6 billion to its own coffers.

But the coming months may well see a further rise in dollar demand from Turkish banks and corporates which borrowed heavily overseas to fund booming domestic growth but will see a record $132 billion come due in the coming year, including coupons.

RBS compared the predicament to Russia's in 2008, when a third of FX reserves vanished in the rouble's defence.

"Russia suffered badly back then because it had $160-80 billion in external debt liabilities falling due; and yet it got into trouble even with $590 billion in FX reserves, which now underscores the risks in Turkey's case," RBS said.

RESERVES OR RATES

So apart from praying for a quick resolution of the euro zone crisis, what can Turkey's central bank do next?

Tufan Comert, strategist at Garanti Securities in Istanbul said the central bank could try for a swap line with the U.S. Federal Reserve, which stepped in to provide liquidity to many emerging central banks in 2008. Or it could lend dollars to banks on forex deposit instead of selling, he said.

What markets would really like to see is an interest rate rise. Turkey's policy rate, the one-week repo rate, is at 5.75 percent, a negative rate in real terms, though the one-year bond yield is still in positive territory at 8.3 percent.

Yet the central bank admitted this week end-2011 inflation would be significantly above-target.

But a rate rise would mark an immense U-turn for the bank which has eased policy several times this year to engineer lira depreciation. It would argue a rate hike now will put Turkey at a disadvantage, given growth at home and abroad is slowing.

"I would have liked to have seen the central bank defending the lira with interest rate weapons as well, rather than only intervention," said Namik Aksel, chief executive of HSBC Asset Management Turkey. "Obviously this policy is a risk but they do have a point. Growth is going to be the main driver in 2012."

He too reckons no more than $5-$10 billion can be spent from now in the lira's defence. After that circumstances may force the central bank's hand -- the bank's strategy clearly hinges on a reversal of the global bearish market sentiment.

"I do believe they may hike overnight borrowing rates if we see another round of heavy sell-off," Aksel added.

(Editing by Catherine Evans)

EUR/USD rises 0.2% to 1.0933. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0939 GMT - ECB President Christine Lagarde says the central bank will continue to increase rates in July, but she refrained from commentary about future meetings. "My intention is not to signal any future decisions, but rather to frame the issues that monetary policy will face in the period ahead," Lagarde told the ECB Forum on Central Banking in Sintra. In other words, she refuses to get pinned down on the decision in September, according to Pantheon Macroeconomics' chief eurozone economist Claus Vistesen. While he sticks with a view that the bank will raise its key policy rate by 25 basis points in September, the risks are tilted toward the further hikes in 4Q, especially judging by Lagarde's tone of a second phase of rising inflation that is proving strong and persistent, he says. (edward.frankl@wsj.com)

0936 GMT - A key to tackling persistent inflation may be in whether the services sector takes more of an impact from the effect of higher interest rates than seen so far, according to ECB President Christine Lagarde. Monetary-policy shocks are typically transmitted more quickly and forcefully to manufacturing, reflecting the sector's higher interest-rate sensitivity, while there is a more muted and delayed impact on services, Lagarde told the ECB Forum on Central Banking in Sintra, Portugal. The question is whether services will "catch down", rather than catch up, with manufacturing, which has been seen in previous cycles, or whether it will be insulated from the effects of policy tightening for longer than in the past, given the strength of demand and employment in the sector, she says. (edward.frankl@wsj.com)

While organic sales increased more than 15% in the first three months of its 2023/24 financial year, they rose by 8% in May, JD said, adding that it had expected the slowdown and that it still believed full-year 2023/24 headline pretax profit before adjusted items would match market expectations. The trading slowdown wasn't surprising, given the company had forecast it in its full-year results, Barclays says. title: ANALYSIS-Investors lament lost opportunity after unconvincing Turkish rate hike
text:
(Updates lira's fresh record low and bond prices in paragraph 9)

By Libby George

LONDON, June 23 (Reuters) - Foreign investors hoping for a game-changing rate hike from Turkey's newly appointed central bank chief said Thursday's disappointing move to a key rate of just 15% could keep some money on the sidelines.

The appointment of U.S.-trained banker Hafize Gaye Erkan to lead the bank boosted expectations that it would rapidly raise rates to unravel years of unorthodox policies as quickly as possible.

But the 650 basis point hike - to 15% - was well below the median rate expectation in a Reuters poll of a rise to 21%, leaving some fretting that Erkan might have limited room to aggressively tackle inflation.

"They lost one perfect chance to demonstrate that they mean business," said Viktor Szabo, emerging markets investment director with Abrdn. "Whether it's because they have political constraints, or they're afraid for the banking system, it's not great. It's not a great message."

Newly re-elected President Tayyip Erdogan, a self-described enemy of high interest rates, for years directed a heavily managed economic system, with a tightly controlled lira, rate cuts in the face of galloping inflation and plentiful credit for local borrowers.

Amidst tumbling reserves and fleeing investors, his choice of Erkan at the central bank, and investor darling Mehmet Simsek as finance minister, prompted bets for a quick turnaround to unravel some of these policies.

But analysts said that after Thursday's decision, Erkan and Simsek would need to work even harder to prove the country had indeed shifted course.

"They look less credible now," Eric Fine, portfolio manager of emerging market debt at VanEck, said of the central bank, adding: "They need to hike rates to whatever level prevents the need for currency interventions using reserves. They haven't."

Turkey's lira suffered a second consecutive day of declines on Friday, hitting a fresh record low of 25.74 to the dollar before retracing, while the country's international bonds eked out small gains after tumbling on Thursday.

Already in the week to June 16, foreign investor holdings of Turkish government bonds had fallen by $16.2 million.

"For now, it's not enough, probably, for long-term investors. Because of the magnitude of some of the problems in the economy," said Marek Drimal, a lead strategist at Societe Generale.

CAUTION AND TEMPERED DISAPPOINTMENT

Still, many, including Drimal, saw positive signs, and noted that even Simsek had repeatedly said that gradual rate moves were move likely.

Simsek also promised predictable, market-based economic policies and an inflation-targeting model would enable capital inflows.

"I think investor disappointment should be tempered," said Dan Wood, portfolio manager at William Blair, adding that the bank also signalled that it will keep hiking rates until inflation improved.

"It is clearly positive that a return to a more orthodox economic policy has been signalled."

The associate director of ratings agency Scope Ratings and a sovereign analyst at ratings agency Fitch also said the hike itself was positive - but the core question would be whether Erdogan allows Erkan to stay the course with continued rises.

"I don't think investors will throw in the towel just yet because I think there is still expectation there is more to come in the coming months," said Kaan Nazli, portfolio manager at Neuberger Berman.

"The market is very cautious - so to regain confidence, that will take a long time. I would think that you would need to maintain tight policy for a considerable amount of time for significant, more long-term inflows to come in." (Additional reporting by Karin Strohecker and Marc Jones; Editing by Toby Chopra)
