The LTLC IDRs of Ziraat, Vakifbank , TSKB, Akbank, Isbank and YKB could be downgraded if Turkey's LTLC IDR was downgraded, if Fitch believes the sovereign's propensity to provide support in LC has reduced or our view of the likelihood of intervention risk in the banking sector increases. For Akbank, Isbank and YKB, this would only lead to a downgrade if the banks' VRs were also downgraded.

The banks' GSRs could be downgraded if Fitch concludes the reliability of support for the banks in FC from the Turkish authorities has weakened.

LT IDRS, SSRS AND SENIOR DEBT RATINGS OF FOREIGN-OWNED BANKS

A downgrade of Turkey's sovereign rating would likely lead to similar action on the banks. Increased government intervention risk would likely also lead to negative rating action on the banks' LT IDRs.

The banks' ratings are also sensitive to Fitch's view of their shareholders' ability and propensity to provide support, in case of need. For banks with VRs at the level of their LTFC IDRs, a reduced likelihood of shareholder support would only lead to a downgrade of the banks' ratings if their VRs were also downgraded.

The respective senior unsecured debt ratings are primarily sensitive to changes in the banks' LTFC IDRs.

Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to positive rating action/upgrade:

LT IDRS, GSRS OF TKYB, TURK EXIMBANK , VAKIF KATILIM AND EMLAK KATILIM

Upgrades of the banks' LT IDRs are unlikely given the Negative Outlook on Turkey's sovereign rating. A revision of the sovereign Outlook to Stable would likely lead to similar action on the banks' LT IDRs.

In the medium term, a material improvement in Turkey's external finances and net FX reserves position, that resulted in a marked strengthening in the sovereign's ability to support banks in FC, could lead to positive rating action on the banks' GSRs and LTFC IDRs - with the exception of TKYB, as its rating is already equalised with the sovereign.

Turk Eximbank 's senior unsecured debt ratings are primarily sensitive to changes in the bank's LTFC IDR.

LTLC IDRS, GSRS OF ZIRAAT, VAKIFBANK, TSKB, AKBANK, ISBANK AND YKB

Upgrades of the banks' LTLC IDRs are unlikely given the Negative Outlook on the sovereign rating. A revision of the sovereign Outlook to Stable would likely lead to similar action on the banks' LTLC IDRs.

In the medium term, a material improvement in Turkey's external finances and net FX reserves position, resulting in a marked strengthening in the sovereign's ability to support banks in FC, could lead to positive rating action on the banks' GSRs. However, only a multi-notch upgrade of the banks' GSRs would lead to an upgrade of their LTFC IDRs as their VRs are already rated one (Ziraat, Vakifbank , TSKB) or two (Akbank, Isbank and YKB) notches above their respective GSRs.

LT IDRS, SSRS AND SENIOR DEBT RATINGS OF FOREIGN-OWNED BANKS

Upgrades of the banks' LT IDRs are unlikely given the Negative Outlook. However, a revision of the sovereign Outlook to Stable would likely lead to similar action on the banks' LT IDRs.

A material improvement in Turkey's external finances or net FX reserves position, resulting in a significant reduction in our view of government intervention risk in the banking sector, could lead to an upgrade of the banks' LTFC IDRs to the level of Turkey's LTFC IDR. However, given Turkey's large external vulnerabilities and very weak net FX reserves position, this is unlikely in the near term, in our view.

The respective senior unsecured debt ratings are primarily sensitive to changes in the banks' LTFC IDRs.

SUBORDINATED DEBT RATINGS OF GARANTI BBVA , KUVEYT TURK

The subordinated debt ratings of Garanti BBVA and Kuveyt Turk are primarily sensitive to changes in the banks' LTFC IDRs.

The ratings are also sensitive to a change in notching from their respective anchor ratings due to a revision in Fitch's assessment of the probability of the notes' non-performance risk or loss severity in the case of non-performance.

BANK SUBSIDIARIES

The ratings of Ziraat Katilim Bankasi are sensitive to changes in the LT IDRs of Ziraat.

NATIONAL RATINGS

The National Ratings of all issuers under review are sensitive to changes in their respective LTLC IDRs and their relative creditworthiness to other Turkish issuers.

Best/Worst Case Rating Scenario

International scale credit ratings of Financial Institutions and Covered Bond issuers have a best-case rating upgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a positive direction) of three notches over a three-year rating horizon; and a worst-case rating downgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a negative direction) of four notches over three years. The complete span of best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings for all rating categories ranges from 'AAA' to 'D'. Best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings are based on historical performance. For more information about the methodology used to determine sector-specific best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings, visit https://www.fitchratings.com/site/re/10111579 

REFERENCES FOR SUBSTANTIALLY MATERIAL SOURCE CITED AS KEY DRIVER OF RATING The principal sources of information used in the analysis are described in the Applicable Criteria. Public Ratings with Credit Linkage to other ratings

All banks included in this review have ratings linked to the Turkish sovereign rating, given the ratings either rely on or are sensitive to our assessment of sovereign support or country risks.

ESG Considerations

The state-owned banks - Ziraat, Vakifbank , Emlak Katilim, Vakif Katilim and Ziraat Katilim Bankasi have ESG Relevance Scores of '4' for Governance Structure and Management Strategy (in contrast to a typical Relevance Score of '3' for comparable banks) due to potential government influence over their boards' effectiveness and management strategy in the challenging Turkish operating environment, which has a negative impact on the credit profile, and is relevant to the ratings in conjunction with other factors.

In addition, the Islamic banks' (Emlak Katilim, Vakif Katilim, Kuveyt Turk, TFKB, Ziraat Katilim Bankasi) ESG Relevance Score of '4' for Governance Structure reflects their Islamic banking nature (in contrast to a typical ESG Relevance Score of '3' for comparable conventional banks). These banks' operations and activities need to comply with sharia principles and rules, which entails additional costs, processes, disclosures, regulations, reporting and sharia audit. This has a negative impact on their credit profiles and is relevant to the ratings in conjunction with other factors.

The Islamic banks also have an ESG Relevance Score of '3' for Exposure to Social Impacts (in contrast to a typical ESG Relevance Score of '2' for comparable conventional banks), which reflects that Islamic banks have certain sharia limitations embedded in their operations and obligations, although this only has a minimal credit impact on Islamic banks.

Unless otherwise disclosed in this section, the highest level of ESG credit relevance is a score of '3'/ ESG issues are credit neutral or have only a minimal credit impact on the entity, either due to their nature or the way in which they are being managed by the entity. title: Turkey 's  central bank  to  intervene  again in the market to support the lira
text:
The Central Bank of Turkey today intervened again in the market to prop up the exchange rate of the lira, in what is the third defense of the Turkish currency by the institution so far in December. "The Central Bank of the Republic of Turkeyintervenes directly in the market through sales transactions due to unhealthy price formations in exchange rates," said the monetary institution, as reported by the agency Europa Press. The dollar exchange rate had risen today to 13.9549 Turkish liras, but later eased to 13.8862 liras, when last Wednesday, the date of the first intervention of the central bank of the Eurasian country, the dollar cross also reached almost 14 liras. On December 31, 2020 dollars were exchanged for 7.43 liras, so so far this year the Turkish currency has seen almost half of its value vanish. In recent weeks the currency's plunge has been exacerbated by comments from President Recep Tayyip Erdogan that the country was waging an "economic war".

 The lira also recorded negative developments after the country's central bank cut interest rates by 100 basis points in mid-November, and on the other hand, the country's year-on-year inflation rate climbed to 21.31% in November, compared to 19.89% in October and well above the 14.03% in November 2020. title: Fitch Revises Outlooks on 13 Turkish Banks to Negative on Sovereign Outlook Change
text:
Fitch Ratings-London-10 December 2021: Fitch Ratings has revised the Outlooks on 13 Turkish banks' support-driven Long-Term Foreign-Currency (LTFC) Issuer Default Ratings (IDRs) to Negative from Stable. The Outlooks on 20 banks' support-driven Long-Term Local-Currency (LTLC) IDRs have also been revised to Negative from Stable.

The Outlook revisions follow the change in the Outlook on Turkey's Long-Term IDRs to Negative from Stable. The latter was driven, among other factors, by the Central Bank of Turkey's premature monetary policy easing cycle, and the prospect of further rate cuts or additional economic stimulus ahead of the 2023 presidential election. Together these factors have led to a deterioration in domestic confidence - reflected in a sharp depreciation of the Turkish lira and rising inflation, creating risks to macroeconomic and financial stability and potentially re-igniting external financing risks.

We believe that the risks to macroeconomic and financial stability and external financing could increase the likelihood of government intervention in the banking system. This has driven the revision of the Outlooks on foreign-owned Turkish banks' LT IDRs to Negative. The Negative Outlooks on banks with ratings driven by state support reflect the sovereign Outlook, and the risk of a further weakening of the authorities' ability to provide support in case of need.

The Viability Ratings of the banks under review (where assigned) are unaffected by the sovereign Outlook revision, as are the VRs of other Fitch-rated Turkish banks, whose IDRs are driven by their VRs. This reflects our view that risks to standalone credit profiles are captured in the current ratings and in Negative Outlooks, despite persistent and heightened operating environment pressures. We consider risks to banks' financial profiles and VRs to be skewed to the downside, given macro and financial market developments.

Fitch has assigned Government Support Ratings (GSRs) or Shareholder Support Ratings (SSRs) to all banks under review. This follows the withdrawal of the banks' respective Support Ratings and Support Rating Floors as they are no longer relevant to our coverage following the publication of the updated Bank Rating Criteria on 12 November.

Key Rating Drivers

IDRS, GSRS AND SENIOR UNSECURED DEBT RATINGS OF STATE-OWNED BANKS AND TSKB

The Outlooks on the LTFC IDRs of Turkiye Ihracat Kredi Bankasi A.S. (Turk Eximbank) and Turkiye Kalkinma ve Yatirim Bankasi (TKYB), the state-owned development banks, and Turkiye Emlak Katilim Bankasi A.S. (Emlak Katilim) and Vakif Katilim Bankasi AS (Vakif Katilim), two state-owned participation banks, have been revised to Negative from Stable, mirroring the Outlook on the sovereign, reflecting increased risks to the sovereign's ability to provide support in case of need.

Fitch regards the Turkish authorities as having a high propensity to support the four banks, given their majority state-ownership, policy roles (development banks), strategic importance to the authorities and the record of support.

TKYB's LTFC IDR is equalised with Turkey's sovereign rating, as reflected in its 'bb-' GSR, reflecting its small size relative to sovereign resources, still largely treasury-guaranteed funding base and the medium-term tenor of its non-guaranteed funding (as a result of which its potential need for support over the medium term is likely to be limited).

Turk Eximbank's 'b+' GSR, one notch below Turkey's LTFC IDR and TKYB's GSR, reflects the bank's strategic policy role as the country's export credit agency but also its considerably larger balance sheet and volumes of external market funding when compared with TKYB. This is an important rating driver in light of Turkey's weak net foreign exchange (FX) reserves position.

The senior unsecured debt ratings of Turk Eximbank have been affirmed in line with its FC IDRs.

Fitch has assigned GSRs of 'b' to four state-owned commercial banks - Turkiye Cumhuriyeti Ziraat Bankasi A.S. (Ziraat) and Turkiye Vakiflar Bankasi T.A.O. (Vakifbank), both considered systemically important and the two participation banks, Emlak Katilim and Vakif Katilim, and the privately-owned development bank Turkiye Sinai Kalkinma Bankasi A.S. (TSKB). Their GSRs are two notches below Turkey's LTFC IDR despite a high sovereign propensity to provide support, reflecting Turkey's weak financial flexibility to provide support in FC, in case of need.

The LTLC IDRs of Ziraat, Vakifbank, Emlak Katilim, Vakif Katilim, Turk Eximbank, TKYB and TSKB are equalised with the sovereign rating at 'BB-' on the basis of support, reflecting a high sovereign propensity and ability to provide support in LC. The revision of the Outlooks to Negative from Stable mirror the sovereign rating action.

LTLC IDRS AND GSRS OF AKBANK, ISBANK AND YKB

The LTLC IDRs of Akbank T.A.S. (Akbank), Turkiye Is Bankasi A.S. (Isbank) and Yapi ve Kredi Bankasi A.S. (YKB), have been affirmed at 'B+', one notch below the sovereign rating, and their Outlooks revised to Negative from Stable, mirroring the sovereign Outlook. At this rating level, the three banks' LTLC IDRs are now underpinned by both sovereign support and their standalone credit profiles. Our view of support is based on the banks' systemic importance, solid market shares and franchises, but also considers their private ownership.

The three banks' LTFC IDRs, also B+/Negative, continue to be driven by the banks' VRs, reflecting our view that sovereign support in FC cannot be relied upon - as reflected in their GSRs of 'b-'.

IDRS AND SSRS OF FOREIGN-OWNED BANKS, SENIOR UNSECURED DEBT RATINGS

The LTFC IDRs of nine foreign-owned Turkish banks (Alternatifbank A.S., Burgan Bank A.S., Denizbank A.S., Kuveyt Turk Katilim Bankasi A.S. (Kuveyt Turk), ING Bank A.S., Turkiye Garanti Bankasi (Garanti BBVA), Turk Ekonomi Bankasi (TEB), Turkiye Finans Katilim Bankasi A.S. (TFKB), QNB Finansbank A.S. are driven by shareholder support from higher-rated parent banks.

Fitch's view of support reflects the banks' strategic importance to their respective parents, ownership, integration and roles within their wider groups. Senior debt ratings, where assigned, are aligned with the banks' LT IDRs, reflecting average recovery prospects in case of default.

Fitch's view of government intervention risk caps the foreign-owned banks' LTFC IDRs at 'B+', one notch below the sovereign LTFC IDR. This reflects our assessment that weaknesses in Turkey's external finances make some form of intervention in the banking system that would impede banks' ability to service their FC obligations more likely than a sovereign default, given the weak external financial position. We believe government intervention risk could increase following the latest market volatility, driving the revision of the Outlooks on the banks' LTFC IDRs to Negative.

The foreign-owned banks' LTLC IDRs - which are also driven by shareholder support - have been affirmed at 'BB-', one notch above their LTFC IDRs, reflecting our view of a lower likelihood of government intervention in LC. The Outlooks have been revised to Negative from Stable, mirroring the sovereign Outlook change.

The respective senior unsecured debt ratings have been affirmed along in line with their FC IDRs.

SUBORDINATED DEBT RATINGS OF KUVEYT TURK, GARANTI BBVA

The subordinated notes' ratings of Kuveyt Turk - issued through its SPV KT21 T2 Sukuk - and Garanti BBVA are notched down once from their support-driven IDRs and have been affirmed along with their anchor ratings. The notching in each case includes one notch for loss severity and zero notches for non-performance risk (relative to their anchor ratings).

BANK SUBSIDIARIES

Ziraat Katilim Bankasi A.S.'s ratings are equalised with those of its parent (Ziraat) reflecting its role as a core subsidiary. Our view of support considers its strategic importance in helping develop participation banking in Turkey, its role as the sole provider of Islamic banking products for the Ziraat group, its high integration and shared branding. The Outlooks on the bank's LT IDRs mirror those on its parent.

NATIONAL RATINGS

The National Ratings of all issuers included in this review have been affirmed following the sovereign rating action. This reflects our view that their creditworthiness in LC relative to other Turkish issuers has not changed as a result of the revision of the Outlooks on their LT IDRs.

Rating Sensitivities

Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to negative rating action/downgrade:

LT IDRS AND GSRS OF TKYB, TURK EXIMBANK, VAKIF KATILIM AND EMLAK KATILIM

Negative rating action on Turkey would likely lead to similar action on these banks. The banks' GSRs could be downgraded, and as a result their LTFC IDRs also downgraded, if further stress in Turkey's external finances materially reduces the reliability of support in FC for the banks from the Turkish authorities.

A downgrade of Vakif Katilim's GSR would only lead to a downgrade of its LTFC IDR if the bank's VR was also downgraded.

TKYB's GSR could be downgraded by one notch and its LTFC IDR downgraded, if its proportion of non-guaranteed funding increases materially - particularly if Fitch believes this to be indicative of a weakening in TKYB's policy role - or if its balance sheet size sharply increases. Turk Eximbank's GSR could be downgraded due to a material weakening in the bank's policy role.

All four banks' LTLC IDRs could be downgraded if Turkey's LTLC IDR was downgraded, Fitch believes the sovereign's propensity to support the banks has reduced or Fitch believes there is an increased likelihood of intervention risk in LC.

Turk Eximbank's senior unsecured debt ratings are primarily sensitive to changes in the bank's LTFC IDR.

LTLC IDRS AND GSRS OF ZIRAAT, VAKIFBANK, TSKB, AKBANK, ISBANK AND YKB

The LTLC IDRs of Ziraat, Vakifbank, TSKB, Akbank, Isbank and YKB could be downgraded if Turkey's LTLC IDR was downgraded, if Fitch believes the sovereign's propensity to provide support in LC has reduced or our view of the likelihood of intervention risk in the banking sector increases. For Akbank, Isbank and YKB, this would only lead to a downgrade if the banks' VRs were also downgraded.

The banks' GSRs could be downgraded if Fitch concludes the reliability of support for the banks in FC from the Turkish authorities has weakened.

LT IDRS, SSRS AND SENIOR DEBT RATINGS OF FOREIGN-OWNED BANKS

A downgrade of Turkey's sovereign rating would likely lead to similar action on the banks. Increased government intervention risk would likely also lead to negative rating action on the banks' LT IDRs.

The banks' ratings are also sensitive to Fitch's view of their shareholders' ability and propensity to provide support, in case of need. For banks with VRs at the level of their LTFC IDRs, a reduced likelihood of shareholder support would only lead to a downgrade of the banks' ratings if their VRs were also downgraded.

The respective senior unsecured debt ratings are primarily sensitive to changes in the banks' LTFC IDRs.

Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to positive rating action/upgrade:

LT IDRS, GSRS OF TKYB, TURK EXIMBANK, VAKIF KATILIM AND EMLAK KATILIM

Upgrades of the banks' LT IDRs are unlikely given the Negative Outlook on Turkey's sovereign rating. A revision of the sovereign Outlook to Stable would likely lead to similar action on the banks' LT IDRs.

In the medium term, a material improvement in Turkey's external finances and net FX reserves position, that resulted in a marked strengthening in the sovereign's ability to support banks in FC, could lead to positive rating action on the banks' GSRs and LTFC IDRs - with the exception of TKYB, as its rating is already equalised with the sovereign.

Turk Eximbank's senior unsecured debt ratings are primarily sensitive to changes in the bank's LTFC IDR.

LTLC IDRS, GSRS OF ZIRAAT, VAKIFBANK, TSKB, AKBANK, ISBANK AND YKB

Upgrades of the banks' LTLC IDRs are unlikely given the Negative Outlook on the sovereign rating. A revision of the sovereign Outlook to Stable would likely lead to similar action on the banks' LTLC IDRs.

In the medium term, a material improvement in Turkey's external finances and net FX reserves position, resulting in a marked strengthening in the sovereign's ability to support banks in FC, could lead to positive rating action on the banks' GSRs. However, only a multi-notch upgrade of the banks' GSRs would lead to an upgrade of their LTFC IDRs as their VRs are already rated one (Ziraat, Vakifbank, TSKB) or two (Akbank, Isbank and YKB) notches above their respective GSRs.

LT IDRS, SSRS AND SENIOR DEBT RATINGS OF FOREIGN-OWNED BANKS

Upgrades of the banks' LT IDRs are unlikely given the Negative Outlook. However, a revision of the sovereign Outlook to Stable would likely lead to similar action on the banks' LT IDRs.

A material improvement in Turkey's external finances or net FX reserves position, resulting in a significant reduction in our view of government intervention risk in the banking sector, could lead to an upgrade of the banks' LTFC IDRs to the level of Turkey's LTFC IDR. However, given Turkey's large external vulnerabilities and very weak net FX reserves position, this is unlikely in the near term, in our view.

The respective senior unsecured debt ratings are primarily sensitive to changes in the banks' LTFC IDRs.

SUBORDINATED DEBT RATINGS OF GARANTI BBVA, KUVEYT TURK

The subordinated debt ratings of Garanti BBVA and Kuveyt Turk are primarily sensitive to changes in the banks' LTFC IDRs.

The ratings are also sensitive to a change in notching from their respective anchor ratings due to a revision in Fitch's assessment of the probability of the notes' non-performance risk or loss severity in the case of non-performance.

BANK SUBSIDIARIES

The ratings of Ziraat Katilim Bankasi are sensitive to changes in the LT IDRs of Ziraat.

NATIONAL RATINGS

The National Ratings of all issuers under review are sensitive to changes in their respective LTLC IDRs and their relative creditworthiness to other Turkish issuers.

Best/Worst Case Rating Scenario

International scale credit ratings of Financial Institutions and Covered Bond issuers have a best-case rating upgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a positive direction) of three notches over a three-year rating horizon; and a worst-case rating downgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a negative direction) of four notches over three years. The complete span of best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings for all rating categories ranges from 'AAA' to 'D'. Best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings are based on historical performance. ESG Considerations

The state-owned banks - Ziraat, Vakifbank, Emlak Katilim, Vakif Katilim and Ziraat Katilim Bankasi have ESG Relevance Scores of '4' for Governance Structure and Management Strategy (in contrast to a typical Relevance Score of '3' for comparable banks) due to potential government influence over their boards' effectiveness and management strategy in the challenging Turkish operating environment, which has a negative impact on the credit profile, and is relevant to the ratings in conjunction with other factors.

In addition, the Islamic banks' (Emlak Katilim, Vakif Katilim, Kuveyt Turk, TFKB, Ziraat Katilim Bankasi) ESG Relevance Score of '4' for Governance Structure reflects their Islamic banking nature (in contrast to a typical ESG Relevance Score of '3' for comparable conventional banks). These banks' operations and activities need to comply with sharia principles and rules, which entails additional costs, processes, disclosures, regulations, reporting and sharia audit. This has a negative impact on their credit profiles and is relevant to the ratings in conjunction with other factors.

The Islamic banks also have an ESG Relevance Score of '3' for Exposure to Social Impacts (in contrast to a typical ESG Relevance Score of '2' for comparable conventional banks), which reflects that Islamic banks have certain sharia limitations embedded in their operations and obligations, although this only has a minimal credit impact on Islamic banks.

Unless otherwise disclosed in this section, the highest level of ESG credit relevance is a score of '3'/ ESG issues are credit neutral or have only a minimal credit impact on the entity, either due to their nature or the way in which they are being managed by the entity. title: Turkey's  central bank  comes to the rescue of the lira again after strong inflation figures
text:
The Central Bank of Turkey has intervened again on Friday in the market to prop up the exchange rate of the lira, in what is the second defense of the Turkish currency by the institution so far this week. This intervention comes after inflation data that has surprised on the upside in the Ottoman country.

"The Central Bank of the Republic of Turkeyintervenes directly in the market through sale transactions due to unhealthy price formations in exchange rates," the institution has confirmed.

In a nutshell, the Turkish bank comes to the defense of the lira using its dollar reserves. The central bank undertakes to drain some of the lira supply in the market (investors or agents who want to sell the Turkish currency) by offering in exchange dollars or other 'hard' currencies that make up the reserves accumulated by the central bank. This may temporarily reduce the downward pressure on the exchange rate, as the Turkish central bank has limited reserves (estimated at around $50 billion).

The only way to prevent the lira from depreciating further without resorting to foreign exchange market interventions is through interest rate hikes or structural reforms to improve the country's competitiveness.

Second intervention The dollar exchange rate had risen as high as 13.8898 Turkish liras on Friday, but later eased to 13.7244 liras. Last Wednesday, the dollar cross reached almost 14 liras, forcing the Turkish central bank to intervene.

On Dec. 31, 2020, dollars were trading at 7.43 liras, so so far this year the Turkish currency has seen almost half of its value vanish.

In recent weeks, the currency's plunge has been exacerbated by comments from President Recep Tayyip Erdogan that the country was waging an "economic war". The lira also saw negative developments after the country's central bank cut interest rates by 100 basis points in mid-November.

Separately, the Turkish Statistical Institute (TurkStat) announced that the country's year-on-year inflation rate climbed to 21.31% in November, up from 19.89% in October and well above the 14.03% in November 2020.

title: Turkish finance minister resigns amid lira slump crisis
text:
Ankara, Dec 2 (EFE) - Turkey's Finance Minister Lutfi Elvan resigned Thursday in the midst of the crisis of devaluation of the lira, which lost 30% of its value last month, while the country's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan continues to defend a policy of low interest rates. Turkish media report that Elvan's departure had been expected for weeks, as the former minister had been privately rejecting Erdogan's monetary strategy and his continued intervention in the work of the Central Bank.Elvan's resignation and the appointment of the new minister, Nureddin Nebati, until now deputy finance minister, was published after midnight in the official state gazette, with a decree signed by the president. The document notes that the resigning minister requested to be relieved of the post and that his request was accepted by Erdogan.Nebati is the third finance minister since November, when Erdogan's son-in-law Berat Albayrak resigned from the post.

 At the opening of the Turkish market today, the lira fell 1.47% against the dollar and 1.75% against the euro, trading at 13.52 and 15.31 respectively against those currencies.Last November was the worst in the history of the Turkish lira, with a cumulative loss of nearly 30%. The Turkish media had been speculating two weeks ago with the resignation of Elvan for what they claim was his opposition to Erdogan's strategy of keeping interest rates low, arguing, contrary to the opinion of most economists, that this helps to combat inflation, which is at 20%. "We have abandoned the policy of high interest rates and have moved to a strategy of growth by investment, employment and production," said the president yesterday in a speech to his party, the Islamist AKP, in power since 2002.The devaluation of the lira is affecting the purchasing power of the Turks and in recent days there have been demonstrations and protests against the government, while the opposition calls for early elections. The Turkish currency soared yesterday by 10% against the euro and the dollar immediately after the Central Bank of Turkey announced that it is intervening in the foreign exchange market through sales to influence the exchange value of the national currency.

title: Erdogan promises more rate cuts as Bank of Turkey steps in to try to stabilise the lira
text:
The Bank of Turkey (CBRT) has been forced to intervene in the foreign exchange market in the face of the new collapse of the currency. For the first time in seven years, the bank is getting rid of foreign currency. The lira has risen as much as 7% but has fallen in high volatility. The previous falls have been caused by Tayyip Erdogan's statements. The president has promised more interest rate cuts.

Erdogan had warned that there will be more interest rate cuts before the election to "free the economy" from dependence on "short-term foreign cash". He has also promised more jobs and lower inflation thanks to the interest rate cuts, which the central bank is making.

The elections are scheduled for 2023. CBRT at its last meeting hinted that the cuts would stop in December, after lowering rates to 15% from 16%. For some time now, the entity has lost its credibility because of Erdogan's interference. Last week it issued a statement blaming the market itself for the lira's decline.

The Turkish lira has bounced as much as 10% to $0.0764 after the Bank of Turkey announced that it is "directly intervening in the market... for unhealthy price formations in exchange rates," according to the statement.

In the year the Turkish lira accumulates a depreciation of 43% by Erdogan's insistence on an unorthodox and interventionist economic policy. The country suffers an inflation rate close to 20%. Any economics textbook would advise raising interest rates to try to contain the price escalation. The CBRT's inflation target is set at 5%. Real interest rates (discounting inflation) are in very negative territory, almost -4%.

Erdogan has come to control the CBRT with an iron fist and has imposed his economic theories despite the risk to the country's financial stability. Last March he dismissed the governor of the institution, after the last rate hike that the central bank undertook in order to control inflation. Since then the Turkish lira has continued to plummet.

title: Lira plunge leaves Turkey in turmoil
text:
Turkey is right now a serial with no guaranteed happy ending. You only have to sit in a barbershop in Ankara to hear the same litany, before you've even taken off your mask. "The economy is bad, pretty bad." By the time the barber finishes with the scissors and moves on to singeing ear hairs with a spectacular flare, the lira is already worth less than when he started.

The country is not on fire, but it is in a bain-marie, like the frog in the story, while the temperature of the water keeps rising. If there is no panic, no queues at the bureaux de change, it is because Turkey, because of its recent history, is cured of its fright.

There are millions of Turks who have part of their savings denominated in euros or dollars, or bundles of banknotes under their mattresses. However, the combination of galloping inflation and the lira in free fall is something else this time.

Different from the meltdown of 2018, though still incomparable to the crisis of two decades ago, when an even worse inflationary wave threw the old forces into disarray and brought the ship of Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his Justice and Development Party (AKP) to power.

Barber Sinan, with premises in the affluent neighbourhood dedicated to the pirate Barbarossa, says he pays 8,000 liras in rent. This is Çankaya - the heart of republican Turkey, with embassies and star-studded hotels - and it used to be a lot, but today the exchange rate is less than 640 euros. Even so, Sinan needs two hundred haircuts just to cover the rent. To this must be added "the four months of closure due to the pandemic".

The economy that is bad, quite bad, is his own, in small letters, and that of millions of Turks who have been squeezed by high inflation and low wages. But the economy in capital letters, that of the official reports, conveys a more nuanced message, despite the spectacular collapse of the currency.

Support The central bank has given up on supporting the lira, a year after burning through its reserves.This has been worsened by the umpteenth cut in interest rates - on Thursday to 15% from 16% - contrary to orthodoxy which preaches that to contain inflation rates should be above this - officially, 19.9%.

Although the bars in Barbaros are full even on weekdays, a liquor store in the same neighbourhood - with good wines and better malt whiskies - confesses to having lived in more comfortable times, when the lira had a price tag. "I have to change the price tags every day," says Hassan. Upwards, of course.

His Angora cat glides among the hundreds of bottles, more expertly than others among the interest rates. "He has never broken any of them," says Hasán, before adding: "Before, the customer would come in and take three wines almost without looking. Now he checks what each one is worth and in the end he only gets one, rather cheaply".

The straw that breaks the camel's back is "the 65% tax on imported wines and 300% on champagne," he exclaims. Erdogan has a strained relationship with Macron and the Penedès is a collateral victim.

So this time it's different, because almost no one is spared. Suddenly, the neighbor with the white BMW opens her heart to lament "how much the Turks are suffering", before confessing her own struggles to pay her daughter's rent in Boston. Suddenly, a thousand dollars has become a mountain, following the lira's 30% depreciation so far this year.

If this is happening in the airy diplomatic zone, truffled with secular followers of Atatürk and without a veil for two kilometres around, it's easy to imagine the hardship in the working-class neighbourhoods.

For the first time, the possibility of the end of the Erdogan era seems to be floating in the air. The same is true in the middle and upper class neighborhoods of Istanbul or throughout Izmir. But the portrait of Turkey is somewhat more complex.

It is true that, four years ago, Turks were shaking their heads because one euro was already worth four liras and today it is worth twelve and a half. But it is not so much an accident as a model, based on low wages and exports.

Impact Inflation and the decline in the value of the lira have undermined the confidence of all classes of people.A banker who has been based in Turkey for many years, but likes his anonymity, is reluctant to see the glass half empty. "If the lira is falling, it is because they are letting it fall. Because the priority is no longer to support the lira, but to avoid at all costs a downgrading by the rating agencies".

For several weeks now, ID cards have been required to exchange foreign currency. But Erdo?an knows that a "corralito" would be his political death. The aim is therefore to present a healthy current account balance and growing reserves.

All this after Erdogan's son-in-law almost exhausted the latter in vain to support the lira a little over a year ago. Berat Albayrak was then relieved of his post as finance minister, but the governor of the Central Bank was soon replaced by an economist more sensitive to Erdogan's theses and interventionism.

The export locomotive is going like a shot and Turkey wants to jump on the post-pandemic bandwagon that advocates cutting supply chains. A small China bordering the EU. With heavy tariffs, moreover, on Chinese products.

Not in vain, 56% of its exports go to the EU, with which it has an advantageous customs agreement, despite the fact that its minimum wage - in exchange, 225 euros - borders on social dumping.

However, not all companies are grateful for the rate cuts. The employers' association Tusiad, which brings together 600 large family-owned conglomerates, criticises the indifference to inflation and the depreciation of the lira.

In any case, according to Trade Minister Mehmet Mus, Turkey's GDP grew by 21.7% in the second quarter. This is largely due to the fact that exports have reached a record figure of 160 billion euros in the first ten months, helping the unemployment rate to fall slightly. Even so, one out of every nine Turks looking for work is unemployed.

But the devaluation is a double-edged sword and if the Turkish industry gains competitive advantage, on the other hand frown those who have invested in property in Istanbul, Ankara or Antalya. It is not always transparent money that seeks security, they say, rather than profit.

Hydrocarbon importer The country has seen a severe rise in transport, import and production costs.President Erdogan, a former mayor, after the previous bout of inflation, in 2018, threw a lifeline to "his people", setting up temporary markets for vegetables and pulses at highly subsidised prices. But with no election in sight, the aces are still hidden up his sleeve.

Although he abhors the data, Erdogan clings to the fact that Turkey was one of the few economies that grew last year - 1.75% - and that he expects to end 2021 with 10% growth. To this, or to bottlenecks in global supplies, Ankara attributes part of the inflation, and not only to the rate cut.

"As long as I am president, I will continue my fight against high interest rates," Erdogan told parliament on Wednesday, couching his arguments in the Koranic condemnation of usury.

His party bench applauded him, but not Finance Minister Lütfi Elvan, which has been interpreted as a possible sign of an early handover.

It is true that, even now, the Turkish interest rate is double that of countries with much weaker economies, such as Pakistan.

Against the tide, with the help of its CEO, Onur Genç, BBVA has just doubled its Turkish bet, with the takeover bid for 51% of Garanti bank, which it does not yet control. On Wednesday, in the palace of a thousand and one rooms, Erdogan thanked them for their "trust", with Pedro Sanchez to his right.

Be that as it may, the dream of getting Turkey out of the middle-income trap is looking increasingly distant and it does not seem that it can be carried out by Erdogan, nor his generation.

title: Turkish Lira Continues to Fall and Reaches an All-Time High against the Dollar
text:
Istanbul, Oct 12 (EFE) - The Turkish lira marked Tuesday for the first time a value of 9 units per U.S. dollar, its lowest point since the currency reform in 2005, in line with the downward path that follows since the beginning of last September. The sharp fall of the lira in the last 12 hours is also observed against the euro, although in this case has not yet reached the level of 10.5 units per euro recorded last June, although it is close to 10.45 units.Turkish analysts link today's decline with the speech of the governor of the Central Bank, Sahap Kavcioglu, on Monday, when he defended the decision to lower interest rates from 19% to 18%, taken on September 23.

 The move came as a surprise to financial markets, which did not expect a rate cut when the year-on-year inflation rate stands at 19.25%.Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has insisted for years on keeping rates low, saying that, contrary to what economists believe, high interest rates accelerate inflation rather than curb it. Some analysts link the lira's new decline to a speech by Erdogan yesterday, in which he promised to "do whatever it takes in Syria," which is interpreted in the Turkish press as a possible signal of a new military intervention in that country, where Turkey controls several border areas.

title: *Fitch Affirms Alternatifbank at 'B+'; Outlook Stable
text:
5 Oct 2021 12:58 ET  Press Release: Fitch Affirms Alternatifbank  at 'B+'; Outlook Stable


 
 
The following is a press release from Fitch Ratings : 
      Fitch Ratings-Frankfurt am Main-05 October 2021: 

Fitch Ratings has affirmed Alternatifbank A.S .'s (Alternatifbank ) Long-Term Foreign-Currency (LT FC) Issuer Default Rating (IDR) at 'B+' with a Stable Outlook. It has also affirmed the bank's Viability Rating (VR) at 'b-'.

In addition, Fitch has affirmed the support-driven LT FC IDR of Alternatif Finansal Kiralama A.S at 'B+' with a Stable Outlook, which mirrors that of the parent Alternatifbank .

A full list of rating actions is at the end of this Rating Action Commentary.

Key Rating Drivers

IDRS, SUPPORT RATINGS

The bank's LT FC IDR is driven by institutional support from its 100% shareholder, The Commercial Bank (P.Q.S.C.) (CBQ; A/Stable). Our view of the propensity and ability of CBQ to provide support reflects Alternatifbank 's ownership, strategic importance, integration and role within the wider group.

Fitch's view of government intervention risk caps the bank's LT FC IDR at 'B+', one notch below Turkey's rating. This reflects our assessment that weaknesses in Turkey's external finances make an intervention in the banking system impeding banks' ability to service their FC obligations more likely to happen than a sovereign default.

The LT LC IDR, which is also driven by institutional support, is one notch above the bank's LT FC IDR, reflecting our view of a lower likelihood of government intervention in LC.

The Stable Outlook on the bank's LT IDRs mirrors that on the sovereign rating.

VR

Alternatifbank 's 'b-' VR is constrained by its weak core capitalisation, and weak, below-sector-average profitability. The VR also reflects the bank's limited franchise and the concentration of operations in the volatile Turkish market, adequate asset quality for its rating and manageable refinancing risks.

The Turkish operating environment remains volatile amid weak monetary policy credibility, exposure to investor sentiment (due to high FC debt), deposit dollarisation, and inflationary pressures. The lira depreciated by 11% against the US dollar in 8M21, exacerbated by the replacement of the central bank's governor in March 2021, and has come under further pressure following the latest 100bp cut in the policy rate.

Nevertheless, we have revised the outlook on the operating environment score to stable, reflecting our view that the inherent uncertainty and volatility in the Turkish operating environment is captured at the 'b+' level, despite some persistent downside risk to banks' financial profiles. The outlook considers Turkey's resilient growth prospects (Fitch's 2021 GDP forecast: 9.2%; 2022: 3.5%), the easing in short-term external financing pressures and the Stable Outlook on the sovereign rating (BB-/Stable) - given the high interlinkages between the banking sector and sovereign balance sheets.

The impact of the gradual removal (expected from 4Q21) of most regulatory forbearance measures that have supported reported asset quality and capital metrics during the pandemic, is likely to be limited for Alternatifbank .

Alternatifbank has market shares of assets, loans and deposits of below 1%. Its growth has moderated in recent years (1H21: lending contracted by 4% (FX-adjusted); sector: up 4%), due to operating environment and capitalisation constraints. FC lending is still high (46%; sector: 37%), despite deleveraging, inflated by the lira depreciation.

Alternatifbank 's non-performing loans (NPLs) ratio at end-1H21 (3.0%; end-2020: 4.8%) is below sector average. Foreclosed assets comprised a further 2% of total assets (24% of common equity Tier 1 (CET1)). Stage 2 loans were a fairly high 12% of loans (50% restructured) - broadly in line with the sector - largely comprising FC, including legacy construction and real estate loans.

Asset-quality risks are high though they have partly eased given the resilient growth outlook. Risks reflect concentrations (end-1H21: the top 25 cash loans comprised about 42% of total loans (4.3x of CET1)) and exposure to the construction (17%, including real estate development), energy (7%) and logistics (5%) sectors.

Total NPLs reserves coverage rose to 128% at end-1H21 (sector: 139%), mainly reflecting NPL collections. Specific Stage 3 coverage (61%) reflects reliance on collateral, though Stage 2 reserves coverage was adequate (12%).

Core capitalisation is very weak given concentration risks, the lira depreciation (given the inflation of FC risk-weighted assets) and weak internal capital generation. Leverage is also high (end-1H21: 6.3% tangible equity/tangible assets). Its CET1 ratio was 8.1% at end-1H21 (7.8% net of forbearance), implying less than a 100bp buffer above its 7% minimum regulatory requirement, though we expect capital support from CBQ to continue to underpin compliance with regulatory minimums. Unreserved NPLs (net of specific reserves) were equal to 12% of CET1 at end-1H21. Pre-impairment operating profit (annualised) comprised just 0.4% of average loans.

The total capital ratio is higher (end-1H21: 16.6%), reflecting additional Tier 1 capital from CBQ, which provides a partial hedge against lira depreciation.

CBQ has provided regular capital support to Alternatifbank (USD225 million since 2018), including a USD25 million cash injection (equal to 9% of end-2020 equity) in 1Q21, with a further USD25 million budgeted in 4Q21, which would provide about 60bp uplift to its CET1 ratio, and USD50 million by end-2023.

Alternatifbank 's below-sector-average profitability in recent years reflects the loan book clean-up and low economies of scale. Margins have also tightened significantly since 3Q20 (1H21: 1.8%; sector: 3.7%) due to the high lira interest-rate environment, given that the bank's liabilities reprice quicker than its assets, and the bank's concentration in low-yielding corporate lending and expensive term deposit and FC wholesale funding. It reported an operating profit loss in 1H21, reflecting low growth and revenue generation, and the full absorption by loan impairments of pre-impairment operating profit.

We expect performance to remain weak and under pressure in the medium term. However, margins should benefit from lower lira interest rates and growth in granular deposit funding.

Customer deposits were 57% of total funding at end-1H21, of which 46% is in FC (sector: 56%). The bank's gross loans/deposits ratio of 130% underperforms the sector (105%), reflecting reliance on FC wholesale funding (43% of total funding). Excluding parent funding, FC wholesale funding is lower, but still high (28%). Refinancing risks remain high, as for the sector, but are partly mitigated by the presence of CBQ.

The bank's funding and liquidity profile is adequate, and supported by the presence of CBQ. FC wholesale funding maturities are fairly diversified, while FC liquidity is sufficient to cover short-term FC non-deposit liabilities (net of parent funding) due within a year, in addition to about 10% of FC deposits at end-1H21. Nevertheless, FC liquidity could come under pressure from prolonged market closure or deposit instability, if not offset by shareholder support.

NATIONAL RATING

The affirmation of the National Rating reflects our view that Alternatifbank 's creditworthiness in LC relative to other Turkish issuers has not changed.

SUBSIDIARY RATING

The ratings of Alternatif Finansal Kiralama are equalised with those of the parent, reflecting Fitch's view that it is a core and highly integrated subsidiary and the sole provider of leasing products within the group. Our view of support also considers Alternatif Finansal Kiralama's full ownership and shared branding. The Stable Outlook mirrors that of its parent bank.

Rating Sensitivities Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to negative rating action/downgrade:

LT IDRs, SUPPORT RATING

The bank's LT IDRs are sensitive to Fitch's view of government intervention risk in the banking sector, and could be downgraded if Fitch assesses this risk as having increased. The ratings could also be downgraded if Fitch's assessment of the bank's owner's ability and propensity to provide support materially weakens.

VR

The bank's VR could be downgraded due to further erosion of its core capitalisation, given its limited buffer over the regulatory minimum, which could result from a significant increase in impaired loans leading to losses or if unreserved NPLs materially rise.

The VR is sensitive to a marked deterioration in the operating environment, given the concentration of its operations in the domestic market. A sharp weakening in asset quality, likely resulting from high concentration risks, or a weakening in the bank's FC liquidity position due to deposit outflows or an inability to refinance maturing external obligations, could result in a downgrade if not offset by shareholder support.

SUBSIDIARY RATING

The ratings are sensitive to adverse changes in Alternatifbank 's ratings; and Fitch's view of the ability and willingness of the parent to provide support in case of need.

Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to positive rating action/upgrade:

LT IDRs, SUPPORT RATING

An upgrade of Turkey's LT IDRs or a revision of the Outlook to Positive would likely lead to a similar action on the bank's LT IDRs. A material improvement in Turkey's external finances or a marked increase in its net FX reserves position, resulting in a significant reduction in our view of government intervention risk in the banking sector, could lead to an upgrade of the bank's LT FC IDR to the level of Turkey's LT FC IDR. However, given Turkey's large external vulnerabilities and weak net FX reserves position, this would take time, in our view.

VR

Upside to the VR is unlikely at present unless there is a material strengthening in the bank's core capitalisation and underlying profitability.

SUBSIDIARY RATING

An upgrade of Alternatifbank would likely lead to a similar action on the subsidiary's ratings.

NATIONAL RATING

5 Oct 2021 12:58 ET  Press Release: Fitch Affirms Alternatifbank  at -2-

The National Rating is sensitive to changes in the bank's LT LC IDR and its creditworthiness relative to other Turkish issuers.

Best/Worst Case Rating Scenario

International scale credit ratings of Financial Institutions and Covered Bond issuers have a best-case rating upgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a positive direction) of three notches over a three-year rating horizon; and a worst-case rating downgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a negative direction) of four notches over three years. The complete span of best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings for all rating categories ranges from 'AAA' to 'D'. Best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings are based on historical performance. Unless otherwise disclosed in this section, the highest level of ESG credit relevance is a score of '3'. title: *Fitch Affirms Burgan Bank Turkey at 'B+'; Outlook Stable
text:
5 Oct 2021 15:50 ET  Press Release: Fitch Affirms Burgan Bank Turkey at 'B+'; Outlook Stable


 
 
The following is a press release from Fitch Ratings : 
 

Fitch Ratings -London-05 October 2021:

Fitch Ratings has affirmed Burgan Bank A.S.'s (Burgan Bank Turkey) Long-Term Foreign-Currency (LTFC) Issuer Default Rating (IDR) at 'B+'. The Outlook is Stable. The bank's Viability Rating (VR) has been affirmed at 'b-'. A full list of rating actions is below.

Key Rating Drivers

IDRs

Burgan Bank Turkey's 'B+' LTFC IDR is driven by institutional support from its 99.4% shareholder, Kuwait-based Burgan Bank K.P.S.C. (Burgan Bank Kuwait; A+/Negative), in case of need. This reflects the bank's ownership and integration with the group, common branding and the record of support. Burgan Bank Turkey is Burgan Bank Kuwait's largest international subsidiary, and represented 15% of the parent's consolidated assets at end-2020.

Government intervention risk, which might impede banks' ability to service FC obligations, caps the bank's LTFC IDR at 'B+', one notch below Turkey's rating. The bank's LT Local-Currency (LC) IDR is one notch above its LTFC IDR, in line with Turkey's rating, given lower intervention risk in LC. The Stable Outlook on the LT IDRs mirror that on the sovereign rating (BB-/Stable).

VR

The VR reflects the bank's exposure to Turkish operating environment risks, weak operating profitability and high asset quality risks, in light of which, and notwithstanding the record of capital support from its parent, we consider core capitalisation to be tight. Burgan Bank Turkey has a limited franchise (end-1H21: 0.4% of sector assets) and limited competitive advantages.

The Turkish operating environment remains highly volatile amid weak monetary policy credibility, banks' exposure to investor sentiment (due to high foreign currency debt), high deposit dollarisation, lira weakness and inflationary pressures (Fitch forecast: 17.2% inflation at end-2021). The lira depreciated 11% against the US dollar in 8M21, exacerbated by the abrupt replacement of the central bank governor in March 2021, and has come under further pressure following the latest 100bp cut in the policy rate.

Nevertheless, we have revised the outlook on the 'b+' operating environment to stable, reflecting our view that the inherent uncertainty and volatility in the Turkish operating environment is captured at the 'b+' level, despite some persistent downside risk to banks' financial profiles. The stable outlook considers Turkey's resilient growth prospects (Fitch's 2021 GDP forecast: 9.2%; 2022: 3.5%) and the easing in short-term external financing pressures supported by a narrowing current account deficit and a recovery in gross sovereign FX reserves position, among others. It also reflects the Stable Outlook on the sovereign rating, given the high interlinkages between the banking sector and sovereign balance sheets.

The gradual removal (expected from 4Q21) of regulatory forbearance measures poses a risk to the bank's nonperforming loan (NPL) ratio, which is significantly higher net of forbearance.

The bank's asset quality metrics significantly underperform the sector (end-1H21: NPLs: 10.6% of loans; sector: 3.7%) and Stage 2 loans (19%). Exposure to FC lending (including project finance) reduced to 54% at end-1H21 (sector: 36%) from 59% at end-2020 but remains high.

In addition, exposure to single-name risk, and the risky tourism (11%), real estate (9%) and contracting (9%) sectors is material. The 25 largest cash exposures amounted to an exceptionally high 57% of gross loans (5.8x equity). Total reserves coverage of NPLs (80%; 88% including free provisions) is significantly below the sector average (139%), reflecting low specific reserves coverage (35%) due to a highly collateralised portfolio. However, reserves (24%) against Stage 2 loans are above the sector average. Provisions are calculated as per IFRS 9 methodology.

Operating profitability is weak and likely to remain under pressure, given a tighter net interest margin (1H21: 2.8%; 2020: 3.5%, including swap costs), limited economies of scale (Fitch-adjusted cost/income ratio: 62%; sector: 37%) and asset quality risks. The bank made a TRY9.8 million operating loss in 1H21 excluding gains from the sale of fixed assets of TRY96.3 million, which Fitch considers as non-recurring income, following a TRY300 million operating loss in 2020 (equal to 18% of common equity Tier 1 (CET1)). However, the latter included TRY195 million of free provisions (equal to under 1% of loans) set aside for unexpected losses, which were not released in 1H21 and are not expected to be fully released in the short term. The bank's after-tax profit was TRY75.9 million in 1H21, compared with an after-tax loss of TRY267 million in 2020.

The bank's CET1 ratio improved to 8.6% at end-1H21 (end 2020: 7.5%), following the conversion of subordinated debt from its parent. Core capitalisation remains very weak, given thin buffers over regulatory requirements, unreserved NPLs (equal to 22% of CET1), weak internal capital generation, concentration risks, and the lira depreciation (which inflates FC risk-weighted assets). We expect ordinary support from Burgan Bank Kuwait to support the bank's compliance with its 7.0% CET1 regulatory minimum.

The bank's total capital adequacy ratio (end-1H21: 18.7%) is supported by FC Tier 2 debt from its parent, which provides a partial hedge against lira depreciation. In 2020, the bank converted USD50 million of subordinated debt from its parent to a perpetual loan, supporting its Tier 1 ratio (end-1H21: 10.4%).

Customer deposits (end-1H21: 67.5% of total funding) are mainly in FC (63%; sector: 56%) and from retail depositors (72%). The deposit base is moderately concentrated, with the 20 largest deposits comprising 17%. A high loans/deposits ratio (end-1H21: 134%, including finance leases), reflects a high share of both loans and wholesale funding.

FC wholesale funding comprises 30% of total funding, but a lower 10% net of group funding, mitigating refinancing risks. FC liquidity is adequate, with additional comfort provided by the presence of the bank's parent, and is broadly sufficient to cover FC wholesale funding falling due within 12 months. However, it could come under pressure in the event of prolonged market closure or FC deposit outflows.

Rating Sensitivities Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to negative rating action/downgrade:

IDRs, VR

The bank's LT IDRs are sensitive to a change in the sovereign rating and Fitch's view of government intervention risk in the banking sector. Its ratings are also sensitive to our view of the parent's ability and propensity to provide support, in case of need.

The bank's VR could be downgraded due to further erosion of its core capitalisation, given its limited buffer over the regulatory minimum, which could result from a significant increase in impaired loans leading to losses or if unreserved NPLs materially rise.

A marked deterioration in the operating environment given the concentration of its operations in the domestic market, or of the bank's FC liquidity position due to deposit outflows or an inability to refinance maturing FC debt, if not offset by shareholder support, could also result in a downgrade of the VR.

Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to positive rating action/upgrade:

IDRs, VR

An upgrade of Turkey's LT IDRs or revision of the Outlook to Positive would likely lead to similar action on the bank's LT IDRs. A material improvement in Turkey's external finances or a marked increase in its net FX reserves position, resulting in a significant reduction in our view of government intervention risk in the banking sector, could lead to an upgrade of the bank's LTFC IDR to the level of Turkey's LTFC IDR. However, given Turkey's large external vulnerabilities and weak net FX reserves position, this would take time, in our view.

The VR could be upgraded upon a marked strengthening of its core capitalisation, combined with an easing of asset quality risks and a sustained, significant improvement in underlying profitability.

OTHER DEBT AND ISSUER RATINGS: KEY RATING DRIVERS

NATIONAL RATING

The National Rating has been affirmed at 'AA(tur)' with a Stable Outlook, reflecting our view that the bank's creditworthiness in local currency relative to other Turkish issuers has not changed.

OTHER DEBT AND ISSUER RATINGS: RATING SENSITIVITIES Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to negative rating action/downgrade:

NATIONAL RATING

The National Rating is sensitive to a negative rating action on the bank's LTLC IDR or a worsening in its relative creditworthiness to other Turkish issuers.

Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to positive rating action/upgrade:

NATIONAL RATING

The National Rating is sensitive to changes in the bank's LTLC IDR and also in its relative creditworthiness to other Turkish issuers.

International scale credit ratings of Financial Institutions and Covered Bond issuers have a best-case rating upgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a positive direction) of three notches over a three-year rating horizon; and a worst-case rating downgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a negative direction) of four notches over three years. title: Fitch Affirms Alternatifbank at 'B+'; Outlook Stable
text:
Fitch Ratings-Frankfurt am Main-05 October 2021: Fitch Ratings has affirmed Alternatifbank A.S.'s (Alternatifbank) Long-Term Foreign-Currency (LT FC) Issuer Default Rating (IDR) at 'B+' with a Stable Outlook. It has also affirmed the bank's Viability Rating (VR) at 'b-'.

In addition, Fitch has affirmed the support-driven LT FC IDR of Alternatif Finansal Kiralama A.S at 'B+' with a Stable Outlook, which mirrors that of the parent Alternatifbank.

A full list of rating actions is at the end of this Rating Action Commentary.

Key Rating Drivers

IDRS, SUPPORT RATINGS

The bank's LT FC IDR is driven by institutional support from its 100% shareholder, The Commercial Bank (P.Q.S.C.) (CBQ; A/Stable). Our view of the propensity and ability of CBQ to provide support reflects Alternatifbank's ownership, strategic importance, integration and role within the wider group.

Fitch's view of government intervention risk caps the bank's LT FC IDR at 'B+', one notch below Turkey's rating. This reflects our assessment that weaknesses in Turkey's external finances make an intervention in the banking system impeding banks' ability to service their FC obligations more likely to happen than a sovereign default.

The LT LC IDR, which is also driven by institutional support, is one notch above the bank's LT FC IDR, reflecting our view of a lower likelihood of government intervention in LC.

The Stable Outlook on the bank's LT IDRs mirrors that on the sovereign rating.

VR

Alternatifbank's 'b-' VR is constrained by its weak core capitalisation, and weak, below-sector-average profitability. The VR also reflects the bank's limited franchise and the concentration of operations in the volatile Turkish market, adequate asset quality for its rating and manageable refinancing risks.

The Turkish operating environment remains volatile amid weak monetary policy credibility, exposure to investor sentiment (due to high FC debt), deposit dollarisation, and inflationary pressures. The lira depreciated by 11% against the US dollar in 8M21, exacerbated by the replacement of the central bank's governor in March 2021, and has come under further pressure following the latest 100bp cut in the policy rate.

Nevertheless, we have revised the outlook on the operating environment score to stable, reflecting our view that the inherent uncertainty and volatility in the Turkish operating environment is captured at the 'b+' level, despite some persistent downside risk to banks' financial profiles. The outlook considers Turkey's resilient growth prospects (Fitch's 2021 GDP forecast: 9.2%; 2022: 3.5%), the easing in short-term external financing pressures and the Stable Outlook on the sovereign rating (BB-/Stable) - given the high interlinkages between the banking sector and sovereign balance sheets.

The impact of the gradual removal (expected from 4Q21) of most regulatory forbearance measures that have supported reported asset quality and capital metrics during the pandemic, is likely to be limited for Alternatifbank.

Alternatifbank has market shares of assets, loans and deposits of below 1%. Its growth has moderated in recent years (1H21: lending contracted by 4% (FX-adjusted); sector: up 4%), due to operating environment and capitalisation constraints. FC lending is still high (46%; sector: 37%), despite deleveraging, inflated by the lira depreciation.

Alternatifbank's non-performing loans (NPLs) ratio at end-1H21 (3.0%; end-2020: 4.8%) is below sector average. Foreclosed assets comprised a further 2% of total assets (24% of common equity Tier 1 (CET1)). Stage 2 loans were a fairly high 12% of loans (50% restructured) - broadly in line with the sector - largely comprising FC, including legacy construction and real estate loans.

Asset-quality risks are high though they have partly eased given the resilient growth outlook. Risks reflect concentrations (end-1H21: the top 25 cash loans comprised about 42% of total loans (4.3x of CET1)) and exposure to the construction (17%, including real estate development), energy (7%) and logistics (5%) sectors.

Total NPLs reserves coverage rose to 128% at end-1H21 (sector: 139%), mainly reflecting NPL collections. Specific Stage 3 coverage (61%) reflects reliance on collateral, though Stage 2 reserves coverage was adequate (12%).

Core capitalisation is very weak given concentration risks, the lira depreciation (given the inflation of FC risk-weighted assets) and weak internal capital generation. Leverage is also high (end-1H21: 6.3% tangible equity/tangible assets). Its CET1 ratio was 8.1% at end-1H21 (7.8% net of forbearance), implying less than a 100bp buffer above its 7% minimum regulatory requirement, though we expect capital support from CBQ to continue to underpin compliance with regulatory minimums. Unreserved NPLs (net of specific reserves) were equal to 12% of CET1 at end-1H21. Pre-impairment operating profit (annualised) comprised just 0.4% of average loans.

The total capital ratio is higher (end-1H21: 16.6%), reflecting additional Tier 1 capital from CBQ, which provides a partial hedge against lira depreciation.

CBQ has provided regular capital support to Alternatifbank (USD225 million since 2018), including a USD25 million cash injection (equal to 9% of end-2020 equity) in 1Q21, with a further USD25 million budgeted in 4Q21, which would provide about 60bp uplift to its CET1 ratio, and USD50 million by end-2023.

Alternatifbank's below-sector-average profitability in recent years reflects the loan book clean-up and low economies of scale. Margins have also tightened significantly since 3Q20 (1H21: 1.8%; sector: 3.7%) due to the high lira interest-rate environment, given that the bank's liabilities reprice quicker than its assets, and the bank's concentration in low-yielding corporate lending and expensive term deposit and FC wholesale funding. It reported an operating profit loss in 1H21, reflecting low growth and revenue generation, and the full absorption by loan impairments of pre-impairment operating profit.

We expect performance to remain weak and under pressure in the medium term. However, margins should benefit from lower lira interest rates and growth in granular deposit funding.

Customer deposits were 57% of total funding at end-1H21, of which 46% is in FC (sector: 56%). The bank's gross loans/deposits ratio of 130% underperforms the sector (105%), reflecting reliance on FC wholesale funding (43% of total funding). Excluding parent funding, FC wholesale funding is lower, but still high (28%). Refinancing risks remain high, as for the sector, but are partly mitigated by the presence of CBQ.

The bank's funding and liquidity profile is adequate, and supported by the presence of CBQ. FC wholesale funding maturities are fairly diversified, while FC liquidity is sufficient to cover short-term FC non-deposit liabilities (net of parent funding) due within a year, in addition to about 10% of FC deposits at end-1H21. Nevertheless, FC liquidity could come under pressure from prolonged market closure or deposit instability, if not offset by shareholder support.

NATIONAL RATING

The affirmation of the National Rating reflects our view that Alternatifbank's creditworthiness in LC relative to other Turkish issuers has not changed.

SUBSIDIARY RATING

The ratings of Alternatif Finansal Kiralama are equalised with those of the parent, reflecting Fitch's view that it is a core and highly integrated subsidiary and the sole provider of leasing products within the group. Our view of support also considers Alternatif Finansal Kiralama's full ownership and shared branding. The Stable Outlook mirrors that of its parent bank.

Rating Sensitivities

Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to negative rating action/downgrade:

LT IDRs, SUPPORT RATING

The bank's LT IDRs are sensitive to Fitch's view of government intervention risk in the banking sector, and could be downgraded if Fitch assesses this risk as having increased. The ratings could also be downgraded if Fitch's assessment of the bank's owner's ability and propensity to provide support materially weakens.

VR

The bank's VR could be downgraded due to further erosion of its core capitalisation, given its limited buffer over the regulatory minimum, which could result from a significant increase in impaired loans leading to losses or if unreserved NPLs materially rise.

The VR is sensitive to a marked deterioration in the operating environment, given the concentration of its operations in the domestic market. A sharp weakening in asset quality, likely resulting from high concentration risks, or a weakening in the bank's FC liquidity position due to deposit outflows or an inability to refinance maturing external obligations, could result in a downgrade if not offset by shareholder support.

SUBSIDIARY RATING

The ratings are sensitive to adverse changes in Alternatifbank's ratings; and Fitch's view of the ability and willingness of the parent to provide support in case of need.

Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to positive rating action/upgrade:

LT IDRs, SUPPORT RATING

An upgrade of Turkey's LT IDRs or a revision of the Outlook to Positive would likely lead to a similar action on the bank's LT IDRs. A material improvement in Turkey's external finances or a marked increase in its net FX reserves position, resulting in a significant reduction in our view of government intervention risk in the banking sector, could lead to an upgrade of the bank's LT FC IDR to the level of Turkey's LT FC IDR. However, given Turkey's large external vulnerabilities and weak net FX reserves position, this would take time, in our view.

VR

Upside to the VR is unlikely at present unless there is a material strengthening in the bank's core capitalisation and underlying profitability.

SUBSIDIARY RATING

An upgrade of Alternatifbank would likely lead to a similar action on the subsidiary's ratings.

NATIONAL RATING

The National Rating is sensitive to changes in the bank's LT LC IDR and its creditworthiness relative to other Turkish issuers.

Best/Worst Case Rating Scenario

International scale credit ratings of Financial Institutions and Covered Bond issuers have a best-case rating upgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a positive direction) of three notches over a three-year rating horizon; and a worst-case rating downgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a negative direction) of four notches over three years. The complete span of best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings for all rating categories ranges from 'AAA' to 'D'. Best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings are based on historical performance. Unless otherwise disclosed in this section, the highest level of ESG credit relevance is a score of '3'. This means ESG issues are credit neutral or have only a minimal credit impact on the entity, either due to their nature or the way in which they are being managed by the entity.
