title: Erdogan's  Central Bank  Shuffle Unsettles Investors -- WSJ
text:
This article is being republished as part of our daily reproduction of WSJ.com articles that also appeared in the U.S. print edition of The Wall Street Journal (March 22, 2021).

Turkey's newly appointed central bank governor sought to reassure markets on Sunday as investors braced for turmoil following the abrupt firing of his predecessor by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Sahap Kavcioglu, a former member of parliament from Mr. Erdogan's Justice and Development Party who was named to the post late Friday, said the bank's main objective is to achieve "a permanent fall in inflation."

In a statement, Mr. Kavcioglu outlined the importance of tackling inflation, saying it "will foster macroeconomic stability" by lowering borrowing costs and reducing "country risk premiums," helping set the stage for sustainable growth.

The change in command atop the central bank -- a day after it again raised interest rates -- prompted concern among economists and investors about the trajectory of the economy in Turkey, an aspiring global power whose influence extends through the Middle East, Europe and beyond.

The previous governor, Naci Agbal, who was appointed in November of last year, had repeatedly raised interest rates in an effort to tame inflation. His dismissal has prompted concerns that his successor could move less aggressively to tighten monetary policy.

Mr. Kavcioglu, who had been working as a columnist at a pro-government newspaper, has publicly sided with Mr. Erdogan's preference for lower interest rates.

Economists were predicting a steep drop in the value of the Turkish lira when markets open on Monday morning, as investors move to scale back their exposure to Turkish assets until the likely course of policy becomes clearer. In early trading, the lira fell more than 12% against the dollar, according to FactSet.

"It will cause chaos for the Turkish economy. You will see tomorrow morning when the markets are open," said Durmus Yilmaz, a former governor of the Turkish central bank and currently a member of parliament with the centrist opposition Iyi Party.

A sharp decline in the value of Turkey's currency would ratchet up inflation, raise the cost of imported goods including oil, and hurt living standards for ordinary Turks, economists warned.

"It really is puzzling. It makes no economic sense whatsoever," said Refet Gurkaynak, a leading Turkish economist at Bilkent University in Ankara, referring to Mr. Agbal's removal.

The firing of Mr. Agbal was the third time Mr. Erdogan has replaced a central bank chief in less than two years. Before the bank chief's ouster, the Turkish economy was already struggling due to the coronavirus pandemic, which wiped out tourism and slowed international trade, as well as a currency crisis that began in 2018.

The change also comes as Mr. Erdogan has expanded his power within Turkey's political and economic system and asserted Turkey's influence abroad, intervening in wars in Syria, Libya, and the Caucasus region in recent years.

Within Turkey, the government is also intensifying a clampdown on some of Mr. Erdogan's opponents. Last week, a top Ankara prosecutor called for the banning of one of Turkey's largest political parties, the leftist People's Democratic Party, which the government accuses of having ties to a Kurdish militant group that is banned as a terrorist organization.

In the same set of decrees in which he fired Mr. Agbal, Mr. Erdogan withdrew Turkey from an international treaty known as the Istanbul Convention designed to combat violence against women, sparking criticism from women's groups and a rebuke from President Biden. Mr. Biden called the decision "a disheartening step backward for the international movement to end violence against women globally."

After years of unpredictable policy-making, Mr. Agbal's tenure inspired confidence from foreign investors. When Mr. Agbal began raising interest rates last year, investors poured a net $4.6 billion back into Turkish lira assets. Turkey remains dependent on foreign funds to finance its current-account deficit.

As a result, Mr. Agbal's removal surprised investors and economists. The most recent interest-rate increase came on March 18, when the bank lifted its benchmark rate to 19% from 17%, triggering a surge in the value of the lira.

The rate increases put Mr. Agbal at odds with Mr. Erdogan, who has repeatedly expressed a preference for low interest rates, espousing the unorthodox view that high interest rates lead to inflation. "I don't believe my country will develop with high interest rates," he said in a speech to a business group in January.

The new central bank chief, Mr. Kavcioglu, also criticized the rate increases in his newspaper columns, fueling concerns among investors that he will reverse Mr. Agbal's policies.

"There's a disappointment to the investment case that a lot of people, including me, were building that there would be a cap on inflation and now that looks much less likely," said Kieran Curtis, an emerging-markets fund manager at Aberdeen Standard Investments.

The surprise change at the central bank is also fueling anxieties among some regular Turkish people who are worried about the country's economic and political trajectory.

"In general, there is a problem with stability in the country," said Cihan Ilter, the 35-year-old manager of two restaurants in Istanbul.

"In the past, this wasn't so. We felt the effects of such higher level economic decisions, perhaps in a year or more. But now, because the Turkish economy is very fragile, we feel the effects immediately," he said.

The decision is also likely to have a long-lasting impact on the credibility of Turkey's central bank, making it difficult to assuage concerns over higher inflation and price stability, said Maya Senussi, a senior economist at Oxford Economics.

Under Mr. Agbal's predecessor, Murat Uysal, cheap lending rates intended to boost growth created gaping holes in the country's current account as Turkish businesses and households imported more than they exported.

Concerns over the current-account deficit and interest rates below that of inflation caused foreign investors to pull a net $13.4 billion out of local currency bonds and stocks in the first 10 months of 2020.

The capital flight accelerated the lira's decline. The central bank opted to sell foreign currencies, from its own reserves and dollars borrowed from domestic banks, to buy the lira.

"Like many people I'm pretty flabbergasted," said Erik Meyersson, a senior economist at Swedish bank Handelsbanken. "Because of the appointment of Agbal, you've gotten investors to come back and that's pretty extraordinary. Now those portfolio flows, they will most likely reverse."

title: *Fitch Affirms ING Bank A.S at 'B+'; Outlook Negative
text:
4 Feb 2021 06:16 ET  Press Release: Fitch Affirms ING Bank A.S at 'B+'; Outlook Negative


 
 
The following is a press release from Fitch Ratings : 
      Fitch Ratings -London-04 February 2021: 

Fitch Ratings has affirmed ING Bank A.S.'s (INGBT) Long-Term Foreign-Currency Issuer Default Rating (LTFC IDR) at 'B+'. The Outlook is Negative. At the same time, the agency has affirmed the bank's Viability Rating (VR) at 'b+'.

A full list of rating actions is at the end of this commentary.

Key Rating Drivers

IDRS, SUPPORT RATING AND NATIONAL RATING

The LTFC IDR of INGBT is underpinned by both potential institutional support from its 100% owner, ING Bank N.V . (ING; AA-/Negative) and the bank's standalone creditworthiness (as defined by its VR). INGBT's '4' Support Rating reflects the bank's strategic importance to, integration and role within the wider ING group, and small size relative to ING's ability to provide support, if needed.

Fitch's view of government intervention risk caps the bank's LTFC IDR at 'B+', one notch below Turkey's LTFC IDR (BB-/Negative) and is also the main driver of the Negative Outlook on the bank. This reflects our assessment that weaknesses in Turkey's external finances would result in some form of intervention in the banking system that would impede banks' ability to service foreign-currency (FC) obligations more likely than a sovereign default. The sovereign's significantly weaker net FC reserves, together with weak monetary-policy credibility, have exacerbated external financing risks and this is a key driver of the Negative Outlook on the sovereign rating.

INGBT's 'BB-' Long-Term Local-Currency (LTLC) IDR, which is also driven by institutional support, is one notch above the LTFC IDR, reflecting our view of a lower likelihood of government intervention that would impede the bank's ability to service obligations in local currency (LC). However, the LTLC IDR is also on Negative Outlook, mirroring the sovereign Outlook, reflecting our view that the likelihood of government intervention that would impede the bank's ability to service obligations in LC is not lower than the probability of a sovereign default in LC obligations.

The affirmation of INGBT's National Rating reflects our view that the bank's creditworthiness in local currency relative to other Turkish issuers' remains unchanged.

VR

The affirmation of INGBT's VR at 'b+', a level that is in line with that of the largest, systemically important banks in the sector despite the bank's only small size, reflects the bank's record of solid performance, adequate loss absorption buffers and a below-peer-average risk appetite. However, the VR also consider the concentration of the bank's operations in the high-risk Turkish operating environment, limited franchise, moderate market shares and limited competitive advantages.

We see downside risks to INGBT's VR given uncertainty over the impact of the pandemic and potential further market volatility. A deeper and more extended economic contraction than expected would exacerbate operating-environment risks, heightening pressure on the bank's asset quality, capitalisation and performance metrics. In addition, regulatory forbearance measures, which are currently providing uplift to banks' reported asset quality and capital metrics, are due to expire at end-June 2021.

INGBT has pursued a conservative growth strategy by deleveraging its loan book from end-2018 to end-2020, largely reflecting a reduction in FC loans. The loan book contracted 3% in foreign-exchange (FX) adjusted terms in 9M20, despite the asset ratio requirement (AR), designed to stimulate sector loan growth, coming into force in May 2020. The bank aims to slightly increase loan growth in 2021, which will be focused mainly on LC, while it will avoid high-risk sectors such as real-estate, energy and infrastructure projects.

High FC lending (end-9M20: 42% of gross loans) heightens credit risks given that not all borrowers will be fully hedged against lira depreciation. INGBT adopts a cautious approach to new FC lending and has appetite mainly for export and manufacturing loans. It does not, as a matter of internal policy, undertake real-estate development projects and has a conservative policy towards energy projects.

The bank's impaired loans improved to 5.7% of total loans in 9M20 (2019: 7%), due primarily to collections and, to a lesser extent, regulatory forbearance. Stage 2 loans comprised 12.5% of gross loans at end-9M20, having declined significantly in recent years (2019: 10%; 2018: 24%). This decline should partly be considered in light of the high starting point resulting from the bank's conservative classification approach (mostly in line with ING Group standards). INGBT has subsequently reviewed its significant increase in credit risk (SICR) thresholds for large corporates by adjusting its portfolio accordingly.

Impaired loans were only 63% covered by specific reserves at end-9M20 reflecting reliance on collateral, which could be challenging to realise in the challenging Turkish market. Including Stage 1 and Stage 2 reserves, total loan loss allowance coverage increased to 80%, which was still significantly below the sector average (9M20: 127%).

We believe the improving growth outlook in Turkey (Fitch forecasts 3.5% real GDP growth in 2021), recent appreciation of the lira and greater market stabilisation should be moderately supportive of Turkish banks' asset quality and collection capacities. Nevertheless, risks remain to the downside given uncertainty over the pandemic, operating-environment volatility and a higher lira interest-rate environment.

The bank's profitability metrics deteriorated in 9M20 due to a slight decline in margins, loan-book contraction, but also to lower fees (due largely to regulatory restrictions) and weaker trading income. Cost growth remained muted in 2019 and 9M20, reflecting sound cost control.

Loan impairment charges (LICs) have remained manageable (9M20: equal to 25% of pre-impairment profit; 2019: 27%) but the bank reports weaker reserve coverage than peers. The bank's operating profit/risk-weighted assets (RWAs) declined to a still reasonable 2.6% at end-9M20 (sector: 2%) from 4% at end-2019.

Fitch expects further contraction in net interest margin (NIM) in 2021, given higher lira interest rates and that liabilities reprice more quickly than assets, as for the sector, which may only be partially offset by higher loan growth. We believe that the cost of risk (LICs/ gross loans) should remain manageable in 2021, given the improving macro backdrop and the front-loading of provisions.

Capitalisation is reasonable. INGBT's CET1 ratio was above peer average at 17% (excluding uplift from forbearance) at end-9M20. Its total capital ratio was a higher 23.3%, significantly above the 12% recommended regulatory minimum, supported by USD524 million of FC subordinated debt from ING, which provides a partial hedge against FC RWAs. However, as for the rest of the sector, capitalisation remains sensitive to lira depreciation (due to the inflation of FC RWAs) and asset-quality deterioration.

Unreserved non-performing loans (NPLs) amounted to 6% of CET1 capital at end-9M20, although pre-impairment operating profit (amounting to 4.3% of average loans at end-9M20, annualised) provides a significant buffer to absorb losses through the income statement before hitting capital.

The bank is largely deposit-funded (end-9M20: 68% of total funding) and its deposit base is fairly granular, reflecting a high proportion of retail deposits. Customer deposits contracted 9% in FX-adjusted terms in 9M20. Combined with loan deleveraging and a reduction in wholesale funding (largely from the ING group) in recent years, this led to further improvement in the gross loans-to-deposits to, albeit still high, 126% at end-9M20 from an exceptionally high 163% at end-2018 (end-2019: 116%).

Parent funding remains material (around 23% of total funding at end-9M20), but has been declining, reflecting INGBT's strategy to become increasingly self-funded, largely through customer deposits. External wholesale funding - comprising largely trade-finance and bilateral loans - amounted to a low 4% of total funding at end-9M20, mitigating refinancing risks.

The bank's available FC liquidity - comprising cash and interbank balances (including balances placed with the Central Bank of Turkey ), maturing FX swaps and government securities - fully covered short-term non-deposit FC liabilities falling due within a year at end-9M20. This means INGBT should be able to cope with a short-lived market closure. Consequently, and given its moderate external debt exposure, refinancing risks should be manageable, particularly considering potential liquidity support from ING. Nevertheless, FC liquidity could come under pressure from deposit instability or a prolonged loss of market access.

RATING SENSITIVITIES

Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to negative rating action/downgrade:

The bank's LT IDRs and Support Rating are primarily sensitive to a change in Turkey's sovereign rating or in Fitch's view of government intervention risk in the banking sector. A sovereign downgrade, particularly if triggered by further weakening in Turkey's external finances or in the country's FX reserves, or an increase in intervention risk, would likely result in a downgrade of INGBT's LT IDRs.

A marked reduction in Fitch's view of ING's propensity or ability to support INGBT (not our base case) could also result in a downgrade of the LTFC IDR, but this would only occur if at the same time Fitch also downgrades the bank's VR.

title: *Fitch Affirms Denizbank at 'B+'; Outlook Negative

4 Feb 2021 07:00 ET  Press Release: Fitch Affirms Denizbank at 'B+'; Outlook Negative


 
 
The following is a press release from Fitch Ratings : 
      Fitch Ratings -London-04 February 2021: 

Fitch Ratings has affirmed Denizbank A.S.'s Long-Term Foreign Currency (LTFC) Issuer Default Rating (IDR) at 'B+' with a Negative Outlook and Viability Rating (VR) at 'b+'.

The support-driven ratings of the bank's subsidiary Deniz Finansal Kiralama A.S. (Deniz Leasing), which are equalised with the parent, have also been affirmed. A full list of rating actions is below.

Key Rating Drivers

IDRS, SENIOR DEBT RATING, SUPPORT RATING AND NATIONAL RATING

Denizbank's 'B+' LTFC IDR and senior debt rating are underpinned by shareholder support and the bank's standalone creditworthiness, as reflected in its VR.

Denizbank's '4' Support Rating reflects its strategic importance to its 100% owner, UAE based Emirates NBD Bank PJSC (ENBD, A+/Stable), given its increasing integration and role within the wider group following Denizbank's acquisition from Sberbank of Russia (BBB/Stable) in July 2019. ENBD's LTFC IDR is driven by an extremely high probability of support from the UAE authorities given its flagship status in Dubai. We believe support for Denizbank would flow through from the UAE authorities via ENBD, in case of need, given ENBD's systemic importance to the UAE banking sector.

Integration between Denizbank and ENBD continues to increase, particularly in terms of the banks' risk management and control frameworks. Denizbank continues to be run largely by local management, but ENBD representatives dominate the bank's board, while a number of key ENBD management members, including the credit risk officer, are closely involved in the Turkish bank's operations and oversight.

Fitch's view of government intervention risk caps the bank's LTFC IDR at 'B+', one notch below Turkey's LTFC IDR (BB-/Negative), and is also the main driver of the Negative Outlook on the bank. This reflects our assessment that weaknesses in Turkey's external finances would make some form of intervention in the banking system that would impede banks' ability to service their foreign-currency (FC) obligations more likely than a sovereign default. The sovereign's significantly weaker net FC reserves position together with weak monetary policy credibility have exacerbated external financing risks, and this is a key driver of the Negative Outlook on the sovereign LT IDR.

Denizbank's 'BB-' Long-Term Local-Currency (LTLC) IDR, which is also driven by institutional support, is one notch above its LTFC IDR, reflecting our view of a lower likelihood of government intervention that would impede the bank's ability to service obligations in local currency (LC). However, the Outlook on the LTLC IDR is also Negative, mirroring the sovereign Outlook, reflecting our view that the likelihood of government intervention that would impede the bank's ability to service its obligations in LC is not lower than the probability of a sovereign default in LC obligations.

The affirmation of Denizbank's National Rating with a Stable Outlook reflects our view that the bank's creditworthiness in local currency relative to other Turkish issuers' is unchanged.

VR

The affirmation of Denizbank's 'b+' VR reflects the bank's reasonable strategy, moderate, but weakened, profitability record and adequate funding and liquidity profile. However, the VR also considers its moderate franchise (end-9M20: 3.3% of sector assets; unconsolidated basis) in the challenging Turkish operating environment, high exposure to risky sectors, asset quality that is weaker than peers, and only adequate core capitalisation.

Nevertheless, we see downside risks to Denizbank's VR given uncertainties over the impact of the pandemic and potential further market volatility. A deeper and more extended economic contraction than expected would exacerbate operating environment risks, heightening pressure on the bank's financial metrics. In addition, regulatory forbearance measures, which are currently providing uplift to banks' reported asset quality and capital metrics, are due to fall away at end-June 2021.

Denizbank's strategy has been largely unchanged since its acquisition by ENBD. It continues to target more granular SME and retail lending, primarily in lira, while also serving corporate and commercial customers. The bank also has a strong presence in the niche agriculture segment with a 13% market share of sector loans, supported by its large branch network.

Asset-quality risks were already high for Denizbank entering the crisis, exacerbated by the below-trend growth in Turkey and high exposure to risky segments and sectors. The bank reports above-sector-average foreign-currency (FC) lending (52% of loans at end-3Q20; peer average, 37%), which heightens credit risk where borrowers are not fully hedged against lira depreciation (the lira depreciated by 19% against the US dollar in 2020). However, about half of FC loans at end-3Q20 were issued by the bank's Austrian subsidiary Denizbank AG , half of which were to EU -based companies with access to FC revenues, or cash collateralised, partly mitigating the risks. FC exposures include significant project finance (about a fifth of total loans, equal to 1.6x common equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital at end-3Q20), which mainly comprise long-term, slowly amortising energy and infrastructure loans, meaning asset quality problems are likely to feed through only gradually.

Denizbank's impaired loans ratio fell moderately to 6.9% at end-3Q20, from 7.5% at end-2019, despite operating environment pressures, primarily reflecting regulatory forbearance in respect of loan classification and high nominal loan growth (22% in 9M20; or 5% on an FX adjusted basis). Net of forbearance, we estimate Denizbank's impaired loans ratio was 100bp higher. We expect impaired loans to rise moderately in absolute terms as government stimulus measures subside, regulatory forbearance is phased out (expected by end-1H21) and due to maturing pandemic-related loan deferrals.

Asset quality is also vulnerable to above-peer average Stage 2 loans (17% at end-9M20; flat on end-2019) of which about half were restructured, which could migrate to Stage 3 as loans season, and significant exposure to the risky SME segment (24% of loans). Denizbank had outstanding loan deferrals equal to 4% of gross loans at end-3Q20, of which 20% were classified as Stage 2. Exposures to the troubled energy (11% of loans at end-3Q20), tourism (11%) and construction (6%) sectors, which make up a high share of Denizbank's Stage 2 and restructured loan portfolios, are also sources of risk. Energy loans largely comprise project finance, which benefits to some extent from a government-guaranteed feed-in tariff set in US dollars. Similarly a high share infrastructure loans also benefit from state debt and revenue assumption guarantees, partly mitigating the credit risks.

Denizbank's total loan loss allowances increased materially to 125% of impaired loans at end-3Q20 (end-2019: 90%), which compares well with the peer average, partly reflecting the frontloading of pandemic-related provisions, but also higher reserve coverage of impaired loans and Stage 2 loans. We believe the improving growth outlook in Turkey (Fitch forecasts 3.5% real GDP growth in 2021), recent appreciation of the lira, and greater market stabilisation should be moderately supportive of Turkish banks' asset quality and collection capacities. Nevertheless, risks remain to the downside given uncertainty over the pandemic, operating environment volatility and the higher lira interest rate environment.

The bank's profitability metrics are weaker than most peers and have come under pressure since 2018 from significant loan impairment charges (LICs). LICs absorbed a high 73% of pre-impairment operating profit in 9M20 (78% in 2019). As a result, the bank's cost of risk (LICs/average gross loans: 4.4% in 9M20; 2019: 4%) significantly underperforms peers, although to some extent this is a consequence of conservative loan provisioning since the bank's acquisition, and in 9M20, the frontloading of provisions against the pandemic and increased provisioning against exposures to high risk sectors, in particular in FC.

Despite this, Denizbank's annualised operating profit/risk-weighted assets (RWAs) ratio moderately increased to 1.6% in 9M20, from 1.0% in 2019, as rapid loan growth in 2Q and 3Q20, accompanied with falling funding costs supported net interest income. Nevertheless, asset-quality weakness is likely to continue to weigh on performance, given operating environment risks and loan book seasoning and as forbearance measures are removed. We expect earnings to remain broadly flat in 2021 given the high interest rate environment, but margins could start to normalise in 2H21 if interest rates stabilise. In addition, pre-impairment operating profit (9M20: 6.3% of average loans; annualised) provides a significant buffer to absorb unexpected credit losses through the income statement.

We view Denizbank's capitalisation as only adequate for it its risk profile, given high asset quality risks, credit concentrations, weakened internal capital generation and sensitivity to lira depreciation (given a high share of FC loans). The CET1 ratio increased to 12.6% at end-3Q20 (from 10.4% at end-2019), supported by a TRY2.4billion capital increase from ENBD in 1Q20 (the equivalent of 1.4% of end-2019 RWAs), although net of regulatory forbearance (set to expire at end-1H21) it was a lower 10.7%. The total capital adequacy ratio was a higher 17.1% (14.7% net of forbearance) supported by US dollar-denominated, Tier-2 subordinated debt (from ENBD, for which the tenors were extended in 2Q20).

We expect capitalisation to remain under pressure in the near term due to an increase in RWAs (as forbearance is removed), asset quality risks and weaker profitability, although it should remain adequate, supported by the bank's significant pre-impairment profitability buffer and increased provisioning (unreserved NPLs were equal to minus 15% of CET1 capital at end-3Q20). We also believe ordinary capital support would be forthcoming from ENBD, if needed.

Denizbank is largely customer deposit-funded (78% of total funding at end-3Q20), mainly from retail customers (about 70%). A significant 71% of total customer deposits were in FC at end-3Q20. This reflects both sector-wide dollarisation but also deposits from Denizbank AG (equal to 35% of the total), given that these are mainly in euros (85%) and US dollars (15%). The share of FC deposits in Denizbank's unconsolidated accounts is a lower 55%, in line with the sector average. Wholesale funding (22% of total funding at end-3Q20), nearly all in FC, comprises short-term borrowings (8% of total funding), long-term borrowings (6%), subordinated debt (3%) and bank deposits (2%). Net of parent funding (6% of total funding) it was a more reasonable 16%. Wholesale funding could increase over the medium term, given that the bank is no longer subject to EU sanctions under its new owner and the bank is looking to diversify and extend the tenor of its funding.

Denizbank's loans/deposits ratio increased to a still reasonable 106% at end-3Q20, from 100% at end-2019, as loans grew faster than deposits in 9M20 as the bank complied with the asset ratio requirement. Denizbank reported good liquidity coverage ratios (LCR) at end-3Q20 (total LCR: 168%; FC LCR: 375%), while its available FC liquidity was sufficient to cover maturing FC wholesale debt over 12 months plus a moderate share of FC deposits.

FC liquidity comprises mainly FC swaps (primarily with the Turkish Central Bank (CBRT)), cash and interbank placements, and FC placed under the reserve option mechanism at the CBRT. Given only moderate FC market funding exposure and good FC liquidity, we believe refinancing risks at the bank should be manageable, particularly considering potential liquidity support from ENBD and improved market sentiment. However, FC liquidity could come under pressure from a change in investor sentiment, a prolonged loss of market access or FC deposit instability.

SUBSIDIARY AND AFFILIATED COMPANIES

Deniz Leasing's IDRs are driven by potential support from its 100% owner Denizbank. Our view of parental support reflects its strategic importance to and close integration with Denizbank, including the sharing of risk-assessment systems, management resources, branding and also customer referrals.

RATING SENSITIVITIES

Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to negative rating action/downgrade:

The bank's LT IDRs are primarily sensitive to a change in Turkey's sovereign rating or in Fitch's view of government intervention risk in the banking sector. A sovereign downgrade, particularly if triggered by further weakening in Turkey's external finances or in the country's FX reserves, or an increase in intervention risk would likely result in a downgrade of Denizbank's LT IDRs.

A marked reduction in ENBD's ability and propensity to support Denizbank could also result in a downgrade but only if the bank's VR was simultaneously downgraded. This is not our base case, given Denizbank's only recent acquisition and its strategic importance to ENBD.

The bank's VR could be downgraded due to a marked deterioration in the operating environment - as reflected in adverse changes to the lira exchange rate, interest rates, and economic growth prospects - or if economic recovery was not as swift as currently expected by Fitch. In addition, a greater than expected deterioration of Denizbank's asset quality and a protracted weakening in operating profitability would likely lead to a downgrade of the VR. The headroom at the current VR level would reduce and Denizbank's VR would likely be downgraded, if its CET1 ratio fell and remained below 9% for a sustained period or if we viewed capitalisation as no longer commensurate with the bank's risk profile.

The National Rating could be downgraded if the bank's LTLC IDR was downgraded and Fitch believed Denizbank's creditworthiness had weakened relative to other rated Turkish issuers.

Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to positive rating action/upgrade:

An upgrade of the bank's LTIDRs is unlikely in the near term given the Negative Outlooks. The Outlook on the LT IDRs could be revised to Stable if Fitch believes that the risk of government intervention in the banking system has abated, for example as a result of greater confidence in the sustainability of Turkey's external financing position. A significant reduction in intervention risks, likely reflected in a sovereign upgrade or resulting from a marked improvement in Turkey's net FX reserves position, could result in an upgrade.

Upside for the VR is limited in the near term in light of the challenging Turkish operating environment, the bank's moderate franchise, and the 'BB-' LTFC IDR of the Turkish sovereign. However, a record of resilient financial metrics notwithstanding the pandemic, an improvement in underlying asset quality and the maintenance of adequate core capitalisation in line with its risk profile would reduce downside risks to the VR.

The National Rating could be upgraded if Fitch believed Denizbank's creditworthiness had improved relative to other rated Turkish issuers.

SUBSIDIARY AND AFFILIATED COMPANIES

Deniz Leasing's ratings are sensitive to changes in Denizbank's Long-Term IDRs.

Best/Worst Case Rating Scenario

International scale credit ratings of Financial Institutions and Covered Bond issuers have a best-case rating upgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a positive direction) of three notches over a three-year rating horizon; and a worst-case rating downgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a negative direction) of four notches over three years. The complete span of best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings for all rating categories ranges from 'AAA' to 'D'. Best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings are based on historical performance. Summary of Financial Adjustments

An adjustment has been made in Fitch's financial spreadsheets of Denizbank that has had an impact on the core and complimentary metrics. Fitch has taken a loan that was classified as a financial asset measured at fair value through profit and loss in the bank's financial statements and reclassified it under gross loans as we believe this is the most appropriate line in Fitch spreadsheets to reflect this exposure.

title: *Fitch Affirms Turk Ekonomi Bankasi at 'B+'; Outlook Negative
text:
4 Feb 2021 07:22 ET  Press Release: Fitch Affirms Turk Ekonomi Bankasi  at 'B+'; Outlook Negative


 
 
The following is a press release from Fitch Ratings : 
      Fitch Ratings -London-04 February 2021: 

Fitch Ratings has affirmed Turk Ekonomi Bankasi A.S .'s (TEB) Long-Term Foreign-Currency Issuer Default Rating (LTFC IDR) at 'B+' with a Negative Outlook and Viability Rating (VR) at 'b+'. A full list of rating actions is below.

Key Rating Drivers

IDRS, SENIOR DEBT RATING, SUPPORT RATING AND NATIONAL RATING

TEB's 'B+' LTFC IDR and senior debt rating is underpinned by its standalone creditworthiness as reflected in its VR, and potential institutional support from its majority owner, BNP Paribas S.A . (BNPP; A+/Negative), as reflected in the bank's '4' Support Rating.

Fitch's view of institutional support reflects TEB's strategic importance to, integration with and role within the wider BNPP group and small size relative to BNPP's ability to provide support. TEB is 55%-owned but fully controlled by TEB Holding, in which BNP Paribas Fortis (BNPPF; A+/Stable) has a 50% stake. TEB is fully consolidated by BNPPF, a core subsidiary of BNPP. BNPP ultimately holds a 72.5% stake in TEB, including a 23.5% stake held directly.

Fitch's view of government intervention risk caps the bank's LTFC IDR at 'B+', one notch below Turkey's LTFC IDR (BB-/Negative), and is also the main driver of the Negative Outlook. This reflects our assessment that weaknesses in Turkey's external finances would make some form of intervention in the banking system that would impede banks' ability to service their foreign-currency (FC) obligations more likely than a sovereign default. The sovereign's significantly weaker net FC reserves position together with weak monetary policy credibility have exacerbated Turkey's external financing risks, and this is a key driver of the Negative Outlook on the sovereign rating.

TEB's 'BB-' Long-Term Local-Currency (LTLC) IDR, which is also driven by institutional support, is one notch above its LTFC IDR, reflecting our view of a lower likelihood of government intervention that would impede the bank's ability to service obligations in local currency (LC). However, the Outlook on the LTLC IDR is also Negative, mirroring the sovereign Outlook, reflecting our view that the likelihood of government intervention that would impede the bank's ability to service its obligations in LC is not lower than the probability of a sovereign default in LC obligations.

The affirmation of TEB's National Rating with a Stable Outlook reflects our view that the bank's creditworthiness in local currency relative to other Turkish issuers is unchanged.

VR

The affirmation of TEB's VR at 'b+' considers the bank's asset quality metrics, which are better than peers, reasonable profitability and adequate funding and liquidity profile. However, the VR also reflects TEB's moderate franchise (end-3Q20: 2.2% of banking sector assets; unconsolidated basis) in the challenging Turkish operating environment, high exposure to the fairly high-risk SME segment (end-3Q20: 34% of gross loans at end-3Q20) and only adequate core capitalisation.

Nevertheless, we see downside risks to TEB's VR given uncertainties over the impact of the pandemic and potential further market volatility. A deeper and more extended economic contraction than expected would exacerbate operating environment risks, heightening pressure on the bank's financial metrics. In addition, regulatory forbearance measures, which are currently providing uplift to banks' reported asset quality and capital metrics, are due to fall away at end-June 2021.

TEB has historically pursued a fairly conservative growth strategy, typically reporting below sector average loan growth. However, lending grew by 9% (FX adjusted basis) in 9M20 (peer average: 6%), despite operating environment pressures, and in response to the asset ratio requirement introduced by the regulators to stimulate sector growth during the pandemic (but was subsequently removed at end-2020). The asset ratio requirement also drove an increase in government securities and swaps with the Turkish Central Bank (CBRT) at TEB. In 2021, TEB aims to continue focussing on granular SME and retail lending, following a clean-up of the loan portfolios since 2018.

Asset-quality risks were already high for TEB entering the crisis, exacerbated by the below-trend growth in Turkey, above-sector-average exposure to the risky SME segment and exposure to the troubled construction and real estate (6% of loans) and energy (5%) sectors. Exposure to the pandemic-hit tourism sector (3%) is relatively low. A moderate share of foreign-currency (FC) lending (18% of loans at end-3Q20; peer average: 37%) also increases credit risks given that not all borrowers are likely to be fully hedged against lira depreciation (the lira depreciated by 19% against the US dollar in 2020). However, exposure to long-term FC investment and project finance loans is limited.

TEB's impaired loans ratio fell moderately to 4.6% at end-3Q20, from 5.8% at end-2019, despite operating environment pressures, primarily reflecting regulatory forbearance in respect of loan classification and high nominal loan growth (16% in 9M20). Net of forbearance, we estimate the impaired loans ratio was about 75bp higher. We expect impaired loans in absolute terms to rise moderately as government stimulus measures subside, regulatory forbearance is phased out (expected by end-1H21) and due to maturing pandemic-related loan deferrals.

In addition, TEB reported fairly high, albeit below peer average, Stage 2 loans at end-3Q20 (9.9% of loans; about one-fifth restructured), which could migrate to Stage 3 as loans season. Loan deferrals were equal to about 5% of gross loans at end-2020 and about a third were classified as Stage 2. Total reserve coverage of impaired loans was below the sector average at 104% at end-9M20, partly reflecting the bank's focus on SME, and therefore collateralised, lending.

The improving growth outlook in Turkey (Fitch forecasts 3.5% real GDP growth in 2021), recent appreciation of the lira and greater market stabilisation should be moderately supportive of Turkish banks' asset quality and collection capacities. Nevertheless, risks remain to the downside given uncertainty over the pandemic, operating environment volatility and the higher lira interest rate environment.

TEB's profitability is moderate (9M20: operating profit/risk-weighted assets (RWA) of 2.3%), although broadly in line with peers', dampened by its high cost base, limited economies of scale (costs/assets of 2.8%), and asset quality pressures. The bank reports an above-sector average net interest margin (NIM; 9M20: 6.0%, or 5.1% FX swap-adjusted), reflecting its focus on higher-margin, SME lending. However, we expect recently increased interest rates to put pressure on profitability in 2021, given that TEB's liabilities reprice faster than its assets, although margins could normalise in 2H21 if interest rates stabilise.

TEB's cost of risk (loan impairment charges/average gross loans ratio) compared well with the peer average in 9M20 (0.9% versus 2.1%) reflecting the clean-up of its loan book prior to the pandemic (since 2018), ensuing identification of, and adequate provisioning against, higher risk exposures and relatively high non-performing loans (NPL) collections in 9M20 (equivalent to about a third of end-2019 impaired loans). Nevertheless, we believe loan impairment charges (25% of pre-impairment operating profit in 9M20; 2019: 50%) could increase in 2021 as regulatory forbearance measures are withdrawn and given the only moderate loan loss coverage of problematic exposures. Pre-impairment operating profit (9M20: 3.5% of average loans; 2019: 4.2%) provides a reasonable, although reduced, buffer to absorb losses through the income statement.

We view TEB's core capitalisation as only adequate for its risk profile, internal capital generation and asset quality pressures. The common equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio increased to 13.0% at end-3Q20 (from 12.0% at end-2019), but would have been a lower 10.8% excluding uplift from regulatory forbearance (set to expire by end-1H21). The total regulatory capital ratio was more comfortable at 18.8% (or 15.9% net of forbearance) supported by FC subordinated Tier 2 debt from BNPP, which provides a partial hedge against potential lira depreciation.

We expect capitalisation to remain under pressure in the near term due to an increase in RWAs (as forbearance is removed), asset quality risks, sensitivity to lira depreciation and weaker profitability. However, it should remain adequate, given the bank's moderate buffers over minimum regulatory requirements and adequate reserves coverage (net unreserved NPLs: minus 1% of CET1 at end-3Q20). We also believe ordinary capital support would be forthcoming from BNPP, if needed.

TEB is largely deposit-funded (75% of total funding at end-3Q20) and its loans/deposits ratio (end-9M20: 95%) outperforms peers and the sector average. Customer deposits, primarily from retail customers, are sticky despite being contractually short term and also fairly granular, although FC deposits are significant (end-9M20: about half, albeit slightly below the sector average). Wholesale funding is nevertheless fairly high (end-9M20: 25% of total funding) and is largely in FC, but it includes material BNPP group funding. Net of the latter, external market funding amounted to a more moderate 18% of total funding at end-3Q20.

TEB reports good liquidity metrics (Liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) at end-3Q20: 168%; FC LCR: 375%). At end-3Q20 available FC liquidity was also sufficient to cover maturing FC wholesale debt over 12 months plus a moderate share of FC deposits. FC liquidity comprises mainly FC swaps (primarily with CBRT), FC cash and interbank placements and FC placed under the reserve option mechanism at the CBRT. We believe refinancing risks at the bank should be manageable given low FC debt exposure, good FC liquidity, potential liquidity support from BNPP and improving market sentiment. However, FC liquidity could come under pressure from a change in investor sentiment, FC deposit instability or a prolonged loss of market access.

RATING SENSITIVITIES

Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to negative rating action/downgrade:

The bank's LT IDRs are primarily sensitive to a change in Turkey's sovereign rating or in Fitch's view of government intervention risk in the banking sector. A sovereign downgrade, particularly if triggered by further weakening in Turkey's external finances or in the country's FX reserves, or an increase in intervention risk, would likely result in a downgrade of TEB's LT IDRs.

A marked reduction in BNPP's ability and propensity to support TEB could also result in a downgrade but only if the bank's VR was simultaneously downgraded.

The VR could be downgraded due to a marked deterioration in the operating environment - as reflected in adverse changes to the lira exchange rate, interest rates, and economic growth prospects - or if economic recovery was not as swift as currently expected by Fitch. In addition, a greater than expected deterioration of TEB's asset quality and a protracted weakening in operating profitability would likely lead to a downgrade of the VR. The headroom at the current VR level would reduce and TEB's VR would likely be downgraded, if its CET1 ratio fell and remained below 9% for a sustained period or if we viewed capitalisation as no longer commensurate with the bank's risk profile.

The National Rating could be downgraded if the bank's LTLC IDR was downgraded and Fitch believed TEB's creditworthiness had weakened relative to other rated Turkish issuers.

Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to positive rating action/upgrade:

An upgrade of the bank's LT IDRs is unlikely in the near term given the Negative Outlooks. The Outlook on the LT IDRs could be revised to Stable if Fitch believes that the risk of government intervention in the banking system has abated, for example as a result of greater confidence in the sustainability of Turkey's external financing position. A significant reduction in intervention risks, likely reflected in a sovereign upgrade or resulting from a marked improvement in Turkey's net FX reserves position, could result in an upgrade.

Upside for the VR is limited in the near term in light of the challenging Turkish operating environment, the bank's moderate franchise, and the 'BB-' sovereign LTFC IDR. However, a record of resilient financial metrics notwithstanding the pandemic, an improvement in underlying asset quality and the maintenance of adequate core capitalisation in line with its risk profile would reduce downside risks to the VR.

The National Rating could be upgraded if Fitch believed TEB's creditworthiness improved relative to other rated Turkish issuers.

Best/Worst Case Rating Scenario

International scale credit ratings of Financial Institutions and Covered Bond issuers have a best-case rating upgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a positive direction) of three notches over a three-year rating horizon; and a worst-case rating downgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a negative direction) of four notches over three years. The complete span of best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings for all rating categories ranges from 'AAA' to 'D'. Best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings are based on historical performance. For more information about the methodology used to determine sector-specific best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings, visit [ https://www.fitchratings.com/site/re/10111579 ]

Public Ratings with Credit Linkage to other ratings

TEB IDRs are either driven or underpinned by institutional support from its majority shareholder, BNPP.

ESG Considerations

Unless otherwise disclosed in this section, the highest level of ESG credit relevance is a score of '3'. This means ESG issues are credit-neutral or have only a minimal credit impact on the entity, either due to their nature or the way in which they are being managed by the entity. TEB's impaired loans ratio fell moderately to 4.6% at end-3Q20, from 5.8% at end-2019, despite operating environment pressures, primarily reflecting regulatory forbearance in respect of loan classification and high nominal loan growth (16% in 9M20). Net of forbearance, we estimate the impaired loans ratio was about 75bp higher. We expect impaired loans in absolute terms to rise moderately as government stimulus measures subside, regulatory forbearance is phased out (expected by end-1H21) and due to maturing pandemic-related loan deferrals.

In addition, TEB reported fairly high, albeit below peer average, Stage 2 loans at end-3Q20 (9.9% of loans; about one-fifth restructured), which could migrate to Stage 3 as loans season. Loan deferrals were equal to about 5% of gross loans at end-2020 and about a third were classified as Stage 2. Total reserve coverage of impaired loans was below the sector average at 104% at end-9M20, partly reflecting the bank's focus on SME, and therefore collateralised, lending.

The improving growth outlook in Turkey (Fitch forecasts 3.5% real GDP growth in 2021), recent appreciation of the lira and greater market stabilisation should be moderately supportive of Turkish banks' asset quality and collection capacities. Nevertheless, risks remain to the downside given uncertainty over the pandemic, operating environment volatility and the higher lira interest rate environment.

TEB's profitability is moderate (9M20: operating profit/risk-weighted assets (RWA) of 2.3%), although broadly in line with peers', dampened by its high cost base, limited economies of scale (costs/assets of 2.8%), and asset quality pressures. The bank reports an above-sector average net interest margin (NIM; 9M20: 6.0%, or 5.1% FX swap-adjusted), reflecting its focus on higher-margin, SME lending. However, we expect recently increased interest rates to put pressure on profitability in 2021, given that TEB's liabilities reprice faster than its assets, although margins could normalise in 2H21 if interest rates stabilise.

TEB's cost of risk (loan impairment charges/average gross loans ratio) compared well with the peer average in 9M20 (0.9% versus 2.1%) reflecting the clean-up of its loan book prior to the pandemic (since 2018), ensuing identification of, and adequate provisioning against, higher risk exposures and relatively high non-performing loans (NPL) collections in 9M20 (equivalent to about a third of end-2019 impaired loans). Nevertheless, we believe loan impairment charges (25% of pre-impairment operating profit in 9M20; 2019: 50%) could increase in 2021 as regulatory forbearance measures are withdrawn and given the only moderate loan loss coverage of problematic exposures. Pre-impairment operating profit (9M20: 3.5% of average loans; 2019: 4.2%) provides a reasonable, although reduced, buffer to absorb losses through the income statement.

We view TEB's core capitalisation as only adequate for its risk profile, internal capital generation and asset quality pressures. The common equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio increased to 13.0% at end-3Q20 (from 12.0% at end-2019), but would have been a lower 10.8% excluding uplift from regulatory forbearance (set to expire by end-1H21). The total regulatory capital ratio was more comfortable at 18.8% (or 15.9% net of forbearance) supported by FC subordinated Tier 2 debt from BNPP, which provides a partial hedge against potential lira depreciation.

We expect capitalisation to remain under pressure in the near term due to an increase in RWAs (as forbearance is removed), asset quality risks, sensitivity to lira depreciation and weaker profitability. However, it should remain adequate, given the bank's moderate buffers over minimum regulatory requirements and adequate reserves coverage (net unreserved NPLs: minus 1% of CET1 at end-3Q20). We also believe ordinary capital support would be forthcoming from BNPP, if needed.

TEB is largely deposit-funded (75% of total funding at end-3Q20) and its loans/deposits ratio (end-9M20: 95%) outperforms peers and the sector average. Customer deposits, primarily from retail customers, are sticky despite being contractually short term and also fairly granular, although FC deposits are significant (end-9M20: about half, albeit slightly below the sector average). Wholesale funding is nevertheless fairly high (end-9M20: 25% of total funding) and is largely in FC, but it includes material BNPP group funding. Net of the latter, external market funding amounted to a more moderate 18% of total funding at end-3Q20.

TEB reports good liquidity metrics (Liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) at end-3Q20: 168%; FC LCR: 375%). At end-3Q20 available FC liquidity was also sufficient to cover maturing FC wholesale debt over 12 months plus a moderate share of FC deposits. FC liquidity comprises mainly FC swaps (primarily with CBRT), FC cash and interbank placements and FC placed under the reserve option mechanism at the CBRT. We believe refinancing risks at the bank should be manageable given low FC debt exposure, good FC liquidity, potential liquidity support from BNPP and improving market sentiment. However, FC liquidity could come under pressure from a change in investor sentiment, FC deposit instability or a prolonged loss of market access.

RATING SENSITIVITIES

Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to negative rating action/downgrade:

The bank's LT IDRs are primarily sensitive to a change in Turkey's sovereign rating or in Fitch's view of government intervention risk in the banking sector. A sovereign downgrade, particularly if triggered by further weakening in Turkey's external finances or in the country's FX reserves, or an increase in intervention risk, would likely result in a downgrade of TEB's LT IDRs.

A marked reduction in BNPP's ability and propensity to support TEB could also result in a downgrade but only if the bank's VR was simultaneously downgraded.

The VR could be downgraded due to a marked deterioration in the operating environment - as reflected in adverse changes to the lira exchange rate, interest rates, and economic growth prospects - or if economic recovery was not as swift as currently expected by Fitch. In addition, a greater than expected deterioration of TEB's asset quality and a protracted weakening in operating profitability would likely lead to a downgrade of the VR. The headroom at the current VR level would reduce and TEB's VR would likely be downgraded, if its CET1 ratio fell and remained below 9% for a sustained period or if we viewed capitalisation as no longer commensurate with the bank's risk profile.

The National Rating could be downgraded if the bank's LTLC IDR was downgraded and Fitch believed TEB's creditworthiness had weakened relative to other rated Turkish issuers.

Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to positive rating action/upgrade:

An upgrade of the bank's LT IDRs is unlikely in the near term given the Negative Outlooks. The Outlook on the LT IDRs could be revised to Stable if Fitch believes that the risk of government intervention in the banking system has abated, for example as a result of greater confidence in the sustainability of Turkey's external financing position. A significant reduction in intervention risks, likely reflected in a sovereign upgrade or resulting from a marked improvement in Turkey's net FX reserves position, could result in an upgrade.

Upside for the VR is limited in the near term in light of the challenging Turkish operating environment, the bank's moderate franchise, and the 'BB-' sovereign LTFC IDR. However, a record of resilient financial metrics notwithstanding the pandemic, an improvement in underlying asset quality and the maintenance of adequate core capitalisation in line with its risk profile would reduce downside risks to the VR.

The National Rating could be upgraded if Fitch believed TEB's creditworthiness improved relative to other rated Turkish issuers.

Best/Worst Case Rating Scenario

International scale credit ratings of Financial Institutions and Covered Bond issuers have a best-case rating upgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a positive direction) of three notches over a three-year rating horizon; and a worst-case rating downgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a negative direction) of four notches over three years. The complete span of best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings for all rating categories ranges from 'AAA' to 'D'. Best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings are based on historical performance. title: *Fitch Affirms QNB Finansbank at 'B+'; Outlook Negative
text:
3 Feb 2021 12:06 ET  Press Release: Fitch Affirms QNB Finansbank  at 'B+'; Outlook Negative


 
 
The following is a press release from Fitch Ratings : 
      Fitch Ratings-Frankfurt am Main-03 February 2021: 

Fitch Ratings has affirmed QNB Finansbank A.S.'s Long-Term Foreign-Currency (LTFC) Issuer Default Rating (IDR) at 'B+' with a Negative Outlook and Viability Rating (VR) at 'b+'.

The support-driven LTFC IDRs of the bank's subsidiaries QNB Finans Finansal Kiralama A.S. (QNB Finansleasing) and QNB Finans Faktoring A.S. (QNB Faktoring), which are equalised with that of their parent, have also been affirmed.

A full list of rating actions is detailed below.

Key Rating Drivers

IDRS, SUPPORT RATING, NATIONAL RATING, SENIOR DEBT RATING

QNB Finansbank 's 'B+' LTFC IDR and senior debt rating is underpinned by both potential institutional support and its standalone creditworthiness, as measured by its VR. The Support Rating of '4' reflects its strategic importance to its 99.9% owner, Qatar National Bank (Q.P.S.C.) (QNB; A+/Stable), integration with and role within the wider QNB group and small size relative to QNB's ability to provide support, if needed.

Fitch's view of government intervention risk caps the bank's LTFC IDR at 'B+', one notch below Turkey's LTFC IDR (BB-/ Negative), and is also the main driver of the Negative Outlook on the bank. This reflects our assessment that weaknesses in Turkey's external finances would make some form of intervention in the banking system that would impede banks' ability to service their foreign-currency (FC) obligations more likely than a sovereign default. The sovereign's significantly weaker net FC reserves position together with weak monetary policy credibility have exacerbated external financing risks, and this is a key driver of the Negative Outlook on the sovereign ratings.

QNB Finansbank 's 'BB-' Long-Term Local-Currency (LTLC) IDR, which is also driven by institutional support, is one notch above its LTFC IDR, reflecting our view of a lower likelihood of government intervention that would impede the bank's ability to service obligations in local currency (LC). However, the Outlook on the LTLC IDR is also Negative, mirroring the sovereign Outlook, reflecting our view that the likelihood of government intervention that would impede the bank's ability to service its obligations in LC is not lower than the probability of a sovereign default in LC obligations.

The affirmation of QNB Finansbank 's National Rating with a Stable Outlook reflects our view that the bank's creditworthiness in local currency relative to other Turkish issuers is unchanged.

VR

QNB Finansbank 's 'b+' VR is in line with that of the largest, systemically important banks in the sector despite the bank's small size. The affirmation of the VR considers the concentration of the bank's operations in the challenging Turkish operating environment, which exposes it to market volatility and political and geopolitical uncertainty. However, the VR also considers the bank's moderate franchise (end-9M20: 4% share of banking-sector assets; unconsolidated basis) and ensuing limited competitive advantages.

QNB Finansbank provides a mix of services to corporate and commercial customers (a segment where it is looking to increase its market shares) small and medium-sized companies (SMEs, which are highly sensitive to the macro outlook) and retail customers. As a key subsidiary of QNB, we also see increasing integration with the wider group in its risk management and control environment and policies and procedures.

We see downside risks to QNB Finansbank 's VR, given uncertainties over the impact of the pandemic and potential further market volatility. A deeper and more extended economic contraction than expected could exacerbate Turkish operating environment risks, heightening pressure on the bank's asset quality capitalisation and performance metrics. In addition, regulatory forbearance measures, which are currently providing uplift to banks' reported asset quality and capital metrics, are due to fall away at end-June 2021.

Loan growth at the bank was 11% in FX-adjusted terms in 9M20, despite operating environment pressures. However, growth was below sector average (of 19%) as the bank curtailed its expansion plans (targeting both retail and business lending) in response to the weaker growth environment and pandemic-related disruption.

The bank's impaired loans ratio improved to 5.7% at end-9M20 (sector average: 4.1%) from 7% at end-2019, due to lower inflows (reflecting regulatory forbearance) and the denominator impact from nominal loan growth. Fitch calculates the impaired loans ratio would have been 30bp higher net of regulatory forbearance. Stage 2 loans were also fairly high (8.1% of gross loans at end-9M20), although below the peer average, and nearly two-thirds were restructured. Total reserve coverage of non-performing loans was solid at 120% end-9M20 (sector average: 127%), with specific reserve coverage of 76% (sector: 74%) and average Stage 2 reserve coverage of 19%.

Asset-quality risks were already high for QNB Finansbank entering the crisis, exacerbated by the below-trend growth in Turkey, exposure to troubled sectors and segments and high, although slightly below the sector average, FC foreign-currency (FC) lending (35% of loans at end-3Q20; sector: 36%), given that not all borrowers are likely to be fully hedged against lira depreciation (the lira depreciated by 19% against the US dollar in 2020).

FC loan exposure mainly relates to the corporate and commercial segments and includes significant project finance (end-9M20: around a fifth of gross loans), whereby loans are long term and slowly amortising, meaning asset quality problems will feed through only gradually. Project finance comprises public-private-partnership loans (PPPs, 48%), largely covered by state government revenue and debt assumption guarantees, and energy loans (15%), including renewable energy projects eligible for government-guaranteed feed-in tariffs set in US dollars. As a result, around 60% of the bank's project-finance exposure was covered by some form of state guarantee, mitigating the credit risk. Real estate comprised a further 27% of total project finance.

QNB Finansbank 's sectoral exposures are reasonably diversified, typically at 10% or less of the loan book. However, the bank has exposure to the troubled construction and real estate sector (9%) and energy & commodities sector (8%). Borrower concentration is moderate compared with peers, with the top 25 cash loans equal to 19% of loans or 1.6x common equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital.

We believe the improving growth outlook in Turkey (Fitch forecasts 3.5% real GDP growth in 2021), recent appreciation of the lira, and greater market stabilisation should be moderately supportive of Turkish banks' loan portfolios and collection capacities. Nevertheless, risks are to the downside given uncertainty over the pandemic, operating environment volatility and the higher lira interest rate environment.

QNB Finansbank 's profitability metrics remained in line with the sector average in 9M20. It reported an operating profit/risk-weighted assets (RWA) ratio of 2.1% (annualised) at end-9M20 (sector: 2.0%). Its performance in recent years has been underpinned by its above-sector-average net interest margin (reflecting its historical focus on higher-yielding but more risky segments), above-sector-average growth and only moderate impairment charges. However, loan impairment charges rose to 45% of pre-impairment operating profit in 9M20 (2019: 36%) and remain sensitive to asset-quality weakening.

The bank's cost efficiency is weaker than the sector average as the bank does not benefit from economies of scale. However, cost efficiency ratios have improved steadily in recent years (9M20: cost/income ratio of 41%; sector: 32%) and are in line with that of mid-sized bank peers as the bank has focused on optimisation measures and network rationalisation and achieved efficiency gains through volume growth.

Core capitalisation is only moderate given the bank's risk profile (end-9M20: CET1 ratio of 11.3% including forbearance uplift), growth appetite, sensitivity to lira depreciation (due to the inflation of FC RWAs) and asset-quality risks. The CET1 ratio would have been even lower at 9.1% excluding the impact of regulatory forbearance (set to expire at end-1H21). The bank's total regulatory capital is stronger, at 16.7%, and comfortably above the regulatory minimum, supported by FC subordinated debt from QNB, which provides a partial hedge against potential lira depreciation. Pre-impairment operating profit (9M20: equal to 4.5% of average loans) also provides a solid buffer to absorb losses through the income statement.

The bank is mainly customer deposit funded (9M20: 66% of total funding) and deposits are sticky despite being contractually short term. Deposits are fairly granular with retail accounts comprising 72% of the total. Customer deposits rose by 10% in FX-adjusted terms in 9M20 mainly driven by FC deposits. The bank reports an above sector average share of FC deposits (63% versus 54% for the sector). It also reports a slightly above-sector-average loans/deposit ratio (119% at end-9M20, sector: 108%), reflecting reliance on wholesale funding. FC wholesale funding amounted to 30% of total funding at end-9M20. However, parent funding comprised 4% of the total, resulting in net FC debt exposure of 26%.

FC liquidity is adequate and was broadly sufficient to cover the bank's short-term liabilities maturing within one year as at end-9M20, meaning it should be able to cope with a short-lived market closure. Available FC liquidity comprises cash and interbank placements (including balances with the Central Bank of Turkey ), maturing FX swaps and government securities. Refinancing risks are also mitigated by potential liquidity support from QNB. However, FC liquidity could come under pressure from prolonged loss of market access or FC deposit instability.

Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to negative rating action/downgrade:

The bank's LT IDRs and Support Rating are primarily sensitive to a change in Turkey's sovereign rating and in Fitch's view of government intervention risk in the banking sector. A sovereign downgrade, particularly if triggered by further weakening in Turkey's external finances or in the country's FX reserves, or an increase in intervention risk, would likely result in a downgrade of QNB Finansbank 's LT IDRs.

A marked reduction in QNB's ability and propensity to support QNB Finansbank could also result in a downgrade but only if the bank's VR was simultaneously downgraded. However, this is not our base case, given the bank's strategic importance to QNB.

The headroom at the current VR level would reduce and QNB Finansbank 's VR would likely be downgraded, if its CET1 ratio fell and remained below 9% for a sustained period or if we viewed capitalisation as no longer commensurate with the bank's risk profile.

The National Rating could be downgraded if the bank's LTLC IDR was downgraded and Fitch believed QNB Finansbank 's creditworthiness had weakened relative to other rated Turkish issuers.

Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to positive rating action/upgrade:

An upgrade of the bank's LTIDRs is unlikely in the near term given the Negative Outlooks. The Outlook on the LT IDRs could be revised to Stable if Fitch believes that the risk of government intervention in the banking system has abated, for example as a result of greater confidence in the sustainability of Turkey's external financing position. A significant reduction in intervention risks, likely reflected in a sovereign upgrade or resulting from a marked improvement in Turkey's net FX reserves position, could result in an upgrade.

Upside for the VR is limited in the near term in light of the challenging Turkish operating environment, the bank's moderate franchise, and the 'BB-' sovereign LTFC IDR. However, a record of resilient financial metrics notwithstanding the pandemic, an improvement in underlying asset quality and the maintenance of adequate core capitalisation in line with its risk profile would reduce downside risks to the VR.

The National Rating could be upgraded if Fitch believed QNB Finansbank 's creditworthiness had improved relative to other rated Turkish issuers.

SUBSIDIARY AND AFFILIATED COMPANIES

The ratings of QNB Finansleasing and QNB Faktoring are sensitive to changes in QNB Finansbank 's Long-Term IDRs.

Best/Worst Case Rating Scenario

International scale credit ratings of Financial Institutions and Covered Bond issuers have a best-case rating upgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a positive direction) of three notches over a three-year rating horizon; and a worst-case rating downgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a negative direction) of four notches over three years. The complete span of best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings for all rating categories ranges from 'AAA' to 'D'. Best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings are based on historical performance. For more information about the methodology used to determine sector-specific best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings, visit [ https://www.fitchratings.com/site/re/10111579 ]

Summary of Financial Adjustments

An adjustment has been made in Fitch's financial spreadsheets of QNB Finansbank that had an impact on core and complimentary metrics. Fitch has taken a loan that was classified as a financial asset measured at fair value through profit and loss in the bank's financial statements and reclassified it under gross loans as we believe this is the most appropriate line in Fitch spreadsheets to reflect this exposure.

Public Ratings with Credit Linkage to other ratings

All IDRs of the rated entities are either driven or underpinned by institutional support from their respective shareholders.

title: Press Release: Fitch Ratings : Turkey Improves Policy Mix but External Finances Still Weak
text:
The following is a press release from Fitch Ratings : 
 

Related Fitch Ratings Content:

Turkey: Policy Mix Improved but External Finances Are Still Weak

Fitch Ratings -London-02 February 2021: Positive steps have been taken to improve policy credibility but this process will take time, as will rebuilding Turkey's depleted foreign exchange reserves, Fitch Ratings says in a new report. Fitch's revision in August 2020 of the Outlook on Turkey's 'BB-' Issuer Default Rating (IDR) to Negative from Stable was driven by greater external financing risks, partly reflecting lower foreign-exchange (FX) reserves and weak monetary policy credibility. Since then, policy tightening has been stepped up through a more orthodox approach, and a new economic team has placed strong emphasis in communications on sustaining disinflation and repairing external finances. The real average cost of funding from the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey (CBRT) has risen 7.4pp since June and credit stimulus has been withdrawn. As a result, Turkey has seen a moderate rise in capital inflows and in gross FX reserves since November. However, this change in policy was precipitated by lira weakness, FX pressure (net reserves excluding FX swaps fell by near USD70 billion in 2020), a higher deposit dollarisation ratio, widening current account deficit (5.2% of projected GDP in 11M20), and high inflation. CBRT has limited independence and the combination of the government's current targets for GDP growth, inflation and the current account lacks credibility. How policymakers will resolve the trade-offs over time between boosting economic growth and reducing external and domestic imbalances remains unclear. It will take time to rebuild policy credibility, which was already weak ahead of significant loosening and large CBRTFX interventions earlier in 2020. Similarly, Fitch forecasts a stabilisation in Turkey's external finances but not a sharp near-term improvement in FX reserves. External financing positions of the private sector have remained resilient, a feature that has provided support to the sovereign rating during periods of stress. title: EMERGING MARKETS-Stocks,  currencies  eye best week in 5 months as Biden edges closer to victory
text:
* MSCI's EM stocks index rises 6% this week

* Rouble weakens as Biden edges close to winning U.S. vote

* Turkey FX interventions top $100 bln year-to-date - GS

By Shreyashi Sanyal

Nov 6 (Reuters) - Emerging market stocks and currencies were set for their best weekly gains in five months on Friday, as Democratic candidate Joe Biden inched close to winning a tight U.S. election that has also weakened bets for a major U.S. fiscal stimulus.

MSCI's index for emerging market stocks has risen 6% so far this week, while currencies are up 1.3%, driven by Asian and other markets seen as benefiting from the potential departure of Donald Trump from the White House.

Mexico's peso, sensitive to Trump's drive to keep jobs in the United States and impose more tariffs on trade, has gained 2% this week while China's yuan has seen its best performance in a month, gaining more than 1%.

"The large bounce in equities this week creates an opportunity for investors to reassess and rebalance their portfolios in preparation for a President Biden and divided Congress," said Mark Haefele, chief investment officer at UBS Global Wealth Management.

The prospect of a divided Congress has also strengthened expectations that the burden of economic stimulus over the months ahead would remain with the Federal Reserve and other central banks funnelling yet more cash into the financial system.

The more bonds the Fed buys, the more tends to trickle to higher-yielding emerging markets like Indonesia, South Africa or Mexico.

Elsewhere, Russia's rouble, expected to weaken if Trump loses the presidency, has been bolstered by oil prices this week. It was down 0.4% against the dollar on Friday but up almost 3% this week.

Turkey's lira, which has struggled for months, shed 0.3% and was on track for its tenth weekly loss, after a media report said Turkey's Finance Minister Berat Albayrak ruled out an intervention to support the currency.

Goldman Sachs estimated Turkey has spent $101 billion to intervene in its currency markets so far this year.

Analysts at Morgan Stanley say credit supply in emerging markets dropped significantly this week, but expect a pick-up in the coming weeks, given the conducive market backdrop, "with expectations of $25 billion worth of sovereign supply and around $5 billion worth of quasi sovereign supply materializing before end of the year."

Hungary's forint dropped against the euro, leading declines among Central European currencies while the Czech crown edged lower against the euro a day after the country's central bank held interest rates as expected.

title: Turk cenbank to  intervene  if exchange rate swings.
text:
ANKARA, March 3 (Reuters) - Turkey's central bank said on Monday it would intervene in the currency market in the event of extreme fluctuations as financial markets slid after parliament struck down a motion to allow U.S. troops on Turkish soil in return for billions of dollars in aid.

text:

title: UPDATE 2-Turkish CB defends lira as Iraq woes hit mkts.
text:

 Concerns that a conflict next door could destabilise Turkey's fragile economy have sent the unit tumbling in recent days, alongside falling shares and debt prices. 

 The lira recovered to close at best bids of 1,676,000 to the dollar after the central bank's intervention, still weaker than Monday's close of 1,650,000. 

 "We've been saying the lira should be falling, we've been saying it's overvalued," said Charles Robertson, emerging Europe economist at ING Baring. "It looks like the central bank is just trying to manage the decline."

 Benchmark December 3, 2003 debt was also weaker at yields of 58.01 percent from Monday's close of 56.25 percent. 

 Dealers said foreign investors had largely withdrawn from the market ahead of the year-end and local players were also winding down business. 

 Turkey fears that war in Iraq could damage its fragile economic recovery and the IMF pact underpinning it, and could spread over Turkey's southern border. 

 A close U.S. ally, NATO member Turkey is expected to provide reluctant support if Washington strikes against Iraq for allegedly developing weapons of mass destruction. 

 Prime Minister Abdullah Gul told his party's lawmakers that the situation in Iraq had reached a "serious point" and Turkey could not remain indifferent. 

 Gul met senior advisors as well as the president and military chief on Monday night to discuss possible support for the United States and Tuesday's newspapers were full of speculation about what Ankara's role would be in any war. 

 A top Israeli general and an Iraqi Kurdish leader visited Ankara on Tuesday for talks. 

 "Even though it's been expected for a long time (dollar) prices have gone up because a war in Iraq is becoming more concrete," said one banker in the forex market. 

 In addition to Iraq fears, investors are also watching the government for progress on next year's budget and on reforms promised to the IMF in return for a latest $1.6 billion loan tranche due to be paid after a review in January.

title: UPDATE 1-Turk mkts fall on  intervention ,Iraq fears.
text:

 A landslide November election win for the Justice and Development Party (AKP) and optimism about Turkey's EU membership bid have driven markets higher in recent weeks. 

 The lira weakened to close Tuesday at best dollar bids of 1,534,500, below the Central Bank's 1,510,000 point when the central bank intervened to buy dollars and Monday's close of 1,523,000. This is the currency's highest level in more than five months. 

 December 3, 2003, debt fell and yields rose to 47.34 percent from 47.16. July 2, 2003 paper yielded 49.96 percent. 

 "The market has consolidated, taking into account the risk (of lira falls) in the coming days," said a trader. 

 Turkish stocks slipped 1.03 percent to close at 13,226.38 points with brokers citing worries about a possible U.S. attack on neighbouring Iraq. U.S. Deputy Defence Secretary Paul Wolfowitz visited Ankara on Tuesday.
