title: UPDATE 2-Turk lira hits 5mth-high, bucks cbank  intervention .
text:
ISTANBUL, Dec 2 (Reuters) - The Turkish lira closed at a five-month high on Monday on hopes for Turkey's EU membership bid, despite the central bank intervening on foreign exchange markets to sell lira and dampen lira volatility. 

 Bond prices also rose, driving yields to their lowest levels this year, while stocks rose modestly. 

 It was the first time the central bank had acted to weaken the lira since the currency was floated in the wake of a devastating financial crisis in February 2001. The bank has moved in the past to support the currency. 

 The lira ended the day at 1,523,000 to the dollar, off an earlier high at around 1,510,000 but beating Friday's 1,531,000 close, its best since June 11. 

 The Central Bank confirmed it had moved to arrest a persistent rally in the currency after bankers told Reuters it had intervened to buy foreign currency for lira. 

 "A direct intervention in the forex market took place today aimed at preventing an observed fluctuation in the exchange rate," the bank said in a written statement. 

 While lira strength helps Turkey's fight against inflation, it is a handicap for exporters who are expected to drive the country's return to strong growth after the damage of financial crises in 2000 and 2001. 

 The Central Bank announced on Friday it would restart auctions to buy dollars if political conditions continued to fuel lira strength. 

Central Bank chief Sureyya Serdengecti warned earlier last week that investors taking positions on the lira could get their fingers burned. 

 The lira hit a low of some 1,735,000 to the dollar in early November before rallying on the landslide election win for the Justice and Development Party (AKP), Turkey's first one-party government in 15 years. 

 EU OPTIMISM 

 The main factors driving lira strength are high real interest rates on a massive domestic debt load and optimism for Turkey's European Union membership bid. 

 Bond yields fell around three percentage points to their lowest levels this year on Monday as investors bet on a measure of Turkish success for its drive to win a date to start membership talks when the bloc meets at a December 12 summit in Copenhagen. 

 Average yields on December 3, 2003, debt fell to 47.16 percent from a previous close of 50.4 percent. The July 2 papers, also busy, were down to 49.34 percent. 

 Investors said expectations for a central bank rate cut, possibly before the Copenhagen summit, were also helping to drive bond yields down. 

 "Right now investors are focusing on the Copenhagen story and they are coming round to our view Turkey's going to get a result at Copenhagen," said Tolga Ediz, director in global economics at Lehman Brothers in London. 

 Real interest rates on lira assets are still very high, given that inflation looks set to fall well below a 35 percent target for consumer inflation set alongside the IMF. November inflation data are due for release on Tuesday. 

 The treasury auctioned 1,195.3 trillion lira (around $788) 169-day debt on Monday at a maximum yield of 49 percent, in line with expectations. 

 Turkish stocks recovered from earlier falls to close up 0.48 percent at 13,364.17 points with otherwise positive sentiment dampened by worries for the completion of IMF-backed bank reform, compromised by a November court decision to suspend the bank watchdog's seizure of Pamukbank.

title: Dervis pledges low profile role in Turkish "troika".
text:
ISTANBUL, July 13 (Reuters) - Economy Minister Kemal Dervis, torch-bearer of Turkey's $16 billion IMF pact, signalled on Saturday he would keep a low profile in a new centre-left bloc that is staking its claim to power in the crisis-hit country. 

 The United States and European Union, which candidate Turkey aspires to join, have expressed their concern as an unfolding government crisis threatens stability in NATO's sole Muslim state, currently leading peacekeeping efforts in Afghanistan. 

 Seven ministers, including ex-foreign minister Ismail Cem, and more than 37 deputies have fled ailing premier Bulent Ecevit and his Democratic Left Party (DSP) this week, reducing the largest party in parliament to third largest. Further departures are expected. 

 "As long as I remain in government it is not possible to take an active role in the new movement...One has to think about Turkey's economic interests," Dervis told the daily Hurriyet. 

 Turkey's western allies see the presence of Dervis, an ex-World Banker, in the crumbling coalition government as the closest thing to a guarantee the IMF's biggest debtor will implement a reform plan to escape the worst economic recession since 1945. 

 The 77-year-old veteran premier has brushed off talk of early elections his nationalist allies have called for November, insisting his apparently divided three-party government could reach agreement on a dispute over EU reforms. 

 "We must continue with this government until the end," he said in a live television interview on Friday. 

 Ismail Cem, who quit Ecevit's party and resigned as foreign minister this week, said in a statesman-like speech on Friday he had formed a new social democratic "troika" with former deputy premier Husamettin Ozkan and Dervis, brought in after a February 2001 financial crisis ripped through Turkey's economy. 

 Cem pledged on Saturday to support the non-party technocrat as he worked to implement Turkey's IMF programme. 

 "Dervis is very important for this government and he has a very important function to perform," the state-run Anatolian news agency quoted Cem as telling reporters in Ankara. 

 "Appraisals we conduct with Mr. Dervis will be done within a framework of respect (for his position)." 

 The ex-foreign minister said he would hold a meeting in the Turkish capital with defected MPs focusing on efforts to set up a new political party ahead of the next general election. 

 WOLFOWITZ VISIT 

 U.S. Deputy Defense Secretary Paul Wolfowitz will visit Turkey on Sunday before flying on to Afghanistan. A U.S. defence official, who asked not to be identified, told reporters the visit had no connection with Turkey's political turmoil. 

 "They (the Turks) have a functioning government and we have an important relationship," the official said. Wolfowitz would likely broach the issue of Iraq, Turkey's eastern neighbour, he added, amid speculation about a possible U.S. military invasion to depose President Saddam Hussein. 

 Ankara is a staunch supporter of Washington's declared war on terrorism and allows U.S. and British warplanes to patrol a no-fly zone in northern Iraq from an airbase in southern Turkey. 

 Cem said Ecevit's government was no longer able to tackle the country's problems and democratic reforms Ankara must pass to begin membership talks with Brussels. 

 "There is an impasse on the EU issue. We will certainly provide the greatest support to this government or another government," he said. 

 Reacting to news Dervis had joined Cem's camp, coalition Nationalist Action Party (MHP) leader Devlet Bahceli declared on Friday the economy minister's "marginal use had been wiped out" and demanded Ecevit and Turkey's president accept his resignation. 

Turkey's central bank intervened late on Thursday to prop up the free-floating lira currency when Dervis temporarily quit. 

 Dervis later returned to office on the appeal of President Ahmet Necdet Sezer, meeting with an IMF delegation visiting Ankara for the latest review of Turkey's pact. 

 Analysts said the emerging political picture in Ankara may compromise Turkey's economic reforms. 

 "We are worried the IMF programme may take a back seat as Turkey's politics are realigned," Lehman Brothers said in a research note. "The battle... will be carried out at the ballot box. And the elections will effectively be a referendum on EU accession." 

 NEW HAWKISH FOREIGN MINISTER 

 Ecevit expressed his eagerness this week to press ahead with reforms to open the European Union's gates to Turkey but then appointed Sina Sukru Gurel, a man with a hawkish reputation on Cyprus and the EU, as his new foreign minister. 

 Greek Foreign Minister George Papandreou said in a letter to Gurel late on Friday he hoped recent improvements in relations between their nations could continue. 

 Gurel, also installed as deputy premier in Ecevit's revamped cabinet, says his country's foreign policy will not change. 

 Greece and Turkey have been at odds for decades over territorial issues in the Aegean and divided island of Cyprus. 

 "No changes in any of the policies are being considered... Of course we will continue with our foreign policy, keeping with the known principles of this government's programme and the coalition agreement," Gurel told Reuters. 

 Credit ratings agencies Moody's and Standard and Poor's downgraded their outlooks on Turkey to negative this week because of the mounting political turmoil.

 U.S. Deputy Defense Secretary Paul Wolfowitz will visit Turkey on Sunday before flying on to Afghanistan. A U.S. defence official, who asked not to be identified, told reporters the visit had no connection with Turkey's political turmoil. 

 "They (the Turks) have a functioning government and we have an important relationship," the official said. Wolfowitz would likely broach the issue of Iraq, Turkey's eastern neighbour, he added, amid speculation about a possible U.S. military invasion to depose President Saddam Hussein. 

 Ismail Cem, who quit Ecevit's party and resigned as foreign minister this week, said in a statesman-like speech on Friday he had formed a new social democratic "troika" with former deputy premier Husamettin Ozkan and Dervis, brought in after a February 2001 financial crisis ripped through Turkey's economy. 

 Cem said Ecevit's government was no longer able to tackle the country's problems and democratic reforms Ankara must pass to begin membership talks with Brussels. 

 Reacting to news Dervis had joined Cem's camp, coalition Nationalist Action Party (MHP) leader Devlet Bahceli declared on Friday the non-party technocrat's "marginal use had been wiped out" and demanded Ecevit and Turkey's president accept his resignation. 

Turkey's central bank intervened late on Thursday to prop up the free-floating lira currency when Dervis temporarily quit. 

 Dervis later returned to office on the appeal of President Ahmet Necdet Sezer, meeting with an IMF delegation visiting Ankara for the latest review of Turkey's pact. 

 NEW HAWKISH FOREIGN MINISTER 

 Ecevit expressed eagerness this week to press ahead with reforms to open the European Union's gates to Turkey but then appointed Sina Sukru Gurel, a man with a hawkish reputation on Cyprus and the EU, as his new foreign minister. 

 Greek Foreign Minister George Papandreou said in a letter to Gurel late on Friday he hoped recent improvements in relations between their nations could continue. 

 Gurel, also installed as deputy premier in Ecevit's revamped cabinet, says his country's foreign policy will not change. 

 Greece and Turkey have been at odds for decades over territorial issues in the Aegean and divided island of Cyprus. Cem and Papandreou have been credited for a spectacular thawing of relations in the past three years. 

 "No changes in any of the policies are being considered... Of course we will continue with our foreign policy, keeping with the known principles of this government's programme and the coalition agreement," Gurel told Reuters. 

 Ecevit met with Gurel on Saturday at his official residence, but no statement was made after the meeting. 

 Credit ratings agencies Moody's and Standard and Poor's downgraded their outlooks on Turkey to negative this week because of the mounting political turmoil. 

 "The outlook reflects concerns that political instability could persist and jeopardise the IMF-supported economic programme," S&P said.

title: Dervis pledges no active role in Turkish "troika".
text:
ISTANBUL, July 13 (Reuters) - Economy Minister Kemal Dervis, the torch-bearer of Turkey's $16 billion IMF pact, signalled on Saturday he would keep a low profile in a new centre-left bloc that has staked its claim to power in the crisis-hit country. 

 Turkey's western allies see Dervis's presence in Turkey's crumbling coalition government as the closest thing to a guarantee the IMF's biggest debtor will implement a reform plan to pull Turkey out of its worst economic recession since 1945. 

 "As long as I remain in government it is not possible to take an active role in the new movement... One has to think about Turkey's economic interests," Dervis told the daily Hurriyet. 

 The United States and European Union, which candidate Turkey aspires to join, have expressed concern a political crisis sparked by an exodus from premier Bulent Ecevit's government is threatening stability in NATO's sole Muslim state, currently leading peacekeeping efforts in Afghanistan. 

 Ismail Cem, who quit Ecevit's party and resigned as foreign minister this week, said on Friday he had formed a new social democratic "troika" with Dervis, an ex-World Banker, and former deputy premier Husamettin Ozkan. 

 The 77-year-old Ecevit has brushed off talk of early elections, insisting his apparently divided coalition could reach agreement on a dispute over EU reforms that has led his nationalist coalition allies to call for November polls. 

 Nationalist Action Party (MHP) leader Devlet Bahceli on Friday demanded Ecevit and Turkey's president accept Dervis's resignation, saying news the non-party technocrat had joined Cem's camp meant his "marginal use had been wiped out". 

Turkey's central bank on Thursday intervened to prop up the free-floating lira currency when Dervis temporarily resigned. 

 Dervis returned to office on Friday on the appeal of President Ahmet Necdet Sezer, meeting with an IMF delegation visiting Turkey for a latest review of the economic programme.

title: Turk cenbank confirms  intervention  in  forex  market.
text:

title: Dervis sees Turkey meeting export goal, demand up.
text:
ISTANBUL, April 5 (Reuters) - Economy Minister Kemal Dervis said on Friday crisis-hit Turkey could meet an IMF-backed export target for 2002 despite discouraging recent data and predicted a modest recovery in domestic demand. 

 Turkey is looking to exports to achieve economic growth of three percent in 2002 after its economy contracted 9.4 percent in 2001. But exports fell 13 percent year-on-year in February according to preliminary customs data. "The moderate recovery will be driven by a reasonable increase in domestic demand, nothing spectacular, in the order of three to four percent perhaps, and a reasonably good export performance," Dervis told an Istanbul conference. 

 "From the programme we foresee export growth of between six and seven percent is achievable." 

 The preliminary data showed imports were down 35 percent in February, and a Reuters poll of industrial production for that month indicates no immediate recovery in domestic demand. 

 The survey sees a 4.2 percent decline in industrial production in February after falls of 3.1 percent in January. 

 Dervis has said Turkey must resist the urge to stimulate economic growth at the expense of cutting consumer inflation to a targeted 35 percent by year-end from 65.1 percent in March. 

 On Friday he ruled out any government intervention to encourage a cheaper lira, something Turkey's firms have sought as a means to increase export growth. 

 Dervis said a gradual rise in imports would help the lira towards a dollar rate that could help stimulate exports. 

 "It will be necessary in the medium term to have a competitive real exchange rate," he said. 

 The Turkish lira recently hit highs of some 1,290,000 to the dollar after slumping to an all-time low of 1,650,000 lira to the dollar last October. 

 The currency was at best bids of 1,306,000 against the greenback on the local interbank market on Friday. 

 The lira has lost close to 50 percent of its value since it was floated amid last year's financial crisis. 

Central bank governor Sureyya Serdengecti told the same Istanbul conference the bank was not yet happy with expectations for inflation but stressed disinflationary goals would not be sacrificed in the name of growth and exports.

title: Turkish lira slides, traders worry at volatility.
text:
ISTANBUL, Feb 11 (Reuters) - The Turkish lira slipped on Monday to its lowest level against the dollar this year, mostly on selling from London-based banks. 

 The lira fell to 1,408,000 to the dollar on the central bank-brokered spot market from Friday's 1,372,000 lira but firmed slightly to close at 1,385,000 lira. 

 Stocks on the main Istanbul National-100 index ended the day up 3.73 percent at 11,675.15 points as worries subsided over possible U.S. action against neighbouring Iraq, which had led markets down last week. 

 "I don't think it (the lira selling) has anything to do with the Iraq issue. Foreign institutions in London led the (dollar) buying. Local banks that were selling lira reacted to the (dollar's) rise and bought dollars," said one local banker. 

 The lira is now off the highs of some 1,296,000 to the dollar reached last week on IMF approval of a new $16 billion loan pact for Turkey. 

 The central bank has pledged to intervene to stop excessive fluctuations in the currency that Turkish exporters say render pricing difficult, but the IMF pact limits funds the bank can inject into the market in support of the currency. 

 The busiest Turkish bills maturing on February 5, 2003 weakened to average yields of 71.75 percent from 70.33 percent. 

 DOLLAR DANGER 

 Ankara has pledged to make inflation targeting a centrepiece of its monetary and fiscal policy but says fluctuations in the lira and burgeoning inflation should first subside. 

 Bankers said the lira selling did not bode well for a year-end consumer price inflation target of 35 percent and could damage economic recovery. 

 "This game with the dollar is a dangerous one for the year-end inflation target...The manufacturing sector as much as the financial sector cannot take this much volatility," another banker told Reuters. 

 Investors had been unsettled by market speculation about a possible Iraqi reply to Turkish Prime Minister Bulent Ecevit's warning last week that Iraq might face U.S. strikes if it did not allow U.N. weapons inspectors back into the country. 

 But the local press released what they said were the contents of Iraqi President Saddam Hussein's response at the weekend. This contained none of the aggressive rhetoric rumoured last week. 

 Brokers said lower tension over Iraq had helped the stock market post gains, but the lira's weakness had also encouraged buying as stocks had cheapened in dollar terms. 

 "Total losses last week approached 30 percent taking into account the dollar's rise against the lira. Part of that fall has now been regained by this (lira buying) reaction," said Enver Gursoy of Dis Investment in Istanbul.

title: Turkey 's Dervis:  Intervention  Vs Overvalued Lira Needed
text:
ISTANBUL -(Dow Jones)- Turkey's Economy Minister Kemal Dervis said late Tuesday the lira is "excessively" overvalued against the dollar and a central bank intervention might be necessary to reverse the trend. 

 Dervis's statement could be seen by the markets as undermining the independence of the central bank, one of the preconditions of the International Monetary Fund-backed economic program. 

 In a speech to Turkish exporters, Dervis said the "excessively valued lira will be corrected by the market." But he was quick to emphasize that monetary authorities "also need to contribute to this process, as the currency can't drift on its own." 

 Dervis hinted that intervention may come in the form of the central bank selling lira for dollars. 

 He added that the economic program doesn't set a ceiling for the central bank's international reserves. "So the central bank has the right to build up some reserves," Dervis said. 

 "Of course, execution and its timing is up to the central bank as an autonomous institution," he said. 

 After a series of crises saw the lira on a free float on February 2001, Turkey launched a new economic program backed by IMF. 

 The float initially worked against the lira, which shed 60% of its value against the dollar. 

 But since October, amid signs of renewed IMF support for Turkey, the lira reversed, gaining about 20% against the dollar. 

 An overvalued lira increases the probability of a sharp correction, and currency market volatility could be risky to the IMF-backed economic program. 

 The dollar Tuesday closed at TRL1,320,000. 

 While the lira's free float is a key aspect of the new IMF program, the central bank has already announced it can intervene at times of excessive volatility. 

 -By Selim Atalay, Dow Jones Newswires; 90212 2313355 selim.atalay@dowjones.com

title: Turk shares end down on debt worries.
text:
ISTANBUL, Oct 18 (Reuters) - Turkish shares slid more than one percent on Thursday after a government minister said Turkey needed to urgently restructure its debt, but held above key support levels while the market awaits fresh foreign loan news, brokers said. 

 Sales mostly hit leading mobile phone operator Turkcell , which fell 10.29 percent to 6,100 lira after recent sharp gains chasing New York stocks. 

 The International Monetary Fund on Wednesday said it was too soon to talk about increased lending for Turkey but it was in broad agreement with Ankara on budget targets for 2002. Turkey is hoping to secure up to $13 billion in foreign cash to plug a financing gap in its 2002 budget. 

 The main ISE National-100 index ended 1.59 percent lower at 8,818.09 points after fluctuating between 8,724 and levels approaching 9,000 points. It had gained nearly 6.3 percent during the previous three trading days. 

 "The index has been testing the 8,900-9,000 levels for the last two days. The main resistance is at 9,100. In order to pierce these levels, we need to see goverment decisiveness and positive remarks about additional loans," said Kadir Ozkaya at Acar Securities in Istanbul. 

 After Industry Minister Ahmet Kenan Tanrikulu called for urgent restructuring of Turkey's domestic debt mountain, the central bank had to intervene in forex markets to support the lira, sending bonds lower. 

 Tanrikulu later said he had been misunderstood, but brokers said the initial panic had been enough to affect sentiment in equities. 

 "This statement led to a rise in bond yields and falls in the index too," said Ebru Sengul of Datek Securities. 

 Consumer electronics and television exporter Vestel was the most active share, rising 2.15 percent to 2,375 lira. The stock is still enjoying the effects of Tuesday's decision by the European Commission to terminate anti-dumping proceedings on imports of televisions from Turkey. 

 Mostly state-owned flat steel maker Eregli Demir Celik fell five percent to 14,250 lira after posting losses of 173.63 trillion lira ($106 million) in the first nine months of 2001 compared with an 81.7 trillion lira net profit in the same period of 2000. 

 Private commercial bank Garanti Bankasi closed flat at 1,425 lira. Its merger with fellow group bank Osmanli was announced this week. Italy's IntesaBci said on Monday negotiations with Garanti continued but it was not yet considering taking a stake. 

 Daily turnover rose slightly to 483.9 trillion lira (around $297 million) from Wednesday's 461.5 trillion lira. Of the 289 shares traded, decliners outnumbered gainers by 140 to 98, while 51 ended unchanged.

title: TurK CB steps in after debt comments shake markets.
text:
ISTANBUL, Oct 18 (Reuters) - Turkey's central bank intervened to support the lira on Thursday after a minister sent crucial bond yields spiking higher and drove the currency lower with comments he said were misunderstood as calling for domestic debt restructuring. 

 "The central bank action lasted until the close and until bids came up to around 1,630,000 lira (to the dollar)," said one forex trader. 

 The lira had fallen as low as 1,650,000 on the independent interbank market after Industry Minister Ahmet Kenan Tanrikulu urged in a public speech that: "Work on restructuring the domestic debt must be started rapidly". 

 The minister later said he had been misunderstood and such a thing was out of the question. Economy Minister Kemal Dervis also released a statement saying there had been no change in Turkey's debt management policy. 

 "After that the market calmed down a bit," said another foreign exchange dealer said. 

 The lira had closed on Wednesday at 1,637,000 to the dollar on the central bank-brokered spot market . It closed on that market at 1,630,000 after deals of around 1,642,000 in the afternoon. 

 The minister's remarks also sent yields on benchmark bonds spiking more than a percentage point to 88 percent in some trades in a thin market. 

 Average yields on benchmark March 6, 2002, papers were 87.20 percent on Thursday after closing Wednesday just below 86 percent. 

 Any increase in yields is bad news for Turkey's treasury, which is trying to use billions of dollars in IMF support to drive down the cost at which it borrows. 

 The main share index in Istanbul shrugged off the comments, which came during the break between sessions. 

 Shares were trading just under one percent lower with eyes there still fixed on the international lending Turkey says it will need next year to help it roll over a domestic debt stock that reached 101,814 trillion lira (around $65 billion) by the end of August.

title: Turkish  central bank intervenes  to prop up lira.
text:

title: UPDATE 2-Turk mkts slide on U.S. strikes, c.bank vigilant.
text:
ISTANBUL, Oct 8 (Reuters) - Turkish shares, bonds and the lira currency fell on Monday after U.S. and British strikes on Afghanistan overnight, but the falls were limited by the central bank's statement it was ready to support the lira. The main share index in Istanbul fell four percent in early trade but clawed back some of those losses to close the day 1.31 percent lower at 7,499.02 points. 

 Investors said they were tracking the conflict in Afghanistan as well as Turkey's efforts to win further international lending for 2002. It says the global turmoil means it will require additional foreign aid on top of the $15.7 billion IMF-backed crisis rescue pact earmarked for this year. 

 "The dimensions the U.S. intervention takes now and in the near term and the credit the IMF will give are very important," said Cem Gokkan of Anadolu Investment. 

 An IMF team is expected in Ankara on Wednesday for talks set to focus on Turkey's 2002 budget, government officials told Reuters on Monday. 

 Economy Minister Kemal Dervis said last week in Washington after talks with the fund that he saw general agreement that Turkey would need more lending to compensate for global economic turmoil after the attacks on the United States. 

 Investment bank Merrill Lynch said on Monday it had cut Turkish bonds to underweight from market weight in its model portfolio, citing delays in Turkey reaching an agreeement with the IMF on additional funding. 

 "Our market weight position of the past few weeks was not based on economic data releases and the economic outlook but on the market's anticipation of new cash from the IMF," the bank said in a research report. 

 The lira slid on the central bank-brokered spot market , trading at 1,633,000 to the dollar against Friday's close of 1,580,000. That took depreciation since crisis float in February to 58 perent from Friday's 56 percent. 

CENTRAL BANK VOWS SUPPORT 

Turkey's central bank had intervened in forex markets on Friday to pull the lira back from a record low of 1,652,000 to the dollar and reiterated on Monday that it was ready to step in again if needed. 

 "We're watching all markets very closely. We will do whatever is required," central banker Governor Sureyya Serdengecti told Reuters. 

 Bankers estimate the size of Friday's intervention at around $150-200 million dollars, reflecting how thin trade has become on nearly all of Turkey's financial markets as fears of the ramifications of global conflict add to domestic economic woes. 

 "(Friday's intervention) was telling the market, I'm here and you cannot push the rate up as much as you want," said one banker, who asked not to be named. 

 Average yields on the benchmark March 6, 2002 bonds rose under a percentage point to 94.73 percent in very thin trade. 

 Turkey's treasury said on Monday it planned an auction of bills with a 91-day maturity on Tuesday as it sought to service a debt mountain swollen by the bailout of crisis-hit banks. 

 It gave no targeted amount for the borrowing. The treasury sold 434.7 trillion lira of 182-day bonds on October 2 at a maximum yield of 93.56 percent, above a 91 percent average borrowing the treasury targets for 2001. 

 The treasury faces a total 6,728.3 trillion lira ($4.2 billion) in payments on debt interest and principal in October. Of those payments, 3,850.1 trillion lira are to the market with the remainder to state institutions, state banks and banks in receivership.

title: UPDATE 1-Turkish  central bank  steps in to prop up lira.
text:
ISTANBUL, Oct 5 (Reuters) - Turkey's central bank intervened on foreign exchange markets on Friday to arrest a slide in the value of the lira after it hit record lows earlier in the day, bankers said. 

 It was the first confirmed direct central bank intervention on Turkey's volatile forex markets since the crisis in late February which forced the country to float the lira. 

 "The central bank is putting in quotations on the market to buy lira for dollars," one banker told Reuters. Other traders also detected the central bank action. 

 The lira responded, strengthening to 1,580,000 to the dollar on the central bank-brokered spot market in the afternoon after reaching record lows around 1,650,000 lira. 

 The currency had been sliding for days, setting record after record as investors grow anxious over Economy Minister Kemal Dervis's talks with the IMF in Washington and over the likely impact for NATO member Turkey of any U.S. strikes in the Middle East. 

 The central bank has pledged to act to prevent "excessive" fluctuation in the value of the lira, which has lost more than half its value against the dollar since the February float. 

 But its room for manoeuvre is constrained by the provisions of Turkey's $15.7 billion international rescue lending package, which limits how much the central bank's reserves can fall over time. 

 The bank said on Thursday its reserves had risen $1 billion to $18.925 billion in the week ending September 28, swollen by treasury deposits after a dollar and euro-denominated debt offering.

 "The central bank is putting in quotations on the market to buy lira for dollars," one banker said. Other traders also detected central bank action.

title: UPDATE 3-Turkish  intervention  props lira, curbs share losses.
text:
ISTANBUL, Oct 5 (Reuters) - The first direct intervention on the foreign exchange markets by Turkey's central bank since the lira's float succeeded in propping the currency up on Friday, and helped equities claw back some early-session losses. 

 The bank sold dollars after the lira hit a record low of 1,652,000 to the dollar on the central bank-brokered spot market , helping to meet Turkish investors' seemingly insatiable demand for safe-haven hard currency. 

 The intervention, the first such action by the bank since the flotation in late February, pushed the lira to close at 1,580,000 to the dollar. 

 "The central bank is putting in quotations on the market to buy lira for dollars," one banker told Reuters. Other traders also detected the central bank action, which came immediately before the spot market closed. 

 "The central bank has been selling at around 1,600,000 to the dollar," said another banker. 

 Shares, which had been down almost three percent, recovered slightly to close 2.64 percent lower. The main ISE National-100 index ended the day at 7,598.91 points. 

 "The morning rise in forex prices brought some selling, even if it was reluctant. After the intervention some of these came back," said Kerim Sarc of ABN Amro. 

 The currency had been sliding for days, setting record after record as investors grew anxious over Economy Minister Kemal Dervis's talks with the IMF in Washington and over the likely impact for NATO member Turkey of any U.S. strikes in the Middle East. 

 Analysts say Turkey will need billions of dollars in funding from either the IMF or private market sources in 2002. 

 CLUTCHING AT STRAWS 

 "I think they're clutching at straws here. What Turkey needs is a fresh injection of funds and it doesn't seem like they're anywhere near getting that yet," said a London-based analyst. 

 The central bank has pledged to act to prevent "excessive" fluctuation in the value of the lira, which has lost more than half its value against the dollar since the February float. 

 But its room for manoeuvre is constrained by criteria of Turkey's $15.7 billion international rescue lending package, which limits how much central bank reserves can fall over time. 

 The bank said in early September the limit for falls in net international reserves for the September and October period was $3.25 billion, comprising an IMF-agreed $2.5 billion limit and $650 million carried over from unused allowances August. 

 The bank said on Thursday its reserves had risen $1 billion to $18.925 billion in the week ending September 28, swollen by treasury deposits after a dollar and euro-denominated debt offering, indicating it may have more cash at its disposal for any support in defence of the lira. 

 Analysts in London said they needed to know the size of the intervention before commenting on its importance. 

 "It's difficult to assess the motivation behind the move until we get some idea of the amount of dollars they sold. However, it could be justified as a temporary measure to rein in a market that looked to be getting out of hand," said another London analyst. 

 One local banker estimated the central bank and state banks had sold around $150 million to prop up the lira on Friday. 

 Others questioned the wisdom of feeding a desire for foreign exchange that has seen shares and other lira-denominated instruments such as treasury bills avoided by many investors. 

 "It's not very good for credibility when they've said to the market we're only going to do it with dollar auctions," said Sheetal Radia at Standard and Poors MMS in London. 

 "They've now altered the market dynamics. They're selling what everyone wants to buy," Radia said. 

 The central bank had previously restricted action to daily $20 million auctions, largely to process IMF cash and revenue from forex denominated bonds it sold to the market. 

 Average yields on the busiest paper maturing on March 6, 2002 rose more than one percentage point to 94.18 percent. 

 (Additional reporting by Mark Bentley, James Thornhill).

title: Turkish lira slips, record low in sight.
text:
ISTANBUL, Aug 23 (Reuters) - The Turkish lira fell sharply on Thursday raising fears that the troubled currency may again slip to uncharted depths against the dollar. 

 Turkey abandoned a managed currency regime during a financial crisis in February and the currency has since lost more than 50 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar as the government struggles to implement a $15.7 billion IMF rescue pact. 

 The lira was trading at 1,490,000 to the dollar on the central bank-brokered spot market in mid-morning trade, down from Wednesday's 1,460,000 with a record low of 1,515,000 set last week well in sight. "Such a sudden rise (in the dollar) comes down to the fact that there are no dollar sellers," one banker said. 

 Analysts said Turkey's private banks may intervene and begin selling dollars on the central bank's behalf in an effort to prevent the lira currency sinking lower. 

 Representatives of several major Turkish banks met with senior central bank officials last week after the lira set its record mark. 

 The currency then strengthened to around 1,420,000 lira against the U.S. currency with central bank sources saying the banks had discussed ways to intervene to arrest the slide. 

 The IMF pact restricts dollar sales the central bank can make in support of the ailing float. 

 Turkish shares traded on the main Istanbul National-100 index ended the morning session down 0.01 percent at 9,625.01 points after trading lower most of the morning. Yields on the most heavily traded bills maturing on March 6, 2001 rose slightly to 89.21 percent from Wednesday's 89.04 percent. 

 Analysts said news of tax exemptions on bond puchases to be introduced in an effort to provoke a fall in interest rates had helped suppress any rise in yields, but stocks had not escaped the lira rot. 

 "This (the bond tax exemption) was not reflected in the stock market as movements in the dollar prevent this," said Alper Tavukcu of Hak Securities in Istanbul.

title: UPDATE 1-Turkish CB reassures markets on debt, lira.
text:
ISTANBUL, Aug 17 (Reuters) - Turkey's central bank assured markets on Friday the country could handle its hefty debt stock and said recent falls in the value of the lira currency did not reflect economic fundamentals. 

 The written statement, which followed an appearance on television by central bank chief Sureyya Serdengecti, appeared to ease markets, with the lira firming slightly and shares rising nearly two percent in morning trade. 

 "The current debt stock is one that can comfortably be rolled over," the central bank said. 

 The lira hit a record low of 1,515,000 to the dollar on Wednesday amid concerns for Turkey's ability to handle its debt load under a $15.7 billion IMF-backed crisis recovery pact. 

 Financial crises in November and February drove many banks to the wall and the country has issued billions in new domestic debt to bail out ailing state and private banks. 

 But interest rates have stayed well above levels foreseen under the IMF plan, forcing the treasury to raise its prediction of average 2001 borrowing rates to 91 percent from 81 percent and sparking market fears the debt could become unsustainable. 

 The statement stressed Turkey had the financial and monetary discipline needed to push the pact through. 

 "The basic condition of a stability programme, financial and monetary discipline, has been completely established," the statement said, adding first-half indicators pointed to Turkey reporting a primary budget surplus, which excludes payments on debt, of around the target of 11,568 trillion lira or some 6.3 percent of gross national product (GNP). 

 'BUBBLE' WILL BURST 

 The statement said the recent falls in the lira did not reflect those fiscal realities. 

 "A foreign exchange rate that is not justified by economic fundamentals, and a trend to move even further above that level, is only a bubble. Bubbles always burst," it said, adding the switch to a floating rate system to cap market turmoil in February had created natural upheaval. 

 The lira has lost around 50 percent of its value since. 

 "It is only natural that changing the rules of the game creates tension among the players. It is certain that as the rules become accustomed, this tension will disappear," it said. 

 "We fully believe once the realities of the exchange rate movements are understood, the forex market will begin to behave like a normal market," the bank said. 

 It said it had spent $7 billion, partly to stabilise the lira, from the February float to July 31. Recent currency interventions had been limited. 

Turkey's IMF plan limits the amount the bank can spend each month to stabilise the lira.

title: UPDATE 1-Turkish CB head says rates too high, lira too low.
text:
ISTANBUL, Aug 17 (Reuters) - Turkish Central Bank Governor Sureyya Serdengecti said on Friday interest rates of over 90 percent were too high and would come down to 60 percent levels as confidence in Turkey's $15.7 billion IMF pact grows. 

 "Interest rates need to come to the 60 percent level - as doubts are eased, so will rates fall," Serdengecti said, speaking live on private news channel NTV before markets opened. 

 Turkey needs lower interest rates to help it deal with a domestic debt load swollen after months of a banking crisis. Recent treasury borrowing at in excess of 90 percent on three-month bills has increased fears Turkey will struggle to rollover the domestic debt load. 

 "There are two important indicators where we have not reached the point we should be at. One of these is the extremely high level of general interest rates, which raises the issue of domestic debt sustainability," Serdengecti said. 

 "The second is the excessive loss in value of the Turkish lira and the fact that it has not yet found stability," he said. 

 Serdengecti said he believed the recent restructuring of domestic debt held by the central bank to extend its maturity had addressed concerns over the debt schedule. 

 He also said recent falls in the value of the lira against the dollar were excessive but gave no details of how or when the central bank would intervene on currency markets. 

Turkey's deal with the IMF limit the amount the central bank can spend each month to defend the currency. 

 The lira was floated amid financial crisis in late February and has lost around 50 percent of its value since. 

 It hit a record low of 1,515,000 to the dollar on Wednesday but has since recovered, particularly following a meeting on Thursday between Serdengecti and the heads of major banks. 

 "In the last two or three weeks there has been no significant central bankintervention...," Serdengecti said.
