title: ANALYSIS-Turkish  central bank  faces dilemma as lira slides.
text:
ANKARA, Aug 16 (Reuters) - A joke in Istanbul has bankers discussing what they would do if they learned the world was to end tomorrow. 

 The Japanese banker would make a last visit to the golf course, the French banker would visit his mistress, but the Turkish banker has a different plan: 

 "I'd buy dollars," he says. 

 It is a popular option in Turkey where doubts over debt sustainability and a 50 percent depreciation in the Turkish lira since it was floated in February have made the U.S. unit the safe haven of choice. 

 The lira hit all-time lows on Wednesday with dealers saying only determined central bank intevention can stop further falls. 

 But the $15.7 billion IMF crisis rescue pact imposes limits on Turkey's ability to prop up the flagging currency through limits on how much foreign currency reserves may fall each month. 

 "The central bank should sell dollars in an effective manner. If not, I cannot guess how far the dollar can go," said a forex dealer at a private sector local bank. 

 Economy Minister Kemal Dervis has said the slide is an overshoot and will "definitely reverse." Lira depreciation quickly feeds through into Turkey's stubbornly high rate of inflation since the country imports most of its fuel. 

 The lira hit a record low of 1,515,000 to the dollar on Wednesday, bringing the week's depreciation to 9.4 percent. 

 NO WIN SITUATION 

 Turkey's central bank abandoned a policy of unannounced dollar sales in June as hefty purchases by Turkey's banks rendered that policy of limited intervention ineffective. 

 The bank then announced plans of pre-announced dollar sales for July and August to both help curb demand for the greenback and process IMF loans destined for public institutions. 

 But forex dealers now criticise that revised system too, saying those sales also encourage buying. 

 "This auction system is being used as a speculative tool as banks push up prices before the auction," one dealer said. 

 Backing the demand from banks is a widespread public faith in the dollar as a hedge against inflation - running at over 60 percent annually in July - and against lira volatility. 

 The irony is that such currency substitution reinforces inflation and "increases the volatility of the floating exchange rate," according to a recent MSDW research note. 

Forex dealers say Turkey's agreement with the IMF to abandon hefty central bank intervention, the hallmark of exchange rate policy under a previous currency regime, led the central bank to follow a less active and more transparent intervention policy, making its dollar sales less effective. 

 According to the pledges given to the IMF, the central bank can sell $2.5 billion in July and August including leftover allowances from previous months. 

 The bank says it sold $700 million in July and has already announced scheduled auctions to sell a total of $600 million in August, leaving it with leeway to sell more. 

 MORE THAN A BILLION IN HAND 

 Analysts say unused dollars earmarked for lira support in previous months will permit the central bank to spend well in excess of $1 billion in a possible lira rescue mission. 

 Tolga Atac of Bayindir Securities said small intervention by the Central Bank had little chance of arresting the lira's fall. 

 "Now the Central Bank intervenes and it comes down 30-40,000 (lira) but then new buyers step in," Atac said, adding that only large scale intervention would make a difference. 

 During the crisis in November the central bank spent $5 billion in a week with little impact on slowing demand for dollars. 

 In a further effort to prop up the ailing currency and increase confidence in lira-based assets, Turkey took measures in late July to encourage long term lira investments through tax breaks on long-term deposits and bond purchases. 

 Analysts say those measures came too late to stop dollarisation after the switch to a floating rate regime. 

 "You've got an environment of distrust. Nobody wants to own anything Turkish, any Turkish assets," Atac said. 

 Analysts say dollarisation is also being fuelled by exporters reluctant to change foreign earnings to lira and, despite a recent $8 billion debt swap, banks are also purchasing the dollar to close their remaining open forex positions. 

 Difficulty in rolling over syndicated dollar loans leads banks to borrow from the domestic market to repay that debt. 

 While large-scale intervention to prop up the lira may carry both prohibitive cost and dubious result, some analysts say the Turkish government should give clearer signals about where it stands on the intervention issue. 

 "I think (having) no monetary policy would be better than this," said Selim Cevikel of CLSA in Istanbul, referring to the policy of limited dollar sales the central bank now follows. 

 "They're afraid the lira will get weaker but then they're not willing to defend it...It's the worst sign. Which central bank does this kind of intervention?" Cevikel said.

title: WRAPUP-Turkey tackling lira problems as Fischer visits.
text:
ISTANBUL, July 27 (Reuters) - High demand in a forex bond sale on Friday and an overhaul of Turkey's ailing lira borrowing programme shows poor demand for the lira, an issue which Turkey and visiting IMF number two Stanley Fischer must tackle, analysts say. 

 But Fischer said on Friday evening he envisaged no major changes to Turkey's $15.7 billion IMF-bail out pact, including changes to the floating currency regime that analysts say is a major obstacle to government borrowing and business confidence. 

 "We see no major changes taking place in the programme," Fischer told reporters in Ankara when asked if he had discussed changes to the currency regime with Turkey's leaders. 

 In a later statement, Prime Minister Bulent Ecevit said Fischer had warned him against compromising the free float. 

 "I conveyed our problems regarding the floating currency...(He) said the steps taken to abandon the floating currency will lead to negative results. Mr Fischer said such a new evaluation will not be appropriate," Ecevit told reporters. 

 Ecevit said on Thursday he would discuss with Fischer ways to smooth problems caused by the free float currency, which has looked fragile in the face of government infighting and a spat with the IMF. 

 LIRA BEHIND DEBT WORRIES 

 Analysts said the success of a Friday forex debt sale, when demand reached $2 billion for a $500 million one-year dollar and euro bonds sale, shows weakness in the lira. 

 And they said Turkey's abandonment on Friday of its fixed monthly domestic debt auctions, at which last week the government was forced to pay three-figure interest rates, reflected on both lira weakness and Turkey's ability to pay its domestic dues. 

 "There's good (forex debt) demand so maybe the concern of the market is not the repayment risk of the government," said Selim Cevikel of Credit Lyonnais in Istanbul. 

 "The concern is that there's not much confidence in the Turkish lira, in long-term Turkish lira assets," Cevikel said. "If you do this for Turkish lira bonds for one year, you wouldn't get half of this (demand) and interest rates would probably be 95 percent." 

 DOMESTIC BORROWING ADDRESSED 

 Analysts said the major revision to the treasury's borrowing policy is a precautionary measure to keep domestic borrowing costs down amid the volatility that has plagued the lira free float in recent weeks. 

 "Today's auction is the proof that the current exchange rate system was the major deterrent working against treasury debt auctions," said Emin Ozturk, economist at Bender Securities. 

 Rates in treasury lira bond auctions topped 100 percent last week during a spat between the reformist wing of the government led by economy minister Kemal Dervis and coalition nationalists seen as obstructing the IMF programme. 

 An auction immediately following a fateful argument between the prime minister and president in February saw interest rates soar to 144 percent from around 70 percent. 

 Turkish officials and the IMF agree resultant high interest rates and a growing debt load are the greatest threat to the future of the loan pact, which necessitates low interest rates to reverse a recession predicted to bring a GDP contraction of at least three percent in 2001. 

 Turkey hopes the abandonment of a policy of announcing a fixed monthly programme of domestic debt auctions will give it more flexibility to hold sales when conditions are favourable. 

 LESS FLEXIBLE FLOAT? 

 Analysts say the resounding success of the forex bond sale as compared to equivalent lira bond sales may give Turkey a strong case to make alterations to the currency regime. 

 "It could be a tool for the government when they see Fischer," Cevikel said. 

 Turkey's battered lira currency has lost nearly half of its value since its float amid financial crisis in February. A lira pegged to the dollar was the centrepiece of a now-revamped IMF-backed reform programme signed in late 1999. 

 But analysts do not expect Fischer and Turkey to agree on anything but minor adjustments to the free float. 

 "The most likely scenario is when they don't re-label policy but give more flexibility to the central bank in terms of forex interventions," said Ozturk. 

Turkey has already taken measures to promote lira stability by encouraging long term lira investments through tax incentives on long-term lira deposits and bond purchases announced earlier this week. 

 Analysts say further measures to reduce domestic debt redemptions during the rest of 2001 should also ease the pressure on the floating lira-based programme. 

 IMF loans, a swap of Turkish treasury debt held in the central bank and the ability of state banks to roll over their debt means Turkey only has to tap domestic debt markets for a minimum 19,000 trillion lira ($14.4 billion) this year against total debt repayments of 40,000 trillion, a treasury information note showed on Thursday. 

 "In the rest of the year the rollover burden of the treasury is not as large as what it seemed from the redemption side," said Ozturk.

title: ANALYSIS-Turk politics place hugh strain on IMF-rescue plan.
text:
ANKARA, July 12 (Reuters) - Turkey and the IMF look set to solve a row that has delayed the payment of an urgent loan, but domestic political rifts may still keep interest rates sky-high, putting a heavy strain the country's IMF-backed rescue plan. 

 A 10-day deadlock with the IMF - ostensibly over the composition of the board of landline monopoly Turk Telekom, but really a test of Turkey's commitment to reform - has eroded much of what market confidence remained in the country's fractious three-party coalition, analysts say. 

 "The government's obstinacy with the IMF over the Telekom issue hurt market confidence a lot," said an economist with a foreign bank based in Turkey. "Everyone reckons a similar crisis could emerge any time, in a week, in a month." 

 The IMF and World Bank are expected to release more than $3 billion in loans on Thursday when they meet to review steps Turkey has taken to meet fund demands on bank reform and the grooming of Telekom for privatisation. 

 The dispute over the make up of the Telekom board highlighted hostility in the government's nationalist wing to Economy Minister Kemal Dervis, who brokered the rescue deal with the IMF and World Bank. Markets see the Nationalist Action Party (MHP) increasingly as an opposition within the government. 

 CRIPPLING INTEREST RATES 

 Turkish government debt yields - what it costs the country to borrow - are now punishingly high at around 100 percent, reflecting the market's lack of appetite. Investors have seen the value of lira-denominated bonds tumble as the lira has lost almost half its value since the February crisis struck. 

 Such yields, if sustained over coming months, could raise the country's debt burden to levels making the rescue programme unsustainable. 

 The domestic debt stock more than doubled to 84,500 trillion lira by end of May from 36,400 trillion lira at the end of last year and total interest payments will now account for upwards of 85 percent of government revenues in 2001. 

 Yet the crisis recovery plan, backed by $15.7 billion in IMF and World Bank loans, is predicated on a steady fall in rates. 

 "The current interest rate levels reflect investors' risk premiums. It's not because of high inflation expectations but lack of confidence in the programme's future," said Yarkin Cebeci, chief economist at Ottoman Bank. 

 Turkish wholesale inflation was 52.4 percent in June, while the most traded bond yields swing around 90-100 percent. 

 BLAME PUT ON LIRA FLOAT 

 A report by Nomura Equity Research was even gloomier. 

 "Turkey's economy is now clearly falling into severe financial stress. Higher bond yields are now a given, driving the currency lower in a vicious circle. 

 "Inflows of fresh forex receipts from the tourism industry (this summer) are masking what is a very ugly dynamic. Once these tail off in September, unfortunately just in time for the opening of parliament, yields are likely to explode and the lira will head south." 

 Fears of an Argentinian debt default have also added to the economic pressure on Turkey. The IMF appears reluctant to consider any further intervention to shore up Argentina, fund sources arguing political damage is of the country's own making. The warning might apply also to Turkey, which is seen to be unlikely to receive a third international bail-out in under 12 months after packages in November and February. 

 Some analysts argue the floating currency rate system, introduced when Turkey was forced to abandon a crawling currency peg regime in February, is the real cause of the current high interest rates. 

 "Investors cannot guess where the exchange rate can go, so they ask for high risk premiums for their lira investments, pushing interest rates to levels higher than those under a system where exchange rates are predictable," wrote Ercan Kumcu, an economist and columnist at the daily Hurriyet. 

 Overnight interest rates, the only instrument the central bank can use to intervene, are anchored at 63 percent. The bank cannot change the rate, since a cut would prompt dollar demand, and a rise would put a greater burden still on the treasury. 

 "It's true the floating rate puts pressure on interest rates," said Cebeci of Ottoman Bank. "But, if we were still in the crawling peg system, central bank reserves would disappear in a week under such political fears." 

 The central bank has lost about $6 billion of its international reserves since the February crisis. They now stand at $16.5 billion. 

 FLIGHT OF CONFIDENCE 

 Some other analysts argue interest rates should have fallen even under the floating exchange rate system with rising exports, falling inflation and a rosier current account balance. But that premium has been squandered by the politicians. 

 "With confidence so badly torn at home and abroad, we could not even enjoy those benefits the floating rate system could have brought," the foreign bank economist said. 

 The lira briefly traded at a new record low of 1,345,000 against the dollar on Thursday on the central bank-brokered spot market - a fall of almost a half since February's float. 

 Turkish banks and investors still seek solace in dollars, as a safe haven in crisis periods. Banks have recently closed their open foreign currency positions after an $8 billion debt swap, and seem reluctant to turn to lira instruments again. 

 The high dolarisation in the system, makes restoring confidence in the lira much harder, analysts said. According to the latest central bank data, 83 percent of its liabilities are now in foreign currencies. 

 "We are at a turning point," said Funda Gungor, chief economist at Demir Bank. "If the government meets all commitments to the IMF, the programme may have a chance to survive, though hanging by a thread."

title: Turkish stocks expected cautious after party ban.
text:
ISTANBUL, June 25 (Reuters) - Turkish stocks are likely to react cautiously on Monday to a Constitutional Court ban on the main opposition Virtue Party as attention turns to a crisis-racked economy, analysts say. 

 The Court expelled two members of the Islamist party from parliament, relieving investor worries of possible by-elections and doubts over financial reforms crucial for $15.7 billion in lending from the International Monetary Fund (IMF). "It is clear there is no longer a danger of early elections," said Mehmet Ascioglu of Demir Yatirim. "But we do not expect the exchange to rise above 11,250-11,300. There's an auction tomorrow and economic developments are the most important criteria for us now." 

 The ISE National-100 index rose 1.25 percent to close at 11,119.75 percent on Friday before the court made its decision later that evening. 

 The Turkish parliament has passed a swathe of reforms since signing a deal with the IMF in May. The fund is due to meet later on Monday to discuss Turkey's performance in adhering to a stringent economic programme. Brokers say worries over the weakness of the Turkish lira, which lost more than 40 percent of its value after a February crisis, will dampen any optimism in the short term. 

 "The result of the Virtue closure case has brought relief. 

 "There may be a slight rise today but increases will be dampened by the lira-forex dimlemma, demand for foreign exchange due to banks' syndicated loans, lack of cash for investment, and a general lack of confidence in the lira which is causing people to stay in foreign exchange," said Ozgecan Firildak of Kent Portfolio Management. 

 The index ended down 6.08 percent last week on worries over the closure case and the lira, which weakened to around 1,277,000 against the dollar by Friday, a depreciation of some 46 percent since it was floated in February. 

 Analysts say interventions by Turkey's central bank to bolster the currency can only be limited as the government aims to use a weakened lira to increase export earnings.

title: Turk Cbank sees limited  forex  market  intervention .
text:
ANKARA, April 24 (Reuters) - Turkey's central bank will take limited action on foreign exchange markets to prevent "excessive" fluctuation in the value of the recently-floated Turkish lira, Governor Sureyya Serdengecti said on Tuesday. 

 "In the coming period the central bank will take limited action on foreign exchange markets, in keeping with the needs of a floating currency regime to reduce excessive fluctuations," Serdengecti told a meeting of central bank officials. 

 Turkey floated the lira in late February in a bid to cap market turmoil sparked by fears of political instability. The unit has since lost around 45 percent of its value against the dollar and Turkey seeks billions of dollars in new foreign lending to help rebuild the economy from the ruins of a collapsed IMF-backed disinflation plan. 

 Bankers say they believe the central bank has stepped in to sell dollars on the interbank market already, on one occasion to prevent the lira falling below the 1,300,000 lira to the dollar mark.

title: PRESS DIGEST - Turkey - April 10.
text:
ISTANBUL, April 10 (Reuters) - These are the leading stories in the Turkish press on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy. 

 SABAH 

 - Shame on you Gazi Bey: former Central Bank Head Gazi Ercel converts his lira savings into dollars a few days into the financial crisis that has slashed the value of Turkey's currency while assuring people there will be no lira float. 

 MILLIYET 

 - The powerful generals ask the head of the Union Of Turkish Bourses and Chambers, Fuat Miras, to stop widespread street protests by tradesmen and tell them the hardship the country is passing through will be overcome altogether. 

 HURRIYET 

 - Why does Miras visit military headquarters a day before a meeting of his union which is under pressure by its members to step up its calls for the government's resignation? 

 RADIKAL 

 - Parliament faces a busy week and aims to approve three reform bills quickly by working at the weekend, as the economy minister Kemal Dervis seeks to push a total of 15 draft laws through parliament to win foreign support and loans. 

 CUMHURIYET 

 - The cabinet takes a series of measures in order to ease street protests by small businessmen against the financial crisis. The measures include cutting the interest rates for some oustanding bank loans and easing some taxes. 

 DUNYA 

 - The government plans to cut public sector spending by selling cars over 12 years old and providing official vehicles only for ministers and ministry undersecretaries. 

 ZAMAN 

 - Economy Minister Kemal Dervis says the IMF, which is negotiating a new economic programme to replace its gutted $11.5 billion deal with Turkey, cannot intervene in the country's domestic affairs.

title: ANALYSIS-Foreign money needed for Turkish rescue.
text:
ANKARA, March 15 (Reuters) - Turkey must secure billions of dollars in foreign loans to tackle the chief cause of its recent crisis - weakness in the state-dominated banking system. 

 "We no longer have the luxury of doing this operation without foreign support," Ercan Kumcu, a leading economist, wrote in a column for Hurriyet newspaper. 

 A failure to acquire this foreign financing would force the government to rely more heavily on central bank resources, printing money and pumping up inflation to perilous levels. 

 According to Morgan Stanley Dean Witter, Turkey urgently needs foreign financing for bank restructuring to avoid a debt restructuring. It did not give any further estimate about the type of debt restructuring. 

 Bankers say Turkey, with a good past record of foreign debt servicing, is not likely to consider foreign debt restructuring but it may look for ways of rolling over its high domestic debt redemption in coming months. One idea is to convert maturing debt into foreign currency-indexed bonds. 

 "The Treasury may find relief in giving foreign currency papers in return for short-term Turkish lira bonds in bank portfolios," Deniz Gokce of Bosphoprus University said. 

 STATE BANKS TARGET OF REFORM 

 Economy Minister Kemal Dervis unveiled on Wednesday government plans to reform state banks which account for a third of the whole banking system in terms of asset size, a total of $144 billion at the end of September. 

 He did not detail the magnitude, means and sources of financing required but indicated banking would be the target of the injections. The World Bank and IMF have already made clear there can be no more loans with a convincing plan to sanitise the banking system. 

 "According to our estimates, the cost of an all-out and all inclusive clean up of banks would be prohibitively high - including the state banks, banks under administration and potential insolvent banks," said Ercan Uysal of SG EMEA Research. 

 "TRUSTWORTHY AND RESPECTABLE PROGRAMME" 

 There is still no clear sign from the IMF and World Bank of loans but Prime Minister Bulent Ecevit appears optimistic. 

 "I hope our preparation of a trustworthy and respectable programme and its rapid and determined implementation will put foreign resources into action," Ecevit told his deputies. 

 Turkey has so far secured an $11.5 billion IMF loan to carry out its programme devastated by the recent crisis. 

 Philip Poole, head of emerging markets at ING Barings, said the IMF itself was unlikely to contribute significant additional funds given the already sizeable commitment on Turkey's quota. 

 "However, the fact that the direct securitisation of the hole in the state banks has been set below the generally accepted estimate of the size of the problem probably means that additional resources will be forthcoming from the World Bank specifically for this purpose," Poole said. 

 "DUTY LOSSES" BURDEN BANKING SYSTEM 

 Dervis said the government would set up a joint board of independent banking professionals for three state banks - Ziraat, Halk and Emlakbank. The plan proposes an eventual merger of Ziraat and Emlak. 

 The three banks, used by the government as an instrument to subsidise some sectors, has total "duty losses" of around 14,000 trillion lira ($14 billion). These losses place a heavy burden on the banking system. 

 The government plans to eliminate the duty loss stock by issuing government bonds to the banks, short of cash. 

 Most of the state banks must borrow heavily on overnight markets. 

 "This is an urgent problem which threatens the banking system," a text prepared by Dervis's office said. The text, headlined "The measures needed to be taken within the framework of economic programme", was distributed to journalists at Dervis' press conference on Wednesday. 

 "The three banks should be provided with a total resource of 13,000 trillion ($13 billion) for the solution of the problem." 

 It said another $3 billion should be injected into the banks to boost their capital adequacy. 

 Such a radical and costly plan has probably been endorsed by the World Bank and IMF which have been urging Turkey for almost a decade to overhaul its troubled banking system. 

 CSFB estimates the cost of a banking bailout at around "$20-25 billion which is too high for Turkey to finance alone without printing money, which might pave the way for hyper-inflation. 

 "Although it is not only the state banks that will need recapitalisation, the state banks are likely to account for the bulk of the aggregate bailout need," CSFB said in a note. 

 "If the total for the state banks is $16 billion, then the total for the banking system as a whole is probably in the order of $20-25 billion." 

 CRISES RESOLUTION TO TEST BUSH 

 The Turkish crisis sets an early test for the new U.S. administration of President George W. Bush. The Bush camp has advocated a policy of less direct intervention in financial crises, setting itself apart from President Bill Clinton. 

 This might bode ill for Turkey, which received $7.5 billion in new loans from the IMF after a crisis in December. Certainly the United States, while offering general support, has said nothing to commit it to any loans. 

 Professor Alan Makovsky of the Washington-based Institute for Near East Policy believes Turkey's position as a NATO ally at the rim of the Middle East gives it particular significance. 

 "I don't think the 'ideological purity' of non-intervention is going to allow a crucial ally like Turkey to collapse," he said. "That would have serious foreign policy consequences." 

 Uysal of SG anticipates a "partial rehabilitation and restructuring initiative spread over 2-3 years, which might require the liquidation of insolvent banks, the merger of small-to-medium sized commercial banks." 

 "Such an initiative would require a budget of $25-30 billion which can be financed through monetisation and, domestic and external debt financing. We expect a combination of these financing options with respective weights of 30, 40 and 30 percent," Uysal said.

title: Turkish sovereign debt and European telcos led the way down ...
text:
Turkish sovereign debt and European telcos led the way down as the cost of credit protection cheapened. Tom Bergen reports. 

 LONDON, Feb 27 (Reuters) - The cost of credit protection on Turkish sovereign debt fell on Tuesday as turmoil in its financial markets calmed. 

 Credit protection costs on European telecoms debt also fell, helped by a rebound in the sector on European stock markets, with default swap spreads tightening by midsession, dealers said. 

 Default swaps, the most liquid part of the credit derivative market, are insurance-like tools which allow investors to juggle exposure to the risk of an issuer defaulting on an underlying loan or bond. 

Turkey's central bank intervened in the country's money markets for the second day running on Tuesday, providing liquidity at comparatively low interest rates. 

 The stock market and the Turkish lira also recovered from recent lows, contributing to more positive sentiment in the default swaps market. 

 "Turkey is normalising again. People are squaring positions that they weren't able to close last week," a trader with a U.S. bank said on Tuesday. 

 Bid/offer spreads on Turkish one-year default swaps were quoted at 600/900, from 600/1000 on Monday. The two-year swaps were shown at 650/900, in from 700/1100. The three-year swaps had come in to 700/1000 from 800/1200 on Monday. 

 Nonetheless, the trader added there still could be fallout if local banks began selling large quantities of their bond holdings. 

 "The local banks could drive the market back again. They have margin calls in foreign currencies and the easiest way for them to meet these is to sell their dollar bonds. A widespread sell-off would impact the default swaps market," he said. 

 TELECOMS STRONGER 

 A recovery in European technology and telecoms stocks helped to narrow spreads of default swaps on the telecoms sector on Tuesday. A trader with a major European bank said spreads had narrowed by five basis points across the board. 

 Five-year defaults swaps on Deutsche Telekom's debt were quoted at 150/170 from 155/175 on Monday. Vodafone was quoted at 78/82, in from around 82/86 yesterday. France Telecom was shown at 170/178, having traded at 180 on Monday. Swedish handset maker Ericsson was bid at 100 on Tuesday, narrowing from a bid/offer spread of around 107/115 yesterday. 

 No trading was reported in default swaps on banks or the automotive sector.

title: Turkey's  central bank  has offered cash at lower rates...
text:
Turkey's central bank has offered cash at lower rates but the markets are still waiting for a long-term economic Plan B. 

 By Joseph Logan 

 ISTANBUL, Feb 27 (Reuters) - Turkey's central bank on Tuesday again intervened decisively on the money market, offering cash at low interest rates to soothe markets and ease pressure on its newly floated lira. 

 The first lira dollar deals on the interbank market were recorded at 970,000, a depreciation of some 29 percent since the float of the lira last week, only slightly weaker than late Monday, but up from losses of 36 percent in the first days of free trade. At around 1030 GMT the lira stood at 985,000. 

 Turkey abandoned its controlled currency policy, the heart of an anti-inflation programme backed by over $11 billion in IMF loans, last week after a political row sparked panic, sending interest rates to astronomical levels and crushing the peg. 

 The central bank continued to provide cheap credit and abundant liquidity, as it did on the previous day, offering banks three-day dollar and euro lending at 40 percent and overnight lira liquidity at 150 percent in the interbank money market. 

 The first deals on that market were at 100 percent, plunging from around 5,000 percent last week as cash-strapped banks scrambled for liquidity at any price. 

 Analysts said the strategy of the bank, whose chief Gazi Ercel resigned at the weekend after the demise of the currency policy he helped design, was paying off in the short term but that the pressure was on to design an economic policy from the ruins of the plan built around the lira peg. 

 Treasury Undersecretary Selcuk Demiralp, another architect of the gutted currency policy, has also submitted his resignation. Deputies are filling both posts until Turkey's coalition government agrees on successors. 

 "The markets are still short of lira and dollars, people are just trying to survive rather than trying to make money," said Burak Akbulut, a strategist with Istanbul's Bayindir Securities. 

 "The markets are still waiting for a package, a plan B from the government. It's been almost a week that we haven't heard anything clear from the government in terms of what the monetary policy is going to be in this new environment. 

 "Will Turkey follow the old disinflation programme, will that programme survive, or to what extent are we going to obey the rules of the old programme?" he said. 

 The main share index , which has surged since the currency float as investors pumped money into the shares of tourism companies and others seen benefiting from a weaker lira, was down about one percent, as brokers said profit taking set in. 

 "Tomorrow is the last opportunity to get into cash (before a religious holiday next week)," said Alper Ozge of General Fianans. 

 BANK SECTOR SOLUTION NEEDED 

 Akbulut said all Turkish markets welcomed the steps taken till now to cap the crisis, but that a cogent policy that dealt with the country's bloated, creaking banking sector had to emerge quickly or those gains would evaporate. 

 "The markets are not going to buy the expectations, they're going to behave according to solid steps rather than expectations," he said. 

 Analysts say the high rates generated by the financial crisis have boosted pressure on Turkish banks, and that the devaluation may have pushed some with heavy foreign currency obligations to the wall. 

 The head of the country's banking watchdog, which has seized 11 troubled banks, at the weekend said all banks had managed to close their positions. Bankers said much of the sector, including two state giants, had been unable to do so last week. 

 Akbulut said speculation in the media about plans to merge some of the state banks and let some of the shakier Turkish banks go under might be a bitter pill that Turkish policymakers would have to swallow to win the trust of markets. 

 "That's a very radical solution but that's what Turkey should do...a radical and healthy solution is the troubled banks should be wiped out of the system whatever the cost," he said.

title: Emerging  FX -Turkish lira pauses, zloty firm.
text:
LONDON, Feb 27 (Reuters) - The newly-floated Turkish lira steadied on Tuesday as an injection of liquidity by the central bank helped traders pause for breath, while the zloty was upbeat as the Polish central bank's two-day policy meeting began. 

Turkey's central bank intervened on the money market, offering cash at low interest rates to soothe markets and ease pressure on the lira, which was pushed out of its crawling peg regime last week after a political flare-up between the president and prime minister triggered a financial crisis. 

 The first lira-dollar deals on Tuesday's interbank market were at 970,000, a depreciation of some 29 percent since the float and marginally below late Monday levels although up from losses of 36 percent soon after it traded freely. 

 Investors were far from convinced that the lira was out of the woods, given the political uncertainty which clouded the prospects of an effective cure for the troubled banking sector. 

 "At the moment, you've got a short-term containment. Interest rates have come down, the central bank is providing liquidity and we're now in a pause, waiting for a much clearer sense of what the scale of the problem is," said Jerome Booth, head of research at Ashmore Investment Management in London. 

 "The thing that everybody is waiting for - mostly domestically but externally as well - is the sense that the political spat that we saw is not going to be repeated. That's very important because you can have all the policies in place but see the whole thing get out of hand again." On Tuesday, Turkey's central bank offered overnight lira to banks at 150 percent, continuing lending at low rates. The first deals on the interbank money market were made at 100 percent, down from highs of 5,000 percent last week. 

 The central bank also offered three-day dollar and euro lending to banks at 40 percent. 

 ALL EYES ON POLISH MPC Elsewhere, the zloty maintained a firm note as the Polish central bank began its two-day Monetary Policy Council meeting, with many in the market expecting a rate cut of between 1.0-1.5 percentage points. 

 The bank has been maintaining interest rates at 19 to 23 percent - among the highest in Europe - to squeeze out inflation. But real interest rates are very high, with the consumer price index up 8.4 percent in the 12 months to January. 

 "The market is anticipating a rate cut of perhaps 100 to 150 basis points. Polish bonds are slightly better bid as a result, and that goes for the currency as well," said Callum Henderson, currency strategist at Citibank SSSB in London. 

 "Recent emerging market volatility over the last couple of days was of concern to some high-yielding markets but that seems to have calmed down," he added. 

 The zloty hit one-week peaks around 4.0880 to the dollar before trimming gains to around 4.0910/4.0940 by 1153 GMT, according to Reuters data. 

 Against a broadly firmer euro, the zloty was trading at 3.7430/60 to the euro , down marginally on the day but still within sight of Monday's five-day peaks. 

 In South Africa, the rand was softer after gross domestic product growth for the fourth quarter came in at 3.2 percent, a touch below a consensus forecast for 3.4 percent. 

 "Most people were expecting something between 3.4 and 3.8 (percent growth), so 3.2 was a bit of a disappointment," said Henderson at Citibank SSSB. 

 "The key factors for the rand now are the trade data (due on Wednesday), and more importantly, the Anglo American/De Beers deal." 

 Earlier this month, mining giant Anglo American and South Africa's Oppenheimer family agreed to buy diamond miner De Beers in a $17.6 billion deal, and currency traders expect the transaction to generate some rand demand. 

 The rand was trading at around 7.7500/7.7600 to the dollar , down from around 7.72 prior to the GDP data.

title: Turkish Lira Float Not A Threat To Asia - Salomon
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Turkey's decision to float its currency in the aftermath of a political crisis in unlikely to have wide ramifications for Asia, as there are few trade links between Turkey and this region, Salomon Smith Barney said Tuesday. 

 "Routes for contagion to Asia from Turkey's decision are not wide," Salomon Smith Barney said in a report. 

 Salomon noted that total trade between Turkey and Asia was only around $4 billion in 1999. 

 Turkey's exports to Asia are less than 0.5% of the total goods the country sells overseas, with many of these items usually headed for India and South Korea, Salomon said. 

 Financial problems in one emerging market often spill over into neighboring countries and other emerging markets, as investors become more risk-averse. 

 That was the situation in Asia in 1997 when the devaluation of the Thai baht in July quickly led to currency depreciation in Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, and South Korea. 

 On Thursday, Turkey was forced to abandon exchange rate controls and allow its currency to float freely. The Turkish lira lost 36% of its value as early as Friday, with the currency recovering some of its losses early this week following an intervention by the central bank. 

Turkey decided to float the lira after political infighting between
the Prime Minister Bulent Ecevit and President Ahmet Necdet Sezer
triggered a massive loss of confidence in the economy, which translated
to huge outflows of foreign currency by nervous investors.
- - 27/02/01 08-55G



Meanwhile, Salomon Smith Barney said concerns over Turkey's political
and economic stability is not likely to trigger new fears in Asia.



"Certainly there is fragility in some of the region's banking systems,
but nothing that should be new or surprising to investors," the company
said, citing Indonesia, Thailand and China.



More so, Salomon Smith Barney said characteristics of the Asian
financial crisis like huge current account deficits, appreciated
exchange rates, and off-track reform programs are absent in the current
scenario.



Although the currencies of China, Malaysia and Hong Kong are somewhat
pegged, the foreign exchange environment in these three countries are
different from that of Turkey, the company said.



For one, Salomon Smith Barney said Hong Kong's banking system and
fiscal accounts are "solid."



While Malaysia's banking system is not as sound as Hong Kong's, there
has been no major deterioration over the past years, Salomon Smith
Barney said.



China's structural problems in its fiscal and banking systems,
meanwhile, aren't immediate worries for investors, the company said.



-By Rita Raagas De Ramos, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2832-2331;
Rita.DeRamos@dowjones.com

title: Turkey stepped in to calm crisis-racked markets and revive the beleaguered lira ...
text:
ANKARA, Feb 26 (Reuters) - Turkey stepped in to calm crisis-racked markets and revive the beleaguered lira on Monday but top-level talks between political and military leaders produced no sign its premier and president had settled a power struggle. 

 "It was a nice, beneficial, fruitful meeting," Prime Minister Bulent Ecevit told reporters after a meeting of the powerful National Security Council (MGK), scene last Monday of a row that shook markets and changed the face of Turkey in a week. 

 He gave no details before going to talks with government partners and an MGK statement made no reference to the row. 

 Turkey's Central Bank, whose governor resigned at the weekend over the collapse of the country's IMF-backed financial reforms, intervened to force interest rates down by lending money to banks well below last week's sky-high levels. 

 Average deals on the repo market - used to inject money into the system to ensure smooth transactions between banks - were 122 percent compared to 1,300 percent on Friday. 

 The aggressive Central Bank move in a crisis that has reverberated through international emerging markets immediately affected market mood. The squeeze of last week when some banks had trouble squaring accounts eased. 

 FEARS LINGER FOR THE FUTURE 

 Stocks, which lost a third of their value last week after Ecevit accused Sezer of prompting a crisis by belittling his anti-corrution campaign, soared by up to eight percent. The lira, which slumped 36 percent after it was floated on Thursday, clawed its way back to 28 percent below pre-crisis levels. 

 The influx of funds will be welcomed by an 80-strong banking system, Achilles heel of the Turkish economy. A liquidity squeeze stirred a banking crisis in Turkey last November defused only by IMF intervention with a $7.5 billion loan package. 

 Milliyet newspaper said in an unsourced report on Monday that the IMF, whose Turkey desk head is in Ankara to discuss a new counter-inflation programme, may offer more emergency loans. 

 Analysts said that Monday's action would ease immediate fears on the markets, but dangers remained. Banks could use "cheap money" to buy foreign currency. Again, Turkey could be faced with the rush to dollars that shook the system last week. 

 "The Central Bank announcements will go some way towards cooling the markets' fever," said Yarkin Cebeci, chief economist at Ottoman Bank. 

 "This is what we need for the short term, but...we need a revised economic programme for the medium term and we also need the political will to defend it," he added. 

 Political uncertainty lingered, however, after the meeting of the secretive MGK, a body used by powerful generals to impart their views to politicians, especially at times of crisis. 

 For Ecevit and President Ahmet Necdet Sezer, it was the first encounter since Ecevit abandoned the last MGK meeting on Monday accusing Sezer of belittling his efforts to fight graft. He declared a crisis of state that was all too promptly picked up by markets sensitive to recurring political instability. 

 Those present at the abortive meeting said passions ran so high that a book, the constitution, was thrown around - an image not edifying to generals, markets or the general populace. 

 Ecevit has fended off demands that he sack ministers, clearly fearing any reshuffle could upset the delicate balance of his three-party coalition. But Central Bank Governor Gazi Ercel resigned on Friday and official sources said Treasury head Selcuk Demiralp had also decided to go. 

 ECEVIT REMAINS IN SADDLE 

 While Ecevit has been widely faulted for his conduct last week, when key interest rates soared over 5,000 percent, the belief still lingers on markets that his departure could create political chaos and paralyse government. 

 The generals have made it clear they do not want to become directly or publicly involved in the dispute. However Ecevit and Sezer would in effect have been giving account to the General Staff as well as to markets at the MGK meeting. 

 The MGK statement, however, dwelt on Turkey's reform programme to prepare for European Union membership talks - something that seems now more distant following the crisis. 

 IMF Turkey desk head Carlo Cottarelli is in Ankara for urgent talks on measures to renew Turkey's disinflation programme, which had been designed to cut inflation to single figures by the end of next year from up to 100 percent in the 1990s. 

 Humour at least has not died. 

 Milliyet daily carried a front-page cartoon showing Ecevit being searched as he entered the MGK meeting room and hundreds of copies of the constitution spilling onto the floor. 

 "Sorry, sir," says the security officer. "No copies of the constitution in the meeting room."

title: Turkish markets numbed by earthquake.
text:
ISTANBUL, Aug 18 (Reuters) - Turkish bonds yields rose and the lira weakened on Wednesday on concerns about the economic cost of the huge earthquake that crippled the country's most industrialised region. 

 "There was an overall lack of appetite. But there was also dollar demand fuelled by foreign investors' sales in the bond market," said Gokhan Yilmaz, trader at Denizbank. 

 Yields climbed to 97.41 percent, up 3.3 percentage points from their levels before Tuesday's quake. The lira closed at 439,800 against the dollar compared with Monday's close of 438,100. Istanbul's stock exchange has suspended trading until next Tuesday. 

 "Bond sales come mainly from foreigners...due to worries about the effects of the quake on the economy," said Tugrul Ozbakan, Capital Markets deputy manager at Turk Ekonomi Bankasi. 

 Officials say it is too early to give a figure for the total financial cost of the quake which devastated a large area in western Turkey. The earthquake has so far cost some 3,500 lives, including 460 in Turkey's financial capital of Istanbul. 

 It has severely interrupted commercial life in some quake-hit towns like industrial city of Izmit and Adapazari, severing power and telephone links. A tyre factory of Italian Pirelli collapsed near Izmit. 

 Izmit, the epicentre of the quake measuring 7.4 on the Richter scale, is home to many ventures involving foreign companies in the automobile, petrochemical and machinery sectors including companies like Honda , Toyota , Hyundai , Pirelli, Goodyear , Mannesmann  and Lafarge . 

 The quake will also set back the privatisation programme the International Monetary Fund wanted the country to start as one condition for funds. The Tupras oil refinery in Izmit, the country's biggest and top of the privatisation list, has been ablaze since the quake. 

 "It's normal that there will be reactionary sales by foreigners in the bond market, but this must be temporary as this is nothing related to macroeconomics," said Yilmaz. 

Turkey's central bank intervened in the currency market in support of the lira on Wednesday afternoon, as it often does to control the rate of depreciation of the lira. Bankers estimate the central bank sold around $400 million to buy lira. 

 A treasury bond auction was also hurt by the gloom. Average and maximum yields for the three-year floating-rate notes rose to 127.62 and 130.91 percent from 119.54 and 123.25 percent respectively.

title: Turkey officials say no change in  forex  policy.
text:
ANKARA, July 2 (Reuters) - Turkish economy officials said on Friday that ongoing talks with the International Monetary Fund would not bring any radical change in the country's foreign exchange policy. 

 "There will be no change in our foreign exchange policy," central bank head Gazi Ercel told a news conference jointly held with a visiting International Monetary Fund team. 

 Economy Minister Hikmet Ulugbay told the conference that a currency board would not be part of any future arrangement between the IMF and Turkey. 

 The central bank has been keeping the lira's depreciation rate on par with inflation as part of its monetary policy since 1995 through open market operations and interventions. 

 Carlo Cottarelli, head of the IMF's Turkey desk, said earlier that a staff monitoring accord would remain in place as a bridge towards a new programme but did not give a time frame. 

 He said "strategic steps" must still be taken before putting a new programme into practice. 

 Turkish markets had been hoping for news of a new arragement including financial support, but Cottarelli did not mention any amounts. The IMF previously linked new funds to government progress on structural reforms in social security, banking and agriculture.

title: Turkey bank law just step toward reform-JP Morgan.
text:
ISTANBUL, July 1 (Reuters) - Turkey's banking law, passed by parliament last month, is a step in the right direction but more measures are needed to complete reform of the sector, an economist at JP Morgan said. 

 "It is too early to declare that banking reform has been achieved," economist Emin Ozturk said in a recent research note. 

 "If anything, the latest legislative changes may be considered as just the first step in a necessary reform process that in the next step will require careful implementation of the new law with minimum political interference." 

 The law creates a regulatory and supervisory body for the 75-member banking system to monitor policy implementation and rule on the establishment and closure of banks. 

 But analysts are concerned that the body could be shaped by political interests. 

 "Good implementation will depend on the skill of the body and, particularly in the Turkish context, on the absence of political intervention in its decisions," Ozturk said. 

 He said Turkey should also reduce the public sector's share in banking and rehabilitate the undercapitalised state banks which try to finance most of the off-budget deficits. 

 Four state-owned commercial banks make up more than one-third of the system's assets which rose to $116.7 billion at end-1998. 

 "Moreover, all these steps would need to be complemented by a fiscal reform, since high public sector borrowing requirements almost inevitably create major balance sheet risks for the private banks," Ozturk said. 

 The banking sector carries a large portfolio of government securities and a considerable level of short foreign exchange positions, estimated at around $9 billion. 

 Ozturk pointed at the risks of this policy. 

 "One is the risk of a step devaluation or a faster-than-expected depreciation of the lira exchange rate. The other risk arises from the mismatch of maturities on asset and liability sides." 

 On the asset side, the average maturity of the Treasury's borrowing is over one year. On the liability side, maturities of deposits are mainly at around three months while most repurchase agreements (repos) with customers carry maturities from overnight to one month. 

 He said "the deplorable shape" of Turkey's public finances had created strong incentives for banks to carry high levels of such risks. 

 "Reduction of those incentives through a cut in the borrowing requirement of the public sector is a sine qua non for effectively addressing the balance sheet risks in the banking sector." 

 The high cost of lira funding increased by the public sector borrowing need, reserve requirements and taxes on deposits, and the central bank's policy of keeping lira depreciation in line with inflation make short foreign exchange positions attractive for banks. ((Servet Yildirim, Istanbul Newsroom, 90-212-275 0875, fax 90-212-267 2137, istanbul.newsroom@reuters.com)).

text:

 Another trader said a morning intervention might be a sign of a faster lira depreciation and that afternoon trading needs to be seen. 

 Traders see further bank intervention in the afternoon. 

 Around 0850 GMT dollar offers were at TRL414,050, up from early Tuesday's TRL413,350. 

 The euro was at $1.0385, down from $1.0419 and $1.0423 late Monday in New York.

 The Turkish Treasury is also holding two auctions Tuesday to sell paper worth TRL900 trillion to TRL1.1 quadrillion and some of the commercial bank dollar selling is seen related to the auction.

title: Key facts about Turkey.
text:
ANKARA, April 18 (Reuters) - These are the key facts about Turkey, where parliamentary elections are taking place on Sunday: 

 POPULATION: 63 million. 

 AREA: Turkey's 780,576 square km (301,382 square miles) covers Asia Minor and the southeastern toe of Europe. Bordered by Greece and Bulgaria to the northwest, Iran, Georgia and Armenia to the east and Iraq and Syria to the southeast. 

 CAPITAL: Ankara. 

 LANGUAGE: Mainly Turkish. About six million Kurdish speakers and several hundred thousand Arabic speakers. 

 RELIGION: Ninety-nine percent Moslem, mostly Sunni. Alevi Moslem population of roughly 10 million. Small Jewish, Armenian and Greek Orthodox communities. 

 GOVERNMENT: A constitutional republic with a 550-seat parliament as the sole legislative authority. General elections held at least every five years. The president, currently Suleyman Demirel, is elected by parliament for seven-year terms. 

 POLITICS: Incumbent Prime Minister Bulent Ecevit came to power in January, 1999, as a caretaker to guide the country to April 18 elections, held more than a year before they would normally be due. The last general elections were held in 1995. 

 An Islamist party was narrowly the winner of those elections and an Islamist-led coalition emerged after the collapse of a deal between conservative rivals Tansu Ciller and Mesut Yilmaz. But pressure from the powerful secularist military, a major political force, edged the coalition between Ciller and the Islamists from power in 1997. 

 Since then weak secularist coalitions under Yilmaz and then leftist Ecevit have ruled over Turkey's estrangement from the European Union. The same period has also seen an increasingly stern foreign policy force climbdowns from Syria and Cyprus. 

 However, with the Islamists effectively isolated in parliament by military distrust, coalitions between feuding leaders became increasingly hard to build and consensus was reached on the need to hold early elections. 

 ECONOMY: Turkey witnessed a sharp decline in gross national product growth to 3.9 percent last year after rapid growth of around eight percent in recent years. The global financial crises which prompted the slowdown also contributed to downward pressure on chronic high inflation. Anti-inflationary government programmes helped bring annual wholesale price inflation down to 48.2 percent in March from 86.0 percent a year earlier. While keeping the lid on inflation and boosting economic activity, the new government will be expected to rein in gaping public deficits. 

 The central bank maintains a policy of steady lira depreciation in line with inflation, maintained by near-daily interventions in the currency market. 

 The slowdown in growth has also limited growth in exports, which rose to $26.88 billion in 1998 from $26.26 billion the previous year. The trade deficit shrank to $19.04 billion from $22.30 billion last year. 

 The budget deficit fell to 7.0 percent of gross national product in 1998, from 7.6 percent a year earlier. The current account surplus in 1998 stood at $2.69 billion, compared with a deficit of $2.64 billion a year earlier. 

 The political uncertainty of recent months has put privatisations on hold after some progress in sell-offs last year. The government raised some $1.0 billion from privatisations in 1998. 

 MODERN HISTORY: The Turkish Republic was declared in 1923 from the ashes of the Ottoman Empire. The key figure in establishing the new nation was former army officer Mustafa Kemal, later named Ataturk (Father of Turks), whose memory is still widely revered. 

 Kemal led the nationalist movement to victory over occupying powers which dismembered the empire after its defeat in World War One. Until his death in 1938, Kemal, first president and virtual dictator, oversaw Turkey's transformation into a secular, one-party state aimed at Western-style development. 

 Turkey was neutral in World War Two until it joined the allies in early 1945. It became a member of NATO in 1952 and is an associate member of the European Union. Turkey's quest for full membership of the Union is hampered by its poor human rights record, Greek objections and economic problems. Ankara applied for full EU membership in 1987 but was told to wait. 

 Development of multi-party democracy since the 1940s has been dogged by political squabbling, corruption and violence which led to military interventions in 1960, 1971 and 1980. 

Turkey strongly backed the U.S.-led coalition against Iraq during the Gulf crisis, when U.S. planes used Turkish bases. 

 The Cyprus issue has long dogged Turkish-Greek relations. Turkey invaded the island in 1974 to protect the Turkish-Cypriot minority after a Greek-backed coup, and has held the island's northern third ever since, keeping about 30,000 troops there. 

 Turkey upset Iraq and Syria in 1990 by diverting the Euphrates, which flows through all three, to fill a new dam. It has also been at odds with Iran, Iraq and Syria over their alleged support for the Kurdistan Workers Party rebel group. 

 Turkey captured the rebels' leader Abdullah Ocalan in 1999 and plans to try him for treason.

title: Turkey's  Central Bank  -2: Sparked By Banks' Dollar Buying
text:
ISTANBUL (Dow Jones)--Dollar-buying by commercial banks in Turkey caused the Turkish central bank to intervene in the market Monday afternoon, with the bank buying Turkish lira (TRL) for dollars, traders said. 

 The bank intervened to slow the lira's depreciation rate to a monthly 4% against the dollar and euro currency basket. 

 Traders said the intervention had been expected but that they were unsure whether the dollar demand was isolated or marked the start of a general buying trend. 

 There was speculation earlier that some foreign institutions were switching from lira positions to dollars due to political uncertainty connected to the elections on April 18. 

 However, an Istanbul-based trader said that London markets, the main base for Turkey-related transactions, are closed Monday, therefore excluding the "foreign investor exodus" speculation. He said the domestic demand could be purely technical. 

 Local traders don't see any justification for a general exodus and see relative political stability in the post-election period. 

 Traders said the extent of the dollar demand would need to be watched. The central bank has been selling lira for dollars almost every day since Jan. 1. 

 Monday, the dollar closed at TRL374,900, up from Friday's close of TRL373,100.

 ISTANBUL, Aug 4 (Reuters) - Corporate tax payments caused a cash squeeze in Turkey's money market on Tuesday, prompting the central bank to fund banks in the money and forex markets. 

 The bank injected 98.8 trillion lira on overnight deals and 1.5 trillion lira in tomorrow/next money interbank deals at 76 percent after intervening twice in the foreign exchange market, selling lira for dollars. 

 The market was 104 trillion lira short on Tuesday, causing the average overnight money rate to rise to 75.94 percent from 75.37 percent previously. 

 The central bank's tomorrow/next funding followed heavy treasury borrowing in an auction of 359.1 trillion lira of six-month bills compared with repayment of around 266.8 trillion lira, bankers said. 

 The cash squeeze and the firmer cost of funding pushed bond yields up by around 2.5-3 percentage points. 

 The yields on the most active papers rose to 91.8 and 88.28 percent from 89.15 and 85.17 percent respectively. 

 The yield on the last auctioned February 3, 1999 paper rose to 88.19 from 86.90 percent on tomorrow value deals. 

 The average repo rates, indicating the cost of bond funding, jumped to 80.23 percent from 66.08 on tax-free deals and to 85.98 percent from 73.80 percent on taxed deals.

 ISTANBUL, July 21 (Reuters) - A Turkish money market cash squeeze which stemmed from petroleum consumption tax payments and pension salaries eased in the afternoon due to the central bank's intervention to sell lira for dollars. 

 The bank drained 29.2 trillion lira at 41 percent on overnight deals at close of the market. The average overnight money rate ended at 45.43 percent, down from Monday's 63.42 percent after touching 73 percent during the day. 

 "The Central bank stepped in foreign currency market by selling lira for the dollar as daily lira depreciation against the currency reduced below of daily limits on markets' severe demand for the lira," said one banker. 

 Bankers said the bank raised the lira's daily depreciation level to 0.1 percent after the intervetion. 

 The central bank's daily depreciation target is estimated at around 0.08 percent for July after June's 0.1 percent. 

 Higher cost of funding in line with a cash squeeze earlier in the day caused bond yields to rise around three percentage points to around 78 percent levels. 

 The most active papers were March 10 and April 14 yielding 78.12 and 77.96 percent, up from previous 75.16 for both. 

 "Bond yields returned from 80 percent which is seen as offering technical resistance in the day. In line with firmer funding cost and uncertainty about early poll talks, the yields may keep rising tendency in coming days," said one banker. 

 Bankers said renewed political concerns after coalition leaders' statements on early elections also upset the market. 

 Prime Minister Mesut YIlmaz, under pressure from coalition partners to announce a date for early general elections, said on Tuesday parliament would decide in October when to hold the polls. 

 He told a meeting of his Motherland Party that he would call for a summer parliamentary recess from next week to October, adding that the long-awaited tax reform would pass this week. 

 Overnight repo rates, the indication cost of bond funding, remained above of the previous yields by around 20-21 percentage points at 65.94 percent on tax-free deals and 70.30 percent on taxed deals.

title: NO DEVALUATION, NO RATE  INTERVENTION -TURK MINISTER.
text:
ANKARA, July 7 (Reuter) - Gunes Taner, Turkey's state minister for the treasury, said the new coalition government would not go for a one-off devaluation nor intervene in the interest rate policy. 

 "In our practice, there will not be two things -- a devaluation and intervention in interest rates," Taner told Reuters. 

 Taner said the government would manage the economy through "fine tuning". 

 "By saying fine tuning, I mean that there won't be big interventions. To do this, the central bank has some instruments such as open market operations. We will run the economy by using these instruments," Taner said. 

 Turkey had last devalued its currency in early 1994. 

 The republic has led its lira fluctuate in line with supply and demand in the market under the central bank's tight grip since then. 

 Taner hinted that the government may not continue to auction two-year, inflation-indexed bonds -- an instrument heavily used by the former Islamist-led government to raise funds from the domestic market in the past four months. 

 "TUFEX (inflation-indexed bonds) is not a type of borrowing model I prefer," he said. He did not give any further details. 

 The inflation-index bonds make up 15 percent of the domestic debt stock which stood at 4,026.8 trillion lira at end-May.

ISTANBUL (AP-Dow Jones)--The Turkish lira closed lower against the dollar Wednesday despite the Central Bank of Turkey's intervention by selling dollars for the lira. 

 Traders said the bank aims to keep the lira's depreciation rate under its control and added that more dollar selling by the bank might come Thursday if the market pushes for higher rates than the bank's target. 

 Traders said the central bank targets a lira depreciation of 4% against its currency basket in February. The bank's currency basket consists of 1 dollar and 1.5 Deutsche marks. At time time of Wednesday's intervention, the depreciation was over 4.2%, traders added. 

 Traders said the bank sold dollars about 10 minutes before the market's 1300 GMT close. The dollar/lira rates were at 119,800 lira at the time of the intervention and were rolled down to 119,450 lira at the market's close. 

 Traders expect the market to open Thursday morning at a dollar rate of 119,750 lira. 

 An Istanbul bank's foreign exchange manager said the intervention wasn't severe as when the dollar selling started, banks were fast to lower their rates by 100 lira at each round. 

 'If banks were worried, the rates would decrease by 10 lira at each round, not by 100,' he added. 'Banks weren't keen on buying dollars.' 

 In order not to loose reserves, the central bank starts its interventions minutes before the trading session closes, traders believe.

title: WSJ: Turkey Moves To Halt Lira's Fall
text:
ISTANBUL (Dow Jones)--Turkey intervened strongly this week to stop an abrupt slide in its currency, even as foreign corporate investors bet on the economy as a bright spot amid the global doldrums.

The unusual paradox illustrates complex strains in the world economy, as developing nations have had to struggle with sharp ups and downs in their currencies, threatening growth even as they are counted on to shore up struggling developed economies.

Turkey's central bank spent $350 million in an auction to purchase Turkish lira Friday, bringing the week's intervention total to $1.64 billion. At the same time, the bank has been cutting reserve requirements for commercial banks, pumping liquidity into the financial system.

In striking contrast, two U.S.-based private-equity funds this week bet about $1 billion on Turkey for the longer term.

Turkey's economy grew by more than 10% in the first half of the year. It has a strong banking sector, and enjoys low public debt and budget-deficit levels that neighboring European Union economies can envy.

But concerns over the falling lira are the latest in a series of worries some economists have expressed over what lies around the corner for this country of 74 million.

The central bank's moves this week effectively reversed the unorthodox policies it has followed since late last year. The bank cut interest rates despite double-digit economic growth, as it sought to deter volatile speculative inflows that were then flooding emerging markets, and to drive down the value of the lira to boost exports and cut imports. At the same time, it raised reserve requirements to deter bank lending and temper demand.

Now the bank worries that a global downturn--particularly in the European Union, Turkey's dominant trade partner--could take Turkey's booming economy down with it. A too-rapid fall in the lira could stoke inflation, already well above the central bank's 5.5% target, and trigger a rush to the exits by short-term foreign investment that finances much of the country's massive current-account deficit, economists say.

"The central bank's primary concern isn't the value of the lira, but inflation," said Mustafa Akcay, at Moody's economic research, in West Chester, Pa. "The lira dropped around 10% in September alone, and this rapid decline creates inflation."

A core concern remains the size of Turkey's current-account deficit--now above 9% of gross domestic product--and the short-term nature of the foreign-investment flows that finance it. The central bank "is increasingly concerned that a disorderly sell-off in the lira could worsen capital outflows, as investors see the currency as a one-way bet," said a research note Thursday by Capital Economics, a London-based consultancy.

As the global economy darkens, Turkey's central bank has turned to foreign-currency auctions to stabilize the lira, rather than raising interest rates, which could damp growth.

The IMF in September advised the opposite, saying the bank should raise rates and conserve its foreign-exchange reserves. The reserves provide a cushion against any sudden flight of the short-term investment flows, should Turkey have to cover the current-account deficit.

"We don't waste our reserves...but they are not for decoration on our balance sheet," said the Turkish central bank's deputy governor, Ibrahim Turhan, interviewed Thursday at the Global Economic Symposium in Kiel, Germany. As of Oct. 4, the bank's foreign-exchange reserves stood at $85 billion.

The lira was trading at 1.85 to the dollar Friday, down from a peak of just over 1.90 earlier in the week.

The IMF forecasts that Turkey will grow by 2.5% next year, a sharp slowdown from current heady levels, but well above forecasts for most developed economies. And longer term, rising inflows of foreign investment this year suggest investors are willing to overlook Turkey's short-term risks.

Foreign direct investment in the seven months to July was $9.1 billion, according to Turkey's economy ministry, the same total as for all 12 months of last year. This week saw the launch of a new $1 billion fund by one U.S.-based private equity fund, Cerberus Capital Management LP, and the unveiling of a $300 million venture in a Turkish private-school business by another, Carlyle Group.

Investors and Turkish officials point to the country's youthful population. Its median age is 28, compared with 44 for Germany and 37 for the U.S., according to United Nations data. They say that explains their optimism for longer-term growth. Meanwhile, a high-profile foreign policy and robust growth rates over the past year have drawn attention.

"It didn't take us a week to get 30 companies to come with us," on a trip to promote investment ties between the U.S. and Turkey, said Thomas J. Donohue, president and chief executive of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, interviewed in Istanbul on Wednesday. He said those companies included Citigroup and General Electric.

"Look what's happening in Europe, in the Middle East," he said, contrasting the debt crisis in Greece and turmoil in Libya with Turkey's relative stability and strong growth.

Other larger deals this year include U.K.-based Diageo PLC's (DEO) $2.1 billion purchase of Turkish drinks-maker Mey Icki. In another $2.1 billion deal last month, Jersey-based Vallares PLC (VLRS.LN), an investment vehicle run by former BP Chief Executive Tony Hayward, merged with Turkey's Genel Energy Investment Ltd. Genel has significant oil production in Northern Iraq.

-By Marc Champion at marc.champion@wsj.com and Anita Greil at anita.greil@dowjones.com

--Todd Buell in Kiel, Germany, contributed to this article. [ 10-07-11 1614ET ]

title: ANALYSIS-Turkey defending lira with limited  FX  ammunition
text:
ISTANBUL, Oct 6 (Reuters) - Turkey has upped the ante in defence of the lira, but with hard cash reserves far smaller than those of many developing economy peers, FX intervention may not be feasible for long should investors resume their exodus from emerging markets.

Faced with year-to-date lira losses of almost 20 percent to the dollar and rising inflation, the central bank this week mounted its most aggressive defence of the currency yet, selling a record $1.1 billion on Wednesday and Thursday and making changes to banks' reserve requirements.

The action succeeded in lifting the lira well off record lows. But any further FX interventions will put Turkey in serious danger of depleting a reserve stash that is its primary buffer against a large balance of payments deficit.

Reserves stand now at around $85 billion, far short of the hundreds of billions of dollars held by other comparable emerging market countries and down more than 10 percent from July as a result of the central bank's daily dollar auctions.

"This speed of reserve drawdown is not sustainable," said Manik Narain, emerging markets strategist at UBS in London. "Turkey's reserves in terms of external debt coverage or import coverage are among the the lowest in emerging markets."

In contrast, South Korean interventions throughout September cost it $9 billion but made a dent of less than 3 percent in its reserves, the world's eighth-largest.

Central bank data shows $132 billion in external debt payments due in the coming year, mostly private sector. Add in the huge current account gap and the liability mounts to over $200 billion -- more than double its current reserve level.

Turkey in fact is one of only four emerging countries whose FX reserves are insufficient to cover annual trade balance needs and maturing short-term debt, a UBS study shows. The other countries in this position are Bulgaria, Latvia and Belarus.

"The Turkish central bank ... is not Brazil or Korea which have a lot more firepower," said Alia Yousuf, a bond portfolio manager with ACPI Investments in London.

"If this (reserves decline) continues it will obviously lead to more uneasiness with investors. Ultimately if global market uncertainty remains, funding the Turkish current account deficit will become an increasing worry."

BANK UNEASY?

BNP Paribas analysts note that the gross reserves-imports ratio stands at 37 percent while the reserves to short-term debt ratio is at 98 percent, just above levels it says are mentioned by the bank in its reserve management guidelines.

"Our back-of-the envelope calculation yields that if the central bank sells $10 billion more, all FX reserve ratios will decline to or below their critical levels," BNP told clients.

Though the central bank deliberately engineered a depreciation in the lira in the early part of the year, it has appeared increasingly uncomfortable with the scale and pace of the currency's fall.

On Thursday it attempted to soothe analysts' worries, saying in a presentation that its reserve position was quite strong, judging by the ratio of reserves to short term FX debt.

But signs are it is uneasy; hence the decision to allow banks to hold more reserves in dollars, a step that may add $3.6 billion to its own coffers.

But the coming months may well see a further rise in dollar demand from Turkish banks and corporates which borrowed heavily overseas to fund booming domestic growth but will see a record $132 billion come due in the coming year, including coupons.

RBS compared the predicament to Russia's in 2008, when a third of FX reserves vanished in the rouble's defence.

"Russia suffered badly back then because it had $160-80 billion in external debt liabilities falling due; and yet it got into trouble even with $590 billion in FX reserves, which now underscores the risks in Turkey's case," RBS said.

RESERVES OR RATES

So apart from praying for a quick resolution of the euro zone crisis, what can Turkey's central bank do next?

Tufan Comert, strategist at Garanti Securities in Istanbul said the central bank could try for a swap line with the U.S. Federal Reserve, which stepped in to provide liquidity to many emerging central banks in 2008. Or it could lend dollars to banks on forex deposit instead of selling, he said.

What markets would really like to see is an interest rate rise. Turkey's policy rate, the one-week repo rate, is at 5.75 percent, a negative rate in real terms, though the one-year bond yield is still in positive territory at 8.3 percent.

Yet the central bank admitted this week end-2011 inflation would be significantly above-target.

But a rate rise would mark an immense U-turn for the bank which has eased policy several times this year to engineer lira depreciation. It would argue a rate hike now will put Turkey at a disadvantage, given growth at home and abroad is slowing.

"I would have liked to have seen the central bank defending the lira with interest rate weapons as well, rather than only intervention," said Namik Aksel, chief executive of HSBC Asset Management Turkey. "Obviously this policy is a risk but they do have a point. Growth is going to be the main driver in 2012."

He too reckons no more than $5-$10 billion can be spent from now in the lira's defence. After that circumstances may force the central bank's hand -- the bank's strategy clearly hinges on a reversal of the global bearish market sentiment.

"I do believe they may hike overnight borrowing rates if we see another round of heavy sell-off," Aksel added.

(Editing by Catherine Evans)
