title: DJ  Turkey  May  Intervene  In  FX  Market If Lira Weakness Intensifies
text:
-- Turkey might intervene in currency markets if lira weakness intensifies

-- Measures taken so far to stop the currency sliding have had limited success

-- But some analysts say the bank isn't ready to intervene just yet

By Eva Szalay and Yeliz Candemir

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

The Turkish central bank may sell dollars in the currency markets to stop the lira depreciating further if fears of a global slowdown spook investors out of the Turkish currency, analysts said.

Fears of a direct intervention have grown after central bank Governor Erdem Basci said Friday that further lira weakness would be unwelcome. The lira has slipped almost 9% against the dollar in September, which hit a fresh record high against the lira at TRY1.8732 Sept. 28.

"You keep reserves exactly for these type of situations and if fears of a double-dip recession intensify, they won't think twice to use it," said Sengul Dagdeviren, chief economist at ING Bank Turkey in Istanbul.

The central bank has already sold around $3 billion, approximately 3% of its currency reserves of $87 billion, at its weekly auctions to shore up the lira.

So far, attempts to stall the lira's decline seem to have had little success.

Europe's emerging-market currencies have faced increasing pressure in recent weeks as fears of a global slowdown intensified and spooked investors out of currencies such as the lira, the Polish zloty and the Hungarian forint. Polish state-owned Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego stepped into currency markets for the second time in a week Thursday to support the Polish currency by selling dollars against the zloty.

"The risk for the lira is that capital outflows might continue if risk aversion remains strong but the central bank will remain ready to take steps to stabilize the currency." Dagdeviren said. "The question is how significant the outflows will be."

Turkey recovered remarkably from the recession last year, when its economy expanded 8.9% after having shrunk 4.7% in 2009.

Fueling Turkey's red-hot economic growth has been rampant consumer demand, financed by bank loans and credit cards. This has left the country with a big trade deficit because imports are rising faster than exports. Moreover, the rapid, import-led growth led to a yawning current-account deficit. This makes Turkey vulnerable to swings in the mood of international investors, who won't hesitate to withdraw cash once they grow wary of Turkey's ability to withstand the global downturn.

Already the economic outlook has darkened. The International Monetary Fund recently lowered its growth forecast for Turkey to just 6.6% in 2011 from its earlier 8.7% estimate. For 2012, the IMF predicts growth to slow down to just 2.2%.

Some analysts said the central bank will refrain from taking drastic steps for now.

"The lira is cheap already and close to the bottom, said Benoit Anne, head of emerging-market strategy at Societe Generale in London, adding that "no spectacular measures need to be undertaken at this stage."

"The depreciation of the lira is part of the soft landing," central bank Governor Basci said Friday.

But some economists disagreed. Garanti Yatirim analyst Tufan Comert, for example, said no hard data support Basci's argument, and a hard landing could still come.

Already, lira depreciation is stoking investor concerns over the country's inflation, which Basci said may exceed the 5.5% target in 2011.

title: DJ Middle East Turmoil May Spark Emerging-Market  Forex Interventions
text:
LONDON (Dow Jones)--Central banks in emerging markets look more and more likely to intervene on foreign-exchange markets as heightened nerves over the intensifying political crisis in the Middle East and North Africa cause a broad-based rush out of risky bets Tuesday, with a wide range of emerging-market currencies taking a hit.

Markets largely shrugged off the ructions in Tunisia, and showed relatively mild nerves over the overthrow of the Egyptian regime. But as the Libyan protests draw increasingly violent crackdowns from the under-pressure regime, investors are taking fright.

The sell-off Tuesday is indiscriminate, hitting currencies from Eastern Europe, South Africa, Turkey and Israel. Analysts agree that unless this proves to be a short-term blip, authorities across the region could launch foreign-exchange interventions to stabilize their currencies.

'Turkey may suffer, given its oil dependency and regional proximity. As the Turkish lira is now relatively cheap to [sell], we might need to see central-bank intervention to reduce volatility,' said Charles Robertson, head of macro strategy at Renaissance Capital.

For now, the spell of emerging-market currency weakness is marked, but not panicky. At 1027 GMT, the Turkish lira was at TRY1.6004 against the dollar, just off its weakest level since the end of January. The South African rand was at ZAR7.2057, around its weakest level since Feb. 17, and the Israeli shekel was at ILS3.898, around its weakest in a week.

Investors are scaling back on the riskier assets they hold and markets as far away as Korea and Taiwan could be hit, especially as both are energy importers, Robertson at Renaissance Capital said, adding that India, Kenya and Asia may also be affected.

Any sustained currency weakness would push up import prices, stoking inflation--another factor that could provoke currency interventions across the region.

To be sure, a short blast of weakness would probably be welcomed. It may be 'welcome relief' from recent currency strength and such a fall could be 'healthy corrections,' said Werner Gey Van Pittius, an emerging-markets fund manager at Investec Asset Management in London.

But large, abrupt or sustained currency slides would be a different matter, Gey Van Pittius added. 'Central banks may have to act so that they can step away from imported inflation,' he said, referring to the inflationary impact of weak currencies, which boost import prices.

The market's immediate concerns are on how far the political troubles will spread into oil-producing territories. There are already hints of trouble in Iran and Algeria. For investors, any sign it spreading to Saudi Arabia will be crucial.

'If Libya can overthrow its ruler, markets will assume that any ruler may now look unsafe,' said Renaissance's Robertson.

title: Turkey's Unorthodox Policy Potential Template For Tackling Emerging-Market Dilemma
text:
- While other countries have raised rates, Turkey went against orthodox policy and cut them

- Instead, it used reserve requirements to manage inflation and now other countries are copying

- Promisingly, both the lira and prices have moderated, but it's a risky strategy


 
    By Cynthia Lin 
    Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Last year, while other emerging-market central banks felt the frustration of seeing their interest rate increases drive up local currencies and spur inflows of volatile "hot money," Turkey's central bank opted for a less conventional approach to fighting inflation.

Against criticism that it was playing with fire, the country's central bank went the other way: It cut rates, supporting a weaker lira, and instead turned to bank reserve requirements as the primary weapon for containing credit growth and its overheating effects.

Earlier Tuesday, the central bank kept its benchmark rate unchanged at 6.25%, but that was after two consecutive cuts in as many months that left it at an all-time low in January. Now, one month since that surprising move, there is evidence to suggest the Turkish strategy is working, at least for now.

It could even become a model for other emerging-market central banks that are now dealing with a real conundrum: How to beat inflation without attracting volatile short-term money inflows. Those flows are driving up their currencies, undermining export competitiveness, and raising the risk of a destabilizing outflow if and when risk sentiment turns negative.

So far this year, the Turkish lira is down more than 3% on the dollar, a possible sign that hot money inflows have died off in response to the lower rates. But while this might otherwise have raised fears of imported inflation, a central bank survey released last Tuesday showed annual inflation expectations were at 6.56% for 2011, a decline from the previous 6.61% projection. That's likely an outcome of repeated increases in reserve requirements for banks, which since November have gone up from a blanket 5.5% for all deposits to as high as 12% for deposits of immediate access.

The Turkish approach is risky, as it challenges the central bank's credibility, but "the proof is in the pudding," said Neil Shearing, senior emerging-markets economist at Capital Economics, pointing to the weak lira as an early sign the policy is working.

According to Shearing, those countries with structurally similar economies could do well to follow Turkey's approach. He suggested Brazil, which despite being a commodity-based economy where Turkey is not, shares a key similarity "in that neither country saves a lot," which tends to bolster interest rates at home. "Given the high level of real interest rates in Brazil, they should have one eye on Turkey definitely," Shearing said.

In contrast, however, Turkey has seen subdued inflation readings, providing them a unique window of opportunity to use lower rates to target on hot money issues and its currency--a luxury most say will not last for long. "They've been able to (cut rates) because the inflation data has been benign in the past few months so that's given them a window of opportunity to do this," said Paul Biszko, senior emerging-markets analyst at RBC. "Turkey's turn is coming in terms of inflation pressure, but it's not here yet."

In the past, Turkey and Brazil were both seen as avid practitioners of inflation-targeting, but as their policies have diverged, this has pulled their currencies in opposite directions. While Turkey's benchmark rate is now at a record low, Brazil since last year has raised its benchmark rate by 250 basis points to a towering 11.25%. Meanwhile, the real continues to trend stronger against the dollar, despite aggressive dollar-buying interventions by the Brazilian central bank.

Turkey also pursues this costly tactic of currency intervention--as do many emerging-market central banks--but economists say that its $40 million in daily purchases is now aimed more at bulking up its relatively low foreign-currency reserves than reversing currency appreciation.

The International Monetary Fund, however, has warned of the extra liquidity caused by these dollar purchases, which are seen as counterproductive to the slew of tools Turkey has deployed to slow credit flows. Showing its discomfort with Turkey's policy framework, the IMF also recently said that a "greater effort" is needed from Turkey's fiscal policy side to make monetary moves more effective.

Meanwhile, other emerging-market countries are warming to the reserve requirement strategy that Turkey pioneered, seeing it as an alternative means of curtailing bank lending and the strong domestic demand its has fostered.

Biszko said that other countries have started following Turkey's lead. Developing nations such as China, Russia, Poland and India have all hiked reserve requirements. Biszko added that reserve adjustments can help cool import demand and take pressure off Turkey's hefty current account deficit, which was recently estimated to hit about 6% of 2010 gross domestic product.

For the time being, Turkey's measures appear to have stemmed hot money inflows into bank deposits and money markets without also sparking a destabilizing increase in longer-term redemptions. A net $8 billion in short-term hot-money outflows had occurred between mid-December and mid-January although local bonds still saw a net inflow of about $2.2 billion, according to a report in early February citing Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek.

Still, Turkey's success in its risky strategy is by no means assured.

The lira's weakness "cuts both ways," said Nick Chamie, global head of emerging-markets research at RBC. Without a stronger currency to eat away at inflation, prices could yet get away from the central bank's control. Chamie notes that reserve requirements alone are too blunt an instrument, and eventually the sharper tool of higher rates will be needed to fight pricing pressures. Also, if policy makers indeed have to backtrack and aggressively raise rates from "behind the curve" to restore their credibility and contain rising prices, it could make for a harsh landing and economic whiplash.

Although Turkey's January headline consumer price index showed a dramatic decline to 4.9% year-over-year--a 41-year low--it was mostly held down by an easy base comparison against last year's high levels. Both core inflation and producer price readings came in higher than expected, signaling pricing pressures down the line, especially at a time of rising oil and food prices worldwide.

"Did they create trouble down the line? I think no matter what, Turkey in a way is put into a difficult spot," said Christian Keller, chief economist for European emerging markets at Barclays Capital, "not really due to the policy, but the global commodity price developments working against them."

Yet for now, Turkey is the envy of other developing countries. The question is whether they will follow its policy model. If they do, and Turkey turns out to have been wrong, the implications for global inflation could be quite negative.

"They're making a very calculated gamble," Keller says. "They know that with a weaker lira on top of global commodity price increases, there could be a significant pass through into inflation later in the year, but for now they want to take advantage of the historically low annual inflation prints to lower policy rates further."

-By Cynthia Lin, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-4403; cynthia.lin@dowjones.com [ 15-02-11 2150GMT ]

title: FX  COLUMN-Turkish inflation fight may need lira boost
text:
-- Neal Kimberley is an FX market analyst for Reuters. The opinions expressed are his own --

By Neal Kimberley

LONDON, Feb 14 (Reuters) - The Turkish central bank's monetary policy mix, with its attendant objective of weakening the lira <TRY=>, might need some tweaking as the fight against inflation may be set to hot up.

With this in mind, traders might feel the rally in USD/TRY to Monday's 1.5800 from a November low of 1.3830 has run its course.

Policymakers around the world have been turning their fire on inflation [ID:nLDE7091HX], but the Turkish central bank has adopted an unorthodox monetary policy combining rises in reserve requirements with benchmark interest rate cuts. [ID:nLDE70Q0L5]

Ankara's objective has been to make yields less attractive, lessening international investor demand for the lira and aiding Turkish exporters' competitiveness, while simultaneously raising reserve requirements to drain excess liquidity and curb credit growth. [ID:nLDE70O0VF]

If lira weakening is a measure of this policy's success, the central bank will probably be satisfied, but addressing inflation worries may require a different policy tool kit.

A weak currency is no help when seeking to curb inflation.

On Jan. 25, the Turkish central bank raised its mid-point inflation forecast from 5.4 percent to 5.9 percent, citing concern over higher fuel prices, but predicting its current policy mix would remain in place for a long time.

Maybe. But in a Reuters poll of 15 banks, 10 expect the central bank to keep its benchmark one-week repo rate on hold at 6.25 percent when it makes its rate decision on Feb. 15 [ID:nLDE71910N]

On Jan. 25, Brent crude <LC0c1> was trading at $95 a barrel compared to $101 on Monday, which may test even Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek's confidence that Turkey's economy is strong enough to handle current oil prices. [ID:nLDE719075]

Moreover, while Turkey's consumer price inflation slowed to 4.9 percent on an annualised basis, from 6.4 percent in December and well inside the central bank's year-end target of 5.5 percent, the producer price index is on the rise.

Producer prices rose 2.36 percent on the month, exceeding a forecast rise of 1.0 percent, to give an annual increase of 10.8 percent and fanning fears the central bank's recent benchmark rate cuts may leave Turkey unprepared for any later inflation spike. [ID:nLDE7120H1]

State intervention to lower meat prices is already evident with the government having authorised meat imports -- much to the chagrin of domestic producers. [ID:nLDE70B04A]

While ratings agencies Fitch and Moody's are supporting the central bank's unorthodox policy mix [ID:nLDE71809N], traders might feel a further slide in the lira is inconsistent with controlling price pressures.

STRONG RECOVERY

It is not as if Turkey's economy clearly needs a further boost from a weaker lira.

Simsek said on Thursday that economic recovery was strong and that while growth would not be at the pace of 8-9 percent per annum, he expected around 5 percent in 2011. [ID:nLDE71909I]

Data released on Tuesday showed industrial output rose 16.9 percent year-on-year in December, far exceeding a Reuters poll forecast for a rise of 11 percent. [ID:nIST007569]

Of course it is undeniable that the current account deficit, which the central bank's new monetary policy was largely designed to address, is worsening.

The deficit surged 132 percent to a record high of $7.529 billion in December, central bank data showed on Friday, exceeding the median forecast of $7.0 billion in a Reuters poll of 14 analysts. [ID:nLDE71A0H9]

Be that as it may, central bank governor Durmus Yilmaz [ID:nLDE716235], in a Feb. 7 interview with Reuters and Reuters Insider, highlighted the potentially inflationary impact of further lira weakening.

"We are very mindful that any further ... depreciation of the currency, if commodity prices increase further, will impact the inflation outlook in a negative way," Yilmaz said.

Given that Yilmaz also argued that the central bank's efforts to cool inflows of speculative capital seem to be succeeding, perhaps his attention might turn more to inflationary concerns.

The central bank's interest in weakening the currency further might abate, leaving the field open to the lira bulls.

title: Turkish  Central Bank  Chief: We Have Ability To  Intervene  In Market
text:
ISTANBUL (Dow Jones)--Turkey's central bank has the ability to intervene in the foreign exchange market if the lira moves to an undesirable level, Governor Durmus Yilmaz said Thursday.

"We have ability to intervene if developments on exchange rate side become inappropriate with the economy," Yilmaz said in an interview on state television.

The lira moved to 1.5480 against the dollar at 1000 GMT, from 1.5510 on Yilmaz's comments. Like other emerging markets Turkey aims to protect its currency and foreign trade balances against rising unreliable short-term speculative portfolio investments, or so called "hot money", as quantitative easing policies of big central banks has sent investors seeking higher yields.

The bank cut its benchmark interest rate and raised lira reserve requirements last week in order to curb domestic credit expansion, current accounts deficit and "hot money"' inflows. Turkey aims to prevent excessive appreciation of the lira as it hurts exports.

However, the central bank is not expected to allow the lira to depreciate too much, as this could lead to inflation. Yilmaz stressed that Turkey should not target record high growth rates but sustainable and continuing economic growth.

title: UPDATE 2-Turkey may mull steps against "hot money"-finmin
text:
* Finance Minister says taxation an option

* Brazil-style 'Tobin' tax not viewed favourably by govt

* More monetary measures expected first

* Could build forex reserves to between $100-150 billion

(Adds fresh quotes, analysts comments, background)

By Simon Cameron-Moore and Orhan Coskun

ISTANBUL, Dec 3 (Reuters) - Turkey should discuss contingencies, including taxation, to curb portfolio inflows fuelling runaway asset prices, but no evaluations had taken place yet, Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek said on Friday.

Governments in Brazil, South Africa, Thailand and other emerging markets have directly or indirectly intervened in recent months to keep their currencies from strengthening.

Turkey had no plans at present to rein in such "hot money" inflows, but policymakers had options to review, Simsek told broadcaster CNBC-e in an interview.

"The government should discuss 'hot money.' As a principle, I am someone who believes we can't just be observers to portfolio inflows at this time," Simsek said.

"I believe that other measures can be taken, other measures including tax.... These can always be evaluated. But this is not the case now," he said.

Investors have poured money into Turkish stocks, bonds and the lira this year, seeking higher-yielding markets after developed economies slashed interest rates.

"Steps will not be allowed which shock investors and cause them to flee Turkey," a senior member of the ruling AK Party with knowledge of economic policy told Reuters.

"The entry of long-term capital into the country is something which we clearly prefer."

So far, Turkey has used monetary levers to stop foreign speculators overheating its markets and making the lira currency become too strong.

"In Emerging Europe only Turkey and Poland really have to worry about this," said David Oxley, emerging markets economist at Capital Economics in London.

With inflation falling there was little prospect for a hike in the main central bank policy rate through 2011, he said.

Analysts, expect Turkish policymakers to curb credit growth instead through further increases in the reserve requirements -- already back to levels seen before the global financial crisis struck in late 2008.

PREFERENCES

Analysts also foresaw further reductions in the overnight borrowing rate to dampen speculation on the lira appreciating, as the bulk of foreign money is parked in the money market.

The central bank, on Nov. 11, left its policy rate, the one week repo rate, unchanged but slashed its overnight borrowing rate by 400 points to encourage investors to hold lira deposits longer.

The central bank also has stepped up purchases of foreign exchange at weekly auctions, and Prime Minister Tayyip Erdogan has said Turkey needs to build up its forex reserves.

The AK Party official said reserves should be raised to a level of around $100-150 billion. As of Nov. 26 they stood just below $80 billion.

Simon Quijano-Evans, analyst at C.A. Chevreux in Vienna, saw the central bank and government working well together to cool markets.

"First of all they will try to manage expectations, and looking at equity prices and bond yield movements over the last couple of weeks they've done that and it has worked," he said.

Economy Minister Ali Babacan earlier this year expressed skepticism over the merits of Brazil's "Tobin" tax. The Latin American giant has imposed levies on foreigners' purchases of local bonds and stocks.

A senior official in the ruling AK Party told Reuters that this option was not viewed positively, so the tax weapon appears unlikely to be used unless other methods fail.

"Is it likely? It all depends on the continued flows," Quijano-Evans, said. "It's obviously a possibility."

The imposition of a withholding tax had caused the Turkish bond market to dry up a few years ago, and that experience will probably make policymakers reluctant to go that route, though Turkey is in better shape now.

Turkey notched 11 percent growth year on year in the first half of 2010, making it one of the fastest growing economies globally, and the share market has boomed.

While the lira is little changed against the dollar since the start of the year, Turkey's main trading partner is Europe, and the lira has appreciated 10 percent against the euro, raising complaints from exporters.

The main benchmark Istanbul index <.XU100>, which is 70 percent foreign owned, has gained 26.7 percent since the start of the year compared with a 12.6 percent increase in the MSCI benchmark index of emerging stocks <.MSCIEF>.

Simsek also said the government's 2010 budget deficit may be below 44 billion lira ($29.6 billion), a trend that could bode well for Turkey's chances of getting a credit rating upgrade for its sovereign debt [ID:nLDE6A41BN]. The government has previously said it targets an end-year deficit of 44.2 billion lira. (Additional reporting by Ayla Jean Yackley; editing by Stephen Nisbet and Toby Chopra)

title: ANALYSIS-Turkey's enviable growth outlook revives laggard lira
text:
* Lira seen advancing to 1.40-1.35 to dollar

* Lira lagged 2010 gains in Eastern European currencies

* Central Bank not seen intervening in appreciation

* Impending rate hikes could encourage carry trade

By Alexandra Hudson

ISTANBUL, April 28 (Reuters) - Turkey's lira is finally rallying, with economy set to enjoy one of 2010's fastest growth rates, and a tightening policy by the Central Bank that will help spark demand for the currency.

Turkey's projected growth rate this year of 5.2 percent is faster than the euro zone, emerging Europe and the CIS region, according to the IMF's latest economic outlook.

In addition, minimal risk is seen to Turkey's exports from a higher currency, analysts said.

"We expect Turkish interest rates to rise by 200 basis points in 2010, and the country will benefit from this increasing interest rate divergence. The euro-zone looks a mess and we don't think it will be before 2011 that the ECB can raise rates," said Justin Patrie, emerging Europe analyst at Business Monitor International.

Having already rallied almost 3 percent since the start of April to around 1.48 to the dollar, analysts now think the lira could advance as far as 1.35-1.40, as it catches up on gains made by other Turkish assets, and other emerging currencies.

"There is fundamental demand for the lira. Conditions in Turkey are excellent -- certainly much stronger than the United States and the euro zone. Turkey has a strong, healthy credit market, some of Europe's most robust banks and private consumption is a strong recovery story," Patrie added.

The currency is seen as having plenty of room to appreciate, supported by a Central Bank that will allow such moves.

The lira gained just 3 percent to the dollar in 2009, after losing almost a quarter of its value the year before. Turkish equities <.XU100> by contrast doubled in value and bonds yields touched record lows on the country's resilience to the crisis, which earned it upgrades by all major credit ratings agencies.

Economist Tim Ash at Royal Bank of Scotland said the belief the lira had lagged other emerging currencies as well as more convincing signs of recovery had all helped lift the currency.

Turkish ministers predict first-quarter growth will be in double figures, after 6 percent growth in the fourth-quarter.

LAGGARD

Despite April's gains, the lira is still only trading 1 percent higher than at the start of 2010, compared with a gain of almost 5 percent for Poland's zloty <EURPLN=>, 3.5 percent for the Czech crown, and 8.4 percent for the rouble.

A fresh bout of tension in February between Turkey's Islamist-rooted government and the judiciary and military -- bastions of Turkey's secularist foundations -- briefly hit confidence in Turkish assets, but the row has since eased.

Turkey's parliament is discussing contentious reforms to the constitution, intended to bring it into harmony with European-Union norms, but for now the growth story is dominant.

"Investors have come to expect an element of political instability in Turkey and as long as it isn't a major shock it shouldn't affect assets," said economist Paul Biszko at Royal Bank of Canada.

RBC has upgraded the lira to "overweight" from "marketweight", due to its "valuation, attractive carry, growth upside risks and a non-intervening Central Bank."

INFLATION FEAR

Turkey's central bank is expected to tolerate lira strength because the currency is still trading well below highs of around 1.18 to the dollar in August 2008, and because lira appreciation also will help cap energy inflation by reducing the cost of oil.

Turkey's central bank targets inflation of 6.5 percent by the end of 2010 but it is currently running at 9.56 percent. The bank has signalled it will hike rates later this year when it sees recovery less endangered by monetary tightening.

Most analysts expect rate hikes of 200 basis points to follow although the bank has already begun withdrawing liquidity.

If Turkey's Central Bank, as expected, becomes one of the first in the region to tighten policy rates it will likely spur the carry trade, which all but disappeared after it slashed rates by 10.25 percentage points from late 2008 to 2009.

POSSIBLE RISKS

Risks to the lira's upwards trend include Turkey's current account deficit, which fell sharply during the recession, but is rising again. February's deficit of $2.6 billion was more than eight times wider than in February 2009.

Another factor is the substantial holdings of foreign exchange by Turkish citizens and their tendency to switch from one currency to another.

A more expensive lira could also irritate the country's large export sector.

"A stronger lira could be seen as bad for growth dynamics as it hinders export performance. But more than the value of the lira, demand conditions in Turkey's export markets are more significant in my opinion," said economist Levent Durusoy at Yatirim Finansman. (Editing by Neil Stempleman)

title: Q+A-How dangerous is Turkish military plot report?
text:
ANKARA, June 17 (Reuters) - An alleged plot by the Turkish military to destabilise the Islamist-rooted ruling AK Party could pitch the European Union candidate country into political turmoil.

 The government has taken legal action after a report that the military had drawn up a plan to stop the AK Party and an influential religious movement from "destroying Turkey's secular order and replacing it by an Islamist state". [ID:nLG375319]

 WHAT DOES THE REPORT ALLEGE?

 Taraf, a liberal newspaper often critical of the military, published on Friday what it said was a document from the  powerful General Staff office, signed by a senior navy officer.

 The alleged document, entitled "Plan of Action for Combating Fundamentalism" describes plans to discredit the AK Party through a media campaign, stir up party divisions, foment nationalist opposition to the government and plant weapons in houses used by associates of Muslim preacher Fethullah Gulen to suggest the religious movement is involved in militant activities.

 It is not the first time reports have surfaced alleging efforts to undermine the Islamist-rooted AK Party government.

 WHAT CAN HAPPEN NEXT?

 Whether the document proves to be fake or authentic, the controversy has further strained ties between the AK Party and the staunchly secular military, which is already under pressure over a separate investigation into a suspected right-wing network accused of plotting a coup against the government. A trial has already begun.

 Generals and the AK Party, which has roots in political Islam but also embraces centre-right and nationalist elements, have long been at odds over the direction of the mainly Muslim country. Turkey has a secular constitution.

 The story has embarrassed the military and could end up strengthening the government in a long power struggle with hardline secularists over public opinion and Turkey's direction.

 Prime Minister Tayyip Erdogan on Tuesday urged military and civilian courts to "comfort society" and swiftly conclude an investigation into the report. Armed forces chief General Ilker Basbug has declined to say whether he believed such a secret document existed. On Tuesday the two men met for 80 minutes.

 The military has launched its own investigation.

 If the document is genuine, it would fuel accusations by the AK Party that the secular establishment, of which the army is a key pillar, is willing to use anti-democratic means to undermine the political party, which first took power in 2002.

 Secularists have long accused the AK Party and its conservative supporters of harbouring an Islamist agenda and seeking to turn Turkey away from its Western secular values upon which the republic was founded on by Mustafa Kemal Ataturk. 

 AK, which can look to support in the pro-western middle classes, beyond the country's conservative religious heartland, denies it has any such Islamist agenda.

 Secularists also are suspicious of Gulen and his followers who they believe have infiltrated key institutions in Turkey, particularly the police.

 If the row escalates, the government will be dragged into a new confrontation rather than pursuing reforms towards EU membership that help attract more foreign investment.

 Regardless of which camp prevails, analysts say the price could be high for Turkey's political stability. Domestic turbulence has in the past hampered progress in economic and political reforms aimed at gaining EU membership and have been a source of concern for investors.

 IS THERE A RISK OF A COUP?

Turkey's military has a long history of intervening in politics, including staging several coups by force or through pressure, most recently in 1997 when it helped oust an Islamist government. Few believe there is a risk of another coup, partly because the military would not have public backing.

 The military has traditionally been very careful to ensure it remains respected by Turks. The military is frequently viewed as the most respected institution in Turkey, according to polls.

 But recent setbacks for the armed forces and the damage to its reputation could raise the risk that generals may not be able to hold back rebellion among ranks and that rogue elements would resort to clandestine actions in an attempt to sow chaos.

 Open hostilities between the AK Party and the General Staff, deeply suspicious of each other, have eased since the less confrontational Basbug took command of the NATO army last year.

 But the arrests of retired generals and active officers over the past two years for their alleged links to the suspected Ergenekon right-wing group and attacks by pro-government media against the once-untouchable military may force Basbug to take a harder public line to calm brewing discontent.

 The military -- still Turkey's most respected institution according to recent opinion polls -- has taken a back seat in recent years, but a climate of growing government-military confrontation might drag generals into the political arena.

 ARE MARKETS CONCERNED?

 Turkey can barely afford more domestic turbulence, with the economy suffering a sharp slowdown. The International Monetary Fund expects Turkey's economy to shrink 5.1 percent this year, after growing 5.9 percent annually between 2002-2008.

 Traders said markets were for the moment shrugging off the row, but it was expected to pile further pressure on Turkey in coming months. 

 Tensions between the military and the government may add risk to a business environment where the lira currency is seen coming under pressure as the Central Bank continues to cut rates to prop up the economy and with no IMF loan programme in place.

title: Turkish lira weakens, inflation data eyed
text:
ISTANBUL, Dec 3 (Reuters) - Turkey's lira weakened on Monday as Asian stocks fell and investors awaited guidance from Turkish inflation data due later in the day.   

 Traders shrugged off news at the weekend from the Turkish armed forces that they had inflicted heavy casualties on Kurdish separatist militants in a "intense intervention" into northern Iraq.   

 The army said operations would continue and President Abdullah Gul reaffirmed on Sunday Turkey's readiness and right to intervene in northern Iraq.   

 Investors said limited operations against separatist Kurdish guerrillas had been expected. On Friday, the lira had weakened slightly after Prime Minister Tayyip Erdogan said the government had authorised the army to carry out an operation into northern Iraq.   

 The lira <IYIX=> weakened to 1.1830 in early interbank trade, from an official close of 1.1770 on Friday.   

 "I expect the market to be quiet today until inflation," said one trader.   

 "If inflation comes in between 1.5 and 2.0 percent, that is priced in, if it comes in above or below that the market will react," he said, adding that because of a series of holidays in December, investors are already starting to close their books for year-end and position themselves for 2008.   

 Inflation data is due at 1500 GMT on Monday. A forecast from a Reuters poll put the monthly consumer inflation rate at 1.46 percent after the Central Bank warned prices could spike higher in November before returning to a downward trend.   

 Consumer price inflation in Istanbul came in at 1.94 percent in November, the Istanbul Chamber of Commerce said on Monday.   

 Asian stocks weakened on Monday and then yen, which is closely watched by lira investors, firmed in a sign of lower risk appetite. Investors borrow the cheap Japanese currency to invest in high-yielding lira, helping the Turkish currency appreciate almost 20 percent this year.   

 After the market closed on Friday data showed Turkey's trade deficit widened 30.7 percent year-on-year to $5.633 billion in October, just below a Reuters poll forecast of $5.925 billion.   

 On Saturday data from the Turkish Exporters Association showed that in November exports surged 29 percent year-on-year to $11.11 billion.   

 Stocks in focus on Monday will include conglomerates  Koc Holding  and  Sabanci Holding , which posted nine-month results after the market closed on Friday. On Monday Koc's chairman was also quoted as saying revenue would come in at $45 billion this year, rising to $50 billion in 2008.   

 Media group Dogan Yayin , its parent Dogan Holding , and  Turkish Airlines  also published profit figures.   

 On Friday the main stock index <.XU100> rose 1.94 percent to 54,213.82 points. The yield on the Aug. 5, 2009 benchmark bond <0#TRTSYSUM=IS> fell to 16.63 percent from Thursday's close of 16.66 percent.  (Reporting by Irem Koker)

title: PRESS DIGEST - Turkey - Sept 21
text:
ANKARA, Sept 21 (Reuters) - These are the leading stories in the Turkish press on Friday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.   

HURRIYET   

- A professor recalls how lifting the ban on the Muslim headscarf at Ankara University's theology faculty in 1988 quickly led to all women students wearing the garment. She says she fears similar social pressure on uncovered women if the government lifts the headscarf ban now, as it hopes to do.   

RADIKAL   

- Under the planned new constitution, Turkey's ruling AK Party will reduce the powers of institutions that have opposed its rule over the past few years, such as the board supervising universities and the Constitutional Court.   

MILLIYET   

- AK Party members are upset by plans to make religious education in schools optional. The AK Party has Islamist roots and its rank-and-file are conservative and religious-minded.   

REFERANS   

- Turkey's central bank is ready to intervene in the currency markets if the dollar weakens below the 1.20 level to the lira. The lira is now at 1.23. The paper also says Turkish interest rates could be cut by 200 basis points by end-2007.   

CUMHURIYET   

- Turkish university rectors defend their right to comment on and criticise government plans to overhaul the constitution, saying their duty is to enlighten the public. Prime Minister Tayyip Erdogan had blasted the rectors over their criticism, telling them to "mind their own business".   

ZAMAN   

- Architects of Turkey's present constitution, introduced in 1982 after a military coup, back plans for a new "civilian constitution" that boosts individual rights and freedoms.   

VATAN   

- Prime Minister Tayyip Erdogan will lobby other leaders on behalf of Turkey's bid to become a temporary member of the U.N. Security Council when he attends the annual general assembly in New York. He is due to meet 10 presidents, 30 prime ministers and 50 foreign ministers in the coming days.   

YENI SAFAK   

- The head of the state body overseeing religious activity in Turkey, the 'Diyanet', says religious instrucution must remain compulsory in schools. Making it optional would fan divisions between different sects, he says.

title: Turkish assets unfazed by Gul's talk on presidency
text:
ISTANBUL, July 25 (Reuters) - The Turkish lira weakened slightly on Wednesday along with other Turkish assets although comments by Foreign Minister Abdullah Gul that he may make a fresh bid for Turkey's presidency elicited little reaction.   

Turkey's secularists including army generals blocked Gul's first attempt to be elected head of state in May, forcing last Sunday's early parliamentary election, which resulted in a decisive victory for the pro-business AK Party.   

That win prompted the lira shot to a 6-year high and the stock exchange rallied, although profit-taking has since crimped gains slightly.   

The lira <IYIX=> weakened 0.6 percent to close at 1.2420 on the interbank market on Wednesday after it rallied 1.4 percent to close at 1.2340 on Tuesday.   

The main stock index <.XU100>, which surged 5.1 percent to a record close on Monday, closed 0.2 percent lower at 54,832 points on Wednesday amid profit-talking.   

"Gul's comments didn't affect the market, although we are monitoring the presidential elections. Global markets are slightly more important for us as we wait for a clearer picture on the elections," said a bond trader.   

Markets have been boosted by the AK Party winning 47 percent of the vote in Sunday's general election, allowing it to govern alone again and press ahead with a reformist agenda.   

However, the party must now solve the row over a successor to President Ahmet Necdet Sezer, whose term expired in May, and which has pitted secularists against the AK Party.   

Separately on Wednesday, bids at Turkey's Central Bank daily dollar-buying auction were $288 million, more than seven times a maximum buying limit of $40 million, at the first auction since it raised the buying limit.   

The bank bought $40 million, the full amount, at a maximum price of 1.2475 lira <IYIX=>, central bank data showed.   

Raymond James Chief Economist Ozgur Altug said bid volume was the second highest since 2002.   

"This shows that there is plenty of FX supply, which will exert pressure on the exchange rate in the coming period. If this trend continues, the Central Bank of Turkey will be forced to intervene directly in the foreign exchange market," he said.   

Bonds eased with the yield on the May 6, 2009 benchmark bond <0#TRTSYSUM=IS> rising to 17.26 percent from Tuesday's 17.18 percent.

title: FOCUS: Stakes High As Turkey Goes To The Polls
text:
MILAN (Dow Jones--With just a few days to go before Turkey's enigmatic July 22 elections, Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan has upped the ante by pledging to quit politics if his AK Party doesn't emerge with an electoral mandate to form a single-party government.   

Opinion polls and analysts reckon he'll be proven right and that the AKP, which stands for Justice and Development, can remain solely at the helm and steer through reforms to keep fueling the 7% annual economic growth rate of recent years.   

But the road ahead may be bumpier than it seems. A surprise electoral result could plunge Turkish markets into turmoil. Even the expected AKP victory will require delicate footwork to avoid confrontation with the military, which has openly accused the AKP of being a threat to secular institutions.   

Most of all, Turkey's next government will have to move beyond the acclaimed macroeconomic reforms of recent years to find more concrete ways of boosting productivity and employment, goals that will require policies destined to disturb notable swathes of society.   

"The tension is not about the regime, but arises from Turkey's structural transformation," says  Morgan Stanley economist Serhan Cevik.   

In the past, he notes, the Turkish state owned firms and operated subsidy schemes to establish itself as the ultimate distributor of income and wealth. The AKP's more free-market approach has, since 2002, doubled per capita income and exports but has also threatened many perceived privileges.   

More will be needed, says Cevik, who hopes Turkey will adopt a "big bang" approach to reform after the vote.   

The AKP touts plans to liberalize labor markets, bolster ownership and contract laws, and overhaul the tax system.   

It is also keen to pursue large-scale privatization - toll highway concessions are already on the block and energy utilities are ripe to join them - with the aim of promoting greater productivity as well as further cutting state debt.   

Since the AKP took the helm, the Istanbul stock market has quadrupled, rising another 14% since June 26 alone and Turkish inflation has fallen to a near 35-year low. But its record on employment - a daunting challenge given that more than one million Turks join the workforce each year - is weaker: the jobless rate has fallen to only 9.8%% from 10.5% five years earlier.   

Job prospects are a frequent topic on the campaign trail, according to Mehmet Simsek, a former  Merrill Lynch economist who is now an AKP candidate and tipped for an important economics portfolio in the next administration.   

Future job growth is likely to come from Turkey's burgeoning industrial sector - especially in automotive and electronics - which are replacing traditional sectors such as agriculture and textiles. But success in those new areas will require robust productivity gains and, if European experience is any indication, relative wage restraint.   

The economic policies offered by opposition parties appear aimed at tempting vulnerable voters.   

Cihan Pacaci, an Ankara candidate for the right-wing Nationalist Movement Party, or MHP, says the AKP has left a "wrecked economy" with inadequate job creation and too much reliance on foreign capital. He pledges to "implement a currency policy" to boost exports, and to privatize by local public share offerings rather than sell them to foreign investors.   

Algan Hacaloglu, deputy chairman of the left-leaning Republican People's Party, or CHP, says his party will make agriculture "a driving force in Turkey" and hints at more government intervention through an "industrialization policy" that singles out sectors ripe for public support.   

The mercurial Youth Party, led by controversial entrepreneur Cem Uzan, promises to halve the price of diesel fuel and double procurement prices for hazelnuts, a key product along the Black Sea coast.   

The AKP has indulged in some populism of its own, hiking hazelnut prices by seven times the central bank's inflation target, delaying energy price hikes and vowing to slash sales taxes on tourism and agricultural enterprises. But it is the only party that appears to accept rules foreign capital will embrace.   

Turkey is a "good and improving credit story" but it "gets tricky" if the AKP doesn't stay in power, says Tim Ash, an analyst for  Bear Stearns. He notes the AKP is talking up plans to lift the country's credit rating up three notches to investment grade by the end of 2009.   

Recent polls suggest the AKP is on course to win around 41% of the vote, the CHP 18%, MHP 12%, with the Youth Party polling between 6%-10%. Independent Kurdish candidates, mostly from southeastern Turkey, are also expected to win at least 30 seats in Turkey's 550-seat assembly.   

The final numbers will be particularly crucial because parties that win less than 10% of the popular vote aren't assigned any parliamentary seats.   

That stringent threshold explains why, in the 2002 vote, the AKP won a whopping 365 seats - giving it a powerful majority - on the back of just 34% of the vote. Only the CHP won more than 10% of the vote.   

If both the MHP and the Youth Party pass the threshold this time, the AKP will probably not be able to form a government, unless perhaps by inviting the Kurdish deputies into a coalition.   

But the prospect of an "Islamic/Kurdish" government ruling for five years "would be a recipe for serious political crisis and possible military intervention," warns  Goldman Sachs analyst Ahmet Akarli.   

If only the CHP and MHP enter parliament, the AKP will have to win more than 36% of the vote or risk having a majority so slim as to exacerbate factional infighting inside the party, Akarli said.   

Erdogan "will need a tighter but leaner party in his second term," he added.   

Anticipating such a need, the prime minister has replaced more than 150 current AKP deputies with new candidates, often shedding Islamic hard-liners with centrist technocrats such as Simsek.   

Traditionally, Turkish voters tend to turn against incumbent parties, but also reward recent economic performance, and historical patterns suggest the AKP will win 40% of the vote, says says Ali Akarca, a professor of political science at universities in Chicago and Ankara who has carried out extensive research into electoral habits.   

An export surge helped Turkey's economy expand at a 6.8% annual rate in the first quarter, much faster than expected. But private final consumption - presumably what matters to voters - slowed to a meager 1.6%, suggesting swathes of discontent may emerge at the ballot box.   

Small-town merchants are particularly grumpy, as modern supermarket chains are poaching their clients and even the rebounding tourist flows offer little business as vacationers increasingly opt for all-inclusive package deals, Akarca said from his farm on the Aegean coast.   

Markets are priced for the benign scenario in which the AKP retains power on its own but doesn't muster a two-thirds majority enabling it to change the constitution. The odds of such an outcome are 60% to 80%, according to analysts.   

Investors should be wary as that leaves plenty of room for "icebergs in the Mediterranean," says Ali Al-Eyd, emerging markets specialist for Dresdner Kleinwort, who is underweight on Turkish government debt.   

Any outcome other than the "Goldilocks" scenario of a modest AKP victory would likely produce an impasse preventing the new parliament from appointing a new president in the autumn and requiring new elections.   

-By Christopher Emsden, Dow Jones Newswires; +39-02-58-21-99-05; chris.emsden@dowjones.com

title: Emerging Mkt Debt Struggles; Political Tension Hits Turkey
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging market bonds had a hard time keeping afloat Monday, with the asset class falling far behind a rally in U.S. Treasurys.   

Spreads on  JPMorgan's Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus were seven basis points wider at 164 basis points over Treasurys, which gained on tame March inflation data. On Friday, the EMBI+ had closed at 157 basis points, matching a record-tight level set earlier this month.   

One New York-based debt trader said volumes were quiet ahead of Tuesday's May Day holiday, which will shut every major Latin American market, as well as other countries in Asia and Europe.   

Emerging markets showed signs of fatigue last week, with many credits at record-tight spreads but little momentum for further gains.  Merrill Lynch said in a Monday report that valuations on emerging market debt "appear increasingly uncompelling."   

Turkey grabbed headlines Monday as political tension gripped the country. Hundreds of thousands of anti-government demonstrators took the streets in Istanbul Sunday to demand the resignation of the AK Party government. Late Friday, the military issued a statement saying it might intervene to ward off what it described as threats to Turkey's secular institutions. The AKP's presidential candidate, Foreign Minister Abdullah Gul, failed to win the office in voting last week. A second round is scheduled for May 2.   

Turkey's Global 2030 bond tumbled 1 9/16 to 154 5/8 bid, according to Reuters, and its EMBI+ spread mushroomed 16 basis points to 210 basis points over Treasurys. Its five-year credit default swaps were 20 basis points wider at 165 basis points mid-level late in the European session, and the New York-based trader said the CDS were little traded during U.S. hours.   

Central European currencies weakened in line with Turkish assets, but external debt from the region performed slightly better. Poland's EMBI+ spread tightened two basis points to 48 basis points over Treasurys.   

Mexico's Global 2034 rose 3/4 to 111 1/2 bid and its EMBI+ spread widened two basis points to 88 basis points over Treasurys. The credit posted positive returns on the day despite the Bank of Mexico lowering its 2007 forecast for the country's growth to between 3% and 3.5%, compared with a previous projection of 3.25% to 3.75%. Finance Minister Agustin Carstens said in Canada earlier Monday that the ministry will likely revise downward its growth projection to 3.3% from 3.6%.   

Colombia's Global 2033 jumped 1 3/8 to 148 5/8 bid and its EMBI+ spread widened five basis points to 139 basis points over Treasurys. The central bank holds its monthly monetary policy meeting Monday and is expected to raise the benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 8.5%. UBS said policymakers "will have to maintain a hawkish stance" to bring inflation back within the central bank's target of 3.5% to 4.5%.

title: Emerging debt-Market drifts higher in illiquid trade, Turkey up
text:
LONDON, June 29 (Reuters) - Emerging sovereign debt prices rose modestly in quiet trade on Thursday as investors have little impetus to trade in the illiquid conditions ahead of the U.S. Federal Reserve's interest rates decision.  

The benchmark JP Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus (EMBI+) <11EMJ> <.JPMEMBIPLUS> showed yield spreads narrowed by one basis point to 228 basis points over slightly stronger U.S. Treasuries.  

Overall, investors dipping into the market found illiquid conditions ahead of the U.S. Federal Reserve's interest rate decision, widely expected to produce the 17th straight quarter percentage point increase to 5.25 percent.  

Trade in Turkey's sovereign bonds was light but the credit was showing signs of a slight correction higher.  

Turkey's debt has come under pressure as a result of the heavy sell-off in the lira currency. Rising inflation and tightening global monetary policies have conspired against Turkish assets.  

Until this week's concerted efforts by the central bank to raise interest rates, drain lira from the financial system, sell dollars and intervene directly in the market, investors were losing faith in Turkey's much improved economy.  

The benchmark 2030 bond <TRGLB30=RR> on Thursday rose 0.25 points in price to bid 134.00, yielding 8.508 percent.  

Investors have bought the credit back after pushing prices down to 15 months lows earlier this week of 130.75, which in turn pushed the yield up to 8.736 percent.  

"The Turkey 30s have bounced three points from the lows, but this is only a blip compared with the losses of the past three months. Thus, the dead cat bounce, short covering, relief rally, could continue a little while longer," Richard Sega, portfolio strategist at Argonaftis Capital in London wrote to clients.  

"Balanced against this, though, nerves ahead of the inflation data, plentiful broker recommendations to short the 30s against the 34s, 14s and 15s, etc, will limit the gains," he added.  

Turkey's five-year credit default swaps -- insurance like products that protect against default or credit restructurings -- narrowed by about 20 basis points to 300 basis points on Thursday <TURKEY5UA=GFI>.  

While narrowing spreads show a reduction in risk aversion, spreads are just off their widest point in 13 months.  

"We're seeing short-covering off the street after two weeks of permanently softer days, so this is kind of a bounce which started yesterday but I would not characterize it as aggressive client buying," said one Turkish debt trader at a German bank in London.  

"People are looking at the bonds and maybe thinking they are cheap. It is a corrective trade, but we are really waiting to see what Turkey's inflation figures show next week and we have the Fed tonight, so that is keeping a lid on turnover," the trader said.  

Elsewhere, Brazil's benchmark 2040 bond <BRGLB40=RR> rose 0.187 points in price to bid 121.875, yielding 7.624 percent.  

Fitch Ratings upgraded Brazil's credit rating late on Wednesday to 'BB' from 'BB-', citing ongoing improvement in external finances despite the turbulence in emerging markets.  

Russia's benchmark sovereign bond due 2030 <RUSGLB30=RR> rose 0.125 points in price to bid 105.438, yielding 6.521 percent.

title: Emerging debt-Turkey's bonds move to the beat set by the lira
text:
LONDON, June 26 (Reuters) - Turkey's sovereign dollar-donominated bonds fell sharply on Monday in thin trading as investors trimmed positions while weighing the impact of more rate increases and dollar sales by Ankara.  

"If there is stability on the FX side things it will get better on the external side. Bond traders are looking at the lira and more action by the Central Bank of Turkey will be welcomed by the market," said Luis Costa, emerging markets strategist at ING in London.  

On Sunday Turkey's central bank raised interest rates 225 basis points. On Monday it followed through on promises to sell dollars at auction, conducted direct dollar selling intervention as well as draining more lira liquidity from the system with "depo" auctions.  

Trading in the lira was a tug of war on Monday, with initial strength giving way to selling only to be bolstered again with the dollar auction and direct intervention.  

Turkey's benchmark sovereign dollar bond due 2030 <TRGLB30=> was down on the day, clearly the underperformer for the emerging debt sector as a whole, but strength in the lira has helped cut early losses.  

The 2030 bond is down 1.188 points in price to bid 132.375, yielding 8.636 percent.  

The benchmark JP Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus (EMBI+) <11EMJ> <.JPMEMBIPLUS> however showed the sector was holding up much better with yield spreads wider by just one basis point to 229 basis points over U.S. Treasuries.  

Turkey's EMBI+ portion showed yield spreads wider by 16 basis points to 252 over Treasuries.  

"Invstors still trying to unload their neutral and overweighted positions on Turkey, which I think will continue over the next weeks. Unfortunately this is not going to fade away over a number of days," Costa cautioned.  

Given the low liquidity in the market, investors have turned to the credit default swaps market to unload their risk. The CDS market offers sovereign debt holders protection against default or restructuring. Widening spreads show increased risk aversion.  

Turkey's five-year CDS <TURKEY5UA=GFI> spread has pushed the bid price up to 320 basis points, its highest level in over a year and up from 115 basis points in February.  

"The trading in the market overall has been illiquid and erratic. Turkey especially and that's pushing people into CDS. There is still no conviction (the central bank) is going to get it right," said one senior trader at a German bank in London.  

LIMITED MOVES  

The deterioration in Turkish CDS is now on par with five-year CDS from Argentina and Ecuador and worse than Peru and Jamaica. Elsewhere, Brazil's 2040 bond, the most liquid emerging sovereign debt issue, traded up 0.25 points in price to bid 121.938, yielding 7.619 percent <BRAGLB40=RR>.  

Russia's 2030 bond <RUSGLB30=RR> fell 0.438 points in price to bid 105.250, yielding 6.541 percent.  

Separately, dollar-denominated bonds in Russian steelmaker Severstal plunged on news its bid to buy Luxembourg-based Arcelor failed against a higher offer from Mittal Steel that values Arcelor, according to a Reuters calculation, at roughly 25.6 billion euros.  

Severstal's 2014 bond <RU019049060=> was bid down 3.65 points in price to 103.78, pushing the yield up to 8.572 percent. Spreads over the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury widened by 62 basis points.  

Russian politicians slammed Arcelor's deicision, saying it showed an anti-Russian bias in international markets.

title: UPDATE 3-Turkish  central bank  sells dollars to steady lira
text:
(Adds bond yield, quote)  

ISTANBUL, June 23 (Reuters) - The Turkish central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market on Friday, selling dollars after the Turkish currency weakened to a March 2003 low of 1.71/dollar.  

It was the second bout of central bank intervention in less than two weeks and prompted a short-lived rebound in the lira. But the currency then fell back to trade at 1.7000 at 1040 GMT, 0.2 percent weaker on the day.  

It was still more than 20 percent weaker than its level at the end of April. Since then investors have been spooked by sharply higher than expected inflation, political tensions and a flight of funds from emerging markets generally.  

"It was observed that the excessive fluctuations in the exchange rate have continued in recent days, linked to a liquidity squeeze," the central bank said in a statement.  

The size of the intervention was not immediately clear. The central bank has $58.3 billion in foreign currency reserves.  

"The 1.70 level is creating tension in the market, but I think it will test above this level to see how aggressive the central bank will be," said one currency trader.  

Yields on the secondary bond market followed the currency, with the April 9, 2008 benchmark <0#TRTSYSUM=IS> yield climbing to 21.01 percent, the highest level seen since December 2004.  

"The market is a bit nervous and buyers are just following the foreign exchange rates. We have basic fundamental concerns about inflation and further inflation because of rapid devaluation of the lira," one banker said.  

The lira briefly strengthened on Thursday on news of tax cuts for investors, but gave up those gains amid global weakness in emerging markets.  

The central bank last intervened in the market selling dollars on June 13 after a sharp hike in interest rates failed to halt the lira's slide.  

That was its first intervention to support the lira since May 2004 and amounted to some $700 million.  

INTEREST RATE SPECULATION  

The bank made a surprise 175 basis point hike in overnight interest rates earlier this month amid concerns that Turkey will far overshoot its end-2006 inflation target of 5 percent.  

Economists are keenly awaiting the June inflation data on July 3 and will be looking out for the possibility of further rate hikes in the coming months.  

"I do not think the intervention will be enough to calm the markets. The central bank will have to raise interest rates by at least 100 basis points in July. But the real problem is that confidence in the government has been undermined," said one economist, who declined to be named.  

The central bank left key interest rates unchanged this week and said they were more likely to remain stable than go up, but it said it was prepared to tighten monetary policy to rein in inflation.  

The main share index <.XU100> ended the morning session down 1.35 percent at 33,767 points.  

Political tensions centre on the possibility of early general elections, tensions between the Islamist-rooted ruling party and secularists and concerns that the Cyprus problem will obstruct Turkey's progress towards European Union membership.  

Ankara is under pressure to move towards recognition of EU member state Cyprus's internationally accepted Greek Cypriot government. It currently backs breakaway Turkish Cypriots.  

Investors have fled emerging markets generally as higher U.S. rates attract funds and monetary tightening at the Bank of Japan reduces a source of cheap cash.

ISTANBUL, June 20 (Reuters) - The Turkish lira <IYIX=> sank on Tuesday to its weakest level against the dollar since April 2003 and bond yields soared amid domestic political concerns and rising interest rates in the big global economies.  

Markets were especially jittery as the central bank's monetary policy committee was due to announce later in the day whether it was raising interest rates further after last week's 175 basis point hike. Most analysts expect no change for now.  

The lira traded at 1.6275 to the greenback on the interbank market in Wednesday-dated trade, down from a closing level of 1.6170. It has lost more than 18 percent of its value since the end of April.  

The central bank intervened in the currency market when the lira last approached those levels against the dollar a week ago. Bankers estimated the intervention was worth $150 million. Turkey has some $60 billion in foreign exchange reserves.

"I think foreign investors are suspicious about Turkey because of political concerns, because of oil (prices) and expectations of rate rises in the United States and Japan," said one banker.  

Increased expectations of continuing U.S. rate hikes are pulling cash out of riskier markets as higher U.S. rates change the risk-reward ratio. The U.S. Federal Reserve meets at the end of the month and is expected to tighten policy again.  

Investors have also been rattled by Turkey's war of words with the European Union over Cyprus, which threatens to derail Ankara's negotiations to join the EU.

title: PRESS DIGEST - Turkey - June 19
text:
ANKARA, June 19 (Reuters) - These are the leading stories in the Turkish press on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.  

RADIKAL  

- The paper draws attention to the parlous state of Turkey's European Union General Secretariat, which is meant to steer the country's EU membership drive. It says the secretariat lacks sufficient staff and its building, on the outskirts of Ankara, even suffers shortages of basic utilities.  

MILLIYET  

- A Japanese firm building a tunnel between the European and Asian shores of Istanbul beneath the Bosphorus plans to lower the first of the huge tube-like compartments to the water bed in September. It will avoid using divers due to strong currents.  

- Turkish Cypriot leader Mehmet Ali Talat says Turkey must not secretly open its ports to rival Greek Cypriots. Ankara has so far resisted EU pressure to open its ports, saying the EU must first lift trade restrictions against the Turkish Cypriots.  

HURRIYET  

- Turkey's Supreme Court wants a seven-year jail sentence for a lawyer who made sexual advances to a secretary, the paper says. He was originally sentenced to six months.  

- Greece is preparing a new proposal to try to break the deadlock in Cyprus peace talks, according to a Greek newspaper.  

SABAH  

- Some cabinet ministers plan to block the appointment of Yasar Buyukanit as the next head of Turkey's military General Staff, the paper says. Buyukanit, currently head of land forces, is seen as more hawkishly secularist than incumbent Hilmi Ozkok, who is due to retire in August.  

CUMHURIYET  

- Billionaire philanthropist George Soros is in Istanbul to meet government ministers and to enlarge his business activities in Turkey, the paper says.  

- Austria, which holds the EU's rotating presidency, revives the idea of offering Turkey a "privileged partnership" that would fall well short of full membership.  

YENI SAFAK  

- Around 1.5 million young people sat university entrance exams on Sunday. Many found the section of mathematics and science especially difficult.  

- Turkish Airlines cancels some flights over the weekend due to a shortage of air hostesses but insists there is no problem and notches up a record number of passengers on Sunday.  

REFERANS  

- Turkey's central bank may intervene again in the currency market if the lira weakesn to 1.65 against the dollar.

title: UPDATE 4-Turkey tries to boost lira amid inflation woes
text:
(Adds U.S. Treasury official remarks)  

ISTANBUL, June 13 (Reuters) - Turkey's central bank intervened to support the lira on Tuesday for the first time since May 2004, after a sharp rise in interest rates failed to halt its slide following a shock rise in inflation.  

In addition to global stock market jitters and expectations of rising U.S. interest rates, Turkish markets have also been volatile because of domestic political tensions and a large current account deficit.  

Bankers estimated the intervention was worth $150 million, while analysts said it would have a limited impact.  

The lira lost 15 percent of its value in May -- which could fuel inflation -- and is trading at levels seen previously in April 2003, around the time of war in neighbouring Iraq.  

"Due to the international conditions we have observed extreme volatility in the foreign exchange market...and in order to curb extreme volatility the central bank has intervened in the foreign exchange market directly," the central bank said in a statement.  

The lira <IYIX=>, which had traded as weak as 1.6230 -- down some 4.6 percent from its previous interbank close -- strengthened after intervention to close at 1.6050. But that was still 3.5 percent weaker on the day.  

"They've barely stepped in ... I think they were trying to test the environment to see what kind of amounts they would need to put in," said Lars Christensen, economist at Danske Bank.  

He added a further rate rise now seemed more likely after a surprise 175 basis point hike this month, as it showed the central bank was trying to shore up the currency.  

The bank, which targets 5 percent inflation in 2006, had flagged a possible intervention recently, noting it had some $60 billion in foreign exchange reserves.  

"I would be surprised if it worked," one dealer said, adding the lira could move back to 1.65.  

A senior U.S. Treasury official said Turkey had good economic policies and was suffering from a global liquidity squeeze despite sound economic fundamentals.  

"They've got good policies in place," Tim Adams told reporters travelling with him. Adams is in Turkey for consultations with economic officials.  

"What we're seeing is that Turkey is getting caught up as are many countries around the world, in an era of global transition from benign economic conditions...to a set of conditions in which central banks are draining liquidity," Adams said.  

He also praised the Turkish central bank for raising interest rates a larger-than-expected 175 basis points.  

U.S. INFLATION  

Investors said intervention did not take their eyes off U.S. inflation data due on Wednesday, which could argue for higher rates there. Higher U.S. rates pull funds out of emerging markets, by changing the risk-reward pay-off.  

"The Turkish market will need further clarity over U.S. rates ... to recover," Anne-Sophie Beotti, economist at BNP Paribas, said.  

The main Istanbul stock index <.XU100> fell 5.7 percent to 32,384 points on Tuesday, bringing its loss since a 2006 peak to around a third.  

Bond yields, sensitive to inflation and rates, soared to their highest level since January 2005 on Tuesday, with the benchmark bond trading as high as 19.3 percent. That compares with the current cost of funding of 16.2 percent and overnight benchmark borrowing rates of 15 percent.  

A Treasury auction on Tuesday saw weak demand and the third issue of the benchmark April 9, 2008 bond yielded a higher-than-expected 18.97 percent at the sale, and it yielded an average 18.82 percent on the day <0#TRTSYSUM=IS>.  

Central Bank intervention followed comments from rating agency Fitch on Tuesday that the Central Bank was behind the curve responding to inflation -- which came in at 10 percent in May -- and said its large rate hike earlier this month "smacked a bit of panic".  

Governor Durmus Yilmaz earlier justified the bank's decisions, saying the rate hike had positive effects and there was no question the bank might have been late.

text:
ISTANBUL, June 6 (Reuters) - The Turkish lira retreated in early trade against the dollar on Tuesday amid continued worries over inflation ahead of Wednesday's meeting of the central bank's monetary policy committee which seems set to hike rates.  

Overnight falls in global markets will also cloud investors' mood as they await the central bank's decision, bankers said.

The data showed prices rose more than twice as fast as expected during May, eroding the purchasing power of the currency and pushing up the price of borrowing.

ANKARA, May 24 (Reuters) - Turkey's government and central bank are in no hurry to intervene in financial markets, which have fallen sharply due to political and economic jitters, Prime Minister Tayyip Erdogan said on Wednesday.  

"We're not in a hurry to intervene in markets. Our central bank would not think such a thing and our government has no worries about it," Erdogan said in a televised speech.  

The central bank, which prizes its political independence, later issued a short statement making clear it was solely responsible for applying foreign exchange policy.  

"As is known, we work with the government in determining the foreign exchange policy but applying the policy is directly the mandate and responsibility of our bank," it said.  

The Turkish lira <IYIX=> weakened to its lowest level against the dollar in two years on Wednesday, trading as far as 1.5630 against the dollar on the interbank market. It later rebounded slightly to trade at 1.5430 against the greenback.  

In his speech, Erdogan stressed that other emerging markets were also experiencing market volatility and sought to play down the turbulence at home.  

Tera Stockbrokers managing director Emre Tezmen noted that Turkey, a candidate to join the European Union, had been significantly underperforming other markets.  

"Although the underperformance is normal (given) political risks, deteriorating inflation dynamics and existing economic fragilities caused by the widening current account deficit, the sell-off may have been excessive," he said.  

Erdogan rejected suggestions that his government was relaxing fiscal policy to shore up public support and ruled out calling early elections, despite widespread speculation about such a move which has contributed to market jitters.  

The International Monetary Fund (IMF), which completed a review mission to Turkey this week as part of a multi-billion dollar loan programme, has called for a cautious monetary policy and said additional government revenues should be saved.  

"The IMF comments were quite clear in that they called for fiscal adjustment which obviously is tough before the elections," said Claire Dissaux, emerging markets strategist at Calyon in Paris.

title: UPDATE 2-Turkish PM pledges no let-up in inflation fight
text:
(Recasts, brings in separates, adds details, background)  

ANKARA, May 16 (Reuters) - Prime Minister Tayyip Erdogan said on Tuesday Turkey would not make the slightest concession in its fight against inflation, seeking to ease concerns about the economy after a sharp sell-off in assets.  

Foreign investors' selling of the lira currency, bonds and shares accelerated in recent days following the publication on May 3 of worse-than-expected inflation for April, almost double the year-end target of five percent.  

"The basic priority is to reach the inflation target, we will not give the slightest concession from what we have achieved over inflation," Erdogan told a meeting of his Justice and Development Party (AKP) in parliament.  

Turkey has cut its inflation to single-digit levels under an International Monetary Fund-backed programme after decades of double and triple-digit inflation rates.  

But an 8.83 percent year-on-year rise in inflation in April helped push lira down by as much as 13 percent of its value against the U.S. currency over the last week and capital flight is estimated to have been around $4.5-5.5 billion.  

Factors behind the weakness also include a gaping current account deficit -- estimated to reach 6.3 percent of gross national product for 2006 -- political tensions and concerns that possible early elections could loosen spending discipline.  

Minister after minister has sought to ease concerns, stressing the government was committed to its current policies in what is turning out to be the among the most turbulent weeks for the ruling AKP since it came to power in 2002.  

"The upwards and downwards movements in the exchange rate should not be regarded as a source of problems," Economy Minister Ali Babacan said after a meeting with the banking sector in Istanbul on Tuesday.  

"There will be no sacrifice from budget discipline or inflation as elections approach," he told Reuters.  

EARLY ELECTION FEARS  

Fears of an early election and populist spending policies were also a trigger for the recent flight from Turkish assets.  

Erdogan, Turkey's most popular politician, dismissed speculation of early elections on Tuesday. Parliament must appoint a new president by May next year while legislative elections must be held by November 2007.  

"Neither elections nor populism or an election economy is part of our agenda," he said.  

Investors have been spooked by a standoff between the secularist President Ahmet Necdet Sezer and the AKP, which has roots in political Islam. Sezer who retires next year vetoed a key IMF-required social security reform bill last week.  

Turkey's powerful secularist establishment, which includes the military and the judiciary, are deeply suspicious of the AKP and fear the party will seek to loosen the strict separation between religion and the state if -- as expected -- the AKP picks the next president. The AKP denies this.  

The central bank under a recently appointed governor stepped into the ring on Monday, halting its dollar buying auctions under which bought up to $60 million a day.  

But analysts said if there were renewed lira weakness markets would expect more action than foreign exchange interventions or stop-gap monetary measures.  

"Turkey needs to re-anchor its policy framework with IMF support to weather the current storm. A purely monetary defence could prove ineffective, even counterproductive, in stabilising the lira," said analyst Ahmet Akarli at Goldman Sachs.  

Tera Brokers managing director Emre Tezmen said a rebound was likely after the sell-off of the last two weeks. And the lira rebounded slightly on Tuesday.  

"But we recommend investors not to count on a sustainable bullish trend. Politics and international worries are likely to bring back the bears without delay," Tezmen said.  

(Additional reporting by Humeyra Pamuk, Hidir Goktas and Daren Butler)
