title: Turk markets partially recover after capital flight
text:
ISTANBUL, May 16 (Reuters) - The lira partially recovered  on Tuesday from Monday's 8 percent slide, dragging shares and bonds with it despite persistent worries about Turkey's economic and political outlook.  

 The lira <IYIX=> firmed to 1.4600 against the dollar in early interbank trade. It closed at 1.4700 on Monday but spiked in after-hours trade to 1.5150. Last Friday it closed at 1.4005.  

 "This movement is a correction of the (dollar's) rise over the last six days and the central bank statement may have had some impact. Whether it is lasting or not will depend on foreign trade," said Garanti Investment strategist Serdar Pazi.  

 The currency has lost as much as 13 percent of its value against the dollar over the last week and capital flight is estimated to be around $4.5 billion to $5.5 billion.  

 The central bank took action on Monday, halting its dollar buying auctions under which bought up to $60 million a day.  

 But analysts said if there were renewed lira weakness markets would expect more action than foreign exchangeinterventions or stop-gap monetary measures.  

 "Turkey needs to re-anchor its policy framework with IMF support to weather the current storm. A purely monetary defence could prove ineffective, even counterproductive, in stabilising the lira," said analyst Ahmet Akarli from Goldman Sachs.  

 Factors behind the market weakness include a wide current account deficit, high inflation, political tensions and concerns that possible early elections could loosen spending discipline.  

 MODERATE REBOUND  

 Higher inflation was reflected in a rise in the cost of borrowing, but bonds recovered partially on Tuesday.  

 The yield on the benchmark April 9, 2008 bond, which rose to its highest level of 2006 on Monday, fell 15.05 percent from a level of 15.16 percent in after-hours trading on Monday, but still sharply above Friday's level of 14.50 percent.  

 Istanbul's main share index <.XU100>, which slid as much as 5 percent on Monday, rose 1.5 percent to 40,878.01.  

 Tera Brokers managing director Emre Tezmen said a rebound was likely after the sell-off of the last fortnight.  

 "But we recommend investors not to count on a sustainable bullish trend. Politics and international worries are likely to bring back the bears without delay," he said.  

 Investors have also been unsettled by the impact of high oil prices on a hefty net importer, lower tourist numbers, fears of dwindling enthusiasm for EU-sought reforms and international tensions over neighbouring Iran's nuclear programme.  

 Growing political tensions between Turkey's secular establishment and the ruling Justice and Development Party, which has Islamist roots, have also undermined sentiment. President Ahmet Necdet Sezer last week vetoed a key IMF-required reform law. The government plans to send the bill back to Sezer.  

 A weaker lira will stoke inflation, already seen as one of the weak spots in the fast growing Turkish economy. Inflation in Turkey, which suffered a deep financial crisis in 2001, has only recently fallen to single digits.  (Additional reporting by Gamze Alarslan)

title: IMF's Dawson: Turkish Lira Reflects Investor Confidence
text:
WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--Currency market intervention by Turkey's central bank to stem the rise of the Turkish lira has been "appropriate" and doesn't indicate a need to overhaul the floating exchange rate policy, an International Monetary Fund spokesman said Thursday.  

Turkish Economy Minister Ali Babacan has called the intervention necessary to smooth volatility. IMF Director of External Affairs Thomas Dawson told reporters in a regular briefing that currency strength could be viewed as a vote of confidence in wide-ranging economic reforms that have taken place.  

"We are well aware of the strength of the currency and the intervention that is taking place," Dawson said. "Frankly, it is to a degree a vote of confidence in what has been going on - I don't think it calls into question the foreign exchange policy at this point."  

The Turkish central bank regularly intervened and built foreign exchange reserves in 2005. Currency analysts had predicted intervention would become less frequent, now that the central bank has adopted an inflation target.  

However, Turkish exporters complain the overvalued lira is a threat to the economy, citing a large and growing current account deficit as evidence.

title: POLL-Turkish reference bill auction yield seen at 14.43 pct
text:
ISTANBUL, Feb 20 (Reuters) - The Turkish Treasury's auction of six-month reference bills on Monday is seen attracting an average yield of 14.43 percent, according to a Reuters poll.  

The Treasury targets net borrowing of 2.264 billion lira ($1.72 billion) from the reference bill, or 15 percent of its February domestic debt repayments.  

The yields on the reference bills are used to set the rates for floating rate notes (FRN).  

In the Reuters poll of 12 bankers, the yield forecasts ranged between 14.20 percent and 14.60 percent. Bids for the bills are expected to total 3-4 billion lira.  

"The rates of the previous six-month reference bill were higher because it was the first auction on which withholding tax was imposed," said one banker.  

"But the situation is different now. Fresh cash is entering the market. There should be interest in the auction after the (central bank) intervention, thanks to which there is plenty of cash around," the banker said.  

The central bank last week bought more than $5 billion in what amounted to a record volume of foreign exchange market intervention.  

Turkey began imposing a 15 percent withholding tax on financial instruments at the start of this year, which had a negative impact on the bond market.  

In the last six-month reference bill auction last month the average compound yield was 14.73 percent and the maximum yield was 14.95 percent.  

Under its February borrowing programme, the Treasury targets borrowing of 9.3 billion lira while debt redemptions during the month total 12.4 billion lira.  

Borrowing so far this month has amounted to 2.0 billion lira. The Treasury targets borrowing of 5.0 billion lira at two auctions on Tuesday.

title: ANALYSIS-Turk lira seen stronger, but fragility ahead
text:
ISTANBUL, Feb 16 (Reuters) - Turkey's lira is expected to defy central bank intervention in coming months, rising against the dollar as it remains a favourite of investors, but it could weaken further out as risk appetite wanes and elections loom.  

After cries from exporters for a weaker lira <IYIX=>, the Central Bank bought an estimated $4.6 billion from the market on Wednesday, pushing the Turkish currency down.  

But strategists said investors would take the opportunity to pour back into the market at the cheaper level, driving it back up.  

"The Central Bank might be tested again," Deutsche Bank strategist Jens Nystedt said.  

While huge amounts of capital are flowing through global markets looking for returns and risk appetite is high, the particular appeals of the Turkish lira include a booming economy, expectations that rating agencies will upgrade Turkish assets and an attractive 13.5 percent interest rate.  

"Given its yield and the vast improvement in the economy I would expect to see (the lira) stronger," American Express economist Sarah Hewin said, adding she saw the lira at 1.25 to the dollar in three months, helped by dollar weakness.  

It closed at 1.3370 to the dollar on Wednesday but in early trade on Thursday had already crept up to 1.3325.  

Further down the line, the currency may not be so sought after.  

Turkey faces presidential and parliamentary elections in 2007 and some economists believe uncertainty over the fate of Prime Minister Tayyip Erdogan's reformist government could begin to erode the lira's value.  

"Over the past three years, the government has done everything on investors' wish list. As we go forward the risk of political noise or a less benign political backdrop increases," Merrill Lynch economist Mehmet Simsek said.  

Merrill's 12-month lira forecast is 1.42 to the dollar.  

GLOBAL LIQUIDITY, OIL  

Some economists also expect global liquidity gradually to dry up this year, which would hit the lira. If risk aversion increases, the gaping current account deficit -- not for now a problem to finance -- may become more of an issue for investors.  

The current account deficit ballooned 46 percent last year, swelled by high oil prices and surging imports.  

Since Turkey began targeting inflation formally in January, there has been speculation that the Central Bank would intervene less, particularly as it has said 2006 inflation was more likely to come in above its 5 percent target than below it.  

There is also some uncertainty over future policy as Central Bank Governor Sureyya Serdengecti's term expires in March.  

But several economists dismissed the notion that inflation targeting is incompatible with foreign exchange interventions.  

Last year the Bank intervened six times to buy dollars for lira, soaking up $14.6 billion.  

"I think there is this misperception in the market. Under the International Monetary Fund programme previously there were these targets for monetary expansion ... so last year actually the Central Bank was more constrained," CSFB economist Berna Beyazitoglu said.  

But there are reasons not to want to weaken the lira too much. The bank and the government recently discussed the lira's strength in the context of Turkey's gaping current account deficit.  

Turkey's other traditional problem is inflation, which tends to be checked by a stronger lira and the heavily indebted country benefits from a stronger lira when it comes to foreign debt payments.  

A more valuable currency also makes oil cheaper, crucial in energy-dependent Turkey with oil prices around $60 a barrel and persistant geopolitical uncertainties.  

"They can't really tolerate too much lira weakness at the expense of weight on their oil bill," BNP Paribas economist Anne-Sophie Beotti said. "They are really vulnerable to a surge in oil prices."

title: Turkish lira eases after  intervention , shares firm
text:
ISTANBUL, Feb 15 (Reuters) - The Turkish lira weakened against the dollar on Wednesday after the central bank bought the U.S. currency, intervening directly in the forex market in response to lira strength.  

Bonds also weakened while shares firmed in what was generally a cautious mood ahead of the first testimony of the U.S. Federal Reserve's new chairman Ben Bernanke.  

Turkey's central bank intervened for the first time since November giving its usual explanation of "extreme volatility", but analysts said the currency was likely to spring back. Based on provisional data, the bank bought a record $4.6 billion.  

The lira closed at 1.3370 to the dollar on the interbank market, compared with 1.3271 on Tuesday. Intervention started at an asking price of 1.3272 lira to the dollar and went as high as 1.3420, firming again to 1.3310 in Thursday-dated trade.  

"The forex-selling trend is continuing. (The intervention) provided an opportunity for foreigners to enter the market. With lira strengthening set to continue, there is expected to be more intervention," said one banker.  

Yields on the benchmark Sept. 5, 2007 bond rose to 13.89 percent from 13.84 percent, but fell to 13.77 percent in Thursday-dated trade.  

The main Istanbul share index <.XU100> closed 0.68 percent higher at 43,803.98, recovering some of the 1.22 percent loss a day earlier. Trading volume rose slightly to 1.39 billion lira ($1.04 billion) from 1.38 billion a day earlier.  

"All global markets today were waiting for the statements from the Fed... Nobody wanted to change positions because of that," said Info Securities research director Mukrim Hatipoglu.  

After markets closed, Bernanke said the U.S. economy was running so close to capacity that it faced heightened risks of an outbreak in inflation that could require higher interest rates to tame.  

Among active shares, Akbank ended 1.74 percent higher at 11.7 lira after it said it had hired Swiss-based UBS as exclusive consultant to look for acquisition and other partnership possibilities.  

There was little reaction to a finance ministry official saying Turkey will not make concessions on a 15 percent withholding tax on financial instruments which it introduced at the start of this year despite demands from foreign investors.  

The finance ministry had a meeting on Tuesday night with foreign bankers, bolstering hopes that it may show flexibility.  

Investors have stopped trading American Depositary Receipts, Global Depositary Receipts (GDR) and Depositary Receipts on the Istanbul Stock Exchange since the tax was introduced.

Exporters, reeling from competition from China and other emerging economies, have been calling for a weaker lira while Turkey's current account deficit -- the main weak spot in a booming economy -- is widening.  

Analysts said further interventions were expected but the weakening these were likely to trigger would then draw fresh interest in lira assets from investors.

That will likely push the lira up again.  

TESTED AGAIN  

"The central bank could be tested again," Nystedt said.

The market had expected another intervention, but the Bank was seen as less likely to intervene than last year because it has moved to formal inflation targeting and says inflation will more likely come in above the target than below it.

text:

ISTANBUL, Nov 18 (Reuters) - The Turkish Central Bank intervened in the foreign exchange market on Friday, buying so far $2.6 billion for lira to counter the strength of the Turkish currency, bankers said.  

At 1537 GMT, best bids on the lira <IYIX=> stood at 1.3700 against the dollar on the interbank market, compared with 1.3550 before the bank intervened for the sixth time this year.  

Under its floating exchange rate regime, the central bank is committed to intervene in the market at times of excessive volatility.  

The central bank said in Friday's statement that foreign currency sales had increased in recent days because of global liquidity conditions.  

"The volatility in the Turkish currency has become more evident in line with the change in the U.S. dollar's value in international markets," the central bank said in a statement.  

Based on Friday's closing level, the lira has lost 2.06 percent of its value against the dollar this year.  

Positive global investment sentiment and FX inflows into emerging markets have recently fuelled lira appreciation against a foreign currency basket made up of one dollar and 0.77 euro, bankers said.  

The informal basket which is tracked closely by bankers was at 2.58 lira before the intervention, slightly above 2.56 lira when the central bank last intervened on Oct. 4.  

"The intervention was anticipated looking at the basket level. Banks may have been caught in short positions in the dollar," a banker said.  

Some analysts said the central bank might be more aggressive in intervening in the markets on the back of a widening current account deficit and inflation targeting due to start on Jan. 1.  

"In light of the rapid deterioration in the current account balance, and prospects that it may not improve materially next year, there may be a case for more aggressive intervention from the CBT in 2006 to weaken the currency if it aids a narrower deficit," 4CAST analyst Caroline Gorman said.  

The current account deficit jumped to $16.35 billion in the first nine months of 2005 from $10.62 billion in the same period last year, outstripping all original estimates.  

IMF, Turkey's main mentor on economic policies, said the deficit was likely to be around six percent of gross national product in 2005, and it may not decline much next year.  

Yet analysts did not foresee a major change in the central bank's exchange rate regime next year when it would start inflation targeting.  

Next year's IMF-backed CPI target was set at five percent, down from this year's eight percent.  

"However, with the move to formal inflation targeting from January, we suspect the CBT will be wary about instigating any changes to its FX policy that might make its inflation targeting effort more difficult" Gorman said.  

The central bank has bought around $18 billion this year through direct interventions and daily dollar purchasing auctions to strengthen its reserves.  

Central bank foreign currency reserves stood at $41.849 billion in the week ending Nov. 11.

title: POLL-Turkish inflation seen on track on seasonal factors
text:
ISTANBUL, July 29 (Reuters) - Turkish producer prices should fall for a second consecutive month in July while seasonal factors will keep consumer prices down despite high oil prices, a Reuters poll showed on Friday.  

In a survey of 21 banks and brokerages, the median forecast rise in the consumer price index (CPI) month-on-month was 0.15 percent while the producer price index (PPI) was seen down 0.10 percent.  

The median forecast for private sector manufacturing prices was a rise of 0.50 percent.  

"I believe that any negative effect from energy prices will be limited due to positive seasonal conditions," said TEB Investment analyst Banu Kivci Tokali.  

At its monthly meeting in July the Turkish central bank left its key borrowing and lending rates unchanged at 14.25 and 18.25 percent respectively for the first time this year, and said recent data suggested the downtrend in inflation could be slowing.  

The government's IMF-backed inflation target for 2005 is 8 percent, and the bank said next year's target of 5 percent was only achievable if domestic demand was kept under control.  

The central bank's most recent bi-weekly survey shows year-end consumer price inflation at 7.39 percent, lower than a previous forecast and the government target.  

"Appreciation of the lira will support declines in clothing and food price inflation," said Tokali.  

Hefty borrowing by local banks boosted Turkish lira liquidity and its position against other currencies in the last two months, prompting the central bank to intervene in the forex market last week.  

In June, Turkey's consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.10 percent month-on-month for an annual rise of 8.95 percent, and the producer price index (PPI) fell 0.48 percent to produce a annual increase of 4.25 percent.

title: Emerging  FX -Fed drags market down, lira worst hit.
text:
LONDON, March 23 (Reuters) - The Turkish lira led high-yield emerging market currencies down on Wednesday, after a hawkish message from the Federal Reserve stoked expectations of bigger U.S. interest rate rises.   

 In a widely expected move, the Federal Open Market Committee nudged rates higher by a quarter percentage point to 2.75 percent, its 7th rate rise since June.   

 The committee, however, said "pressures on inflation have picked up" and the risks for growth and price stability would only remain balanced with appropriate policy action.   

 "This was overall negative for emerging markets. A lot of capital has been sucked out," said a senior trader at a UK bank. "The market did not react to the statement yesterday because it was too late, but it was really hit this morning."   

 The prospect of faster U.S. rate hikes unnerves emerging market investors because they would erode the relative attractiveness of high yield assets.   

 The lira fell to a two-month low against the dollar, on the interbank market , trading at 1.3630 by 1025 GMT.   

 Tolga Ediz, director of emerging markets research at Lehman Brothers, said part of the lira's woes stem from Turkey's dependence on foreign investors to finance its current account deficit. "When you are essentially dependent on international liquidity, once there is a change in external environment ... you get hit. And at this point there is still a risk of further decline," he said.   

 Another factor, he said, was the delay in sealing a $10 billion loan deal with the International Monetary Fund which is tied to key social security, tax and pension reforms.   

 Adding momentum to lira losses was Turkish Economy Minister Ali Babacan's comment on Wednesday that the central bank would not intervene in the foreign exchange market even if there is a rapid capital outflow.   

Turkey's central bank last intervened in the forex market on March 9 and purchased as much as $2.5 billion as the lira hit four-year highs against the dollar.   

 Babacan also said the central bank would purchase between $9 billion and $10 billion in foreign exchange this year.   

 SLOVAK CROWN SLUMPS   

 Central European currencies were also down across the board, with the Slovak crown the worst hit. It dropped over 1/2 a percent against the euro  to its lowest levels in nearly 4 months at 39.26, though it later recovered some lost ground.   

 Analysts continue to see the most vulnerable currencies as those where major long positions have been built up. The Slovak currency is one of them, having hit a string of record highs this year.   

 "People are not ready to call a bottom on this move yet. They are trying to close down positions where they can, you can see that in the Slovak crown, which is one of the big underperformers today," said Koon Chow, emerging markets strategist at CSFB.   

 Chow said he remained positive on the outlook for the region's currencies over the medium-term, but would not look to get back in yet. "I want to see these markets stabilise first before re-entering, but the signs are there. Euro/zloty is not making new highs today."   

 The zloty was down around 0.4 percent against the euro at 4.12 .   

 Polish asset markets are finding some support from growing expectations for an interest rate cut from the central bank at next week's policy meeting.   

 News on Wednesday of a weaker-than-forecast 2.4 percent annual rise in February retail sales further bolstered the case for reducing key rates from 6.5 percent.

title: WRAPUP 1- Turkey  cuts rates,  intervenes  on surging lira.
text:
ANKARA, March 9 (Reuters) - Turkey's central bank cut interest rates on Wednesday and bought dollars to curb the surging new lira, reflecting falling inflation and buoyant investor demand fuelled by the country's economic renaissance.   

Domestic bond yields are tempting foreign buyers, with interest also boosted by Turkey's strong economic rebound from a 2001 financial crisis and expectations it will start EU entry talks as planned on Oct. 3.   

In a bolder cut than some had expected, the bank reduced the overnight borrowing rate to 15.5 percent from 16.5 percent, and the overnight lending rate to 19.5 percent from 20.5 percent.   

The bank last cut rates on Feb. 9, by 50 basis points, and markets had largely priced in a further cut after February price data confirmed inflation was still on a downward trend.   

But with the new lira creeping towards four-year highs at just over 1.25 to the dollar, the central bank intervened to buy dollars and nudge the Turkish unit back beyond 1.27.   

Analysts said the two moves looked more like a chain of events than a co-ordinated campaign to halt the new lira's seemingly inexorable rise against the dollar, which puts ever greater pressure on Turkey's widening current account deficit.   

"They cut rates, some investors took their money, then others came in from outside, which drove the currency even stronger," said Gregory Kronsten of WestLB in London. "Then the bank stepped in because the lira went too far in one day."   

The strong new lira helps Turkey service its substantial dollar-denominated debt, but has contributed to large trade and current account gaps as it feeds appetite for imports.   

Local bankers estimated the size of the intervention at around $1.5-2.0 billion.   

"(This) will increase the central bank's forex reserves, thus providing for a further calming of any worries on the external balance," said Simon Quijano-Evans of Bank Austria Creditanstalt.   

INVESTOR DEMAND   

The central bank said it entered the foreign exchange market to curb "excessive volatility" although the new lira has been firming more or less steadily since last September, when it was around 1.5 to the dollar.   

Kronsten said while much of this was due to the weak dollar, which has boosted emerging market currencies across the board, it also reflected foreign interest in Turkey's domestic bonds.   

"Turkey is a huge success story for offshore investors," he said. "Nowhere in the European time zone offers the same yield and a liquid market."   

Yields on the benchmark Sept. 27, 2006, bonds were at 15.91 percent on Wednesday afternoon compared with Tuesday's 16.13 percent. The new lira remained around 1.27 to the dollar while stocks were barely changed on the day.   

Inflation has fallen to single digits for the first time in a generation and Wednesday's interest rate move had been widely expected after February inflation data last week showed consumer prices rose by just 0.02 percent month-on-month - well on course for the government's year-end target of 8 percent.   

But the central bank sounded a mild warning note to the government after reform delays that have held up Turkey's new $10 billion standby deal with the International Monetary Fund.   

Economy Minister Ali Babacan said on Wednesday a letter of intent on the new deal would be signed in the first half of April, but some analysts still saw this as disappointingly late.   

"Fiscal discipline and structural reforms are essential for maintaining the fall in inflation in the medium term and establishing permanent macroeconomic stability," the bank said.

title: Emerging  FX -Lira hits new peaks, rand dips from highs.
text:
LONDON, Feb 15 (Reuters) - The Turkish lira hit its best levels in over nine months on Tuesday with appetite seen returning for high-yield currencies, though the South African rand lagged, in part on softer than forecast growth data.  

The dollar's slide to 10-day lows against the euro on Monday continued to lend a bullish backdrop to high yielding currencies, with the Turkish lira one of the main beneficiaries.  

Domestic factors are also leaning in the Turkish currency's favour with an auction of new five-year lira paper on Tuesday seen attracting good foreign demand.  

"Investor appetite for high yield currencies seems to be increasing again. We've seen that in the price action in the Brazilian real overnight," said Koon Chow, emerging markets currency strategist at CSFB.  

The real firmed one percent to 2.579 per dollar in domestic trade on Monday , its strongest since June 2002.  

By 1050 GMT, the lira traded at 1.31 to the dollar on the interbank market , up from 1.3150 at Monday's close.  

"On the Turkish side, there are three good factors arguing for the downside (in dollar/lira)," said Chow.  

Firstly, increased confidence in the lira after its redenomination on Jan. 1 continues to see locals switch foreign currency deposits back into lira.  

Secondly, portfolio inflows, likely to be reflected in Tuesday's bond auction and, finally, inflows associated with the hedging of lira-denominated bonds issued by non-Turkish entities.  

"We've seen around 1.8 billion lira ($1.4 billion) worth of issuance in just over a month, which is a huge amount.  

"These non-Turkish issuers don't have lira cashflow so ultimately they will have to buy lira some way to pay the coupon."  

Investors have been scrambling to gain exposure to lira assets ever since the European Union granted Turkey a date to start entry talks in October.  

Chow added a note of caution on the bullish outlook, saying the central bank would be wary of allowing the lira to rise too far, hurting Turkey's export competitiveness.  

"I wouldn't rule out intervention in the next 24 hours, though it will probably only offer better levels to go long (lira)."  

RAND DIPS  

South Africa's rand paused for breath after four strong rising sessions, with slightly softer than expected fourth quarter GDP growth giving investors an excuse to trim long positions.  

The South African economy grew four percent in the fourth quarter, down from a strong 5.7 percent rate in the third quarter, leaving full year growth at 3.7 percent  

The rand traded was down 0.64 percent at 6.04 to the dollar .  

Expectations of an uptick in Polish inflation in January consumer price data due at 1500 GMT helped the zloty firm back under the four-per-euro mark .  

January CPI is forecast to rise to an annual rate of 4.6 percent, from 4.4 percent in December, adding to the case that interest rates have bottomed out at 6.5 percent.  

Claire Dissaux at Calyon said the data "will be a reminder that inflation is likely to spike this quarter well above the 2.5 percent central bank target, playing for a freeze in interest rates that keeps carry attraction high in the near term."   


The zloty traded at 3.9883 to the euro  from 4.0012 and at 3.0725 to
the dollar        from 3.0848. The Romanian central bank intervened to
try and curb the rising leu, buying around 50-60 million euros
according to traders.
  

The bank stepped in after speculative buying drove the leu up sharply to two-year highs against the single currency on Monday. The leu traded at 36,450 per euro , down over four percent from its highs following the intervention.

title: Emerging  FX -Turkey acts to curb lira, new high for Slovak crown.
text:
LONDON, Jan 27 (Reuters) - Further strengthening in emerging European currencies triggered direct intervention in Turkey and raised the prospect of similar action in Slovakia on Thursday, while the Czech crown calmed ahead of an interest rate decision.  

The Turkish central bank said it bought dollars for lira to curb exchange rate volatility, in its first market intervention since February 2004.  

The new lira has risen to near 10 month highs following the European Union's decision in late December to allow Turkey to start entry talks in October, raising expectations of a surge in foreign investment inflows.  

By 1041 GMT, the new lira was at 1.3440 per dollar in interbank trade , down from pre-intervention highs around 1.3215. Turkish banking sources said the central bank had bought around 150-200 million dollars on the market.  

"It's probably a combination of the size of flows coming into the bond market and the extent of the lira move that has triggered the intervention," said Lucy Bethell, emerging markets analyst at RBS Financial Markets.  

"People had been getting increasingly short (of dollars), but the question now is whether they'll take it as cue to book profits, or an opportunity for better entry levels.  

"Sentiment is so strong on Turkey at the moment that at some point I'd expect people to get back in."  

Foreign trade minister Kursad Tuzmen said he hoped the lira would fall to 1.5-1.6 per dollar. Its strength has contributed to large trade and current account deficits.  

NEW HIGHS FOR SLOVAK CROWN  

Dealers are also on intervention red alert in Slovakia after investors' ongoing enthusiasm for the country pushed the crown to an all-time high against the euro on Thursday.  

The crown was flat percent at 38.44 per euro, having briefly touched a fresh high earlier at 38.376 .  

The Slovak central bank has tried to stem the crown's rise since mid-2003, intervening twice in the last month to keep the unit above 38.50 per euro, but said it had no comment on the latest move.  

The bank could cut rates at its monthly interest rate meeting on Friday, though further intervention is seen as more likely given the crown has grown increasingly immune to rate cuts following a 200 basis point loosening to 4.0 percent last year.  

Even that is unlikely to reverse the crown's uptrend.  

"If you believe the central bank will intervene most people would believe that any setback in the currency would be rather small and temporary," Barclays Capital emerging markets analyst Jeff Gable said. The Czech crown dipped from Wednesday's 28-month highs to trade around 30.12 per euro ahead of an interest rate decision.  

The central bank is widely expected to hold rates steady at 2.5 percent and market watchers will focus on any comments about currency strength arising from an afternoon monetary policy news conference.  

The crown has risen almost 10 percent in the past 12 months, most recently boosted by speculation about the sale of state-owned phone group Cesky Telekom (SPTTsp.PR) for an estimated $3 billion.  

Further evidence of a benign inflation environment in South Africa came from December producer price numbers, with the annual rate well below expectations at 1.9 percent, down from 2.5 percent in November.  

The news had little impact on the rand, which found good support from the buoyant tone across emerging markets. It traded virtually flat around 5.93 per dollar .  

The Romanian leu eased about three quarters of a percent against the euro, weighed by Prime Minister Calin Tariceanu's comment there might be a delay to plans to allow foreigners access to leu deposits from April, following talks with the IMF.  

Analysts said the Fund might call for a delay due to the risk the move triggers a wave of speculative capital, complicating the central bank's task of curbing inflation.  

The leu was down 0.73 percent at 28,938 per euro .

title: UPDATE 1-Emerging  FX -Lira edges up after rate cut.
text:
LONDON, Jan 11 (Reuters) - The Turkish lira nudged higher after a surprise interest rate cut on Tuesday, while the Slovak crown was flat after Monday's intervention from the central bank to weaken it.  

Turkey's central bank cut both its overnight borrowing rate and overnight lending rate by one percent to 17 percent and 21 percent respectively.  

The timing of the move took analysts by surprise, coming hard on the heels of a two percent cut on Dec. 20 following the European Union's decision to grant Turkey a date to begin entry talks, though some said there had been scope for further easing.  

"Inflation expectations are very close to end-year expectations and there was also a tightening impact coming from the strengthening of the lira. There were all the key ingredients to have a rate cut," said Sonal Desai, senior emerging markets economist at Dresdner Kleinwort Wasserstein in Milan  

"It'll have a positive impact on Turkish markets, but the impact on the lira is close to zero," she added.  

The move triggered a half percentage point fall in benchmark Turkish bond yields and also boosted Istanbul's main share index, though the lira ticked only modestly higher.  

By 1345 GMT, the lira traded at 1.3785 to the dollar on the interbank market from 1.3850 at Monday's close.  

The prospect of further inflows into Turkish bonds, on expectations of more easing to come, are seen offsetting the potential negative effect of lower returns on long lira positions.  

SLOVAK CROWN STEADIES AFTER INTERVENTION

The Slovak crown crept higher on Tuesday, resuming its upward path after central bank intervened to weaken it on Monday.  

The bank stepped in after the crown surged to record highs against the euro around 38.5 early on Monday , triggering a move back to 38.74 initially, before the crown recovered some ground.  

Finance Minister Ivan Miklos backed the central bank's stance on Tuesday, saying the crown's firming was too strong and could hurt the new EU members' economy, in comments reported by a domestic news agency.  

Even so, most analysts continue to see the central bank fighting an unstoppable strengthening trend in the Slovak currency, driven by strong foreign investment inflows.  

Carlos Teixeira, analyst at Goldman Sachs, said the Slovaks' latest intervention was no surprise.  

"Their action may stem appreciation temporarily, as last happened in December, but we expect the currency to resume its strengthening," Teixeira said in a research note.  

"This will help the central bank meet its inflation target and leaves the door open to further rate cuts."  

A bigger than expected November trade gap held up the crown's rise only briefly, with the deficit widening to 3.953 billion crowns ($134.5 million), above a market consensus forecast of 2.7 billion.  

The crown was up 0.16 percent on the session at 38.63 per euro.

text:
LONDON, May 11 (Reuters) - Emerging market debt bounced to erase some of the previous sessions' losses on Tuesday, with Turkey taking centre stage after the country's central bank intervened to buy lira, a move traders said calmed the market.   

"The market is higher, although we will see if bonds will hold when New York comes in. Now it seems 'yes' - we have seen some buyers," said a bond trader in London.   

By 1031 GMT, the risk premium for emerging market debt over U.S. Treasuries had narrowed by 13 basis points to 556 basis points on the benchmark JPMorgan Emerging Market Bond Index Plus , its first positive move after a three-day sell-off.   

Investors dumped emerging market debt late last week and on Monday on rising worries U.S. interest rates would rise sooner than expected.   

Higher rates in safe-haven U.S. Treasury notes would make them more attractive, and prompt a flee of investors from riskier emerging market assets.   

"The market couldn't sustain this degree of selling, there was bound to be a bounce-back. But what was going on in 2002 and throughout 2003 with extremely low U.S. and European rates...that story is probably over now," said Charles Robertson, EMEA economist at ING Barings. The risk premium of Turkey's portion of the EMBI+ tightened 37 basis points to 513 basis points.   

Turkey's benchmark 2034 dollar bond recovered from Monday's steep losses to rise two points to 84.5 percent of face value.   

"My feeling is that it is still probably oversold, but probably the wider market is also oversold. People are still in pain after the past week," said Timothy Ash, analyst at Bear Stearns.   

Robertson said Turkey's external debt yields had become too expensive after a plethora of positive news and a global hunt for yield among investors in the past six to twelve months.   

"The sell-off in currency and debt has meant a return to more sensible and sustainable levels," Robertson said.   

INTERVENTION BOOST   

Turkey's central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market earlier on Tuesday, buying lira for U.S. dollars after a sharp weakening in the Turkish currency driven by political and emerging market worries.   

"I'm not sure they intervened heavily, it was probably more a case of dipping their toe in the water and seeing how it goes... but there were no bids in the market so it got quite a big (positive) reaction," said one London trader.   

The bank was reported to have stepped in around 1,565,000 per dollar , helping the lira recover to around 1,535,000.   

Turkish markets have been hammered in recent sessions by broad-based interest rate fears and also on concerns over a row between the government and powerful military on higher education reform.   

Prime Minister Tayyip Erdogan unnerved markets last week when he said the government would talk to the IMF about lowering the primary surplus target.   

On Tuesday Erdogan helped calm the markets by saying the government was determined to maintain fiscal discipline and would keep its primary surplus high to help pay down public sector debt.   

Erdogan, addressing members of his ruling Justice and Development Party in parliament, said relations with the IMF would continue beyond the end of the current $19 billion loan deal next February in order to preserve confidence.   

He did not specify what kind of relations.

title: UPDATE 3-Turkish c. bank  intervenes  to support ailing lira.
text:
ISTANBUL, May 11 (Reuters) - Turkey's central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market on Tuesday, buying lira for dollars to underpin the Turkish currency after a sharp weakening fuelled by domestic and emerging market worries.   

The small-scale interventions - only the second time the bank has intervened to sell dollars since Turkey moved to a floating rate regime in 2001 - triggered a lira rebound from 12-month lows against the dollar.   

Analysts said it showed the central bank would not allow excessive volatility in the foreign exchange market.   

The central bank initially stepped into the market when the lira was around 1,565,000 to the U.S. currency during the morning, pushing it back to 1,530,000, bankers said.   

It intervened again after the official close at a level of 1,553,000 during Wednesday value-dated trade, prompting it to firm to 1,536,000 on the interbank market .   

The volume of the intervention amounted to some $30 million, bankers said.   

"The central bank intervened directly in the foreign exchange market today, selling (dollars) as a result of excessive volatility," the bank said in a statement.   

It said the volatility resulted from a narrowing of foreign currency liquidity. It also lowered rates on its weekly foreign currency lending to banks to six percent from 10 percent.   

Ozgur Altug, chief economist at brokerage Raymond James, said the intervention showed the central bank would not allow excessive volatility in the foreign exchange market.   

"We believe the central bank intervention was at the right time. The upward correction in the lira-dollar rate could continue but at a decelerated pace," he said.   

"The rising volatility in the forex market started to disturb the bond market and consequently the debt dynamics, plus it was having an adverse impact on pricing behaviour in the manufacturing sector," he said.   

The central bank previously intervened to buy lira in December 2002 around a level of 1,700,000 against the dollar. It has also intervened on eight occasions to buy dollars.   

Turkish markets have been hit in recent sessions by emerging market worries about a possible U.S. interest rate hike, a row between the government and the powerful military on higher education reform, and a widening current account deficit.   

There has also been concern that Turkey may veer away from IMF-backed targets. But Prime Minister Tayyip Erdogan said on Tuesday that a key measure of the government's IMF accord, the primary surplus, would be kept high in line with Fund wishes.   

Last week Erdogan unnerved markets by saying Ankara would talk to the IMF about lowering the primary surplus target.   

The central bank governor Sureyya Serdengecti had tried to soothe rattled markets on Monday, calling on the government to curb inflation risks and stick to a key primary surplus target under the country's $19 billion IMF loan accord.   

Serdengecti blamed banks' short trading positions for intensifying pressure on the lira.

title: UPDATE 1-Turkish lira slips in early trade after bombs.
text:
ISTANBUL, Nov 21 (Reuters) - Turkey's lira slipped to best bids of 1,488,000 to the dollar in early trade on Friday after twin bomb attacks in Istanbul killed at least 27 and injured hundreds.  

The lira had fallen to close at 1,478,000 to the dollar on Thursday in thin trade following the suspected suicide attacks, which raised worries over investor confidence in the IMF debtor recovering from a financial crisis that peaked in February 2001.  

Turkey's central bank said it reserved the right to intervene in the foreign exchange market to buy lira if the free-floating currency comes under sustained selling pressure due to the bombings.  

Britain has warned Turkey may be the target of more terror attacks. Thursday's attacks hit the British consulate in Istanbul and the offices of London-based banking giant HSBC (HSBA.L) (HBC.N) in the city's financial district.  

Trade in Turkey's hefty domestic debt was set to begin around 0730 GMT. The busiest December 15, 2004 paper closed Thursday at yields of 29.07 percent, weaker than Wednesday's 28.69.  

The main stock index dived 7.37 percent to 14,617.53 points shortly after the attacks, prompting the Istanbul Stock Exchange (IMKB) to halt trading.  

Turkey's bourse will remain closed until December 1, when a one-week holiday to mark the end of the Muslim month of fasting concludes.  

The volatile lira has been rallying for much of 2003 as the economy showed signs of a full recovery from the financial crisis, helped by $16 billion in IMF lending.  

The lira and debt markets are due to close on Monday afternoon for the religious holiday and to reopen Friday of the same week.

title: UPDATE(2):Turkey Bombings Claim 27 Lives; Al-Qaida Blamed
text:
(Updates with details)  

ISTANBUL (AP)--Truck bombs killed at least 27 people and wounded nearly 450 in attacks on the British consulate and a London-based bank Thursday - days after a bloody terrorist strike on Istanbul synagogues. The worst terror bombings in Turkey's history coincided with U.S. President George W. Bush's trip to Britain and were blamed on al-Qaida.  

Security forces were on highest alert after the blasts at the high-rise headquarters of the HSBC bank and the British consulate, which occurred with 10 minutes of each other at about 11 a.m. Turkey said suicide bombers carried out the attacks.  

An unidentified caller to the semiofficial Anatolia news agency said al-Qaida and the militant Islamic Great Eastern Raiders' Front, or IBDA-C, jointly claimed responsibility for attacks.  

British Consul-General Roger Short was among the dead, Turkish Foreign Minister Abdullah Gul said. "He was blown up immediately," consulate chaplain Ian Sherwood told British Broadcasting Corp. TV.  

Witnesses said one pickup truck exploded just outside the HSBC building, while another truck crashed into the gate of the British consulate destroying annexes to the main consular building.  

"The man came, rammed into the gates," Interior Minister Abdulkadir Aksu told Anatolia, describing the consulate bombing. The attacker then "set it off, blowing himself up."  

The vehicle looked like a catering truck, with explosives placed in food cauldrons, Anatolia quoted police as saying.  

"Cars were flying, there was blood everywhere, I could see fruit and vegetables flying in the air from stalls," said Mehmet Dag, 26, who works for a textile company as a delivery man. He was about 100 meters away from the consulate building.  

The blasts followed a pair of synagogue bombings Saturday that killed 23 people, plus the two bombers. Turkish authorities blamed the attacks on the same groups.  

Turkish Premier Recep Tayyip Erdogan vowed that Turkey will defeat terrorists and he deplored the timing of the attacks, during the Islamic month of Ramadan.  

"Those who bloodied this holy day and massacred innocent people will account for it in both worlds," he said. "They will be damned until eternity."  

Bush, meeting with British Prime Minister Tony Blair, said Thursday's bombings showed "utter contempt for innocent life."  

"The terrorists hope to intimidate, they hope to demoralize. They are not going to succeed," Bush said at a news conference with Blair.  

British Foreign Secretary Jack Straw was scheduled to arrive in Istanbul on Thursday evening. Earlier, he suggested a link to al-Qaida.  

"I'm afraid it has all the hallmarks of international terrorism practiced by al-Qaida," he said in London.  

The Turkish central bank said it was taking steps to prevent financial fallout from the attacks, and would intervene to stop fluctuations in the Turkish currency. Turkey's benchmark index dropped about 7% until the stock exchange was closed.  

In London, the Foreign Office said it would send a rapid deployment team of consular staff and other officials to Istanbul. The BBC reported 16 officers from the British police's anti-terrorist squad were heading to Turkey to help the investigation.  

"The reaction for the moment is sadness and grief but carrying on with what we're here for," Peter Westmacott, British ambassador to Turkey told Cable News Network. He said Short, 58, "will be terribly missed."  

Local staff of the British consulate were also among the victims, including a cook and security guard, Anatolia said. Rescue officials said their was little hope of finding anybody alive in the rubble.  

The double attack was Turkey's worst terrorist bombing and its highest single-day death toll from terrorism since 1977, when gunmen opened fire on leftists celebrating May Day, killing 37 people.  

The first Istanbul blast was at the Turkish headquarters of HSBC, the world's second-largest bank, shearing off the facade of the 18-story building and shattering the windows of nearby skyscrapers in the affluent district of Levent.  

Body parts, the charred shells of cars and broken glass were scattered around a 9-foot-deep crater in the street outside the bank. Water gushed out of the top floors of the building.  

Bystanders, bloodied and covered in dust, looked dazed as they walked past lines of ambulances. Several people helped carry the limp bodies of victims. Road signs laid on the ground, twisted next to fallen tree trunks.  

The second bomb ripped off the wall surrounding the garden of the British consulate in the downtown Beyoglu district, a popular tourist destination with shops, bars, movie theaters and restaurants. The U.S. consulate was moved months ago to a more secure location in another district.  

Television reports initially spoke of up to five blasts, but Turkish authorities later confirmed only two.  

"Once again we are reminded of the evil these terrorists pose to people everywhere and to our way of life," Blair said. "Once again we must affirm that in the face of this terrorism there must be no holding back, no compromise, no hesitation in confronting this menace."  

A U.S. witness was walking near the British consulate when the attack happened  

"I heard a series of explosions. I thought it was echoing. You could see smoke and smell sulfur in the air," Tim Little, a 44-year-old American tourist from Grand Lake, Colorado.  

One witness was traveling on a bus near HSBC when the explosion occurred.  

"I thought somebody hit our bus from the back, then I saw black smoke rising. Cars were damaged all around us. I saw the charred body of a driver at the wheel," said a sobbing Mehmet Altan.  

Witness Hakan Kozan, 29, who was close to the British consulate said the blast came from a white pickup truck. "I heard a slam on the brakes and 10 seconds later the explosion came," Kozan said.  

Mehmet Celik, who was slightly injured, said a light brown pickup truck "exploded in front of the HSBC headquarters."  

In a sign of international concern over safety in Turkey, Europe's soccer authorities postponed two international soccer matches scheduled to be played in the country next week, including a game between Maccabi Haifa of Israel and Spain's Valencia which had already been switched from Israel because of security fears.  

The Istanbul State Security Court imposed restrictions on news coverage of attacks, but Turkish TV stations continued their broadcasts from the scenes.  

Turkish army troops made a brief appearance on the streets in Istanbul, deploying on a major highway and standing guard beside police in Istanbul.  

The deployment was a significant step, since the military is a powerful force that leads the secular establishment in the predominantly Muslim country. In the synagogue bombings, authorities arrested six people Wednesday. A Turkish court charged five with "attempting to overthrow the constitutional structure," which carries a sentence of life imprisonment. The sixth was charged with "helping illegal organizations," punishable by five years in prison, Anatolia said. No trial date was set.  

The two suicide bombers who attacked the synagogues in pickup trucks were identified as Turks. Foreign Minister Abdullah Gul said the two had visited Afghanistan in the past and that investigators were pursuing al-Qaida links.  

On Sunday, Osama bin Laden's terror network claimed responsibility for the bombings in messages to two Arabic-language newspapers, but it was not possible to authenticate those claims. The outlawed Turkish radical group IBDA-C also claimed responsibility, but Turkish authorities said the attack was too sophisticated to be carried out by that group.

title: Turk mkts set to open flat after lira  intervention .
text:
ISTANBUL, Sept 26 (Reuters) - Turkish markets were expected to open flat on Friday, watching for statements on Turkey's $16 billion IMF pact amid a visit by a Fund team, brokers said.   

A central bank intervention on Turkey's foreign exchange market on Thursday to buy dollars for lira pushed the lira back from year highs, but equities and debt rose as investors remained upbeat about the country's economic recovery.   

The central bank repeatedly stepped in to buy dollars as the lira hit levels around 1,350,000 to the dollar from Wednesday's close of 1,353,000. The currency finished Thursday at 1,374,000 on the interbank market .   

The bank may have bought up to $1.5 billion for lira during the intervention, the Turkish press said on Friday.   

"Right now the optimistic atmosphere continues and sales on the stock market should be met by buying," said Pelin Okul at Koc Invest in Istanbul.   

The lira's rally from record lows of some 1,750,000 in March threatens Turkish exports, the engine behind economic growth after a deep recession in 2001, and a year-end target of $7.4 billion for the current account deficit.   

An IMF team arrived in Turkey this week for a latest review of the economic programme, linked to the release of a latest loan tranche.   

Benchmark August 18, 2004, bonds finished Thursday at 34.27 percent from Wednesday's 34.5 percent.   

Shares on the Istanbul bourse's main index closed Thursday one percent higher at 13,935.67 points.   

Okul said the stock market was likely to trade in a band between 13,700 and 14,200 points.   

Brokers said investors would also be watching for the release of an EU report on Turkey's progress on the political reforms needed to begin accession talks with Brussels.

title: UPDATE 1-Turkish lira off year highs after  intervention .
text:
ISTANBUL, Sept 25 (Reuters) - Central bank intervention on Turkey's foreign exchange market pushed the lira currency back from year highs, but equities and debt rose as investors remained upbeat about the country's economic recovery.   

The central bank repeatedly stepped in to buy dollars for lira as the currency hit levels of around 1,350,000 to the dollar from Wednesday's close of 1,353,000. The currency finished the day at 1,374,000 on the interbank market .   

Bankers said the central bank purchased more than $1 billion in its sixth intervention since May.   

The lira's rally from record lows of around 1,750,000 in March threatens Turkish exports, the engine behind economic growth after a deep recession in 2001, and a year-end target of $7.4 billion for the current account deficit.   

But the intervention failed to dampen appetite for high-yielding Turkish debt. Benchmark August 18, 2004, bonds finished at 34.27 percent from Wednesday's 34.5 percent.   

"(The intervention) is likely to prove to be ineffective - interest rates have fallen sharply, but they still provide an attractive backdrop and the new U.S. loan package has also been supportive," said Mehmet Simsek, emerging markets strategist at Merrill Lynch in London.   

Turkey this week inked an $8.5 billion loan deal with the United States that should boost debt-ridden Turkey's coffers and ease the treasury's domestic and foreign debt burden. Domestic debt alone stands at around $130 billion.   

Offers at the central bank's daily auction to buy dollars on Thursday hit $249 million against a maximum sale of $75 million.   

The auctions and the central bank's repeated interventions have boosted its hard currency reserves to record levels. The central bank said on Thursday its forex reserves were at an all-time high of $31.468 billion on September 19.   

Shares on the Istanbul bourse's main index closed one percent higher at 13,935.67 points.   

"Buying is coming as the index reaches support levels. The positive atmosphere is still continuing and because the market is strong, buying has quite an effect," said Utku Yarpuzlu of Vakif Investment.

title: Emerging debt- Turkey  debt shrugs off  intervention .
text:
LONDON, Sept 25 (Reuters) - Turkish debt shrugged off a central bank currency intervention that might have weakened international bond prices in London on Thursday, as investors still expect rates to fall boosting debt valuations. London traders estimated that Turkey's central bank bought between $350 million and $650 million from banks. The central bank confirmed the purchase, but did not give the amount.   


A weaker lira could make domestic interest rates less likely to fall,
as the lira, which has strengthened 21.5 percent this year, has played
a big part in checking inflation. Prolonged high lira rate makes
Turkish bonds as a whole less attractive, because domestic bond buyers
would have less money to spend. But markets were unfazed. "There was a
very muted reaction, the bonds got hit a bit and the bids came back,"
said a trader at a U.S. bank in London. "But we are still expecting a
300 basis point rate cut next month." Turkey's benchmark 2030 dollar
bond  was unchanged at 116.375 percent of face value. The country's
shorter maturity benchmark the $1.5 billion 2010 bond              rose
0.375 points in price at 114.250.
The country's segment  of the industry benchmark, JPMorgan's Emerging
Market Bond Index plus        , fell in yield premium by two basis
points compared with Treasuries.
  

The EMBI+ as a whole was unchanged at 486 basis points over Treasuries. "The lira will weaken a little bit and then it will strengthen again," said Peter Botoucharov, emerging markets economist at Commerzbank in London. "In Turkey we have a positive sentiment. It has entered a virtuous cycle where lower interest rates and falling rates have a positive impact on the fiscal accounts."  

Turkey has been generating rising primary surpluses in recent months, which makes the country's bonds ever more secure assets to hold. Turkey's economy has begun to consolidate a recovery from 2001's 9.4 percent economic contraction, the largest such recession in 50 years.  

The country is implementing a programme backed with $16 billion in International Monetary Fund assistance after a shaky start. The AK Party, which took power following a landslide election victory in November last year, took six months to agree terms with the IMF. But investor confidence has been rising since the programme was agreed and the U.S.-led war in neighbouring Iraq proved shorter than expected. This week, Turkey signed an $8.5 billion loan deal with the United States, further boosting confidence.  

RUSSIA ALSO RISES  

Russian debt nudged lower in yield as Wednesday's moves in Treasuries lifted prices, and on trader talk that the country might soon have it ratings upgraded.  

The benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury rose more than 0.6 percent in New York on Wednesday, although in London the bond fell slightly, by around 0.1 percent.  

"In Russia there is very good demand thanks to rumours that Russia could be upped by two notches to investment grade by October," said the trader.  

Moody's Investors Service placed Russia on upgrade watch at the end of July. It rates the country's foreign currency obligations Ba2, at the upper end of the speculative grade rating range. A move to investment grade Baa3 would open Russia up to a much broader range of investors.  

Commerzbank's Botoucharov said he thought such a dramatic ratings move unlikely.  

Russia's benchmark 2030 dollar bond rose 0.875 to 94.625 percent of face value.

title: UPDATE 1-Turkish  central bank  buys dollars for lira.
text:
ISTANBUL, Sept 10 (Reuters) - Turkey's Central Bank said it had bought dollars for lira on Wednesday, intervening in the forex market to curb the appreciation of the currency.   

Bankers said the central bank began buying dollars at around 1,371,000 lira after it dipped to 1,370,000. The currency was trading at around 1,389,000 after the intervention.   

"A direct intervention to purchase (dollars) was made in the foreign exchange market today to prevent extreme fluctuations," the Central Bank said in a statement.   

The lira has surged in recent months amid upbeat sentiment about an economic recovery after the Turkish unit reached record lows of around 1,750,000 in March on worries the U.S-led war in Iraq would undermine Turkey's economy.   

The Central Bank's last intervention was on July 18, when it stepped in repeatedly as the lira reached levels around 1,375,000 to the dollar. The bank purchased $938 million that day.   

The lira has appreciated by more than 17 percent since the start of the year, raising concerns for Turkey's current account deficit which widened to $4 billion in the first half of the year against a revised year-end target of $7.4 billion.   

The lira's strength could also affect economic growth if exports become too expensive, hitting the manufacturing sector.

title: PRESS DIGEST - Turkey - July 19.
text:

title: Turk c.bank  intervenes  to buy dollars again-bankers.
text:

 The bank began intervention earlier in the day as the lira climbed to around 14-month highs at 1,370,000 to the dollar. The lira was trading at 1,392,000 to the dollar after the bank intervened a second time.

title: UPDATE 3-Turk c.bank  intervenes  to arrest galloping lira.
text:
ISTANBUL, July 18 (Reuters) - Turkey's Central Bank bought dollars for lira on Friday in the most intense wave of interventions since crisis ripped through Turkey's financial markets in early 2001, sending the lira into freefall. 

 This time the bank intervened to curb a rise in the lira as it reached 14-month highs of around 1,370,000 to the dollar, a rally the government fears could undermine exports. 

 The Central Bank said it had stepped in to arrest "lira volatility" but investors suspected the bank was more concerned about the impact of the strengthening currency on the current account deficit, already gaping beyond targets. 

 The lira, traded freely since the financial crisis struck, later weakened to 1,403,000 after what traders said was a whole series of interventions by the bank during Friday trading. 

 "I think the only way this intervention can be justified is for the level of the lira, not the volatility, despite what the Central Bank says," said Tolga Ediz, director in global economics at Lehman Brothers in London. 

 The lira has risen more than 20 percent against the dollar from record lows of around 1,750,000 in March amid fears over the economic impact of war in Iraq on Turkey's economy. 

 The current account deficit has widened to $3.47 billion in the first five months of the year against a year-end target of $6.1 billion under a $16 billion pact with the IMF. 

 Several bankers estimated Friday's total dollar purchases amounted to around $700 million, although the Central Bank did not say how many dollars it bought. 

 DEMAND FOR DEBT DOMINATES 

 "The Central Bank today made a direct intervention in the foreign exchange market to prevent extreme volatility in the exchange rate," the bank said in a written statement released after its initial intervention in the morning. 

 The bank may need to act again as lira purchases continue on confidence Turkey's frail economy is recovering. 

 Analysts said foreign demand for high-yielding local debt was the main driver behind the lira's rise as Turkey works to service some $125 billion in domestic debt. 

 Appetite for the lira was reflected in a daily dollar purchase auction on Friday, when the Central Bank met $50 million of the $214 million offered by investors. 

 "Yields have brought in portfolio flows from abroad...It (the lira's rally) is being principally driven by this ongoing refinancing of domestic debt," said Philip Poole, senior emerging markets analyst at ING Barings in London. 

 The busiest August 18, 2004, debt traded at yields of 46.78 percent on the secondary market on Friday compared to a yearly consumer price inflation target of 20 percent for 2003, a wide profit margin for investors. 

 The bank is bolstering its foreign currency reserves through its purchase auctions of dollars that some analysts say should be raised to $80 million to $90 million daily if the bank is to succeed in arresting the lira. 

 The bank has yet to confirm it stepped in repeatedly in the foreign exchange market during the day. It last intervened to buy dollars on June 9 when the lira posted a previous 12-month high at 1,409,000 to the dollar. 

 Despite its recent rally, the lira has fallen some 50 percent against the U.S. currency after it was floated in 2001. 

 - Additional reporting by Mark Bentley.

title: Turkish cenbank says  intervenes  to buy dollars.
text:
ANKARA, July 18 (Reuters) - Turkey's Central Bank said on Friday it had intervened on the currency market  by buying dollars to prevent excessive volatility, stepping in as the lira currency climbed to around 14-month highs at 1,370,000 to the dollar. 

 The lira was trading at 1,396,000 to the dollar after the bank acted. The bank says it has no target value for the lira but reserves the right to intervene to arrest "lira volatility".

title: Turk cenbank says buys $2.1 bln for lira in May-June.
text:
ANKARA, June 30 (Reuters) - Turkey's central bank said on Monday it purchased $2.115 billion in U.S. dollars during May and June to arrest volatility in the lira's  value and to build up its foreign exchange reserves. 

 The lira has firmed some 20 percent to around 1,415,000 against the U.S. dollar from a record low of around 1,770,000 in March, raising fears for the competitiveness of Turkey's exports and the current account. 

 The bank said it aimed to purchase up to $880 million in July during daily dollar purchase auctions of $40 million. It said it bought $566 million in dollars for lira on June 9 during an intervention in the foreign exchange market. 

Turkey is looking to exports to help it meet a five percent gross national product (GNP) growth target for 2003, set out under a $16 billion IMF pact. 

 The ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) and many businessmen have criticised the central bank for not doing enough to stem the lira's gains against the U.S. currency. 

 The central bank has said its foreign exchange reserves stood at $28.132 billion on June 20 compared with $26.725 billion at the end of 2002. 

 Turkey on Monday reported a 7.4 percent rise in GNP during the first quarter of 2003 against expectations of a 6.2 percent increase.

title: UPDATE 1-Turkish markets in range, awaiting debt plans.
text:
ISTANBUL, June 12 (Reuters) - Turkish stocks and debt fell on Thursday while the lira edged up as investors awaited action over belated International Monetary Fund (IMF) reforms and a large redemption of domestic debt due next week. 

 The main share index closed 1.02 percent lower at 10,489.19 points while average yields on domestic debt maturing on July 7, 2004, rose to 48.72 percent from a previous 48.46 percent. 

 The lira, strong for months as high real interest rates push investors to sell their dollar holdings, firmed to 1,417,500 against the dollar from Wednesday's 1,423,000. 

 But traders said volume was low and attention was focused on the treasury's borrowing plans for next week ahead of a hefty debt repayment of some 6,500 trillion Turkish lira ($4.59 billion). 

 "The market is extremely quiet. There is a bit of activity in forex but there's no volume and it's in a narrow range. The treasury auctions will set the tone," said a treasury official at one major local bank. 

 The central bank has intervened three times since mid-May to tame lira volatility as it hit a year high. The last intervention was on June 9 as the lira hit around 1,409,000 to the dollar. 

 "There is selling (of dollars) but the volume is small," said Banu Tugsavul, foreign exchange director at Oyakbank. "We may see 1,410,000 lira before the weekend but this time I don't expect an intervention." 

Turkey faces a possible delay in winning a $500 million loan tranche from the International Monetary Fund if the government does not move swiftly on a series of pledges to the fund. 

 "The important thing here is not whether the tranche will be paid but whether relations with the IMF are continuing and whether there's agreement," said Ebru Karluk of TSKB Securities.

title: Turkish markets in range, awaiting debt plans.
text:

title: Emerging  FX -Lira recovers post- intervention , zloty firms.
text:
LONDON, May 22 (Reuters) - The Turkish lira recovered on Thursday, after central bank intervention knocked it lower the previous session, while supportive comments from a central banker in Poland helped the zloty firm up. 

 The lira was brought down from 11 month highs against the dollar following the intervention, estimated by dealers to have been worth in the region of $450-$500 million, but resumed its firming trend on Thursday. 

 Upward pressure was said to have come from domestic players selling hard currency holdings to meet corporate tax payments in lira and from investors looking to tap into the country's high yields. 

 "These flows are more or less done...but there is still an extensive degree of dollarisation in the economy, which means that when local institutions have large lira liabilities to meet their first reaction is to sell hard currency," said Gregory Kronsten, emerging markets analyst at WestLB. 

 Kronsten said that residents' foreign exchange deposits as a percentage of money supply stood at a relatively high 50-55 percent in Turkey. 

 Analysts said Wednesday's intervention may only serve to offer better levels for investors to buy lira, particularly if the International Monetary Fund's latest review passes successfully. 

 An IMF team is currently in Turkey assessing the country's progress on economic reforms tied to a $16 billion loan pact. 

 "If the forthcoming fifth review is completely successfully then I'd expect another rally, with the central bank likely to have to intervene more often going forward," said Kronsten. 

 The IMF's disbursement of another $500 million loan tranche was likely to be the trigger for the release of U.S. aid, Kronsten said, with portfolio inflows set to pick up on the back of that. 

 In this positive backdrop, the market is also looking for further interest rate cuts from the central bank. 

 By 0930 GMT, the lira traded at 1,476,000 to the dollar on the interbank market, from 1,489,000 at Wednesday's close. 

 GRABOWSKI LIFTS ZLOTY The Polish zloty climbed off Wednesday's seven-week lows against the euro, helped by comments from senior central banker Boguslaw Grabowski who said it had scope to gain over the coming months. 


Grabowski said he expected the Polish unit to strengthen to 3.5 per dollar
in a year's time, from current levels around 3.72 and to around 4.15/20 per
euro from 4.34          .



Robust Polish retail sales numbers were also said to lend support, showing
an 11 percent year-on-year rise in April, up from 1.7 percent in March.
Meanwhile, the April jobless rate dipped to 18.4 percent, from 18.7 percent
the previous month.



"We saw some (zloty) buying out of Austria after the retail sales data, but
interest is fairly low, it's really just orders driving the market at the
moment," said one London-based trader.



The zloty traded at 4.3406 to the euro  from 4.3678 and at 3.7163 to the
dollar        from 3.7313.

title: Turkish markets seen steady on c.bank action, IMF.
text:
ISTANBUL, May 22 (Reuters) - Turkish markets were expected to hold steady on Thursday after a Central Bank intervention to buy dollars and as the International Monetary Fund began a critical review of Turkey's $16 billion pact. 

 The lira  closed on Wednesday at 1,489,000 to the dollar after the Central Bank stepped in at levels around 1,452,000. It was trading at 1,484,000 early on Thursday. 

 The lira has rallied to levels not seen since last June with the swift end of the war in neighbouring Iraq, worrying exporters and other businesses an over-valued lira could threaten Turkey's current account. 

 The intervention cheered stockbrokers, and the main index  climbed 1.09 percent to 10,540.85 points after weeks of losses or limited gains that many traders have blamed on the strengthening currency. 

 "The Central Bank intervention gave the market a boost in dollar terms," said Emre Balkeser, sales trader at Alfa Securities. "The market shouldn't go below 10,500 today." 

 Balkeser said investors were also pleased with successful Treasury auctions this week and were still expecting the Central Bank to cut key interest rates on signs inflation is falling. 

 Speculation of a rate cut helped debt yields firm, and March 26, 2004, papers finished on Wednesday at 52.12 percent from a previous 53.5 percent. 

 Investors are eyeing the IMF review amid worries the government has dragged its feet on reforms it promised the fund for a latest loan tranche of $500 million. 

 The last review of the pact was delayed for months by a general election, little action on reforms and a lack of agreement on IMF demands for a cost-cutting 2003 budget.

title: UPDATE 1-Turk lira slips on c.bank  intervention , stocks climb.
text:
ISTANBUL, May 21 (Reuters) - The Turkish lira fell back on Wednesday after the central bank intervened to buy dollars as the currency hovered at 11-month highs. 

 Bankers said the central bank stepped in as the lira traded at around 1,452,000 to the dollar on the interbank market . It was closed at 1,489,000, but was quoted at 1,503,000 in Thursday-dated trade. 

 The lira has rallied to levels not seen since last June with the swift end of the war in neighbouring Iraq. Investors had sent the currency above 1,750,000 in March, fearing a protracted conflict next door would hammer Turkey's frail economy. 

 "The Central Bank today intervened on the buying side on seeing a repeat of extreme volatility," the bank said. 

 It said in a statement the lira's strength did not stem from "fundamental economic variables" but from Turkish corporate tax payments that are due and from a delay in the demand for dollars, possibly from importers. 

 The lira's slippage appeared to cheer stockbrokers and the main Istanbul index  climbed 1.09 percent to 10,540.85 points after weeks of losses or limited gains that many traders have blamed on the strengthening currency. 

 "With the overvalued lira, foreign investors have not seen sizeable returns (in dollar terms) from Turkish equities," said Hakan Avci, strategist at Global Securities. 

 Yields on March 26, 2004, debt firmed to 52.12 percent from a previous 53.5 percent, but bankers said the gains were limited as investors wait for International Monetary Fund inspectors to arrive for a crucial review of the $16 billion rescue pact. 

 "The downward trend in interest rates has been slowed ahead of the talks with the IMF and because the Central Bank still hasn't lowered its lending rates," one banker said. 

 The government's slow progress on key reforms it has promised the fund has raised questions about its commitment to the pact. The latest loan tranche of $500 million will only come after the successful completion of the review, the IMF has said. 

 The last review of the pact was delayed for months by a general election, little action on reforms and a lack of agreement on IMF demands for a cost-cutting 2003 budget. 

 Speculation mounted earlier this month the Central Bank would cut its key overnight rates with signs that inflation was inching downward. But a rate cut now appears unlikely until at least after the IMF review.

title: UPDATE 2-Turkish c.bank  intervenes  to curb lira moves.
text:
ISTANBUL, May 21 (Reuters) - Turkey's Central Bank intervened in the currency market to buy dollars for lira on Wednesday afternoon to stem a rise in the lira's value that some investors say poses a threat to exports and the current account. 

 The intervention came as an IMF team arrived in Ankara for the Fund's latest review of Turkey's economic pact. Analysts said potential problems with completing the review may help weaken the lira in the coming weeks and narrow the current account deficit. 

 Bankers told Reuters the bank had stepped in as the lira traded at around 1,452,000 to the dollar. It closed at bids of 1,489,000 on the interbank market . 

 The lira, which closed Tuesday at 1,460,000, has soared around 19 percent from record lows of some 1,772,000 to the dollar seen in March, when investors worried war in Iraq and tensions with the United States might send the country back into recession. 

 "The Central Bank today intervened on the buying side on seeing a repeat of extreme volatility," the bank said. 

 The bank last intervened on May 12 to buy dollars for lira. It had intervened to buy lira for the U.S. currency on December 24, when the currency traded at 1,700,000 to the dollar. 

 The strong lira has sparked complaints from exporters and other business groups who see a weaker currency as helping their export competitiveness in terms of price. 

 Analysts said the Central Bank will most likely intervene again to arrest any future firming of the lira, floated amid a February 2001 financial crisis. 

 IMF TENSIONS MAY SPARK LIRA SALES 

 While seeing no sharp fall in the currency in the coming weeks, analysts said the government's foot-dragging on a swathe of IMF-backed reforms, including measures on public spending and taxation, may weaken the lira if problems arise with a visiting IMF review team. 

 "I think the IMF review might provide some help in preventing the appreciation of the lira...I'm not surprised the Central Bank intervened because the lira in real terms is very strong," said Marco Annunziata at Deutsche Bank in London. 

 "It makes you somewhat concerned looking at the current account prospects going forward." 

 The IMF is due to complete its review of Turkey's $16 billion pact within two weeks. Its board could meet in early June to approve a $500 million loan tranche provided it is satisfied Ankara has met the pact's conditions. 

 Turkey's foreign trade deficit jumped 74.6 percent in the first quarter of the year to $4.08 billion, raising worries for the current account. 

 The current account deficit had jumped to $1.18 billion in the first two months of the year, the latest available data, against a deficit of $286 million in the same period of 2002. 

 The Central Bank said the lira's strength did not reflect economic fundamentals but was linked to widespread sales of forex in recent weeks to meet corporate tax payments in lira. 

 "The extreme volatility does not stem from the balance of payments or reverse currency substitution, it is thought to be the result of forex sales for heavy tax payments...and the delaying of demand for foreign exchange," it said. 

 The lira is now around 54 percent below the level it was at just before the 2001 financial crisis struck. 

 - Additional reporting by Mark Bentley in Istanbul.
