title: UPDATE 1-Turk lira ends slightly down after CB  intervention .
text:
(Adds close, quote, bond tap, alters dateline to Ankara from Istanbul) 

 ANKARA, May 12 (Reuters) - Turkey's central bank intervention on Monday to buy dollars hardly dampened the appetite for lira as upbeat traders saw little incentive to part with the currency. 

 The lira  finished at 1,501,000 to the dollar, down slightly from Friday's 1,498,000, but was trading at that level in Tuesday-dated trade. The currency firmed to around 1,486,000 before the central bank action, traders said. 

 These levels have not been seen since June 2002 and come with the relief of a swift end to the war in neighbour Iraq and signs the Turkey is committed to a $16 billion IMF pact. 

 Shares and debt both edged higher. 

 It was the only the central bank's second intervention to buy dollars. The first came on December 2 when the lira had rallied to around 1,510,000. 

 The bank said it had intervened to defend the lira against excessive fluctuations in value and was not uncomfortable with the lira's levels against the U.S. unit. 

 But some traders saw it as an effort to protect exports, a main source of growth for Turkey's frail economy, and came amid fears the currency was over-valued. 

 "Every one of us was getting concerned about the value of the lira. Although (the central bank) says the level of the lira was not the main reason for the intervention...I think the bank is not happy with a level below 1,500,000 now," said Yarkin Cebeci at JPMorgan. 

 Turkey's year-on-year foreign trade deficit jumped 74.6 percent in the first quarter of the year to $4.08 billion. 

 TURKEY ISSUES DEBT 

 The Treasury said on Monday it would increase its 2013 dollar bond  via Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan, capitalising on strong investor demand for high yielding debt. 

 Traders have been expecting the tap as Turkey's debt yields fall to more acceptable levels for borrowing. 

 Closely-watched May 26, 2004, debt firmed to yields of 50.68 percent from Friday's 51.19 percent on the secondary market. 

 The Treasury on Monday successfully sold 1,536 trillion lira (around $1 billion) worth of three-month papers at a lower-than-expected maximum yield of 41.96 percent. 

 Bankers said in a Reuters poll ahead of the auction they saw the rate at an average 42.6 percent. 

 Some investors believe a central bank rate cut is imminent amid signs consumer price inflation was falling towards an IMF-backed year-end target of 20 percent. 

 Others say the bank may wait until after a latest IMF review of Turkey's $16 billion pact, due to begin on May 21.

title: UPDATE 2-Fitch may revise Turkey outlook after IMF review.
text:
ANKARA, May 12 (Reuters) - International ratings agency Fitch said on Monday it may upgrade Turkey's country rating outlook to stable from negative following the next review of the country's $16 billion IMF pact, due to begin on May 21. 

 Fitch saw no hitches in Turkey tackling a domestic debt load of around $100 billion during 2003 but the heavily indebted country may experience some "stress" in 2004, Fitch analyst Nick Eisinger told Reuters. The agency's worries focused mainly on the budget and fiscal side, he added. 

 "If we see there is a good review without any major problems and we see that the (debt) auctions are continuing to the good and the fiscal numbers above all, we probably would take off the negative outlook," he said. 

 "We are probably looking at over the next four to six weeks." 

 Turkish markets have firmed recently after war in neighbouring Iraq ended. Investors are now looking to the IMF review, key to the release of a $500 million loan for Turkey's frail economy which is tentatively recovering from a deep slump. 

 "Even though the rating is now at negative outlook we certainly don't anticipate any debt repayment problems this year...But we will be looking on 2004 as potential stress here," Eisinger said. 

 Turkey has yet to implement several economic reforms it pledged the IMF it would tackle in April. The fund has said it will press Turkey hard to deliver on its commitments during the May review. A previous review was held up for months due to slow progress on economic reform. 

 "Our concern remains mainly on the budget, on the fiscal side and the potential impact that a debt crisis could have eventually on the balance of payments, but it's certainly not what you would call a traditional balance of payments problem that is pretty strong," he said. 

 Turkey's 2003 budget, a focus of recent talks with the IMF, requires deep spending cuts and measures to raise revenue. The fund says Ankara must stick to its promises to allay fears in financial markets that it is not fully committed to the pact.

title: UPDATE 3-Turkish cbank says  intervenes  to stem lira rise.
text:

 While a stronger lira could help Turkey meet a key IMF-backed target of lowering consumer prices (CPI), analysts say the bank was worried about the impact of a strong lira on export revenues, a major source of growth for its frail economy. 

 The lira  was trading at around 1,495,500 to the dollar in the afternoon on the interbank market after it had firmed to 1,492,000 in morning trade, just before the central bank action. It had closed Friday at 1,498,000. 

 "A direct intervention in the foreign exchange market was made today to buy dollars in an effort to arrest the volatility seen in forex rates," the bank said in a statement.

title: Turkey  Bnk Afternoon  Intervention  -3: Message To Market
text:
Dealers said the central bank gives the message to the anxious market that it continues to have the power to control the rate through interventions. The market nervousness stems from Tuesday's 182-day bill auction by the Turkish Treasury. 

 Market players interpret this recent intervention as an attempt by the central bank to keep banks' bids only 0.3% above the central bank's dollar buying rate.

title: Turkish  central bank  acts to hold jittery mkts.
text:
ISTANBUL,  July 18 (Reuter) - Turkey's central bank frequently intervened in currency, t-bill and money markets this week to maintain control amid jitters over economic policies of the new Islamist-led government, bankers said. 

 "The central bank interventions were effective in easing the immediate shocks in the markets, but this can't last forever, (Central bank dollar) buying must ease," said Bora Cilek, assistant general manager at Midland Bank's Istanbul branch. 

 The bank sold dollars for lira to banks and free market dealers for the fourth day in a row to curtail the US currency's rise despite the dollar's weakness on world markets. 

 It also raised its overnight bid and offer rates to 50-80 percent on Thursday from Wednesday's 45-75 to support the lira. 

 Despite the interventions, the lira closed weaker at 83,110 per dollar after Wednesday's 82,920. 

 The central bank's currency basket, weighted 40 percent dollar and 60 percent mark, gained 1.02 percent against the lira so far this week after 0.8 percent last week. 

 Bankers said the central bank also bought overnight repos and t-bills from time to time this week to control rates. 

 T-bill yields have surged between 12 and 15 percentage points since last Thursday when Islamist finance minister Abdullatif Sener suggested capping domestic borrowing interest rates and introducing new taxes on t-bills and bonds. 

 Sener, speaking during a parliamentary debate on means to boost state revenues, also forecast 1996 budget deficit at 1,300 trillion lira, up sharply from an official target of 861 trillion due to hefty domestic debt servicing. 

 Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan repeated on Tuesday assurances given on Monday by Deputy Premier Tansu Ciller and her conservative ministers that the government did not plan any intervention in free market economy. 

 But conservative State Minister Ufuk Soylemez confirmed government plans on new taxes on t-bills and bonds by saying a withholding tax to be introduced would not be retroactive. 

 Bankers said the t-bill market anxiously awaited clarification by the government on withholding tax plans as well as a solid programme to fight the country's huge budget deficit. 

 Economists and bankers question the coalition's ability to finance an additional 125 trillion lira burden from a 50 percent civil servant pay rise for second half 1996. 

 Erbakan said on Thursday the local foreign exchange market was stable and predicted interest rates would fall gradually. 

 Talking at his Islamist Welfare Party meeting, Erbakan reiterated plans to use untapped resources to finance government projects including the pay rises. 

 The coalition expects a 300 trillion lira income from the planned sale of properties and buildings, Ciller said on Tuesday, but did not give a time span. She added that the tax base would be widened, but tax rates would not be increased. 

 "The increase in overnight rates and speculation over the treasury's heavy use of central bank advances have increased anxiety in the t-bill market," said a private bank dealer. 

 The central bank said in its weekly report the treasury withdrew 83 trillion lira last week, raising its outstanding cash advances to 203 trillion. Central bank advances to treasury cannot exceed 326.3 trillion this year. 

 "Because the treasury used up most of its cash borrowing line with the central bank, it must borrow in next week's t-bill auction. So the rise in interest rates may continue," the banker said. 

 Banks had shunned the Treasury's 204-day t-bill auction on Monday amid uncertainty. 

 The Treasury raised the average yield by 12 points but could sell only 16.4 trillion lira nominal bills for which it collected 10 trillion lira from banks on Tuesday, but injected 91 trillion lira for maturing t-bills in return. 

 Bankers also have worries ahead of Turkey ratings expected to be released by international agencies soon. 

 "Expectations that Turkey's outlook may be lowered and fears over how the treasury will meet its hefty domestic debt repayments in coming weeks are raising tension in the markets and putting upward pressure on the dollar," Cilek said. 

 The treasury faces 51 trillion lira of t-bill maturities on July 25 and 105 trillion on July 31.

title: Turkey's Lira/New Govt -3:  Central Bank  To Guide Path
text:
The government would be the first in Turkey's modern, secular history to be led by an Islamist party. The risk premium alone should push the lira higher against the dollar, the analysts said. 

 Erbakan's Welfare Party led national elections last December with 21% of the vote. It wasn't asked to form a government, however, until an attempted colaition between Ciller's True Path and its rival centrist party, the Motherland, failed last month. 

 But while they agreed the Islamist-led government - once it's confirmed by a vote of confidence - could bring pressure on the lira, they declined to forecast where the dollar-lira rate might go. 

 'We shouldn't forget the central bank,' warned Ergin of Chase Bank. 'Next week, we're going to see intervention from the Central Bank of Turkey.' 

 With about $16 billion in foreign reserves, the Central Bank of Turkey is expected to use a combination of higher money market rates and direct foreign exchange intervention to guard the lira against sharp movements. 

 How high the lira might go against the dollar depends on the strength of the speculation, the level at which the central bank is comfortable, and policy pronouncements from the new government - a combination of factors analysts said is very difficult to predict. 

 'There will be some pressure on the foreign exchange market...(but) the central bank has a relatively huge amount of foreign exchange reserves,' said Haluk Corbacioglu, a senior dealer for Societe Generale in Istanbul. 'We don't know the level the central bank has in mind.'

title: CURRENCY  '96/ Turkey  Lira -4: More  Intervention  Seen
text:
Domestic debt has already climbed to 1.400 trillion lire, about a third of which is held by domestic banks who are fearing a refinancing crush next year and have sent the three-month Treasury annual compound rate soaring to 170%. This is the highest rate level the country has suffered since last spring when the stabilization program was first introduced. 

 Some fear that rates could still rise as far as 300% before the new government is formed and a new austerity program put in place. 

 Despite this, Xafa said, the lira remains under pressure even with this high level of interest rates, underscoring concern about the country's future and helping to worsen a merchandise trade gap that is already expected to widen to $6.5 billion this year. 

 At this rate, Tezan said, a devaluation could be welcomed - although it would put inflation at risk once again, it would help improve Turkey's competitiveness as it lifts barriers with Europe. 

 So far, though, the central bank has showed it isn't planning to allow any swift decline. It has pumped as much as $2.5 billion of its $17 billion official reserves into the market to support the lira over the last month. 

 Dealers said it has also spent about $3 billion in forward dollar quotes to help cap future pressures on the Turkish currency. At the moment, the central bank is quoting a rate of 63,112 lire for Feb. 2, 1996, suggesting that it sees the decline continuing around the current pace with inflation rising about 6% a month. 

 And a Turkish newspaper reported Monday that the IMF doesn't recomment a devaluation of the lira in 1996, preferring instead a gradual depreciation.
